lessons.title: Mitochondrial Function and Ageing / Advancing Human Clinical Research: UTHEVER NMN from NAD+ Metabolism to Sleep Health

speakers.name: Colin Selman
speakers.role: Professor of Biogerontology, Head of School of Molecular Biosciences

lessons.summary:
Two talks shared this slot, on one EffePharm deck. Professor Colin Selman, a biogerontologist at the University of Glasgow who lists EffePharm beside his university, opened on the science. Mitochondria work less well as animals age, and that decline is one of the hallmarks of ageing. His question was whether it can be slowed.

His answers came from animals. Turning down nutrient sensing, eating fewer calories and giving NMN, a precursor of NAD+, all preserved mitochondrial function in mice. Long-term NMN reduced frailty, and in a preprint it extended the lifespan of female mice. None of his evidence was in people.

JianJun Yu then presented UTHEVER, EffePharm's branded NMN. A trial published in 2022 is the brand's base. The new work is a small sleep trial of EffePharm's own, not yet published: 34 adults who stay up late or sleep poorly took NMN or placebo for eight weeks. Sleep quality, insomnia and fatigue scores ended lower than on placebo. Each result is labelled as within the NMN group or against placebo, and not as a treatment claim.

The talk closed on regulation. EFSA published a positive safety opinion in May 2026, and the deck expects EU novel-food approval in November 2026. EffePharm says that opens pharmacy, beauty and mainstream retail across the EU.
takeaways: Selman's case, all from worms and mice: mitochondrial function falls with age, and reduced nutrient sensing, a 30% calorie cut and NMN each preserved it in mice; NMN made mitochondria more efficient without adding more of them (slide 5) (slide 7) (slide 8) (slide 9).

Long-term NMN (about 550 mg/kg a day in drinking water from 13 months of age) is shown reducing frailty in both sexes and extending female lifespan in mice; the source is a 2024 bioRxiv preprint, and the frailty chart is labelled schematic, its values illustrative (slide 10).

UTHEVER's published trial (Frontiers in Aging, 2022): 66 adults aged 40 to 65 randomised, 62 analysed, 300 mg a day for 60 days; the slide reports a 38% increment in NAD+ levels and 6.5% gains in walking endurance and quality of life, read from the slide image, without saying whether against placebo (slide 13).

The sleep trial (EffePharm data on file): 34 adults aged 30 to 60, 600 mg a day or placebo for eight weeks. At day 56 the NMN group scored lower than placebo on sleep quality (PSQI, p<0.05), insomnia severity (ISI, p<0.01) and fatigue (FS-14, p<0.05); within the group the scores fell 36.61%, 48.43% and 48.15% from baseline (slide 14) (slide 15) (slide 16) (slide 17).
Deep sleep rose 27.65 minutes (38.88%) against the NMN group's own baseline (p<0.05); no placebo comparison is shown (slide 18).

EU novel food: filed August 2023, public consultation completed February 2025, positive EFSA safety assessment published May 2026, approval "expected" in November 2026; the US FDA sent an NDI no-objection letter in November 2025, and the UK application is in progress (slide 20) (slide 21).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: NMN is not in our range, but it is sold on cellular energy, fatigue and healthy ageing, the ground CreaWin is moving into. A retail panel at the same summit said creatine is moving from sports into longevity (from-hype-to-healthspan-building-the [19:15]).
- If EU approval lands as the deck expects, NMN can go into EU pharmacy and mainstream retail, not just cross-border e-commerce (slide 20). My reading: expect NAD+ "energy as you age" launches in EU pharmacy in 2027, competing with or stacked beside creatine; Euromonitor's talk the same morning put the NAD+ family close to a price war (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan).
- My reading: EffePharm made NAD+ felt by testing sleep and fatigue rather than biomarkers. Our healthy-ageing pitches for CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea should lead the same way, on outcomes people notice.
- My reading: the deck's reporting is a model to copy. Every figure says whether it is within the group or against placebo, and each sleep slide says it is not a treatment claim (slide 15) (slide 17).
- My reading: the format, an academic on mechanism followed by the brand's human data, is one we could use in our own speaking slots.
quotes: "My research investigates the biological mechanisms of ageing using diverse model systems." (slide 2)
"Reported as a change within the NMN group during supplementation, not as a treatment claim for a clinical condition." (slide 15)
"Novel Food status opens pharmacy, beauty, and mainstream retail channels across the EU — not just cross-border e-commerce." (slide 20)
"Positive EFSA assessment secured, expected approval in Nov. 2026" (slide 21)
lessons.detail:
- Selman: Professor of Biogerontology and Head of the School of Molecular Biosciences, University of Glasgow (since 2013); the slide gives his affiliation as "University of Glasgow; EffePharm". He sits on the editorial boards of Aging Cell and Experimental Gerontology (slide 2).
- Living longer brings age-related disease: cardiovascular, neurodegenerative and liver disease, macular degeneration, sarcopenia, osteoporosis and osteoarthritis, cancer, type 2 diabetes and obesity, and immunosenescence (slide 3).
- Mitochondrial dysfunction is one of the hallmarks of ageing (Lopez-Otin et al., 2013 and 2023), shown across humans, mice, flies and worms (slide 4).
- With age, oxygen consumption falls from about 6.9 at 4 months to 5.7 at 12 months and 4.3 at 21 months (pmol O2 per second per citrate synthase), and ATP content and ATP production fall to roughly 60% and 40% of the younger level, all read from the charts; the species is not named on the slide (Drew et al. 2003; Hempenstall et al. 2012, 2026; Morsci et al. 2016) (slide 5).
- Two routes to preserve mitochondrial function: genetic and dietary (slide 6).
- Nutrient sensing: the insulin, mTORC1 and S6K1 pathway, with IRS and S6K1 marked. The mouse panel lists preserved cognition, immune function, glucose tolerance and cardiac output, less age-related fat, and fewer cataracts, cases of idiopathic dermatitis and osteoporosis (Selman et al. 2008, 2009, 2012; Borland et al. 2024) (slide 7).
- Dietary restriction (30% fewer calories) raised median lifespan in mice from about 22 to about 33 months, "~45–50%", read from the chart. In male mice it raised muscle mitochondrial respiration at 1, 9 and 18 months without adding mitochondrial content (Hempenstall et al. 2012, 2026; Mulvey et al. 2017) (slide 8).
- NMN: male mice given 100 or 300 mg/kg a day in drinking water from 5 to 17 months of age had higher muscle mitochondrial respiration and gene expression with no change in mitochondrial content (Mills et al., Cell Metabolism 2016) (slide 9).
- The summit's partner slide sits between the two talks; EffePharm is a Diamond Partner (slide 11).
- Sleep trial design: randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled; assessments at day 0, 28, 56 and 84, the last four weeks after stopping. The deck shows no day 84 results (slide 14).
- Fatigue (FS-14): 38.52% down at day 28 (−3.06 points) and 48.15% at day 56 (−3.82 points), p<0.001 within the group (slide 15).
- Sleep quality (PSQI): −3.94 points at day 56, p<0.0001 within the group; no day 28 figure is given (slide 16).
- Insomnia severity (ISI): 46.19% down at day 28 (−6.06 points) and 48.43% at day 56 (−6.35 points), p<0.0001 within the group (slide 17).
- Deep sleep: how it was measured is not stated; the slide says a longer duration "suggests more restorative sleep" (slide 18).
- The outcomes slide shows the 36.61% fall in PSQI score as "+36%" overall sleep quality and rounds deep sleep to 28 minutes; its "No Daytime Drowsiness" tile has no figure and no slide behind it in the deck (slide 19).
- The regulatory slide's footer reads "UK Longevity Summit 2026", so it was made for another event. It calls UTHEVER first to file, first through public consultation and first to EFSA final assessment, and says final Union listing is "a procedural next step" (slide 20).
- Elsewhere: Brazil approved at up to 95 mg a day (through partner distributors); Australia, Thailand and India applications in progress; NMN "can be sold normally" in Mexico, Japan and Hong Kong; finished-product declarations in Canada, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam (slide 21).
- Claims on the closing slide: "World's 1st" clinically-proven NMN brand with 3 clinical studies ongoing; 4 quality certifications (Kosher, Halal, ISO 9001, cGMP); No. 1 trademarked NMN ingredient brand in the USA by 2024 B2B sales volume (Euromonitor, research completed December 2025) (slide 22).
- EffePharm also hosted a roundtable, "NAD+ Next Breakthrough: Exploring Latest NMN Clinical Evidence & Regulatory Milestones"; contact deal@effepharm.com, www.effepharm.com (slide 23).

lessons.title: Absorbed or Assumed? Why Pharmacokinetic Testing Matters
lessons.summary:
The recording holds only the last four and a half minutes of Amanda Rao's talk on pharmacokinetic testing, then one audience question. Her argument, in the part recorded: absorption studies are run on the wrong people, in the wrong conditions.

A typical pharmacokinetic study is done on a 25-year-old, while longevity products are typically sold to older women on several medications. GLP-1 medicines slow food through the gut, and studies with paracetamol show lower absorption in people taking them, so they belong in absorption studies. Studies should look at responders and at high and low absorbers, and test products as people take them: with food and coffee, with missed doses and other medications, not fasted and as a single dose.

She sees research moving from single ingredients to whole formulas, and home blood tests making it easy to track blood levels in long-term trials. AI models that predict exposure need good studies to learn from.

Asked about dose, she said a five-dose pharmacokinetic study early on is easier and cheaper than five doses in a long-term trial, and that the industry may need lower doses taken for longer.
takeaways: In the studies she cited, people on GLP-1 medicines absorbed paracetamol 15 to 50 percent less; absorption studies that leave them out are "not you know, collecting the right data" [00:00].

Study populations do not match buyers: a typical pharmacokinetic study is on a 25-year-old, while longevity products are typically sold to 65-year-old women on three medications, with low oestrogen and a history of antibiotics [00:00].
Look at responders and at high and low absorbers, not only at a rise in the blood: "did 90% of people get that?" [00:00].
Test products as they are taken: most pharmacokinetic studies are fasted and single-dose, while real users eat, drink coffee, miss doses and stack medications [00:00].
Long-term trials should measure blood levels as well as outcomes, now that home tests are easy; some nutrients, such as iron and vitamin D, need longer studies [00:00].
On dose, a five-dose pharmacokinetic study early is "easier and honestly cheaper" than five doses in a long-term study; she suggested lower doses for longer [05:14].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high: this is how absorption evidence for ingredients will be designed and judged, and GLP-1 users are named as a population that absorbs differently [00:00].
- My reading: bioavailability claims for enhanced-absorption forms may be challenged where the study used young, fasted adults; the populations in our studies are worth checking before a pitch to a healthy-ageing brand [00:00].
- My reading: products pitched for muscle on a GLP-1 journey (protein, CreaWin) may in time need absorption data in GLP-1 users before brands rely on them [00:00].
- My reading: a multi-dose pharmacokinetic study is a cheap way to set the dose of a new ingredient before an efficacy trial [05:14].
quotes: "So two people, one capsule, different blood levels." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [00:00]
"Your typical PK studies done on a 25-year-old." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [00:00]
"And as we know, real life is messier than the clinic." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [00:00]
"But maybe we need 10 times less for a longer period of time." Speaker 1 (Amanda Rao) [05:14]
lessons.detail:
- Billed 16:15 to 16:35; the recording starts at 16:33, mid-sentence ("Ones that we all we all know and love"), and she closes with "And I think I'm out of time" [00:00]. The start of the talk, her organisation and her slides are not in the folder. Otter merges her talk into one turn, so every point from it cites [00:00].
- Factors she named that change blood levels from one capsule: kidney, liver and hormone changes, medication, genetics, gut microbiome, body composition and BMI, and baseline nutrient status [00:00].
- Sample size: she asked whether a study's sample represents the population the product is for, and answered "probably not" [00:00].
- Finished products: the industry has seen many single-ingredient studies and is moving to how ingredients work together in a whole formula [00:00].
- Home testing: a finger-prick test from a supermarket can show iron deficiency, so long-term studies should add blood concentrations as they go [00:00].
- Methods named: models that predict exposure, stable isotope tracers (Otter: "traces"), and steady-state studies as well as single-point studies [00:00].
- Otter's "using Australian gems" in the GLP-1 passage is unclear [00:00].
- The question came from an audience member (Speaker 4): the dose is often set from 90-day toxicology work, not efficacy; can dose response go into pharmacokinetic studies [04:58]? She said yes; with absorption enhancers the aim is that people feel better, or at least that it gets in without long-term side effects; "it's great to have six times or 10 times more", but lower doses may be needed [05:14].
- The chair (Speaker 3) then moved to wearables, AI and healthspan [06:12], filed as ai-driven-personalization-at-scale.

lessons.title: AI-Driven Personalization at Scale: Turning Wellness Complexity into Clear Guidance
lessons.summary:
Ohad Manor, Vice President of Computational Precision Health at Thorne, argued that supplement shoppers suffer from too much information, not too little. His example was Lena, 47, sleeping badly and wondering about perimenopause, faced with AI answers, social media and influencers.

Personalisation is the answer, he said, but also a double-edged sword: people differ, and so do ingredients, claims and formulations. Thorne has over 250 products, so even its own shoppers struggle to choose. He sees AI as the engine that can personalise at scale, provided it is data-driven, dynamic and educational rather than a black box.

Thorne's answer is Taya, an AI adviser launched in July last year. It works only from Thorne's own products, claims, science and articles, without web access. It asks follow-up questions, narrows its recommendations, adds lifestyle advice and shares articles. By Thorne's count it held over 300,000 conversations in its first year. Manor said it ignores bestsellers and promotions.

He closed by urging supplement companies to build similar tools. Otherwise people go to ChatGPT, which does not know a company's products as its own medical and ingredient teams do.
takeaways: Thorne's own survey, as Manor gave it: roughly 40% of consumers use AI for health questions, and two out of three would use an AI tool they trusted to make decisions [00:23].
Taya is a closed system: built on foundation models, but without internet access and limited to Thorne's products, ingredients, claims and science and over 1,000 articles [00:23].

Thorne's first-year figures for Taya, as Manor gave them: over 300,000 conversations, over 650,000 messages, over 1.2 million product and lifestyle recommendations, over 135,000 articles shared, and about 92% thumbs up [00:23].
In his Lena example, Taya narrowed eight recommendations to two products, explained the ingredients and gave a daily routine with lifestyle tips [00:23].

Taya recommends almost the whole portfolio, not the same five products; its top topics in year one were heart health and sports nutrition, then cognition and focus, bone and joint, and metabolism [00:23].
His call to brands: build such tools, because ChatGPT "doesn't know everything about your products the way you know them" [00:23].
lessons.for_us:
- An AI adviser on a brand's site answers only from that brand's claims and science [00:23]. My reading: the evidence and approved wording we give customers for our ingredients may end up in the knowledge base such a tool reads, so it should be clear and claim-safe.
- Shoppers find ingredient forms confusing; Manor named citrate, glycinate, bisglycinate and threonate forms of magnesium [00:23]. My reading: form-specific evidence is what lets a tool like this choose one product over another.
- Relevance medium: consumer-facing AI at a brand; it touches our ingredients only through the claims and evidence brands feed it.
quotes: "So the problem is not, you know, too little information. It's too much information." Speaker 2 (Ohad Manor) [00:23]
"She doesn't care about bestsellers." Speaker 2 (Ohad Manor) [00:23]
"Otherwise, people are going to ChatGPT, which is great." Speaker 2 (Ohad Manor) [00:23]
lessons.detail:
- Billed 16:35 to 16:55; recorded 16:40 to 16:57. The chair (Speaker 1) introduced him as "Dr. Ohad Manna" of "Thorn" [00:00]. Otter merges his talk into one turn, so every point from it cites [00:23].
- Thorne's survey also found that two of three US consumers believe supplements can help them [00:23].
- Choice overload at Thorne: a search for sleep shows 17 products, and 27 products contain magnesium [00:23].
- Range size: he said both "over 250 products or SKUs" and "over 200 different products" [00:23].
- What he wants from recommendations: data-driven (different people get different answers), dynamic over time, and educational and interactive, unlike past yes-or-no questionnaires [00:23].
- Thorne's articles are written by its medical team, some with the Mayo Clinic [00:23].
- Taya launched in July last year; Manor ran the first-year analysis in August; Thorne keeps updating it to the newest frontier models [00:23].
- He asked the morning's consumer panel whether they use and trust AI [00:23].

lessons.title: Artificial Intelligence to Rapidly Develop, Improve and Expand Use of Natural Ingredients
lessons.summary:
Paul Spagnuolo, a food science professor at the University of Guelph and co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer of Applied Laboratory Technologies (ALT), declared his conflict of interest and explained why he built an AI tool for ingredient discovery.

For 20 years his lab has applied pharmaceutical drug discovery to food molecules, taking two products, one from avocado, from discovery to clinical trial and market. That path is long, costly and mostly fails, and the claim at the end covers only the indication studied.

AMBROSIA, an agentic AI platform built with a computational biologist, aims to shorten the discovery and validation stages. As a retroactive test they gave it the avocado molecule. He said it reached in one day the target and use his lab had taken 10 years and millions of dollars to find. ALT's slide claims the stages shrink from years to days and from millions to thousands.

He said researchers still have to validate in the lab. Finzelberg was the first partner: in less than a week AMBROSIA pointed to how its extract works, which matched Finzelberg's own research. ALT now works business to business, helping companies understand their ingredients and find new markets for them.
takeaways: ALT's slide claims AMBROSIA cuts discovery and validation from "5-10 years" and millions of dollars to "5-10 days" and thousands (photo 1); Spagnuolo said it took AMBROSIA one day to reach what took his lab 10 years [20:14].

In ALT's retroactive test on avocatin B, AMBROSIA analysed 1,284 crystal structures and found 361 potential gene targets, 99 at high confidence, with lipid metabolism and PPAR signalling among the primary pathways (photo 2); Spagnuolo said it pointed to acyl-CoA dehydrogenase and fatty acid oxidation [20:14].

A claim covers only what was studied: a phase two result on cardiometabolic function "that's our claim", not inflammation or longevity [20:14]. ALT pitches AMBROSIA as a way to find new markets for existing ingredients (photo 3) [30:28].
AI does not replace the lab: "you still need to flip the switch", with researchers doing the validation [20:14].

Finzelberg, the first partner, received an answer on its extract in less than a week that matched its own research [30:28]; ALT's slide quotes Finzelberg on Menofelis, its Siberian rhubarb extract for menopause, and AMBROSIA's "multi-target profiles" (photo 4).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high: AI tools that propose mechanisms and new uses change how ingredient evidence is generated, and how fast a supplier can reposition a botanical (photo 3) [30:28].
- A botanical extract supplier, Finzelberg, already uses AMBROSIA to find which compounds in its extract are active and what to study next [30:28]. My reading: a competitor can now get a mechanism map and a study plan for a botanical in days; we should know whether such maps exist for ingredients in our range.
- Spagnuolo was clear that a prediction is not evidence: lab validation and trials are still needed, and a claim covers only the indication studied [20:14]. My reading: an AI target profile could guide a study plan for one of our ingredients, but it supports no claim on its own.
quotes: "...you still need to flip the switch." Speaker 4 (Paul Spagnuolo) [20:14]
"It took my lab 10 years to go from understanding the discovery of a molecule to its applications as a fatty acid oxidation inhibitor" Speaker 4 (Paul Spagnuolo) [20:14]
"We're talking about one specific application." Speaker 4 (Paul Spagnuolo) [20:14]
"Identify new markets for existing ingredients" ALT's slide (photo 3)
lessons.detail:
- Billed 16:55 to 17:10; recorded 16:57 to 17:13. The chair (Speaker 1) introduced him as "Dr. Paul Spandwalo", co-founder and CSO of Applied Laboratory Technologies [17:21]. Otter heard the platform as "asia", "Embroidery" and "Ambrosia" [20:14]; the slides spell AMBROSIA, "Agentic Multi Modal Biology & Research Operations System for Intelligent Analysis" (photo 1).
- Background: undergraduate and master's degrees in food science at Guelph, physiology at the University of Waterloo, drug pharmacology at the Princess Margaret cancer centre (Otter: "Prince's Margaret Hospital"); now also acting associate vice-president of research at Guelph [18:02].
- His lab: about 15 molecules discovered and validated (cancer, diabetes, some Alzheimer's work), over 70 publications, multiple patents, and "a couple of approved products", some on Amazon [20:14]. Over 50 products worked on, of which 15 were new molecules; many failed and were never published [20:14].
- The avocado molecule (avocatin B; Otter: "avocat and B") has completed a phase two trial; he said the product "has been shown in multiple participants to be able to decrease cholesterol, improve GLP-1 status", and that the study did not reach longevity or mitochondrial function [20:14]. The commercial product on the slide is metavo (photo 1).
- He publishes in high-impact journals because a paper elsewhere could be published "tomorrow" for a few thousand dollars [20:14].
- Formulation work includes a human simulated gastrointestinal system and pharmacokinetic studies [20:14].
- AMBROSIA took about six months to build, with a computational biologist [20:14].
- Avocatin B profile, as on ALT's slide: primary targets the FABP family, PPAR delta and alpha and GST-A1; selectivity "100% human targets, 27.4% high-confidence"; 107 lipid metabolism targets across 12 protein families (photo 2).
- ALT's listed benefits: less time from discovery to market, a higher success rate in validation research, lower cost, new markets for existing ingredients, and defining the bioactivity within an extract (photo 3).
- Finzelberg's text on the slide says AMBROSIA "accelerates the development of effective botanical solutions" and, for Menofelis, identified multi-target profiles across hormone signalling, inflammation and detoxification (photo 4).
- ALT was spun out less than a year ago, after Finzelberg asked at a conference in Europe in November last year what it would cost to use; it now works with "a couple other companies" [30:28]. He called it B2B rather than B2C [30:28].
- He ran 16 seconds over [30:28].

AMBROSIA's target profile for avocatin B: 361 potential gene targets, lipid metabolism and PPAR signalling.

lessons.title: From Data to Decisions: Personalizing Longevity
lessons.summary:
Lauren Nicolle of NutraIngredients+ chaired the last session of the day, framed as AI across the product cycle: discovery with Paul Spagnuolo of ALT, clinical validation with Jeff Chen of Radicle Science, and the consumer with Ohad Manor of Thorne.

Chen described Radicle's decentralised, in-house trials, run at home at a scale site studies cannot reach. On hallucinations, Spagnuolo said they happen all the time and ALT keeps its tool inside the scientific literature. Manor said Taya is a closed system and every message is monitored. Chen said narrow knowledge bases and checking agents cut the risk.

Chen argued that home tests, wearables and phones now let trials collect data sites never could, and that machine learning is needed to read it. He wants biomarkers, wearables and surveys combined rather than one trusted alone. Manor said Taya has limits: complicated cases need a healthcare provider, and shoppers should ask who built a tool and on what data.

All three saw true personalisation as some way off. Spagnuolo pointed to genetics and lifestyle, Chen to precision groups first and trial and error over time, Manor to levels of personalisation. Asked about small studies, Chen called for scale and real-world diversity. Stephen Daniells then closed the day.
takeaways: Chen said Radicle Science has put about 100,000 people through double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trials in about six years, and is running a US-government-funded mental health trial of 6,000 people with one shared placebo and 19 treatment arms [34:11].

Guardrails against hallucination: ALT keeps AMBROSIA from going outside the literature [36:40]; Thorne monitors and scores every Taya message and sends flagged ones to regulatory and medical [37:43]; Chen said narrow knowledge bases and checking agents cut the risk [39:03].

Chen: home kits, wearables and phones let decentralised trials collect data sites cannot; agents can automate the "multi-100-step process" of a trial, and machine learning is needed to read the data [39:58]. Biomarkers, wearables and surveys each show one part, so he wants them combined [43:09].

Small studies: an audience member said many industry studies are pilots of 45-50 or 100 people [58:46]; Spagnuolo said nutraceutical trials run to tens or hundreds, against tens of thousands in pharma [59:13]; Chen said the FDA and NIH are shifting funding toward decentralised approaches [59:31].
Spagnuolo called for publishing what did not work, since "There's no journal of unpublishable results" [53:38].
Chen sees a new chance for brands to show consumers, with their own data, that a product delivers its promise [1:02:46].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high: how ingredient evidence will be generated and judged. Large decentralised trials, run at home, can test many products head to head in parallel [34:11] [59:31]. My reading: a brand could test our ingredient against competitors' in one trial; Radicle is worth a call on cost and design.
- Pilot studies of a few dozen people were challenged from the floor and by the panel [58:46] [59:13]. My reading: the small studies behind many ingredient claims may carry less weight as larger, real-world trials become common.
- Chen's point that consumers can see a product work in their own wearable data [1:02:46]. My reading: felt outcomes such as sleep or strength, measured at home, could become part of how brands using our ingredients sell them.
- Spagnuolo's call for negative results [53:38]. My reading: worth knowing which of our ingredients' unpublished studies a brand or regulator might ask about.
quotes: "...so hallucinations all the time." Speaker 4 (Paul Spagnuolo) [36:40]
"We put about 100,000 people through double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials." Speaker 7 (Jeff Chen) [34:11]
"There's no journal of unpublishable results, right?" Speaker 4 (Paul Spagnuolo) [53:38]
"...you can construct a beautiful trial that's just not real world" Speaker 7 (Jeff Chen) [59:31]
lessons.detail:
- Billed 17:10 to 17:45, with the Chair's Closing Remarks at 17:45; recorded 17:13 to 17:46. Speaker labels: Speaker 1 is Lauren Nicolle, Speaker 2 Ohad Manor, Speaker 4 Paul Spagnuolo, Speaker 7 Jeff Chen; Speaker 3 at [58:46], Speaker 8 and Speaker 9 are audience members; Speakers 5 and 6 are fragments. Otter heard "Dr. Ernie Manna", "porn", "Jack Chen" and "Radical Science" [33:02]; the speaker slide gives Ohad Manor, Thorne, Jeff Chen and Radicle Science (photo 1).
- Jeff Chen gave no separate talk in the recording; he introduced Radicle inside the panel [34:11]. Its platform runs what it calls reflexive trials, which get smarter the more trials it runs; it holds several patents and does recruitment, biostatistics, medical writing and safety monitoring in house [34:11].
- The 6,000-person study measures, as Otter heard them, "cardiomyopaths, metabolomics, dual microbiome, continuous glucose monitoring, all in home" [34:11].
- Spagnuolo: AI could replace graduate students in making some decisions quickly; its limit is that validation in the lab, and even a clinical trial, are still needed [35:55]. Building the guardrails took the most time [36:40].
- Manor: Taya could have been built in a day by connecting it to ChatGPT, which "would defeat the whole purpose"; validation simulated thousands of conversations [37:43].
- Chen: a dried blood spot card in the post gives dozens of standard biochemistry panels; phones can take vital signs from a face scan and run cognitive tests [39:58]. He said agentic AI is the newer use, machine learning the original one [39:58].
- Manor on Taya's limits: it knows only what users tell it; people on many medications, pregnant or with a complicated chronic condition should consult a healthcare provider [45:08]. Shoppers should ask who built a tool, on what data, and whether it can explain its answers [47:08].
- Chen: the stated public position of OpenAI and Anthropic is that paid or sponsored content does not go into model training or chat answers; he called healthcare the "golden goose" for AI companies [48:37].
- Spagnuolo on personalisation: coffee was once said to raise and later to lower heart-attack risk, until caffeine metabolism explained the difference; wide individual responses sit behind meta-analysis averages [50:44].
- Chen: start with precision, fitting people into "a cluster or a segment", then reach personalisation by trial and error, which is also an engagement, upsell and subscription opportunity; a static product for everyone "that's going to go away" [52:18].
- Manor: Taya is text-only for now; wearables, blood markers and questionnaires are being worked on [54:31]. Logged-in users can ask for more lifestyle or more product advice, and choose between two voices [1:03:57] [1:04:28].
- Audience question on reading and buying: Thorne tracks whether a session ends in a purchase but cannot see Amazon purchases; many conversations are two or three messages [57:40].
- Manor measures engagement and learning first as a scientist; conversion matters to the business. He sees Taya becoming proactive, for example reading declining sleep from a wearable and checking after a month whether a product worked [1:01:05].
- Chen: Radicle rewards trial participants with their own data rather than payment [1:02:46].
- Chair's Closing Remarks, Stephen Daniells [1:05:01]: presentations that speakers allow will be shared after the post-event survey; a women's health breakfast briefing at 7:30 the next morning; the main programme at 9:00 with "Ancient and Brave"; names for the next day as Otter heard them, including "the creatine OG".

lessons.title: Living better, not just longer: Shifts for women's healthspan innovation
lessons.summary:
Dr Jenna Macciochi, Director of Science & Innovation at Ancient + Brave, opened the second day's women's health session. Ancient + Brave is a UK wellness brand selling collagen and supplements for women. Her question was how the industry should innovate for women who live longer, but not healthier, lives. Women spend 25% more of their lives in poor health than men.

She set out three shifts. First, from normalised to noticed: women have learned to accept being dismissed, and the industry sells to them with "pink" reformulations, fixed age bands, borrowed evidence and fear. Second, from reproductive hormones to whole-body transitions: hormones act on the heart, bone, muscle, metabolism, sleep and brain, and perimenopause is the least studied stage. Her example was the heart: twice as many UK women die from coronary heart disease as from breast cancer. Third, from borrowed evidence to evidence built with women, since research funding and trials largely leave women out.

Her answer was Ancient + Brave's own model: placebo-controlled trials of its products with universities, blinded consumer studies, and citizen science with customers. It also funds a PhD on collagen in midlife women. She closed on four principles: dose to the evidence, design for transitions rather than age bands, test the finished product with women, and say only what the evidence supports.
takeaways: Longer lives, not healthier ones: the gap between lifespan and healthy years is 2.4 years wider for women than for men across 183 countries, and women spend 25% more of their lives in poor health (slide 5).

Women's supplements are under scrutiny for "pink" repackaging, static age bands and borrowed evidence; Which? found many menopause supplements use botanicals at doses too low to match the trials behind them. Fear (ageing as decline, hormones as a problem, hidden threats) is "a common sales tactic" (slide 9) (slide 10).

Menopause as a whole-body transition: hormones act on brain, heart, bone, muscle, metabolism, sleep, gut, liver, immune system and skin; perimenopause is "Years of fluctuation, and the least studied". In the SWAN cohort cholesterol rose sharply around the final period, beyond what ageing alone explains (slide 12) (slide 13).

Heart: 23,000 UK women die from coronary heart disease each year, twice as many as from breast cancer. Ancient + Brave, King's College London and Heart Research UK launch a Women's Heart Health Survey in December 2026, the first UK-wide one in 9 years and the first to add menopausal stage (slide 14) (slide 15).

The evidence gap: under 1% of global research funding went to six female-specific conditions that carry 14% of the women's health burden, and 16.5% of 704 micronutrient studies included only men (slide 18).

Ancient + Brave's evidence model: clinical trials ("Does it work?"), blinded consumer studies ("How does it feel?") and citizen science with its Inner Circle customers; a four-arm sleep trial of True Nightcap against placebo, with and without a wearable; and a funded Loughborough PhD on collagen and co-supplementation in midlife women (slide 19) (slide 20) (slide 22).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high: Ancient + Brave sells collagen and a creatine product, True Creatine+ ("Advanced creatine formula"), pictured on the title slide beside True Collagen and True Nightcap (slide 1). Nick Stene of Euromonitor named it with IM8 as a brand winning on proof on day 1 (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan). My reading: a natural CreaWin prospect; who supplies its creatine now is not known.
- Her principles include "dose to the evidence" and "test the finished product, with women", with results shared whatever they show (slide 23). My reading: a pitch to her needs the doses used in human creatine trials in women, and an offer to support a placebo-controlled study of the finished product.
- Design for transitions: muscle and bone are on her map of what hormones act on, and perimenopause is the least studied stage (slide 12) (slide 13). Stene said women heading into perimenopause are badly served, and that perimenopause still earns a premium while menopause is losing one (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan). My reading: creatine and protein for muscle in perimenopause fit both talks, but the evidence has to be built in women.
- The Loughborough PhD covers collagen "and co-supplementation" in midlife women (slide 22). My reading: worth asking what is co-supplemented; a protein or creatine partner may fit.
quotes: "The ingredient was studied; the product wasn’t." (slide 9)
"Years of fluctuation, and the least studied." (slide 13)
"If the dose isn’t there, neither is the claim." (slide 23)
"What have we normalised as an industry that we should stop accepting?" (slide 23)
lessons.detail:
- The brand: "a mission driven wellness brand with an award winning range of collagen" and supplements, designed to support women's health; its vision is to be the #1 wellness brand in the world, with new standards "for holistic health, sustainability and female empowerment" (slide 2).
- Research: over £400k over the next four years in independent research with Princeton Consumer Research, UEA, Cardiff and Loughborough universities; logos also show Cardiff Metropolitan and Liverpool Hope. Certification logos: B Corp, 1% for the Planet, The Climate Label, Buy Women Built, Rainforest Concern and ESG Mark. The slide's text layer also carries "£100m" with no label; it is not visible on the rendered slide (slide 3).
- The speaker: 25 years in immunology, human performance and health; former Senior Lecturer in Immunology & Biomedical Science at the University of Sussex; leads product development and clinical research at Ancient + Brave; author of three books, most recently Immune to Age (slide 4).
- Product photos: True Nightcap ("Advanced nutrient nightcap"), True Collagen (bovine collagen) and True Creatine+ ("Advanced creatine formula") on the title slide; True Magnesium+ in a photo (slide 1) (slide 7).
- Sources for the healthspan gap: Garmany and Terzic, JAMA Network Open 2024; World Economic Forum and McKinsey Health Institute 2024 (slide 5).
- What women have learned to accept: 84% said there were times they weren't listened to by healthcare professionals (nearly 100,000 respondents, England; DHSC call for evidence 2021); 56% of UK women feel their pain is ignored or dismissed, and 31% didn't want to "waste" a professional's time (Gender Pain Gap Index, Nurofen and Wellbeing of Women); 1 in 10 women who worked through menopause left a job because of their symptoms (Fawcett Society 2022) (slide 8).
- Menopause: average age 51, usually between 45 and 55; symptoms can start years earlier; more than 34 symptoms. "Women already have the ‘Pink Tax’ and now the hormone tax." Shown on the slide: the paper "What is in the bottle? An analysis of the ingredients in menopause supplements" (Sullivan, Boylan and Harper, 2026), a "Menopause gold rush" headline, and Which?, "Menopause markup", September 2026 (slide 9).
- On fear: "Fear sells answers and certainty when we should start by asking better questions", and without collective action a climate of fear persists "because it is commercially lucrative" (slide 10).
- The four transitions: puberty (bone and body composition build), pregnancy and postpartum, perimenopause, and post-menopause ("A new baseline for heart, bone and metabolism"). SWAN: Matthews et al., Journal of the American College of Cardiology 2009 (slide 13).
- Heart: up to 59% higher risk than men of an initial heart attack misdiagnosis; up to 80% of premature cardiovascular deaths are preventable. Sources include Heart Research UK, the University of Leeds (2016), the World Heart Federation (2025) and the Lancet Women and Cardiovascular Disease Commission (2021) (slide 14).
- The survey is ethically approved and designed to inform policy: when menopause is raised in an NHS Health Check, heart risk should be part of the conversation. The last UK-wide survey was Heart Research UK and Damart, 2017 (slide 15).
- England's Renewed Women's Health Strategy (April 2026) names cardiovascular disease as a priority for women and adds a menopause question to the NHS Health Check; the slide says it does not yet join the menopause question to heart health or plan how heart risk is raised in menopause care (slide 16).
- Evidence gap sources: McKinsey Health Institute 2025 (funding 2019 to 2023, 64 conditions); Science Advances 2021; Scottish Health Survey 2017. Over 80% of the micronutrient studies excluded pregnant or lactating women (slide 18).
- The Inner Circle: customers who opt in to research after three months or more on a product; over 900 survey responses in the past year. "Ingredient studies show what a compound can do. We also need to know what a product does in real lives" (slide 20).
- Citizen science runs with ARIA (myaria.health); its founder Georgina Kyriakoudes is quoted, with three participants' comments, one on the double-blind design (slide 21).
- The PhD: Ancient + Brave's first funded PhD, at Loughborough University with Dr Tom Clifford; independent academic research intended for publication; PhD researcher Chloe Errington (slide 22).
- The deck shows study designs but no results for the sleep trial, the consumer studies or the PhD (slide 19) (slide 20) (slide 22).

lessons.title: The longevity paradigm: Healthy appearance as a reflection of internal vitality
lessons.summary:
Serena Tongiani, Chief Portfolio Officer at Indena, the Italian botanical extracts company, argued that a healthy appearance reflects internal vitality and belongs in the longevity conversation.

She opened on the market. Nutrition Business Journal data show healthy ageing as the fastest-growing supplement category, and skin and beauty ageing among the top five concerns people address with healthy-ageing products. Botanicals can meet that need, she said, but they raise three problems: poor solubility and absorption, active content that varies with the harvest, and pesticide residues, even in organic material.

Indena's answer is a Centella asiatica extract standardised in triterpenes and formulated with sunflower lecithin on its phospholipid platform, sourced from Madagascar and grown in solar-powered greenhouses in Sardinia. In human skin cells it beat a standard extract on oxidative stress and collagen; the deck itself says this is not proof of absorption.

The centrepiece was Indena's own placebo-controlled trial in 52 women aged 45 to 60, with the manuscript submitted. After 84 days wrinkle depth at the crow's feet was 16% lower than at the start, and elasticity, firmness, skin thickness, collagen fibre density and the skin's antioxidant power improved. She closed on quality: there is no quality in a finished product without quality in its ingredients.
takeaways: Market (Nutrition Business Journal, 2026): healthy ageing is the fastest-growing supplement category and the only one in double-digit growth, at 14.6% in 2025, projected to reach $2.11 billion in 2029; 51% of consumers used dietary supplements to support healthy ageing or longevity in the last 12 months (slide 5).

Skin and beauty ageing is addressed by 40% of people using healthy-ageing products, fourth after energy and focus (49%), sleep and recovery (47%) and joint and mobility support (45%) (NBJ, January 2026, n=832; read from the chart) (slide 7) (slide 9).

Botanicals' formulation gap, with Centella as the case: limited solubility and bioavailability, total triterpenes varying from 35.5 to 83.2 mg/g across harvest periods, and pesticide residues in trade samples including organic-certified material (slide 9).

In human skin cells (fibroblasts) the phospholipid-formulated extract outperformed a standard extract on oxidative stress, collagen release, collagen breakdown (MMP-1) and wound closure (about 40% after 24 hours). The deck marks this "NOT PROOF OF ABSORPTION", and a footnote says clinical benefit has not been established (slide 9) (slide 14).

Indena's own trial: randomised, double-blind and placebo-controlled, 52 healthy women aged 45 to 60 with dry skin and mild to moderate crow's-feet wrinkles, 150 mg a day for 84 days; manuscript submitted. Primary endpoints: wrinkle depth -11% at 28 days and -16% at 84 days; skin elasticity (R2) +3% and +5% (slide 15) (slide 16) (slide 17).

Secondary endpoints at 84 days: firmness (F4) -7%, skin thickness +2.2 µm, collagen fibre density +10%, fibre anisotropy -7%, skin antioxidant power (FRAP) +26%, TNF-alpha release -10%; fitted to the testing lab's reference data, wrinkle depth corresponds to 4.9 years younger, with "No variations observed with placebo." (slide 17) (slide 18) (slide 20) (slide 21) (slide 22).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: botanicals for skin are outside our range, but the trial targets women in midlife and sells "beauty from within" on collagen structure, the space collagen products hold, and the same NBJ ranking puts joint and mobility support (45%) above skin (40%) (slide 7) (slide 15) (slide 20).
- The sources differ on skin: Indena's NBJ survey ranks skin fourth among consumers' healthy-ageing concerns, at 40% (slide 7), while Nick Stene of Euromonitor said on day 1 that skin's premium on the US shelf peaked in 2025 and hair is next (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan). One measures consumer use, the other shelf premium; both are given.
- My reading: most headline percentages match the change from baseline in the extract group's chart values (wrinkle depth 267.9 to 224.8 µm is -16%), not the gap against placebo; on elasticity the placebo group started higher and the two ended at 0.634 and 0.632 (read from the chart) (slide 16) (slide 17). Buyers comparing suppliers' trial figures will meet this; ours should state which comparison they use.
- My reading: the deck pairs a supplier-funded trial with plain caveats ("not proof of absorption", in vitro only) (slide 9) (slide 14). That is the standard CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea evidence has to meet when pitched for women's healthy ageing.
quotes: "THE REAL GOAL IS NOT JUST LIVING LONGER, BUT ABOUT LIVING BETTER FOR LONGER" (slide 4)
"Market signal opens the question: can botanicals deliver consistent, well-sourced actives?" (slide 9)
"NOT PROOF OF ABSORPTION" (slide 14)
"THERE IS NO QUALITY FOR A FINISHED PRODUCT WITHOUT QUALITY OF ITS INGREDIENTS" (slide 25)
lessons.detail:
- Cites use the PDF page; the numbers printed on the slides differ (the market slide is printed "4").
- Slide 2 is a still reading "Timeless quality of life. Your golden aging starts today." with a "Health Stories" badge; its text layer reads "THINGS TO WATCH 1", probably a video in the original (slide 2).
- WHO: the number of people aged 60 and over is projected to double by 2050, reaching 2.1 billion (slide 3).
- "Same age, different inner and outer appearance": 1950s and today couples labelled "This is 40" and "This is also 40" (slide 4).
- NBJ: healthy ageing supplement sales grow 109.6% between 2023 and 2029, crossing $2 billion in 2029 at $2.11 billion on 12.2% growth. Other ways consumers supported healthy ageing in the last 12 months: devices and wearables 29%, prescription, off-label or practitioner-supervised medicines 22%, lifestyle coaching 22%, at-home diagnostics 15%, personalised supplement subscriptions 15%, in-clinic therapies 12%, AI-driven supplement or nutrition services 12%, peptides 11% (NBJ survey, aged 18 to 75, January 2026, n=1,000; read from the chart) (slide 5).
- The rest of the concern ranking: cardiovascular health 38%, metabolic weight management or blood sugar 37%, immune function 37%, eye health 34%, cognition and memory 31%, microbiome and gut 25%, hormonal balance and menopause support 22% (read from the chart) (slide 7).
- 34% of Britons say preventing signs of ageing is important (YouGov, Great Britain anti-ageing report 2026) (slide 9).
- Indena's frame for maximising healthspan: cellular ageing, body function and healthy appearance (slide 6). Healthy appearance "begins from within", as skin, hair and posture reflect oxidative stress and a declining ability to regenerate (slide 8).
- Sourcing: traditional sources in Madagascar under a responsible sourcing model (sustainable harvesting, biodiversity, long-term value for local communities), and an agricultural hub in Sardinia with fully self-sufficient photovoltaic greenhouses (slide 11).
- Mechanism: four triterpenes (madecassoside, madecassic acid, asiaticoside, asiatic acid), shown down-regulating NF-kB and up-regulating Nrf2 and MAPK signalling; the illustration is labelled "Generated with AI from: Life 2025, 15(7), 1081" (slide 12).
- The phospholipid platform is a solid dispersion of botanicals into a 100% food-grade lecithin matrix, which the slide says inhibits self-aggregation and acts as a wetting agent; it links to Indena's Phytosome page (slide 13).
- The in vitro paper: Nezi et al., Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences 2026 (13:1832045). Its abstract, shown on the slide, names the product Centextra and reports ROS cut to 115 to 174% against 368% with the pro-oxidant, IL-6 about 75% against about 150%, and collagen restored to 85% against 73%; the unformulated extract "showed limited or no activity" in these assays (read from the abstract image) (slide 14). A further footnote cites Indena internal data, manuscript in preparation (slide 9).
- Trial chart values, extract against placebo, at the start, 28 and 84 days (read from the charts): wrinkle depth 267.9, 239.4, 224.8 µm against 275.1, 273.2, 273.6; elasticity R2 0.605, 0.623, 0.634 against 0.625, 0.624, 0.632; firmness F4 9.449, 9.235, 8.864 against 10.103, 10.246, 10.097; epidermis thickness 49.4, 51.2, 51.6 µm against 48.3, 47.8, 48.4 (slide 16) (slide 17) (slide 18).
- At the start and 84 days (read from the charts): dermis density 23.6% to 25.2% against 24.7% to 24.1%; anisotropy 1.9 to 1.7 against 1.8 to 2.0; FRAP 134.4 to 169.9 µM against 129.5 to 132.4; TNF-alpha 3.32 to 2.96 pg/ml against 3.30 to 3.24 (slide 20) (slide 21).
- The slides mark both within-group and between-group significance, for example p<0.001 on wrinkle depth at 28 and 84 days, and p<0.05 between groups on elasticity (slide 16) (slide 17).
- Methods: PrimosCR SF (Canfield Scientific) for wrinkle depth, Cutometer for elasticity and firmness, line-field confocal OCT for thickness and collagen fibres, tape stripping for FRAP and TNF-alpha (slide 15) (slide 16) (slide 17) (slide 18) (slide 21).
- Collagen fibres with age: at 23 the fibre network is heterogeneous with good cross-linking; at 55 it is fragmented; density falls and anisotropy rises with ageing (slide 19).
- "Skin age": mean wrinkle depth fitted to the CRO's archive reference data gives -3.3 years at 28 days and -4.9 years at 84 days, from about 54 at the start (read from the chart) (slide 22).

courses.description: NutraIngredients' one-day sports and active nutrition conference, a single day (9 November 2026), followed on 10 and 11 November by its Nutra Healthspan Summit at the same venue, filed as its own event (nutra-healthspan-summit-2026). lessons.title: A Bigger Sports Nutrition Landscape: Growth, Tensions and What Comes Next
lessons.summary:
Nick Morgan of Nutrition Integrated opened the day with a state of the market. Sports nutrition is obviously going mainstream, he said, but is it growing beyond the motivations that defined it, is it winning consumers while losing its identity, and is the market growing or are its boundaries just moving?

He answered with three rules. Growth does not guarantee value: whey protein prices have never been higher, and brands are going through a structural reset, cutting promotions, shrinking packs, reformulating, launching whey hybrids and trying to sell more higher-margin lines such as creatine and electrolytes. Relevance does not guarantee ownership: creatine is now for everyone, in gummies, chocolate and products for women, and hydration has no agreed formula and new leaders. Opportunity does not guarantee advantage: his company tracks 16,412 product listings in eight categories, and only a few products will succeed, by pulling on format, brand, dose, science and branded ingredients.

His conclusion was that the principles of sports nutrition have gone mainstream, not sports nutrition itself. Brands should think beyond the category, stay true to the industry's DNA, choose where to compete and know their right to win. Everyone has a seat at the table, but not everyone will win.
takeaways: Starbucks' 15 g protein cold foam is his example of the bigger market: Starbucks say one in seven coffees now provides 15 g of protein. A bigger market is not more of the same market [00:00].

Brands are not just mitigating whey prices but going through a "structural reset". New products that cut whey reliance and a shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the "top priority for brands" [00:00] (photo 6).

More "whey hybrids" (sold as whey, blended with milk, soy or yeast to cut cost) launched in the last 12 months than ever; whey milkshakes and whey plus collagen are the next pillars [00:00] (photo 9).
Plant protein still underdelivers on taste. It should sell itself as a very good protein, not as plant [00:00] (photo 10).
Gummies are the fastest-growing creatine format by new launches: 8.0% of creatine products, 36.2% of them added in the last six months, with "lots of conjecture about stability" [00:00] (photo 14).
A quarter of creatine products use a branded ingredient, most of it from one supplier, and he said there is a race to follow; pre-workout is highest at 53% [18:50] (photo 27).
lessons.for_us:
- Brands want higher-margin lines than protein, and he told the room they would like to hear good solutions [00:00] (photo 6). My reading: this is the opening for CreaWin and Oxystorm.
- In creatine, branded ingredients are in 25% of products and mostly one supplier's, and he said others are racing to follow [18:50] (photo 27). My reading: this is the gap a second branded creatine pitches into, on science and story, and a stability story for CreaWin in gummies would land with brands (photo 14). The ON benchmark sets the consumer price at 25p a serve for 3 g (photo 13).
- Plant protein must sell as a very good protein, and taste is the barrier [00:00]. My reading: IsoClr: Pea should be pitched on taste and clarity first. Rocka sells fava and pea blends at EUR 1.27 to 1.65 a serve (photo 10).
- Brands now blend protein sources, including whey plus collagen in clear drinks [00:00] (photo 9). My reading: this opens room for a pea component in clear formats.
- Pre-workout has the highest branded-ingredient penetration, 53%, so it is crowded but receptive to branded actives (photo 27) (my reading, for Oxystorm). Naturalness and short ingredient lists are a prerequisite across the board [00:00] (photo 24).
quotes: "A really important point here is that a bigger market does not simply mean more of the same market." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [00:00]

"They want to sell higher value vitamins, more pre-workout, more electrolytes, more creatine, because they have a better value chain and margin structure. And so, brands would love to listen to you about some really good solutions that you have." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [00:00]

"Creatine, which is my benchmark, one in four products uses a branded ingredient. It wouldn't take you a genius to work out where most of that comes from. There's a race for those to follow, by the way." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [18:50]
"The growth is good, and it creates opportunity. You all have a seat at the table, but it doesn't mean to say you're all going to win." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [18:50]
lessons.detail:
- His three opening questions: is sports nutrition growing beyond the motivations that defined it, winning consumers but losing its identity, and is the market growing or are the boundaries moving [00:00] (photo 31). His three rules: growth does not guarantee value, relevance does not guarantee ownership, opportunity does not guarantee advantage [00:00].
- Starbucks' protein cold foam (15 g) started in Q4 2025 in America and is now in the UK, Central Europe, Singapore and India [00:00].
- Raw whey prices on Vesper's EU index: WPI from about EUR 11/kg in January 2023 to EUR 30.5 by July 2026, WPC80 from about EUR 7 to EUR 27.6, WPC35 from about EUR 3 to EUR 4.3. The slide calls it "the strongest period of price inflation on record", with WPC80 and WPI up about fourfold on 2023 and the sharpest rise in H1 2026: "Demand continues to exceed available WPI and WPC80 production capacity, resulting in the strongest period of price inflation on record." [00:00] (photo 4)
- The brand response: fewer promotions, 1 kg packs cut to 900 g at the same price, some reformulation, a rush of new whey launches, and a push to sell higher-margin lines. He believes protein will "look quite differently in 18 to 20 months" [00:00].
- Consumer prices per kilogram for priority brands in Europe, October 2025 to October 2026: clear whey up 13.6% (EUR 60.14 to 68.32), HWP/WPI 28.0% (47.73 to 61.10), whey blends 28.8% (37.56 to 48.38), whey hybrids 15.0% (35.64 to 40.97), WPC 20.8% (36.66 to 44.29). From the stage he said 15 to 25 percent [00:00] (photo 8).
- The mitigation ladder: price increases (widespread), reduced promotion (increasingly common) and pack architecture (widely adopted globally) are tactical; reformulation is strategic and brand specific; new products and a portfolio shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the top priority, limited by a ground-zero revenue base, brand permission and the risk of alienating core consumers (photo 6).
- Whey milkshakes are whey plus milk; whey plus collagen is typically 10 g plus 10 g, in shakes and clear drinks. GLP-1 and longevity proteins, yeast, mycelium and protein from air are coming through but are still expensive [00:00]. "We have never seen more whey hybrids launched in the last 12 months than ever before. It is a fundamental product pillar." [00:00] The slide's examples: Bulk Daily Whey Protein ("best value protein"), Myprotein's Impact Whey Protein Milkshake (20 g protein, 2.6 g sugar, 1.2 g fat per 29 g serving), Clean Simple Eats Protein Powder + Collagen and Planta (20 g protein, 24 vitamins and minerals, 1,000 mg BCAAs) (photo 9).
- The six pillars of innovation: whey choice risks confusing consumers; communications react more than they solve; hybrid powders are gaining consistency (dairy plus plant in overt blends); caseinate is the new milkshake; plant protein still needs a taste breakthrough; the Myprotein x Nero launch signals a race for the next cafe collaboration [00:00] (photo 12).
- Plant: ranges come in and out; dairy plus plant hybrids are appearing for the first time; caseinates are gaining with milk volatility [00:00]. "What it really wants to say is we're just a really bloody good protein. That is the ideal. By differentiating yourself as being plant, typically lends people to assume it doesn't taste as good." [00:00]
- Rocka's vegan range: Pro Protein, 24 g protein, 122 kcal, 83% fava bean and pea, EUR 37.99 per 700 g (EUR 1.65 a serve); Natural Protein, 21 g, 112 kcal, 86.6% soy, fava, almond and pea, EUR 29.99 per 600 g (EUR 1.50 a serve); Protein Shake, "the tastiest vegan protein powder", 84% blend, EUR 37.99 per 900 g (EUR 1.27 a serve). Plant is moving "from an extended product proposition to a simple product attribute" (photo 10).
- The creatine benchmark is Optimum Nutrition's Micronised Creatine Powder: 3 g creatine monohydrate a serve, GBP 14.00 for 187 g unflavoured (25p a serve, EUR 0.33) and GBP 16.00 for 247 g flavoured (29p a serve), fronted by Lauren James, Chelsea and England footballer (photo 13).
- Creatine formats across 2,639 products: powder 70.1% (13.1% added in the last six months), capsule 17.0% (8.7%), gummy 8.0% (36.2%), tablet 4.2% (14.4%), effervescent 0.4% (10.0%), other 0.3% (44.4%); 378 products, 14.3% of the total, were added in six months (photo 14). "Other" (liquids, foods, chocolate) grew fastest off a tiny base, and most brands now have a route into broader retail [25:59]. Examples: Creatonics' "Creatine+ formulated for women" sachet and Sunday Natural's Nutrachoc creatine chocolate, 20 pieces at 1,000 mg creatine monohydrate, sweetened with tagatose (photo 14) (photo 15).
- Hydration: no agreed electrolyte dose (SiS "all five essential", LMNT 1,000 mg sodium, Precision by sweat rate); Liquid IV is the category leader at £1.50 a stick; effervescents are three times cheaper than a stick pack [00:00]. Shelf prices: Liquid I.V. GBP 1.50 a sachet (GBP 9.00 for 6; GBP 1.00 on Clubcard), Phizz GBP 0.40 a tablet (GBP 8.00 for 20; GBP 0.28 on Clubcard), Evian 750 ml GBP 1.85, Red Bull 250 ml GBP 2.10, Lucozade Sport 500 ml GBP 1.65, each single (photo 16).
- Declared sodium a serve on selected electrolyte powders: 38 mg (ViDrate Boost), 350 mg (SiS Hydro+), 500 mg (Cadence Daily), 570 mg (Liquid I.V. Multiplier), 750 mg (Hunter & Gather), 1,000 mg (LMNT). 69% of powders include four or five electrolytes; 8% claim Himalayan sea salt as a natural sodium source. The slide: "there is no optimal formula" [00:00] (photo 18).
- Hydration powders are positioned three ways: everyday (Humantra, Hunter & Gather, Repowr: routine, natural, sugar-free), superior (SOS "4x faster than water", Ancient + Brave, ARTAH "cellular hydration") and performance (226ERS Hydra Zero on sweat losses, HIGH5 Isotonic carbs plus electrolytes, Precision PH strength options) (photo 22).
- Naturalness: 40% state natural colours, 46% use natural flavours, 43% include stevia. Humantra names grape skin as its colour source, Liquid I.V. declares sugar alongside steviol glycosides, ViDrate covers flavour, colour and sweetening in one proposition, Cadence extends the absence message to fillers [00:00] (photo 24).
- Tracked listings (US and Europe, 16,412 across eight spaces): creatine 3,448 (new-product activity +10% over the latest six months), magnesium 2,833 (+15%), collagen 2,648, energy and focus 2,153, pre-workout 1,869, sleep and mood 1,626, electrolyte 1,487, longevity 348 (+20% new). From the stage: almost 3,500 creatine, almost 2,800 magnesium, over 2,500 collagen. "Only a few will be really successful" [00:00] (photo 23).
- Branded ingredient penetration (share of tracked products with at least one identified branded ingredient): pre-workout 53% (many use more than one), longevity 40%, energy and focus 31%, sleep and mood 25%, creatine 25%, collagen 25%, electrolyte 17%, magnesium 17%. The slide adds that minerals in general are "needing to work harder to prove the benefit" [18:50] (photo 27).
- Longevity takes three approaches: alter the ageing process (cellular health, mitochondria, senescence), optimise the ageing experience (muscle and mobility, cognition, energy, sleep) or personalise to a life stage (ageing athletes, menopause, later life). Example: Cellaro's Vitalize AM, Renew PM and Reset monthly range against the 12 hallmarks of ageing [18:50] (photo 29).
- Longevity and athlete-backed brands compete for the same consumer: Sergio Ramos links sport to longevity through Centenarian ("Real longevity, backed by science. To perform better. To live better."), with normal sports products framed as living better today. The competitive set has never been broader [18:50] (photo 30).
- Brands should engage with gut and microbiome, longevity and GLP-1, but stay true to the industry's DNA; this will be "the biggest challenge you face for your budgets and strategy in 2027 and beyond" [18:50].
- The four closing principles: think beyond the category (new consumers, needs and occasions); stay true to your DNA (capabilities, credibility, differentiation); choose where to compete ("where you could play from where you should play"); know your right to win (where you can create distinctive value). "Growth creates opportunity. Understanding change creates advantage." [18:50] (photo 32)

key_slides.caption: The whey price mitigation ladder: three tactical moves, reformulation, then new products and a portfolio shift as the top priority.
Creatine for all people and occasions: the format split, with gummies and "other" formats growing fastest.
Branded ingredient penetration by category, from pre-workout at 53% to minerals at 17%.
His four closing principles for winning in a bigger market.

lessons.title: Unfiltered: An Insider's View of the Whey Protein Market

speakers.name: Alan Johnstone
speakers.role: Owner (as introduced; formerly Arla Foods Ingredients)

lessons.summary:
Alan Johnstone, who has spent most of the last decades selling whey protein, most recently at Arla Foods Ingredients, and now runs Nutrilution, explained why whey prices hit records this year and what buyers should do about it.

His answer starts with milk. Whey protein comes from cheese, and cheese production grows only about one and a half percent a year, while demand for whey protein grows by 10% or more: sports nutrition, GLP-1 users, protein in everyday food, and clear whey. Filtration plants are expensive and take years to build, and producers have put the whey they have into isolate, so concentrate was short when brands had just switched to it.

Prices then swing further than supply and demand alone would explain, because buyers stock up when prices rise and wait when they fall. That is happening now: concentrate is falling fast, isolate is correcting, and the proteins brands moved into are rising.

His advice was plain. Do not try to time the bottom. Keep buying steadily if today's price lets you make money. And accept that whey will stay expensive, because the supply limit is structural.
takeaways: The core constraint: cheese production grows about 1.5% a year, while whey protein demand grows over 10%. He called it the most important conclusion of the talk [00:16] (photo 7) (slide 5).
Producers chose isolate. Over five years WPI grew 15.0% a year and WPC80 1.5%; clear WPI is now about a quarter of all isolate (photo 9) (slide 8).
Between 25 August and 4 November 2026, WPC80 fell 40.7% to €16.00/kg and WPI 20.3% to €25.50/kg, while MPC85 rose 13.5% to €15.80/kg (photo 18) (slide 12).
New capacity will not close the gap: he forecast WPI at 7 to 11% a year and WPC80 at 4 to 7% to 2030, and both cannot reach the top of their range [00:16] (photo 11) (slide 9).
Mainstream buyers choose on taste and texture, not protein source, and whey is the easiest protein to make taste good [00:16].
For buyers: "Don't try to time the market. Keep inventory steady. Whey will be expensive." (photo 20) (slide 13)
lessons.for_us:
- The structural case for non-dairy protein comes from a whey insider: supply is capped by cheese and he expects whey to stay expensive [00:16]. My reading: this is the opening for IsoClr: Pea.
- He also set the bar. Mainstream consumers care about taste and texture, not source [00:16]. My reading: a clear pea isolate has to win on taste and clarity before it wins on supply.
- Clear whey is almost all WPI, where supply is tightest (photo 9). My reading: a clear pea isolate is positioned exactly there.
- Brands have just reformulated and are reviewing protein blends while WPC80 falls (photo 18). My reading: now is the time to be in front of formulators, before WPC80 settles.
quotes: "...certainly the more mainstream you get with protein products, the less people care about the protein source. I think what people always care about is taste and texture. And whey protein is delicious." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
"...if WPI is growing 11% a year, then WPC 80 has to be more like four because there's not enough whey." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
"So over the last few weeks, WPC80 has been falling pretty hard. WPI still expensive, but definitely correcting." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]

"...whey protein will be expensive. It should be expensive. It's the best protein source for so many uses. It's got a structural supply restriction, and the amount of protein is not really going away." Speaker 2 (Alan Johnstone) [00:16]
lessons.detail:
- His full deck arrived after the talk (files/alan-johnstone-whey-market-deck.pdf, 14 pages). Slide numbers here are the file's pages; the slides print their own numbers, which run behind from page 6 because some slides have a page per build. The deck confirms every labelled figure read from the photos; only the chart readings below moved.
- Prices this year, as he said them: WPI went from around €7/kg in 2023 to over €30/kg; WPC80 held around €12/kg, then rose to €28/kg in about six weeks. WPC80 was the bigger risk for brands because they had already moved their sourcing into it [00:16].
- His monthly chart differs from the spoken WPC80 figures. It peaks at about €27.4/kg in June and July 2026, not €28, and the rise from about €12.5 in November 2025 takes about seven months, steepest from about €17.7 in March to €25.4 in May; all read from the chart (slide 2). The WPI figures agree: a low of about €7.4 in June 2023 and a peak of about €31.8 in August 2026, read from the chart (slide 2).
- The monthly chart (Vesper VPI, EU monthly prices in €/kg, December 2019 to October 2026), read from the chart: WPC80 between €4.5 and €5.6 through 2020, a peak of about €12.2 in April 2022, a low of about €4.7 in May 2023, about €12 through 2025, the 2026 peak of about €27.4, and about €18.9 in October 2026; WPI about €8 in early 2020, a peak of about €18.0 in spring 2022, the 2023 low of about €7.4, about €22 in March 2025, the 2026 peak of about €31.8, and about €28.1 in October 2026 (slide 2). The photo reading had put the 2026 peaks at about €26 to 27 (WPC80) and €31 (WPI), and the October points at about €18 and €27 (photo 2). The slide headline: "Record highs this summer (WPC80 up roughly 6x since 2020, WPI near €32/kg), now correcting" (photo 2) (slide 2).
- Another speaker's view of the same price: Tess Plaquet (Rousselot, whey-collagen-the-protein-power-couple) showed WPC80 at US$5.7k a tonne in June 2023 and US$31.7k in June 2026 (US$5.70 and US$31.70 a kilogram), with Mintel and Vesper as her slide's sources. His series is Vesper's EU price in euros a kilogram: about €5.2 in June 2023 and €27.4 in June 2026, read from the chart (slide 2), and €27.00 in the week of 25 August 2026 (slide 12). The two differ in currency and unit; both show close to a sixfold rise.
- Demand drivers: traditional sports nutrition at 10% a year on Euromonitor, which he thinks underestimates it; GLP-1 users as new demand; protein going mainstream (Starbucks, Papa John's, Dunkin'); and clear whey, which barely existed five years ago and is almost all whey [00:16].
- The demand slide: the 2024 global sports nutrition market splits 48% protein powders, 26% protein bars, 17% non-protein and 9% protein RTD, growing 8 to 10% a year; clear whey SKUs are up 35% a year; 12% of US adults take a GLP-1 medication, with protein spend up 20% (KFF 2025, BCG 2026) (photo 3) (slide 3).
- Milk by weight: water 87.3%, lactose 4.7%, fat 3.9%, casein 2.8%, minerals 0.7%, whey protein 0.6% [00:16] (photo 4) (slide 4).
- The route from milk: cheese keeps the casein and fat; liquid whey goes through ultrafiltration and drying to WPC (35 to 80% protein), microfiltration or ion exchange to WPI (90% or more), then acidification or hydrolysis to clear or hydrolysed WPI. Sweet whey powder (about 12% protein), permeate, lactose, demineralised whey (D70, D90 for infant nutrition) and whey cream are the other outlets for the same whey [00:16] (photo 4) (slide 4).
- Three bottlenecks: factories ("CAPEX intensive, less flexible than people expect, takes years to start commercial production"), liquid whey, and by-products, "a major influencer of producer value". Making WPC80 leaves permeate and lactose, which are easy to sell; WPI makers must also sell a fatty protein stream, shown on the slide as whey cream (Procream or WFC) [00:16] (photo 6) (photo 7) (slide 5) (slide 6).
- Global production: WPC80 334,000 t in 2020 and 360,000 t in 2025; WPI 80,494 t and 161,800 t (40,450 t clear, 121,350 t standard); total 414,494 t and 521,800 t, up 26% (4.7% a year). Clear WPI at 40,450 t is, he said, the top of the estimate range; standard WPI grew 8.6% a year, below the category [00:16] (photo 8) (photo 9) (slide 7) (slide 8).
- Announced US capacity (McCully Consulting, approximate; WPC80 converted from million pounds): 24,400 t of WPC80 and 7,500 t of WPI in 2026, 41,600 t and 20,300 t in 2027, 45,900 t and 22,900 t in 2028; each block on the chart is one company. UK, EU and Oceania: FrieslandCampina (WPI), Fonterra (speciality) and Polmlek (WPC, WPI) in 2026; Tirlán (WPC, WPI, clear) and Liprovit (WPI) in 2027; Arla's mozzarella plant in 2028. He said the European list is incomplete [00:16] (photo 11) (slide 9).
- The buying cycle, using COVID as the example: longer lead times, more stock, rising demand, buyers competing, rising prices and an incentive to buy early; then the reverse, with the 2022 peak as logistics freed up and buyers destocked, and the 2023 trough as buyers waited with stocks too low [00:16] (photo 13) (photo 14) (photo 15) (slide 10) (slide 11).
- Now: new US plants planned three or four years ago are commissioning; isolate, WPC35 and sweet whey powder are better uses of whey, so WPC80 output should fall; substitutes (MPC85, MPI, caseins, plant proteins) are rising, and WPC80 and milk protein "should never meet" [00:16].
- Weekly Vesper prices, 25 August to 4 November 2026: WPC80 €27.00 to €16.00; WPI €32.00 to €25.50; MPC85 €13.92 to €15.80. On 4 November WPC80 was still €0.20 above MPC85 (photo 16) (photo 18) (slide 12). Read from the chart, WPC80 held about €27 for two weeks, then fell every week, to about €19 by 14 October; MPC85 was about €16 from 7 October (slide 12).
- Forces for the next move. WPC80, up: strong other derivatives, rising alternatives, long-term protein demand; down: high inventories, powerful momentum, demand destruction. WPI, up: smaller share of brand costs, healthy inventories on both sides, harder to replace; down: demand destruction, production increases due (photo 16) (slide 12).
- Where prices go: "structurally rising but volatile"; the correction "may overshoot below trend" before demand pulls prices back up. The slide's line is the average of EU WPC80 and WPI (Vesper, monthly to October 2026, lightly smoothed), and it says the trend and forward path are "directional, not a forecast" (photo 19) (slide 13).
- He quoted Keynes, that markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent, so WPC80 and MPC85 touching does not mean they part at once, "but it can't go on forever" [00:16].
- Nutrilution sells niche, higher-value ingredients and advises buyers on whey and dairy protein sourcing, including cross-continental supply chains [00:16]. Contact on the closing slide: alan@nutrilution.com (slide 14).

key_slides.caption: Supply bottlenecks: cheese production +1.5% a year against whey protein demand of 10%+.
Five years of supply growth: WPI the growth engine, clear WPI a quarter of all isolate.
The last ten weeks: WPC80 and WPI falling while MPC85 rises to meet WPC80.
Where prices go from here, with his three takeaways for buyers.
