lessons.title: Martin Bauer: RhoSera, cultivated Rhodiola rosea against anabolic resistance
lessons.summary:
Dr Ralf Spreemann of MartinBauer Nutraceuticals, a new unit of the family-owned Nature Network, introduced RhoSera, an extract of cultivated Rhodiola rosea for the ageing muscle. His question was what goes "beyond protein" for older people.

His case started with anabolic resistance. Ageing muscle responds less to protein and training, and he said hardly any ingredient addresses that gap. Wild rhodiola is overharvested, adulterated and now needs trade permits. So the group has spent decades breeding its own elite lines, grown in Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands. The cultivated root carries several times more of some compounds than wild material. In human muscle cells it switched on two stem-cell markers that wild material did not.

The human trial put 140 inactive adults aged 55 to 75 on training and protein, with RhoSera or placebo on top. Muscle soreness fell by about half on RhoSera, far more than on placebo. Strength, balance and fatigue also improved. He called them the best results of his career with a botanical. The trial is not yet published.

He closed with a typical dose of 250 to 350 mg and a regulatory note. Rhodiola has no authorised EFSA claim, so brands pair it with magnesium or B vitamins for fatigue claims.
takeaways: The gap he names is anabolic resistance: ageing muscle "responds less to protein and training", so protein advice rises from 0.8 to 1.2 g, and "hardly any ingredient" addresses it (slide 3) [00:00].

Wild Rhodiola rosea is overharvested and adulterated with non-rosea species. Rhodiola spp. has been in CITES Appendix II since February 2023, so roots and extracts traded across borders need CITES documents (slide 4). He said it was listed "as an endangered species"; the slide says CITES Appendix II, which differs [00:00].

In primary human muscle cells only the cultivated extract raised Pax7 and MyoD, the muscle stem-cell markers; wild harvest had no effect. Published as Iannuzzo et al., Antioxidants 2024;13:1000 (slide 8) [00:00].

Trial: 12 weeks, 140 inactive adults aged 55 to 75, RhoSera 400 mg a day or placebo, both arms on the same training programme plus 60 g protein a day (slide 9). He described it as double-blind and placebo-controlled [00:00].

Muscle soreness (DOMS) fell 46.3% in men and 51.7% in women, against 18.1% and 10.6% on placebo (slide 9, read from the chart); p = 0.004 and p < 0.001. He rounded these to 46%, 52%, 18% and 11% [00:00]. The data are "on file" and the manuscript is "in preparation" (slide 9).

No authorised EFSA claim for rhodiola. On-hold areas (stress, physical and mental performance) are usable if substantiated, per national rules; pair with magnesium or B vitamins for authorised fatigue claims (slide 11) [00:00].
lessons.for_us:
- This is the most direct talk for us. RhoSera is pitched "beyond protein": its closing slide says protein builds muscle and RhoSera tells it to (slide 10). Both trial arms got 60 g protein a day (slide 9). My reading: a stacking partner for IsoClr: Pea and CreaWin in healthy-ageing and active-nutrition products, not a substitute, and the framing of protein plus an enabler is one our customers will hear again.
- The soreness and performance figures are the speaker's, from a trial not yet published (data on file, manuscript in preparation). The slide itself says they "do not constitute a registered health claim" (slide 9). Carry them with that caveat.
- His point that a brand needs a secure, cultivated, traceable supply and a clean regulatory story is one we can make for creatine too (my reading).
- The group offers "science to shelf" to brand owners, formulators and CDMOs, including the RhoSera brand and logo (slide 11): a botanicals supplier selling to the same CDMOs we want to reach.
- Relevance stays high: muscle, protein utilisation and active nutrition for the over-55s. The deck confirms protein was given to both arms.
quotes: "...there is hardly any ingredient on the market which is really trying to fill this gap by enabling a muscle cell to utilize protein more efficiently, and that was our motivation." Speaker 1 [00:00]
"I'm in this business now 31 years, and it was the best results I've ever seen with a botanical." Speaker 1 [00:00]
"The marker does not predict the effect." (slide 7)
"You don't have EFSA claims. You have only on old claims, or you can borrow claims like magnesia, or for magnesium, or for instance, vitamin B, to claim loss on fatigue." Speaker 1 [00:00]
lessons.detail:
- The Nature Network: privately owned, fourth generation. MartinBauer (founded 1930, "the vanguard of botanical solutions": cultivation and sourcing, big in tea and RTD drinks), Finzelberg ("the experts in botanical efficacy": extracts for pharma and supplements; he said 1875 and that he came from there) and PhytoLab (third-party lab: reference substances, contaminants) (slide 2) [00:00].
- Group figures: 90+ years, 30+ manufacturing sites and sales units, 4,300+ employees, 650+ million euro consolidated revenue (slide 2). Otter heard "over 30 here in Poland"; the slide's 30+ is the group's sites and sales units, which differs [00:00]. The deck names no Polish sites.
- The ageing population: people aged 60+ rise from 1.0 billion in 2020 to 2.1 billion in 2050, and from 12% of the world's population in 2015 to 22% in 2050 (WHO/UN; slide 3, read from the chart). He said "probably over 2 billion" by 2050 [00:00].
- 10 to 27% of people aged 60+ live with sarcopenia, depending on the definition (Petermann-Rocha et al., J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle 2022) (slide 3).
- RhodioFarm cultivation: own fields in Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands; young plants raised in Germany; a 3-year cycle; K.I.A. standard, "no chemical pesticides as a rule, none in the 6 months before harvest"; a PA avoidance programme and full batch traceability (slide 5). He said "Central Europe", three to four years to harvest and that farmers may not use pesticides; the slide's 3 years and pesticide wording differ [00:00].
- Cultivation history: 242 accessions collected 25+ years ago; 210 were true R. rosea (32 were not) and 143 survived cultivation (67 failed in the field); only 6 to 11% met single targets (root biomass, rosavin and salidroside, reproducibility) and none met all; about 1% entered breeding; today 3 elite lines (slide 6). He said "over 10 years" to reach the three elite lines; the slide says "decades of selective breeding followed", which differs [00:00].
- Cultivated against wild, by HRMS peak area: rhodiolin 4.8 times, quercetin glycoside 3.6 times, rhodiocyanoside A 3.4 times (Iannuzzo et al. 2024) (slide 7). He said a "four to five-fold concentration" of the precursors; the slide's range is 3.4 to 4.8 times [00:00]. Otter's "rhodiolene, glycosyl, rhodiocyanide A" are these compounds.
- The "salidroside paradox": the wild extract had 1.4% salidroside and RhoSera 0.8%, yet only RhoSera switched on Pax7 and MyoD (slide 7).
- Cell work: primary human myoblasts, 48 hours, 30 µg/mL (slide 8). Pax7 rose about 1.5-fold and MyoD about 2.3-fold over untreated with the cultivated extract; myogenin did not change (slide 8, read from the chart). The clinical tests to date on rhodiola used wild material, he said [00:00].
- He said the cultivated extract also triggers folate and polyamine pathways, so spermidine, spermine and putrescine are made in the cell [00:00]. The slide gives an estimated 2.5-fold "dose advantage" on folate and polyamine pathways against wild extract, "calculated from metabolite ratios, in vitro" (slide 8). He said wild material concentrated 2.5 times shows similar effects in cells [00:00].
- Trial population: slight muscle loss but no sarcopenia, considered healthy [00:00]. Registered as CTRI/2025/04/083930. No serious adverse events (slide 9).
- Other results, as % change from baseline to week 12 in each arm (slide 9): chair stand +36 to +40% against +9 to +14% on placebo; single-leg balance with eyes closed +35 to +48% against +3 to +18%; handgrip in women +13% against +5%; bench press in men +13% against +6%; all significant against placebo. Fatigue fell and social engagement and quality of life rose, significant in men and women; sleep quality improved significantly in women. He also named leg press as improved "statistically highly significant" [00:00]; the slide does not show it.
- Formulation: 250 to 350 mg a day typical in finished products; the study used 400 mg (slide 11). Hydro-ethanolic (70%) extract on maltodextrin; vegan, non-GMO, caffeine-free, preservative-free (slide 11).
- Formats: the slide lists capsules, soft-gels, tablets, instant powders and beverages (slide 11). He named tablets, capsules, bars and V caps, and called beverages a challenge because rhodiola is very bitter [00:00].
- Supply: "100% EU grown", zero wild sourcing, "CITES-compliant by design" (slides 10, 11). Otter's "100% cytosy compliance" is CITES [00:00].
- Support offered: a clinical study summary (data on file), the RhoSera ingredient brand and logo, regulatory guidance and formulation support from their NPD team (slide 11).
- RhoSera is a trademark of MB-Holding GmbH & Co. KG, marketed by MartinBauer Nutraceuticals; contact details are on the last slide (slide 12). No slide is marked confidential.

lessons.title: Remember it. Make it. Prove it. Three things your brief forgot to ask
lessons.summary:
Thomas Beadnall, presenting for Solabia Nutrition, opened with the brief every brand writes and every CDMO receives: clinically proven, clean label, cost-effective, innovative, ready in Q3, two-year shelf life. He called it impossible and replaced it with three questions: will they remember it, can you make it, can you prove it.

On memory, the name decides. MicrobiomeX, a citrus flavanol with a prebiotic effect, went nowhere as a "flavobiotic" and was repositioned as the co-pilot for your probiotic. An aronia berry extract named Brainberry is now Solabia's second biggest and fastest growing product.

On making it, briefs now ask for several grams of creatine and collagen plus botanicals in one soluble format. Creatine adds its own problem: brands want it in gummies, but heat turns it into creatinine. Solabia and the Polish CDMO Tantus avoided this with a cold-pressed tablet of creatine and Solabia's citrus extract WATTS'UP.

On proof, he said "science-backed" means nothing on its own. What counts is the dose, the population, the endpoints and the study design. Solabia has run randomised placebo-controlled trials on all its ingredients and put each study on its website, with the olive leaf extract Bonolive as his example. He closed by inviting brands to bring their briefs to Solabia.
takeaways: The standard brief is "impossible"; judge a launch on whether they will remember it, whether you can make it and whether you can prove it [00:01] (slide 2) (slide 4).

Naming decides memory: "Flavobiotic" did not fly and MicrobiomeX became "The co-pilot for your probiotic", while Brainberry, an aronia extract with the benefit in its name, is now Solabia's second biggest and fastest growing product [00:01] (slide 7) (slide 8) (slide 10).

Briefs now ask for three to five grams of creatine and five to ten grams of collagen plus a botanical extract and a vitamin complex in one format that is soluble and mixes well [00:01]. The slides show these only as pictures, with no figures (slide 12).

Creatine in gummies: heat applied over time gives creatinine, which "doesn't really do much"; Tantus's answer was a cold-pressed tablet, no heat, of creatine plus WATTS'UP [00:01] (slide 13) (slide 14).

"Science-backed" means nothing on its own. The slide's open-evidence test is dose (how much?), population (tested on whom?), endpoints (what changed?) and study design (how was it tested?); he also named the change against placebo [00:01] (slide 16) (slide 17).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high (unchanged): creatine is being briefed at three to five grams a serving alongside collagen and botanicals, and brands want it in gummies and chewables, not only powder [00:01]. The heat problem in gummies is an opening for a stable creatine and for formats that avoid heat. My reading: a CreaWin pitch to CDMOs should carry stability data for cold-pressed and chewable formats.
- Tantus (Poland) is a CDMO already making a creatine chewable with Solabia's WATTS'UP [00:01]; neither deck names the creatine's source (tantus-longevity-concepts, slide 7). My reading: a direct CreaWin prospect, and a sign that Polish CDMOs co-develop concepts with ingredient suppliers rather than only buying to spec.
- Solabia's open-evidence test (dose, population, endpoints, study design) is how an ingredient marketer expects evidence to be shown (slide 17). My reading: our CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea materials should lead with those four items, study by study.
- A benefit in the name beat a mechanism word [00:01] (slide 7) (slide 10). My reading: relevant to how we name concepts for customers.
quotes: "We want a clinically proven, clean label, cost-effective, innovative product, which is ready in Q3, and it's got a two-year shelf life. Sounds like a great brief. Sounds like a great product, but unfortunately, it is impossible." Thomas Beadnall [00:01]
"Only problem with gummies is when you apply the heat over time, what happens? Creatinine." Thomas Beadnall [00:01]
"It's probably one of the most used phrases in the industry, and it's also probably one of the most dangerous because it means absolutely nothing, really science-backed." Thomas Beadnall [00:01]
"Brainberry is now the second biggest product in their portfolio and the fastest growing." Thomas Beadnall [00:01]
lessons.detail:
- The deck is "Remember it. Make it. Prove it.", subtitled "Three things your brief forgot to ask." and "A different way to think about a successful launch.", by Thomas Beadnall of Solabia Nutrition (slide 1). Spoken, the subtitle was "three things that your brief forgot to tell you" [00:01]. His role is not on the slides; he said he has worked with Solabia "for a while now in their ingredient portfolio" [00:01].
- MicrobiomeX is a "Citrus flavanol with a prebiotic effect on gut microbiome" on the slide (slide 6); spoken as a "flavonol" that is not a prebiotic but has a prebiotic effect [00:01]. The slide's word and the spoken word differ.
- The rejected name on the slide is "Flavobiotic." (slide 7); Otter heard "flavorbiotic". The industry does not need another "biotic" [00:01].
- The new line: "The co-pilot for your probiotic", with "Low dose. Non-fermenting" (slide 8). The slide's screenshot (an image; text read from it) of Solabia's page says MicrobiomeX is upcycled from immature Mediterranean citrus, a "low-dose, non-fermenting precision prebiotic" that shifts the microbiome toward butyrate-producing bacteria, "without the bloat or gas of traditional fibres" (slide 8). These are Solabia's claims.
- Brainberry is an aronia berry extract clinically studied for cognitive health; "the key is in the name" [00:01]. The slides show a berry-to-brain picture and the Brainberry logo (slide 9) (slide 10).
- WATTS'UP is the citrus extract Otter heard as "WhatsApp". Solabia's deck does not name it; Tantus's slides do, as 400 mg WATTS'UP with 3 g creatine in the chewable (tantus-longevity-concepts, slide 7). The speaker said it helps nitric oxide and blood flow, and that the tablets melt in the mouth and could be tasted at Solabia's stand [00:01].
- Bonolive is the olive leaf extract Otter heard as "Bun Olive" (slide 17). It was marketed for bone health and is now studied for skin health and menopause symptoms; all its studies were in women, by female-led research teams [00:01].
- The slide's screenshot of Solabia's Bonolive page (an image; text and figure read from it) lists three applications: menopause capsules and softgels ("one 250 mg dose, one simple menopause claim"); combination stacks with calcium and vitamins K2 and D, marked "For claiming in EU"; and beauty-from-within blends with collagen, marked "Nutricosmetic pairing" (slide 17).
- You can always find an article to back an idea, and "ChatGPT will probably find you five" [00:01].
- Solabia rebuilt its website over the summer so each ingredient has study summaries and each study can be read (solabianutrition.com) [00:01] (slide 17) (slide 19).
- The last slide repeats the three questions: "Thinking of a new product? bring us your brief!" (slide 19).
- No slide is marked "Confidential".
- The host introduced Tantus as a Polish contract manufacturer of dietary supplements working in tablets and hard capsules, with formulation, development and some packaging [08:23].
- The talk was one unbroken Otter turn, so every spoken passage sits in the same [00:01] block; the slides give the order of points.

lessons.title: Longevity - from a trend to a product

speakers.name: Mateusz Korgul
speakers.role: Clinical dietician and business development manager

speakers.name: Victoria Lesiovski
speakers.role: Certified herbalist; sales and business development

lessons.summary:
Mateusz Korgul and Victoria Lesiovski of Tantus, a Polish CDMO, asked how a longevity trend becomes a product people actually take. A trend changes nothing on its own. It matters only once a product reaches the market and becomes part of a daily routine.

Consumers want healthspan, not only lifespan: years spent active, capable and independent. The industry answers with ever more complex formulas, but they argued the real question is what makes biological sense in a product, not what else can be added. Longevity is a marathon, so format, dose and ease of use decide whether people keep taking it.

Their process has four steps: trend, ingredient, formula, market. Suppliers are partners who bring research, safety dossiers and formulation know-how, not vendors filling separate orders.

They showed three concepts. The first, made with Solabia, is a chewable tablet of 3 g creatine and 400 mg of Solabia's citrus extract WATTS'UP, sold on physical function with age rather than sport: "Chew it, don't shake it." The second is a daily healthy-ageing capsule of Kaneka Ubiquinol, VitaCholine and active B vitamins. The third is a tablet of Nuritas's PeptiStrong plant peptides for muscle with age. Their close: keep it simple, make it last.
takeaways: A trend does not change anything on its own; longevity becomes a product "when it fits real life - and stays there" [00:31] (slide 13).
Complexity is not the answer: the question is never what else to add, but what "genuinely makes biological sense in this specific product" [01:05] (slide 4).

Concept one: 3 g creatine plus 400 mg WATTS'UP in a chewable tablet, formulated by Tantus and Solabia, for mobility and muscle resilience "without requiring athletic sports positioning" (slide 7). Spoken as "400 grams" of a hesperidin-based ingredient [04:45]; the slide's 400 mg differs from what was said. The slides do not name the creatine's source.
The slide's image gives four reasons people stop taking creatine powder: water needed, a shaker to carry, grit and aftertaste, and it will not dissolve ("Half of it sits at the bottom") (slide 8).

Concepts two and three, from the slides only: Anti-Age by Tantus, one capsule a day of 100 mg Kaneka Ubiquinol, 300 mg VitaCholine and an active B-complex; and a PeptiStrong tablet co-developed with Nuritas and Vivatis Pharma (slide 9) (slide 10) (slide 12).
Tantus wants long-term suppliers who bring clinical research, safety dossiers, technology know-how and new concepts, not transactional orders [03:09] (slide 6).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high (unchanged): creatine is Tantus's lead concept. A 3 g creatine chewable is built and sampled with an ingredient supplier, but the slides name only "3 g Creatine", not its source (slide 7). My reading: Tantus is a direct CreaWin prospect, and the first question is whose creatine is in the tablet and whether that is fixed.
- Creatine is sold here on mobility and muscle resilience with age, without sports positioning (slide 7). My reading: the ingredient we sell into sports brands has a second customer in longevity brands reached through CDMOs like Tantus.
- The four reasons people stop (water, shaker, grit and aftertaste, poor dissolving) are the case for the chewable (slide 8). My reading: a CreaWin pitch for chewables and tablets should answer taste, grit and tabletting with data.
- Tantus prefers suppliers who bring dossiers and formulation help over suppliers who sell powder [03:09] (slide 6). My reading: our pitch to CDMOs should include stability and formulation support, not price alone.
- Muscle health is framed as healthspan, and the slot is filled by plant peptides with an open pipeline on dose, format and endpoints (slide 11). My reading: Tantus builds muscle-with-age concepts with ingredient partners; a CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea concept could be offered the same way.
quotes: "We know that longevity is a marathon. It's not a sprint, and that's why the most promising formulations don't make sense when users are not willing to use it consistently." Speaker 2 (Victoria Lesiovski) [02:09]
"At Tantus, we aim to build long-term relationship with our suppliers, rather than treating every order as a separate transaction." Speaker 1 (Mateusz Korgul) [03:09]
"We didn't want to develop just another creatine powder that you have to scoop and shake and mix and drink." Speaker 2 (Victoria Lesiovski) [04:45]
"Longevity becomes a product when it fits real life - and stays there." (slide 13)
lessons.detail:
- Speakers as on the slides: Mateusz Korgul, clinical dietician and business development manager; Victoria Lesiovski, certified herbalist, sales and business development (slide 2). Otter heard "Mateus Kollu" [01:05] and the host said "Matthias Korgol" (solabia-launches transcript, [08:23]); the slide spelling is used.
- The deck's title is "Longevity - from a trend to a product", subtitled "How Tantus turns the language of healthy ageing into products people can understand, use, and keep using." (slide 1). The host introduced it as "longevity in action, from a trend to a product" (solabia-launches transcript, [08:23]).
- Lifespan counts the years we live; healthspan the years "spent active, capable, and cognitively well". The opportunity is a shift from vague anti-ageing promises toward everyday functional preservation: mobility, mental clarity and independence (slide 3) [01:05].
- The over-formulation trap: the market piles on ingredients, "stacking theoretical pathways into overly complex formulas". Benefits compound only with uninterrupted adherence, so a formula must earn its daily place (slide 4) [02:09].
- The four steps on the slide: trend (read the market and consumer need with partners), ingredient (evidence-backed, not just strong marketing), formula (combine around one concrete product function), market (from first concept to a manufacturable product) (slide 5). Spoken, the market step means making the product first to show clients [03:09].
- Concept one: the slide says it combines "reference-standard cellular energy support with citrus bioflavonoid efficiency" (slide 7). Victoria said it was developed with Solabia, could be tried at Solabia's stand and turned out "very delicious" [04:45]. Otter's summary also gives 400 mg (files/otter-summary.md).
- Slide 8 is an image only: a WATTS'UP visual carrying the Tantus and Solabia logos, "Creatine minus the shaker. Chew it. Don't shake it." (slide 8).
- WATTS'UP is the ingredient Victoria called hesperidin-based [04:45] and the slide calls a citrus bioflavonoid (slide 7). In Solabia's talk it is the citrus extract in the same cold-pressed tablet (solabia-launches).
- Concept two, "Healthy ageing as a system not a magic ingredient": 300 mg VitaCholine (choline, by Balchem), 100 mg Kaneka Ubiquinol (the reduced form of coenzyme Q10) and active B vitamins (B1, B2, B3, B5, B6 as P-5-P, B7, B12 as methylcobalamin, folate as Quatrefolic), designed around energy metabolism and nervous-system function; 60 vegan capsules, one a day (slide 9) (slide 10). Kaneka's own talk at this event: kaneka-ubiquinol.
- The concept visual (an image; text read from it) says choline "contributes to normal lipid and homocysteine metabolism and to the maintenance of normal liver function", and that the B vitamins support "normal energy-yielding metabolism" and help "reduce tiredness and fatigue" (slide 10).
- Concept three, "Muscle health is healthspan": muscle mass, strength and mobility underpin functional autonomy and metabolic health with age. PeptiStrong is described as "AI-discovered bioactive plant peptides", and dose, delivery format and clinical endpoints are open for joint development (slide 11). Nuritas's own talk at this event: nuritas-peptistrong.
- The concept is titled "Peptiforce" (Nuritas×Tantus) on the slide, while the prototype pack in the slide's image reads "Peptide Bite", "Longevity · Prototype 01", 40 tablets, two a day; the two names differ (slide 12).
- The closing takeaways: start with the problem, not the ingredient count; choose evidence, focus and repeatable formats, since "A supplement has no value if left in the cabinet"; anchor innovation in durable partnership (slide 13).
- No slide is marked "Confidential". Slides 10 and 12 are marked "Concept visual · not for sale" (slide 10) (slide 12).
- The recording ends after concept one [04:45] [06:40]; concepts two and three come from the slides only.
- The host introduced Tantus as a Polish contract manufacturer of dietary supplements in tablets and hard capsules, with formulation, development and some packaging (solabia-launches transcript, [08:23]).

lessons.title: How a novel food ingredient unlocks new solutions for the Health & Wellness market. What can you learn from successful US brands?
lessons.summary:
Thijs Bosch, CEO of The Protein Brewery and formerly a seller of dairy and fava proteins, presented Fermotein, a whole-food mycelium powder grown by biomass fermentation in Breda, in the Netherlands. His pitch was that one ingredient can carry protein, fibre and longevity bioactives together.

Fermotein is 50% protein and 30% fibre, and is rich in spermidine and vitamins. EFSA gave its safety opinion in 2025 and EU authorisation followed in 2026; approval took five years, he said. While waiting, the company built its market in the US, in "all-in-one nutrition": powders between protein powder and meal replacement, priced against the whole supplement basket. Ka'Chava is the model, growing fast in measured retail without discounting. In Europe the brands still sell meal replacement, and he asked the CDMOs in the room to embrace the all-in-one concept.

His evidence so far is laboratory work: prebiotic effects in a gut model, GLP-1 release in human colon tissue, and longer lifespan in nematodes. The slides say plainly that this is not evidence of an effect in humans. Two human trials with Wageningen come next.

He closed on scale: 10 million servings sold in 2026, three active US customers and €70 million raised. The company is not yet profitable.
takeaways: Fermotein is 50% protein with a complete amino acid profile, 30% fibre ("unique fungal fibres"), spermidine at "7x more than wheat germ", vitamin B6, vitamin B4, calcium, iron, zinc, phosphorus and magnesium (slide 5). Spoken: chitin and chitosan fibre, spermidine at about 1,700 mg per kilo, seven times "beet germ" as transcribed, and choline [00:00].

Approvals: self-affirmed GRAS in the US and Singapore (SFA) approval in 2024, EFSA safety approval in 2025, EU authorisation and market launch in 2026 (slide 3). He said "since the summer of this year" after five years, with Australia and Canada pending [00:00].

All-in-one nutrition is worth $0.5 to 1bn in the US against $8.6bn for protein supplements and $4.9bn for meal replacement (2025), and is priced at about $5 to $7 a serving against $1 to $2 for protein powder and $4 to $6 for meal replacement (slide 6) [00:00].

Ka'Chava: $47.2M measured retail sales excluding direct sales, up 24.4% in dollars and 39.9% in units over 52 weeks to 07/12/2026 (SPINS); single-serve multipacks grow fastest, up 254% to over 1,000%, at the highest price per serving (slide 8). He called it "super profitable" [00:00].

Evidence is preclinical: in a TNO gut model Fermotein raised butyrate, propionate and acetate and microbial diversity; in TNO human colon tissue it raised GLP-1 against a blank; in NemaLife's C. elegans study median lifespan rose 21.7%, 28 against 23 days (slide 11) (slide 12). He said 22% [00:00].

Next: a 16-week human RCT on biological ageing clocks in adults aged 40 to 60, led by Dr Pol Grootswagers of Wageningen; a human spermidine bioavailability trial; and a NemaLife follow-up on lifespan and muscle health (slide 13). He said the ageing-clock trial starts in quarter one [00:00].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high, unchanged: a non-animal protein ingredient for active nutrition, now authorised in the EU, competing for the same brief as IsoClr: Pea (slide 3) (slide 5) [00:00]. My reading: at 50% protein it sells protein plus fibre plus longevity, not protein content; it will meet us in all-in-one and superfood blends, not in clear protein drinks.
- All-in-one is priced against the whole basket, at about $5 to $7 a serving against $1 to $2 for protein powder (slide 6). My reading: a premium European format where IsoClr: Pea and CreaWin could be the protein and performance pillars; the European meal-shake brands on his slide, BOL and vybey, are worth approaching (slide 10).
- He says Europe has not yet adopted all-in-one messaging (slide 10) [00:00]. My reading: a CDMO pitch for a European all-in-one shake, built on our ingredients, is open.
- The longevity science is laboratory-only and the company labels it so (slide 11) (slide 12). My reading: a fair benchmark for how plainly to present preclinical data in our own collateral.
quotes: "And we are the first mycelium protein company that has EFSA approval. So since the summer of this year, we can finally sell in Europe" Speaker 1 (Thijs Bosch) [00:00]
"...it's mainly into the all-in-one nutrition segment, which hasn't really evolved yet." Speaker 1 (Thijs Bosch) [00:00]
"Preclinical in vitro, ex vivo and invertebrate-model results; not evidence of an effect in humans." (slide 11)
"Packs got smaller. Price per serving did not." (slide 8)
lessons.detail:
- Title slide: "Remedy Gdańsk – October 2026 – Thijs Bosch, CEO" (slide 1). His 15+ years in proteins run through Fonterra, Cosun and The Protein Brewery (slide 2); he said he ran a European dairy protein business at Fonterra, then sold fava proteins at Cosun [00:00].
- Slide 8 is marked "Property of The Protein Brewery · Strictly Private and Confidential" (slide 8). Its Ka'Chava figures stay internal.
- History: founded in 2020 by Wim de Laat; a 3,000 L pilot plant in 2021; a commercial demo plant and nine patents granted in 2024; two US customers booked all capacity for 2026 (2025); 150 tonnes run-rate capacity in 2026; the commercial plant has two 85,000 L fermenters (slide 3) [00:00].
- Funding: Series A €22M, Series B €30M and a Series B extension €18M, €70M in all (slide 3). He named Novo Holdings (transcribed "Nova Holdings") as the biggest shareholder and said the company is not yet profitable [00:00]; the slides name no shareholders.
- Process: a fungal strain grown in bioreactors forms hyphae of protein, prebiotic fibre and bioactives, and downstream processing turns it into a powder for shakes [00:00].
- Fermotein won the Vitafoods Europe Startup Innovation Challenge 2026 category "Most Innovative Sustainable Solution", and carries allergen-free, certified gluten-free, kosher and non-GMO marks (slide 5).
- Segments: protein powder skews younger, male, urban and athletic and is priced per gram of protein; all-in-one buyers are 30+, slightly female and "health optimisers"; meal replacement serves the time-poor and patients through carers. Growth: protein supplements +11.0% a year to 2032, meal replacement +6.9% to 2033, Ka'Chava +24.4% in 2026 (slide 6).
- Ka'Chava price per serving: $5.20 for the 2 lb bag (14.6 servings), $4.88 for the 15.31 oz tub (7 servings), $6.20 to $6.80 for the single-serve 5-pack (slide 8). He said the price rises as the format gets smaller [00:00]; on the slide the tub is cheaper per serving than the bag and only the single-serve pack costs more.
- US examples: Shakeology (plant protein and superfoods, "over 1 billion servings sold") with its own comparison against Vega One, Orgain and Ka'Chava; Ka'Chava as "Whole Body Nutrition" with 25 g plant protein, 26 vitamins and minerals and 85+ superfoods (slide 7). Vita Hustle ONE Superfood Protein, 20 g plant protein, 86 superfoods, under 160 calories, pre- and probiotics and ashwagandha, set against typical protein and greens powders such as AG1 (slide 9) [00:00].
- European examples are meal replacements: BOL "A meal in a bottle" (25 g+ protein, 9 g+ fibre) and vybey Complete Meal Shake (plant based, 29 g protein, with lion's mane and Bacillus coagulans) (slide 10). He named recent sales of meal replacement brands to Danone and Nestlé [00:00].
- TNO studies, both on Fermotein predigested by the INFOGEST method: gut-model fermentation over 24 h (TNO 2026 15116) at 38 mg/mL, equal to 12 g Fermotein (~4 g fibre); colon tissue over 1 h (TNO 2026 15096) at 15 mg/mL, about 5 g (slide 11).
- Alpha-diversity rose from 2.728 to 2.969 with Fermotein, while inulin's fell from 3.089 to 2.004, as labelled on the chart; the slide says inulin was tested undigested against a different control, "a platform benchmark, not a like-for-like comparator" (slide 11). GLP-1 reached about 440 pM against near zero for the blank, read from the chart (slide 11).
- NemaLife, a Texas Tech University spin-off founded by Prof. Siva Vanapalli, fed nematodes the water-soluble fraction (229.6 mg/mL, n=137 against 102 on standard diet; p<0.0001, log-rank). The dose equals 14 mg spermidine or about 8 g Fermotein, which the slide calls "indicative only" and "not a health claim" (slide 12). Otter's "Nema Live" is NemaLife [00:00].
- Upcoming studies: NemaLife at 7 and 14 mg human-equivalent spermidine, measuring lifespan, muscle health and RNA expression; a human spermidine bioavailability trial measuring blood spermidine and spermine, GLP-1, glucose and insulin; the Wageningen ageing-clock RCT, Fermotein against control, measuring autophagy, DNA methylation and hair growth (slide 13). Otter's "Paul Gössfaifers" is Pol Grootswagers [00:00].
- Progress: 10M servings sold in 2026, 3 active US customers, 80+ prospects in the EU pipeline, €70M raised, factory at scale (slide 14). He said the US customers are mainly in active nutrition, also all-in-one [00:00].
- Slide 14 shows Clean Machine MycelPro-1, a "whole-food mycelium protein" with 20 g protein, 10 g prebiotic fibre and 69 mg spermidine, labelled "Best Protein 2026" by Plant Based News (slide 14). My reading: one of the US customers.
- Slide 15 shows a concept pack, "PRIME Foundation+", "for illustration purposes, not for sale", and a vote for the Protein Production Technology International shortlist (slide 15) [00:00]. Samples, neutral and iced coffee, were at the company's table [00:00].
- The talk was one unbroken Otter turn, so every spoken passage sits in the same [00:00] block.

lessons.title: Translating Longevity Science into Relevant Consumer Outcomes
lessons.summary:
Alex Glover, Holland & Barrett's Global Product Formulation Lead, runs the team that formulates its own-label products worldwide. He asked how longevity science becomes something a customer will buy. His answer: consumers may buy a story, but they judge a product on the outcomes they feel.

He opened with a tortoise to argue that ageing badly is not biologically fixed, so the category is about living better, not longer. H&B's data on millions of customers show that repeat purchase goes to products with one clearly communicated benefit, such as joint function or brain function. Shoppers ask when they will feel it, whether they can measure it, and what it costs. His slides set the test an ingredient must pass: evidence, dose, outcome, communication and consumer relevance.

Two case studies followed. NAD boosters have a strong molecular rationale but very limited functional outcome data, and of over 1000 customers surveyed, not one knew what NAD was. Curcumin, H&B's second best-selling ingredient, shows the other path: a meta-analysis of 11 trials found it improved knee osteoarthritis pain scores. He also named cheap basics with strong evidence: fibre, vitamin D, calcium and protein.

His conclusion for suppliers: bring ingredients with both a biological rationale and human outcome data, and help retailers translate the science without over-promising.
takeaways: Mechanisms make promises and sell, but outcomes retain customers (slide 6). Shoppers ask whether and when they will feel it, whether they can measure it, and what it costs (slide 8); when trials show a benefit at four, six or eight weeks, H&B can sometimes put that on pack [00:25].

H&B's test for an ingredient has five parts: evidence (high-quality science), dose (the effective, studied dose), outcome (which endpoint improves), communication (legal and responsible) and consumer relevance (does it matter in everyday life) (slide 6).

The outcomes consumers buy are energy, memory, strength, mobility, sleep, appearance and feeling younger or better, not NAD+, sirtuins, telomeres or PARPs (slide 8). H&B's biggest own-label sellers carry one clear benefit, such as joint function, joint comfort or brain function [00:25].

NAD: of over 1000 customers surveyed, not one knew what NAD was [00:25]. NR reliably raises blood NAD metabolites and NMN or NAM raise it in some studies, but functional outcome improvements are "very limited" (slide 13).

Curcumin is the "tangible outcomes" case: a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (n=1258) found curcuminoids improved VAS and WOMAC pain scores in knee osteoarthritis against comparators or placebo, and formulation matters because bioavailability varies widely (slide 15).
Cheap interventions with strong evidence (fibre, vitamin D, calcium, protein) beat novel technologies on evidence and cost; US shelves are "protein plus fiber" [00:25]. None of this is on his slides.
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance stays medium: a major retailer's test for ingredients, adjacent to our range; the slides name none of our ingredients.
- The formulation lead at one of our customers' biggest retailers checks evidence, dose, outcome, communication and consumer relevance (slide 6), and wants ingredients with "both biological rationale and human outcome" data (slide 17). My reading: CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea dossiers for retail-led brands should lead with the studied dose, the endpoint that improves and when the user feels it, before any mechanism.
- Strength and mobility are two of the seven outcomes he says consumers buy (slide 8). My reading: a healthy-ageing pitch for CreaWin and pea protein should speak of strength and getting out of a chair, not muscle protein synthesis.
- "Everything is protein plus fiber" in the US, and protein is among his cheap, evidence-rich longevity interventions [00:25]. My reading: pea protein with fibre is a brief European brands will copy, and IsoClr: Pea's taste and clarity are the arguments inside that blend.
quotes: "Customers are not buying into the mechanism. They are buying your product based off how they feel and how they continue to feel taking your product." Speaker 2 (Alex Glover) [00:25]
"Not a single customer knew what NAD was. There was over 1000 people that we surveyed." Speaker 2 (Alex Glover) [00:25]
"I'm sure if anybody's been to the US in the last six months, everything is protein plus fiber." Speaker 2 (Alex Glover) [00:25]
"Longevity science is rich in mechanisms, but consumers experience outcomes." (slide 17)
lessons.detail:
- The deck names him Alex Glover MSc, RNutr, Global Product Formulation Lead, Holland & Barrett (slide 1). Every slide carries the date 04/11/2026; none is marked confidential (slide 2).
- Agenda in five parts: from lifespan to healthspan; consumers don't buy longevity, they buy outcomes; the longevity evidence gap; NAD, NR and NMN as a "molecular outcomes" case study; joints as a "tangible outcomes" case study (slide 2). He skipped it in the talk [00:25].
- The tortoise: a photo, then a survival chart labelled with an average lifespan of about 72-80 years for humans and 150-200 years for the tortoise (slides 3-4). He said humans live about 10 to 12 years with a disability or poor health, while a tortoise lives most of its life without [00:25]. In his words, "we're not in the business of making people live longer; we're making them live better" [00:25].
- H&B's data on millions of customers show what they buy and how often. A customer panel, the "Stay Healthies" around 50, talked about playing with grandchildren and getting out of a chair, not sirtuins or telomeres [00:25].
- The evidence chain on his slide runs mechanism (pathway), biomarker (surrogate), function (performance), clinical outcome (quality of life, disease endpoint) (slide 9). He said suppliers get "stuck" in the first two; his sleep example was the Pittsburgh scale, which means nothing to a shopper [00:25].
- Biomarkers are real signals but often not validated surrogates; a biomarker change is not a change in how someone feels or functions; in supplements, biomarker shifts often precede but do not guarantee outcome benefits (slide 10).
- NAD: a central redox cofactor that declines with age, behind the hypothesis "boost NAD = boost healthspan"; blood NAD is not muscle or mitochondrial NAD, and more in blood does not guarantee more where it matters; measurement is improving but interpretation is still hard (slide 12). NR can raise the muscle NAD metabolome, with mixed outcomes; NMN and NAM outcomes are mixed or early (slide 13).
- The NAD paper: he spoke of an April 2026 meta-analysis and one trial on walking speed in the over-60s [00:25]. The slide shows a different source: a review published 13 October 2025, "NAD+ precursor supplementation in human ageing: clinical evidence and challenges" (Vinten et al., Nature Metabolism 7, 1974-1990), beside three trials: chronic NR in healthy middle-aged and older adults (Martens et al.), NR in aged human skeletal muscle (Elhassan et al., 2019), and a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled NMN trial in healthy middle-aged adults (published 8 December 2022) (slide 13). The spoken date and the slide differ; the walking-speed trial is not on the slide.
- Curcumin is H&B's second best-selling ingredient globally, about "one bottle a minute"; he gave the on-hold claim as joint flexibility and comfort, with evidence on knee osteoarthritis, movement, function and systemic inflammation [00:25]. The slide cites Hsiao et al., a meta-analysis of high- and low-dose curcumin in knee osteoarthritis, and a critical review of curcumin reviews (Chen et al.): adverse events were similar at high and low dose, and curcumin sometimes compares favourably with NSAIDs (slide 15). Systemic inflammation is not on the slide.
- His conclusions: the most compelling retail categories are those where consumers can feel or measure the outcome (mobility, cognition, vision); curcumin, UC-II and anthocyanins show mechanism aligning with real-world outcomes; NAD boosters show strong rationale but limited evidence for tangible benefits "so far"; the retailer's challenge is to translate emerging science without over-promising (slide 17).
- Fibre, vitamin D, calcium and protein: he said the nutrition slide was missing from the deck [00:25]. He gave about 9% lower coronary heart disease risk for every seven grams of fibre, called fibre one of the biggest nutritional predictors of longevity, and costed vitamin D at about two cents per 10 microgram serving from H&B's own label [00:25].
- He believes about 80% of how we age can be influenced. He closed on an 81-year-old sprinter he named as Kenton Brown, who ran 100 metres in 14.4 seconds [00:25]; the slide shows the sprinter in a USA vest without a name (slide 16).
- The talk was one unbroken Otter turn, so every spoken passage sits in the [00:25] block.

lessons.title: 2waves: one platform for brands, manufacturers and ingredient suppliers

speakers.name: Matthew Kwembowski
speakers.role: Co-founder; IT architecture and data security (surname as transcribed)

lessons.summary:
Viktor Tsevsky and Matthew Kwembowski, co-founders of 2waves, pitched a platform for the three sides of the supplement market: brands, manufacturers and ingredient suppliers.

They started from a growing market, which Grand View Research puts at more than 60 billion dollars by 2030, and from how badly its sides find each other. Brands have no view of their category, offers come in no common format, inquiries are incomplete or do not fit, one inquiry runs across many email threads, and many get no answer at all. That costs time and lost business.

Their answer is a first module for new partnerships, quoting and negotiation. One inquiry reaches every manufacturer or supplier in the category. Offers come back in one structure to compare, the negotiation history stays in one place, inquiries are matched to who can make them, and every decline carries a reason. Matthew had begun on data security, with every company verified before joining, when the recording ended.

The conference organiser, Pawel Gruszczynski, sits on the project's board as strategic advisor.
takeaways: The market is framed as three sides, brands, manufacturers and ingredient suppliers, with Grand View Research's forecast of over 12 percent growth a year to more than 60 billion dollars by 2030 [00:13].
The cost of today's process is operational (hours organising inquiries, hunting agreements in email threads) and lost opportunity (offers never received, inquiries never answered) [01:50].
One inquiry reaches all manufacturers (or suppliers) in the category; offers come back in one structure, "two offers or 15", ready to compare [02:46].
For suppliers and manufacturers: inquiries are matched to what you can produce, so you see opportunities that today never find you [02:46].
Every company is verified before joining; the security module answers losing control of information once it sits in an inbox [07:42].
Pawel Gruszczynski (Remedy, the conference organiser) is strategic advisor and board member of the project [02:46].
lessons.for_us:
- If it gains users, 2waves would put Polish CDMOs' ingredient inquiries in front of any verified supplier in the category [02:46]. My reading: worth registering early as a creatine and pea protein supplier to see briefs we are not asked for today, and a signal of how Polish CDMOs may buy.
- It also commoditises: offers "in the same structure" ready to compare favour price comparison [02:46]. My reading: our differentiation (IsoClr: Pea's clarity, CreaWin's stability data) has to fit a template.
- The organiser's board seat means the Remedy network of CDMOs is the launch audience (my reading).
- Relevance medium: how brands, CDMOs and suppliers find each other, not our ingredients directly.
quotes: "...this industry grew up without a tool of its own, and now it has one, and it's called two ways." Speaker 2 (Viktor Tsevsky) [02:46]

"One inquiry automatically reaches all manufacturers in that product category you are searching for, we open up the market and reduce the time it takes to find the right partner." Speaker 2 (Viktor Tsevsky) [02:46]
"And no decision without a reason. If your inquiry or offer is declined, you will get the reason why." Speaker 2 (Viktor Tsevsky) [02:46]
"On two ways, every company is verified before joining. Verified company, always talk to a verified company." Speaker 3 (Matthew Kwembowski) [07:42]
lessons.detail:
- The problems named: no visibility in your category, no single offer format, incomplete inquiries, one inquiry in many email threads, inquiries that do not fit, no answer at all [00:13].
- Module one is "new partnerships, quoting, and negotiation" [02:46].
- Structured templates per product category, quoting variants and negotiation history one click away, and a reason for every declined inquiry or offer [02:46].
- Matthew began on data security when the recording ended [07:42].
- Pricing, launch date and current users were not given before the recording ended (my reading).

lessons.title: Closing panel: evidence, regulation, supply and AI in nutraceuticals

speakers.name: Alex Glover
speakers.role: Leads the product formulation team (own-label); retail and consumer perspective

lessons.summary:
The day's closing panel brought together a retailer (Alex Glover, Holland & Barrett), a CDMO (Martina Pavlová, FAVEA), an ingredient company (Matts Johansen, chief executive of Aker BioMarine), a food lawyer (Joanna) and a pharmaceutical company (Alexandra). The moderator asked what each wants in the next two or three years, then turned to regulation, supply and AI.

They agreed that the consumer comes first. Alexandra wanted evidence-based claims and better communication, Martina a focus on what consumers actually need, and Alex a few claims done well, starting from the consumer's problem rather than piling on ingredients. Matts wanted a revolution in clinical trials: high-dose studies in people with real problems, published where consumers' chatbots will find them.

On regulation they differed in tone. Joanna wants food law to be a shield for innovators, though the claims system was written for vitamins. Matts was blunter: a three-year longer approval in Europe than in the US almost makes innovation impossible.

On supply, Matts warned of a fish oil shortage reaching shelves next summer. Alex described pre-bought stock and protecting the claim shoppers buy. Joanna said blaming the supplier is no defence.

On AI they wanted a human in the loop and peer-reviewed sources, and Matts warned that anyone who cannot use AI will not be able to work in two years.
takeaways: Matts: trials in this industry study healthy people for short periods, so effects look small; he would run high-dose studies in people with real problems and publish, because consumers will find it through chatbots [02:52].
Alex: consumers want evidence but not the EFSA wording; "throwing the kitchen sink" (90 plus ingredients, 35 claims) muddles the message; do a few things well for a defined audience [08:33].

Joanna: EU food law and the claims regulation were written for vitamin C and D; innovators must combine what is legally possible with showing what trials found; food law should be "a shield", not "a heartbreak" [05:36].
Matts: same safety package, three years longer approval in Europe than the US; cost today, income later, so the delay "almost makes the innovation impossible" [14:53].
Matts: fish oil supply is collapsing for aquaculture now and reaches supplement shelves next summer; aquaculture buys the alternatives with higher willingness to pay [18:48].
Alex: H&B holds up to nine months of pre-purchased stock on core lines; shoppers give three or four seconds at shelf, so protect the claim they buy (heart, eye) and find the alternative [19:36].
lessons.for_us:
- Two of five panellists take creatine daily, including H&B's formulation lead [00:30], [00:57]. My reading: creatine is now a default daily supplement for industry insiders, which supports CreaWin's move into everyday and healthy-ageing products beyond sports.
- A retailer and a CDMO both say the brief is the consumer problem and a few claims done well [08:33], [11:13]. My reading: our customer-facing materials should give one outcome per ingredient with the trial that shows it, not a list.
- The fish oil shortage [18:48] is not ours, but H&B's response, protect the benefit and find the alternative, shows how a retailer treats any supply shock. My reading: supply continuity and traceability for CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea are selling points to put in front of buyers now.
- Europe's three-year approval lag [14:53] means novel protein and creatine formats will launch in the US first (my reading).
- Chatbots rank peer-reviewed science [03:45]. My reading: publishing the CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea evidence where AI assistants can find it is now part of marketing.
- Relevance medium: regulation, supply and retail views, adjacent to our ingredients.
quotes: "I see so many brands throwing the kitchen sink at everything. It's 90 plus ingredients. It's got 35 claims on the front of the pack, and then your message gets muddled." Alex Glover (H&B) [08:33]
"Three years delay, cost of fortune almost makes the innovation impossible, and I think that's a big, big problem for Europe." Speaker 5 (Matts Johansen) [14:53]
"The idea is to say it's my supplier's fault. It's not the solution." Speaker 3 (Joanna) [22:09]
"I think with AI, if you can't operate AI, you have you can't work two years from now." Speaker 5 (Matts Johansen) [25:42]
lessons.detail:
- Wants for the next two or three years: evidence-based claims and better communication to consumers (Alexandra [02:10]); a "revolution" in clinical trials, high-dose studies in people with real problems, published (Matts Johansen [02:52]); a focus on what consumers actually need (Martina [04:30]); food law as "a shield" for innovators (Joanna [05:36]).
- Matts, in his words: "I would do high dose studies, you know, much higher than what you sell, but do people that have actually real problems, and then publish it, and then the consumer is going to find it through their chatbots" [02:52].
- Matts: AI assistants rank credibility, peer-reviewed science and university pages, after LinkedIn and Reddit were gamed; the language in published studies matters [03:45], [03:59].
- Alex: H&B's own label has "customer missions" (joint, bone and muscle care; skin; weight management); where it wants to win it runs primary research with universities, clinical trials and standardised or branded ingredients; the lesson of seven years is start with the consumer problem [08:33].
- Martina: legislation is an obstacle for a CDMO; do not fill every gap, stick to one piece and explain it; the customer, not the CDMO, has the power to sell [11:13], [12:26].
- Alexandra: "what is on the box should be in the box during the shelf life"; brand means trust and quality [13:33].
- Matts: micro-influencer social selling arriving from China via the US is "almost impossible to regulate" [14:53].
- Matts on fish oil: "it's not going to hit us on the shelves, on your shelves, until next summer, because we have a much longer value chain" [18:48]. The risks are losing consumers to other ways of managing health, and shortcuts where traceability is absent [21:19].
- Alex: rhodiola's endangered listing brought about 400 customer emails [19:36].
- Joanna: liability stays with you; share responsibility by contract; "it's my supplier's fault" is not a defence [22:09].
- AI: a human in the loop for anything legally binding and for IP (Joanna [23:33]); peer-reviewed databases, not blogs (Alexandra [24:59]); a ChatGPT over factory sensors (Matts Johansen [25:42]).
- Panellists' own supplements: Alex takes creatine daily, omega-3, astaxanthin, vitamin D in winter and pre-workout; Matts protein, creatine, magnesium, zinc, vitamin D; Martina magnesium and krill oil [00:30], [00:51], [00:57].
- Closing asks: "speak the language of the consumer" (Alex [30:07]); bring lawyers in at the laboratory stage (Joanna [27:27], [28:09]); talk to people outside your company (Matts Johansen [28:55]); think what you want, not what the market says (Martina [29:34]).

lessons.title: Beyond Probiotics: Where the Biotics Category Is Really Heading
lessons.summary:
Marit Veenstra of HMT, the Healthy Marketing Team, a food and health branding and innovation agency, opened the probiotic programme. Her question was how to win in a biotics market that has grown into a jungle of products. Use keeps rising, yet in seven of eight European countries consumers do not feel informed about probiotics.

She traced four eras. Yakult made good bacteria a daily ritual. Activia made the benefit tangible, and brands began competing on CFU counts. Then survival technology became the story. Now the shift is from adding bacteria to nourishing the gut ecosystem, with the gut barrier as the gateway to the rest of the body.

From that she drew four rules: quality and proof over "more is better", feeding the ecosystem, benefits consumers can measure and feel, and everyday food formats. Her examples were mostly American: Pendulum's Akkermansia products for metabolic health, a prebiotic fibre brand, a digestive brand that sets expectations week by week, and Poppi.

Her conclusion: in Europe most of these claims cannot be made, so the brand has to carry them. Value is moving from what is inside the product to what the consumer gets. A strong probiotic needs a "Double IP": the science and the brand.
takeaways: Biotics have never been more popular: probiotic use among US adults rose 287% from 2009 to 2023, and European online probiotic sales have grown 15-25% a year since 2020 (slide 2). Yet in 7 of 8 European countries consumers do not feel informed about probiotics (slide 6); she said this without figures [00:24].

Rule 1, from "more is better" to quality and proof: a number on its own no longer builds trust, so be an expert brand in a niche (slide 14). Shelves show 50, 80 or 100 billion CFU [03:59]; her niche example is Pendulum, an Akkermansia-based US brand for metabolic health (slide 14) [03:59].

Rule 2, from adding bacteria to feeding the ecosystem: "eat more plants" instead of strain names, plants and fibre consumers can see, and a gut they feed themselves (slide 15); fibre brands lead this language [03:59].

Rule 3, from belief to measurable and felt benefits: early adopters measure with microbiome tests, apps and personal scores; the mass market wants less bloating, regularity and energy, and buys again only if it notices a difference (slide 16). Her example sets expectations at week 1 and months 1, 2 and 3 (slide 17); she said "for one week, for one month" [03:59].

Rule 4, from supplement to everyday food and formats: products designed for the person, not the bacteria; "the best biotic is the one people actually take every day" (slide 18). Poppi is her example [03:59].

In Europe you cannot claim most of it, so the brand carries it: BioGaia's baby drops say "for colic & digestive discomfort" in the US but "one of the world's most researched lactic acid bacteria strains" in Europe (slide 20), and Activia names its strain, Bifidus ActiRegularis (slide 21) [03:59].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance stays medium: nothing in the talk or slides covers protein, creatine or sports nutrition, but the branding argument transfers to our customers' categories.
- The question has changed from "what's in it?" to "what does it do in me?" (slide 11). My reading: the same shift faces sports and active nutrition brands, and it favours ingredients whose effect a user notices; that is how a CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea pitch should be framed.
- Activia's branded strain on its ingredient list and BioGaia's research claim show how a European brand carries what it cannot claim (slides 20-21). My reading: an argument for branded ingredients, and for getting the CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea names onto customers' packs with a story told within claim rules.
- HMT lists B2B2C communication among its services, with Suntheanine as the case (slide 24). My reading: HMT is an agency, not a buyer; it could brand our ingredients to end consumers or support a customer's launch.
quotes: "...there are too many options out there, but there's not enough clarity in this industry." Speaker 2 (Marit Veenstra) [00:24]
"...numbers alone don't build trust anymore with the consumer" Speaker 2 (Marit Veenstra) [03:59]
"So in Europe, you can't claim most of it, and that's when the brand has to carry it." Speaker 2 (Marit Veenstra) [03:59]
"...science opens the doors, but it's a brand that keeps you in the room." Speaker 2 (Marit Veenstra) [03:59]
lessons.detail:
- The deck is "Beyond Probiotics: Where the Biotics Category Is Really Heading", HMT - Healthy Marketing Team, October 2026 (slide 1). Otter heard the agency as "H and D" and "HMDs" [00:24] [03:59]. Slides carry "© 2026 – Healthy Marketing Team" (a few © 2023 or © 2025); none is marked confidential. The last slide offers the slides by QR code and gives marit@thehmt.com (slide 25).
- HMT describes itself as "Your Expert Partner in Food & Health Branding & Innovation, Since 2007", with three services and a case each: brand repositioning (Concordix), B2B2C communication (Suntheanine, Tomorrow's Nutrition) and launching new ingredients (Curaderm) (slide 24). The chair placed HMT as helping companies connect what they can develop with what consumers understand and value [00:00].
- Sources for slide 2: an NHANES analysis (n=54,776) via Nutrition Insight, September 2026, and Lumina Intelligence via NutraIngredients, January 2025 (slide 2).
- "The Jungle": a collage of biotic products including Activia kefir, Biotiful kefir drink, bio-kult gummies, GoodBelly juice, Bioglan Biotic Balance ChocBalls, Wild Nutrition Biotic Gummies and H&B Expert Triple Action Biotic (slides 3-4). Then the shopper's question, "Which one is right for me?" (slide 5).
- Era 1: Yakult, one strain, one small bottle a day, made popular by the Yakult Ladies delivering door to door; the category was born as a daily ritual (slide 8) [00:24].
- Era 2: Activia gave consumers "a benefit they could feel, and a number they could count"; billions of CFU on packs and supplements, "the more, the better" (slide 9) [03:59].
- Era 3: survival became the promise: gastro-resistant capsules, cold-chain liquids and research on gut survival; Lactoday's (South Korea) Q Shield is pictured (slide 10).
- Era 4: from adding to nourishing, with a new language: ecosystem, barrier, balance, holistic, outcome led, fermentation, whole food approach; Nordic Rebalance's OatBiotics Gut Barrier (ReFerm) is pictured (slide 11). Moving the focus to the gut barrier, where the gut meets the rest of the body, "exploded the category" (slide 12) [03:59].
- The four rules slide reads from "More = Better", "Adding bacteria", "Belief & promise" and "Functional supplement" to "Quality & proven ingredient", "Feeding the eco-system", "Measurable & Felt Benefits" and "Everyday food" (slide 13).
- Rule 2's pictured example is LOAM Prebiotic Fiber Formula (slide 15); she added that the language has moved from one prebiotic fibre to plant diversity [03:59].
- Rule 3's example is the be levels digestive product, whose own claims shown on the slide are 90% less bloating and gas, 92% an overall improvement in digestion and 89% more regular bowel movements; its timeline runs from lighter digestion in week 1 to balanced digestion by month 3 (slide 17). She said this framing is "maybe not so science-based" but easier for consumers to understand [03:59].
- Rule 4: Poppi, "not because it's a good quality product necessarily, but because they really turned it into a format that people like" [03:59]; Poppi cans are pictured (slide 18).
- The Double IP: rational IP is intellectual property (the science, the innovation); emotional IP is intellectual positioning (the story, the brand), called the "HMT formula for transformation" (slide 22). She said the brand gives longer-term protection and value [03:59].
- "Alex", who spoke on day 1 about the consumer wanting to know which product is right for them [00:24], is probably Alex Glover of Holland & Barrett (alex-glover-holland-barrett) (my reading).

lessons.title: Novonesis and Montefarmaco: the Lactoflorene partnership, from science to consumer product

speakers.name: Ariel Annoni
speakers.role: Responsible for the Human Health business across Central and Eastern Europe, Middle East and Africa (as she said it)

lessons.summary:
Ariel Annoni runs Novonesis's human health business across Central and Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Her argument was that a successful probiotic product needs the right science, quality, manufacturing partner and brand strategy, not just a good ingredient.

She introduced Novonesis, formed from Novozymes and Chr. Hansen, with a broad portfolio and some of the most documented strains in the world. Science is strain specific, she said, and documented strains protect the reputation of the brand a manufacturer makes. The European probiotic market is growing beyond the gut, consumers read labels and expect evidence, and probiotics are no longer a niche.

Alessia of Montefarmaco, an Italian family pharmaceutical company, then told the Lactoflorene story as the proof. The partnership began in the early 2000s with an Italian requirement for a high count in a small capsule. Novonesis supplied the potency and stability, the core formula has barely changed in almost 20 years, and Montefarmaco ran a clinical study on the finished product. Lactoflorene is now third in Italy.

Their shared conclusion: a probiotic brand is built through a long-term partnership, not one ingredient. The chair closed by saying both morning talks came back to the consumer asking "what's in it for me".
takeaways: Novonesis pitches to CMOs and CDMOs directly: probiotic solutions "already supported by research, market experience, and technical know-how", with the aim of a product the consumer will trust and repurchase, not only an ingredient sale [00:42].
Science is strain specific; some strains have limited documentation, others decades of study, and documented strains protect the reputation of the brand the manufacturer makes [00:42].

Four probiotic trends: more specialised needs, professional-recommended probiotics, applications beyond gut health, digital channels and emerging markets; "probiotic are no longer a niche category" [00:42].

Lactoflorene: partnership since the early 2000s, started by an Italian requirement of at least 1 billion CFU in a limited-volume cap; Novonesis gave the potency and stability; core formula unchanged for almost 20 years; a clinical study on the finished product beyond what Italy demanded [09:06].

Lactoflorene is third in Italy with around a 7% share; the three reasons given were clinical evidence, delivery innovation (the MCAP system for liquid shots) and formats for different ages and occasions [09:06].
The partnership's value beyond ingredients: formulation expertise, consumer and marketing support, access to a pipeline of new bio-solutions [13:10].
lessons.for_us:
- Medium relevance: a probiotic case, but the partnership model is the one our branded ingredients compete against for a formulator's attention.
- My reading: a supplier that brings formulation help, consumer insight and a finished-product study, and keeps a formula stable for 20 years, is what a brand means by a partner; a CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea pitch to a brand or CDMO should offer the same (application work, stability, a finished-product story).
- My reading: Novonesis selling to CDMOs as a route to brands is the channel this conference exists for, and Polish CDMOs are a route for our sports ingredients too.
- Lactoflorene sells through Italian pharmacies, not our channel. No protein, creatine or sports nutrition was mentioned.
quotes: "...in probiotic, success is not only about having a good ingredient. It's about having the right science, the right quality, and the right manufacturing partner, and the right brand strategy" Speaker 2 (Ariel Annoni) [00:42]
"Our objective is not only to sell an ingredient. Our objective is to help create successful product the consumer will trust and repurchase." Speaker 2 (Ariel Annoni) [00:42]
"Novonasis offered the potency and stability we needed, and the core formula has remained essentially unchanged for almost 20 years." Speaker 3 (Alessia, Montefarmaco) [09:06]
"...a successful probiotic brand is not built around one ingredient alone. They are built through a long, long-term partnership" Speaker 2 (Ariel Annoni) [13:10]
lessons.detail:
- Novonesis is the combination of Novozymes and Chr. Hansen, with more than 100 years of expertise and a portfolio of probiotics, postbiotics, enzymes, vitamins and HMOs; its strains (Otter heard "GGM BB 12") are, she said, among the most documented in the world [00:42].
- Growth areas named for the European probiotic market: digestive health, immune health, women's health, healthy ageing; new categories cardiovascular and mental health [00:42].
- Consumers are more informed, read labels and expect evidence, so quality and documentation matter more than ever [00:42].
- Montefarmaco is an Italian family pharmaceutical company founded in 1945 [09:06].
- The chair's point: it is the audience and the consumer who ask "What's in it for me?" [14:17].

lessons.title: From cell to scale: Patented strains & custom fermentation power
lessons.summary:
Sacco System's speaker presented the company as a family-owned probiotic maker and CDMO that sells speed and flexibility. The recording joins mid-introduction, and the slides do not name him. Sacco dates from 1872 and turned over €195 million in 2025.

He described its offer: probiotics, postbiotics and tailor-made mixtures, strains screened to EFSA safety requirements, custom fermentation at any scale, and next-generation strains developed for third parties. Sacco has recently invested in clinical studies and patents in two areas, women's health and healthy ageing, and he gave one strain for each.

CA15, a patented strain isolated from a healthy woman, was tested in two placebo-controlled trials in women with vaginal imbalance. He reported fewer symptoms after ten days, held a month after intake stopped.

Synbio, a patented mix of two strains isolated from elderly people in Marche, was tested over six months in 97 healthy people over 65. He reported more beneficial bacteria and butyrate, a 43% fall in a marker of inflammation, higher IGF-1, which he linked to muscle maintenance, and slower shortening of telomeres.

His close was an invitation: Sacco will take on unusual projects quickly and work closely with the customer.
takeaways: Its pitch as a CDMO is speed and flexibility: a low time to market, agile family decisions, custom fermentation from 1 L to 40,000 L, and a new kind of production if asked (slide 6) (slide 8) [00:00].

CA15 trials: two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies, 60 women in 2023 and 200 in 2025, one capsule of 10 billion CFU a day for 10 days and a 30-day wash-out (slide 14). They differ from the talk, which gave a six-woman exploratory study and "10 mil per capsule" [00:00].

CA15 results: symptom scores fell 78% for discomfort, 66% burning, 64% itching, 62% secretions and 56% inflammation (slide 15). On the Amsel criteria 98% of women had a corrected pH, 92% a negative amine test, 79% no clue cells and 75% normal discharge, as labelled on the chart (slide 16); he gave the first three the same [00:00].

Synbio trial: L. rhamnosus IMC 501 and L. paracasei IMC 502, 5 billion CFU a serving for six months in 97 healthy people over 65, randomised, double-blind and placebo-controlled (slide 21) (slide 23); spoken as "five mil" daily [00:00].

Synbio results, end of study against start: hs-CRP down 43%, IL-8 down 83%, IL-6 67%, MIP-1α 60% and TNF-α 23% (slide 25); total short-chain fatty acids up 23% and butyric acid up 33% (slide 26) [00:00].
Sacco says Synbio "increases IGF-1 levels", which it calls key for muscle maintenance in ageing, and that it slowed telomere shortening against placebo (slide 27) (slide 28) (slide 29) [00:00].
lessons.for_us:
- Medium relevance, unchanged by the slides. Sacco makes probiotics and runs a CDMO, so it is a possible partner, not a buyer of our ingredients.
- Synbio is pitched to over-65s on muscle maintenance, through IGF-1 and nutritional status (slide 27) (slide 29). My reading: a "gut plus muscle" healthy-ageing pairing with CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea is a possible co-formulation pitch.
- Sport is one of Sacco's ten therapeutic areas (slide 9), though the talk covered only women's health and healthy ageing. Worth asking what it has for sports nutrition.
- The claims are Sacco's. The hs-CRP, cytokine and fatty-acid charts compare the end of the study with its start; only the IGF-1, nutrition and telomere charts show the placebo group (slide 25) (slide 26) (slide 27) (slide 28). My reading: ask for the placebo comparison before citing any of it.
quotes: "If you have got something crazy, we like to do that." Speaker 1 (Sacco System) [00:00]
"...we observe a 43 percentage reduction of the high sensitivity C reactive protein, which is a marker of inflammaging" Speaker 1 (Sacco System) [00:00]

"...an improvement in the production of insulin growth factor one, that is a hormone correlated with the protein synthesis as well as the maintenance of the muscle mass, the so-called sarcopenia" Speaker 1 (Sacco System) [00:00]
"Rapid effect, making asymptomatic 6 out of 10 women in 10 days" (slide 19)
lessons.detail:
- The deck is titled "From cell to scale: Patented strains & custom fermentation power", subtitled "Targeted solutions for healthy ageing & women's health" (slide 2). No slide names the speaker. No slide is marked confidential.
- Sacco's numbers: more than 6,500 strains in its bank, more than 600 people, 11 production plants, €195 million turnover in 2025, more than 110 export countries, more than 40 university collaborations (slide 4).
- Presence: headquarters in Italy (Sacco System and CSL, Centro Sperimentale del Latte), CSL USA, and Sacco System companies in France, the Nordics, Japan, China, Australia, Brazil and Uruguay (slide 5). He named plants in Como, Milan (CSL, pharmaceutical API probiotics) and Wisconsin, and a Brisbane pilot for next-generation and exotic strains [00:00].
- Offer: CultureScience, clinically documented strains; CultureSelect, strains screened for EFSA safety and function (at least 30 species); Made For You, development of next-generation probiotics and live biotherapeutics (slide 7) [00:00].
- Manufacturing: GMP pharma plants and pilot labs, qualified persons and validation experts, religious certifications, a hypoallergenic production system (slide 6); food-grade GMP, an anaerobic pilot plant for next-generation strains, and uses in supplements, pharma, food and drinks (slide 8).
- Therapeutic areas: gut, immune, skin, healthy ageing, metabolic, sport, women's, oral, infant and children, mental health (slide 9).
- CA15 is Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus CA15 DSM 33960, isolated in 2022 in Sicily from a healthy woman (slide 11). Otter's "in CCD" is Sicily [00:00].
- CA15 in vitro: more than 95% survival in simulated gut transit; adhesion of 36% to intestinal Caco-2 cells, 34% to vaginal VK2/E6E7 cells and 12% to intestinal mucus; produces lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide (slide 12).
- In the SHIME gut model a 10-billion capsule survived the small intestine and colon, fasted and fed, alone and with fluconazole 200 mg; the slide cites Vaccalluzzo A et al, Food Res Int (2025) (slide 13). He said the University of Catania ran the clinical studies [00:00]; the slides neither name Catania nor cite the trial papers.
- CA15 outcomes: primary, microbiota rebalance, no signs or symptoms of dysbiosis, normal Amsel and Nugent scores; secondary, quality of life (slide 14).
- Nugent score: CA15 moved women from the dysbiotic band (7 to 10) to normal (0 to 3) by day 10 and held at day 30, while placebo stayed in or near the dysbiotic band, read from the chart (slide 17).
- Vaginal counts: Lactobacillus rose from about 3.5 to about 7 log10 CFU/ml in 10 days; Enterococcus, Staphylococcus, Gardnerella, Candida and E. coli fell, and both held 30 days after the last dose, read from the chart (slide 18) [00:00].
- CA15 key messages also claim better quality of life, resistance to fluconazole, and remission "not only maintained, but further increased" (slide 19).
- Synbio strains were isolated in 2021 in Marche from elderly people (slide 21); he said the ratio is 1 to 1 and the region has one of Europe's highest shares of centenarians [00:00]. The slide says Synbio is backed by "over 50 scientific publications" and more than 1,000 people in human studies (slide 21).
- The Synbio trial slide carries a "ProBioSenior" logo. Primary outcomes were hs-CRP, gut microbiota and fatty-acid production; secondary, cytokines, IGF-1 and nutritional status (slide 23).
- Gut changes after six months: Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus and butyrate up, inflammation down (slide 24) [00:00].
- Chart values, read from the charts: hs-CRP from about 4 to 2.3 mg/l (slide 25); fatty acids from about 57 to 70 µmol/g and butyric acid from about 9 to 12 µmol/g (slide 26). Each is marked significant by t-test (P<0.05).
- IGF-1 rose from about 118 to 145 pg/ml with Synbio and from about 118 to 120 with placebo; normal nutrition on the questionnaire rose from about 28% to 57% of the Synbio group, and malnourished fell from about 18% to 7%, with placebo little changed, read from the charts (slide 27) [00:00].
- Telomere length (estimated marginal means): placebo fell from about 1.025 to 1.00 and Synbio rose from about 1.018 to 1.027 over 180 days, read from the chart; the chart carries no significance mark (slide 28). He said there was "a decrease in the reduction in the length" [00:00].
- Otter heard the mix as "Symbio" [00:00]; the slides spell it SYNBIO (slide 20). He used Gemini to find the shoelace metaphor for telomeres, which the slide repeats (slide 28) [00:00].
