lessons.title: SPI Pharma and Nordic Biotic: new dosage forms and clinically tested strains
lessons.summary:
Two suppliers shared this slot. Miguel of SPI Pharma, an ABF Ingredients company, presented "From platform to product". His case: consumers buy formats first, so the gap is not another active but a format people will take. Last year SPI Pharma showed probiotics can be tableted. This year it showed what that tablet becomes.

He showed three concepts, each on an SPI platform. A mint chewable probiotic for adults, pressed gently on a low-moisture platform so the cultures survive. A fizzy electrolyte and energy stick for sport, kept stable by a modified sodium bicarbonate; a light fizz also masks bitterness. A vanilla fast-melt for healthy ageing that needs no water. The packs were illustrative concepts. His close: do not ask the consumer to swallow another capsule. The deck also asked the room for ideas, as SPI Pharma looks to grow in nutrition.

Mihail Jakubowski of Nordic Biotic then presented a supplier of clinically tested probiotic strains, sold with exclusivity by territory. He showed a stress and sleep blend tested on 227 students at exam time, saying the results, received the week before, proved efficacy on sleep quality and stress. He also showed a blend aimed at microplastics, with its human study still in progress. He closed with an invitation to develop products together.
takeaways: Chewable probiotic: Compressol ProTab is a low water activity direct-compression platform that compresses at low force, so live cultures survive; the concept is an adult mint chew, "Gut Performance Chew" (slide 5) (slide 7) [00:01].

Effer-Soda is a surface-modified sodium bicarbonate, stable across packing forms, "not only desiccant tubes": 15–25% of a tablet or sachet formula as the effervescent system, or 1–4% for sparkle in a chewable or fast-melt; the concept is a fizzy electrolyte and energy stick for sport (slide 8) (slide 10) [00:01].

Fast-melt: Advantol 300 with Effer-Soda 12 disintegrates in under 10 seconds, 20–40% faster than typical direct-compression competitors, and uses standard packaging, not lyophilised blisters (slide 14) (slide 15). It is aimed at children and older people who cannot or will not swallow [00:01].
Nordic Biotic: full exclusivity by territory at strain level; genomics, then metabolomics (630 molecules, "the postbiotics actually"), then functional testing, then human studies [09:25].

Mental Balance: eight-week study, 227 students started, 219 completed, "one of the largest study in stress in probiotics in the last decade"; results received last week; he said statistical efficacy was proved in sleep quality and stress [09:25].
Nordic Biotic has a GLP-1 companion product with its Swiss sister company Azento [09:25].
lessons.for_us:
- Medium relevance, unchanged by the deck: formats, not ingredients. The deck names no creatine or protein. Its sport concept, a fizzy electrolyte and caffeine stick made for athletes, is the kind of format our sports customers sell, and SPI Pharma's platforms are what a CDMO uses to make it.
- My reading: a CreaWin chewable and a creatine effervescent stick are format questions to put to SPI Pharma and the CDMOs that use its platforms. A fast-melt suits small doses better than a gram-level creatine serving, so the chew and the stick are the likelier fits. Favea, shown making a live chewable, is a CDMO to know.
- My reading: SPI Pharma asked the room which dosage forms need new excipients and whether a fully formulated delivery system would interest them. That is an opening to propose a joint CreaWin format concept.
- My reading: Nordic Biotic's GLP-1 companion product is the adjacent opportunity for IsoClr: Pea, since protein for muscle preservation on GLP-1 drugs is a brief our customers already have; its exclusivity-by-territory model is a pattern a branded ingredient supplier can study.
- All efficacy claims are the speakers'. The Mental Balance study is unpublished as of the talk, and SPI Pharma's market figures carry no sources except on swallowing difficulty.
quotes: "The gap is not another strain. It is a chewable adults will actually take." SPI Pharma deck (slide 5)
"...don't ask your consumer to swallow another capsule." Speaker 1 (Miguel, SPI Pharma) [07:50]
"We are not the biggest probiotic company in the world. However, in our opinion, we play in a Champions League from the scientific perspective." Speaker 4 (Mihail Jakubowski, Nordic Biotic) [09:25]

"We received the results last week, so I just want to tell you that we have proved the statistical efficacy was proved in sleep quality and stress." Speaker 4 (Mihail Jakubowski, Nordic Biotic) [09:25]
lessons.detail:
- The deck fills the start of the SPI Pharma talk the recording missed: the agenda (the shift, the concepts, the platforms, how to work together), the thesis and the portfolio (slide 2) (slide 3) (slide 4). The recording picks up at the chewable [00:01].
- "Consumers buy formats first. Convenience, taste, and lifestyle decide the SKU." (slide 2)
- Thesis: in 2025 SPI Pharma showed Compressol ProTab for probiotics (high compactibility, low water activity, strain survival in direct compression, no wet granulation); in 2026 it shows chewables, effervescents and fast-melts as end products (slide 3).
- Platform names, settled by the deck: Compressol ProTab (heard as "composol pro tab"), Effer-Soda 12 and Advantol 300 (slide 2) (slide 15) [00:01]. Hybrids go to "Pharmasolutions" (slide 15).
- The three concepts are SPI-branded packs, each "Illustrative concept only": Gut Performance Chew (adult mint chewable, 30 chews), Sport Performance Infusion Energy (Berry Volt fizzy stick) and Age Performance Melt (vanilla fast-melt, 20 melts) (slide 5) (slide 6) (slide 8) (slide 11) (slide 13). He called his images AI-generated [00:01].
- The sport stick's pack lists 100 mg caffeine, B vitamins and five electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium, chloride), a 6 g stick for 8–12 oz of water, made for athletes such as runners, cyclists and golfers (slide 9, read from the pack image).
- Probiotic market as the deck gives it: global supplements USD 10.5 billion in 2025, toward USD 17.5 billion by 2033; chewables and gummies gaining share (slide 5). The Europe figures differ on the same slide: the headline reads 2.2B with no year, the text "above USD 3 billion by 2030" (slide 5).
- Hydration market as the deck gives it: hydration supplements USD 38.7 billion in 2025, near USD 89.4 billion by 2036; effervescent drink tablets USD 12.6 billion by 2031; electrolyte tablets and powders "win on portability, sugar control, and flavor" (slide 8).
- "Hydration left the gym. The winning SKU is a stick pack that fits a gym bag." (slide 10)
- Healthy ageing market as the deck gives it: USD 36 billion in 2025 toward about USD 79 billion by 2035, with industry forecasts of 6 to 8 percent-plus CAGR; "Fast-melts beat capsules on ease, premium feel, and adherence after 50." (slide 11)
- Swallowing: 15% of older adults worldwide live with dysphagia and only 22.7% of those affected sought care; 1 in 25 US adults is predicted to have swallowing problems; sources given as Pharmaceutics 2020 and the American Academy of Pediatrics 2023 (slide 12).
- Advantol with Effer-Soda: "Sublingual-capable rapid onset" and "Differentiation without changing the active" (slide 14).
- Effer-Soda, as he described it: sodium bicarbonate partly transformed to carbonate, forming a protective layer; plain bicarbonate with an acid is hygroscopic and may not survive shelf life [00:01]. The slide says a physical mix "cannot match it" because local acid contact still triggers premature reaction (slide 10).
- A "delicate fizz" in chewables or fast melts is also a way to distract the tongue from bitterness [00:01].
- The chewable was also shown as a live product at the SPI Pharma stand under Favea's branding; Martina had it [00:01]. The deck does not name Favea.
- SPI Pharma's role, as he put it, is creating product concepts so a CDMO can expand into new dosage forms; "we do not limit there" [00:01]. The deck: "Bring the active. We bring the delivery system." (slide 15)
- The deck says SPI Pharma "is looking to expand in the nutra market and would appreciate input from Remedy". It asks which trends and dosage forms need new excipient solutions, and whether a fully formulated delivery system would interest the room (slide 16).
- His close is worded slightly differently on the slide: "Do not ask the consumer to swallow another capsule." (slide 17) [07:50]
- Nordic Biotic, a silver sponsor, supplies clinically tested probiotics to brand owners, CDMOs and distributors; CFU is measured to milligrams [09:25].
- Mental Balance (Northbiotic Mental Balance): strains chosen for what they produce, Lactobacillus plantarum 140 (GABA) and Bifidobacterium breve 010 (a B vitamin); tested in students at exam time [09:25].
- Microplastic blend: Lactobacillus acidophilus 120 aggregates (binds) microplastic, Lactobacillus fermentum 160 pushes it away; offered as a standalone or an add-on to a gut, detox or clean-label formula; human study in progress, with an invitation to a "plastic gut-free initiative" [09:25].
- Gut-skin, gut-bone and gut-brain technologies were named [09:25].
- WIPO innovation index as he cited it: of 12 countries, seven are European; in the region Latvia, Czechia, Hungary and Poland lead [09:25].
- His closing line: "We will not proudly invent the the next wheel in the next week, but I'm pretty sure we can create something new together." [09:25]
- The chair's aside: Coca-Cola was first sold as a medicinal tonic for brain and nerves [08:30].

courses.name: Active Nutrition Summit 2025
courses.description: NutraIngredients' three-day active nutrition summit in Vienna, hosted by its journalists Nikki Hancocks, Stephen Daniells, Olivia Haslam and Lauren Nicolle (advance programme). Filed from the archive in November 2026, from the speakers' decks, Nathan's Otter recordings and the advance programme (files/).

lessons.title: Active Nutrition Summit 2025: Key Insights & Industry Trends
lessons.summary:
This is a secondary synthesis of the whole summit, not a talk. It is a 20-page written report of unknown authorship and date that says it "synthesizes all presentations". Its figures are the report's own, as it states them, not the speakers' figures as given in the room.

It groups the summit into themes: market dynamics and consumer trends, gut health and the microbiome, weight management and GLP-1, female athlete nutrition, personalisation and AI, longevity and "ageless" consumption, mind health, and regulation and trust. It closes with white spaces, investment areas and an outlook.

It opens with a global market of USD 30.6 billion in 2024, Europe at 19%, and growth projected from USD 28.4 billion to USD 37.8 billion by 2028; the two figures do not agree and no source is given. It then summarises most named talks, from Paul Cotter's athlete microbiome research to Luca Bucchini's regulatory update.

It is useful as a map of the programme and of talks with no session of their own. Some attributions are loose: buyer figures from Biogena's talk also appear under the Avea talk, and some sections reword the hosts' closing recap.
takeaways: By generation, the report names creatine as a hero ingredient for Millennials and Generation Z, with protein for all four generations (page 2).
Euromonitor data as the report gives it: new product launches up 33%, electrolytes and creatine leading, milk protein supplements down 21%, "no added sugar" claims up 32% (page 2) (page 3).
Rousselot's Nextida GC collagen peptides, which the report says boost GLP-1 secretion, with a 42% reduction in glucose spike taken before a meal (page 6).
Creatine as a semi-essential nutrient for the general population, with food fortification as a public health route (Ostojic, as the report puts it) (page 11).

Misinformation figures attributed to Alice Millbank: only 2.1% of social media nutrition content aligned with public health guidelines; 59% of the accounts studied had no formal health qualification (page 14) (page 15).
lessons.for_us:
- Creatine appears as a growth segment, a hero ingredient for younger buyers and a candidate for food fortification (page 2) (page 11). My reading: three angles for CreaWin, to check against the talks themselves.
- Rousselot positions a collagen peptide directly for GLP-1 and glucose control (page 6). My reading: a competitor claim to watch in the GLP-1 companion space.
- Citicoline appears among the mind-health ingredients (page 12). My reading: a prompt for CogniWin, with the talk (singer-biogena-cognitive-health) as the better source.
- Relevance is medium: a useful map of the summit, but secondary and unsourced; leaders should rely on the session records.
quotes: "This comprehensive report synthesizes all presentations, research findings, and industry insights organized by key topic areas" (page 1)
"Global market size: USD 30.6 billion (2024)" (page 1)
"Projected growth: $28.4B to $37.8B by 2028" (page 1)
lessons.detail:
- The original is filed unchanged: files/active-nutrition-summit-2025-key-insights-industry-trends.pdf. It names no author, publisher, date or sources for its market figures (page 1).
- Talks the report covers that have no session of their own in this event: Rousselot's Nextida GC collagen (page 6); Professor James Morton's evidence-based fuelling framework for female athletes, which may belong to the women-in-sports-nutrition session (page 7); Perfect Day, named as a mature precision-fermentation example under investment areas, not clearly a talk (page 19). Professor Susan Jebb is quoted inside the Gilbert section, not as a speaker (page 6).
- Talks it covers that are filed here: Cotter (cotter-athlete-microbiome, page 3); minutia.ai (minutia-gut-microbiome-sports, page 5); Mark Gilbert (gilbert-weight-loss-long-term, page 5); Balchem (balchem-branded-ingredient-partnerships, page 7); Nathan Price (price-ai-scientific-wellness, page 8); Mariette Abrahams (abrahams-glp1-ai-personalised-nutrition, page 9); Marimiina Pykälistö (pykalisto-nutrigenomics, page 9); Sophie Chabloz (chabloz-avea-longevity-supplements, page 10); Sergej Ostojic (ostojic-creatine-lifelong-nutrition, page 11); Kristiina Singer (singer-biogena-cognitive-health, page 12); Eric Puro of Nordic Mushrooms (nordic-mushrooms-functional-mushrooms, page 13); Alice Millbank (millbank-nutrition-by-algorithm, page 14); Marit Veenstra (veenstra-hmt-branding, page 15); Luca Bucchini (bucchini-essna-regulatory-update, page 16). The NutraIngredients Global Survey (page 1), the generational segments (page 2) and the Euromonitor data (page 2) match consumer-health-survey, holland-barrett-fitness-generations and euromonitor-sports-nutrition-trends, though the report names no speaker for them.
- Sessions filed here that the report does not name: lux-functional-ingredient-trends, neutral-labs-startup-pitch, sports-nutrition-innovation-panel, personalised-health-panel and tonic-health-fireside (its "social media regulation gaps" section may draw on the fireside, page 16).
- Market: Europe 19% of the global market, over 80% of it Western Europe; Latin America the highest two-year growth, then Europe (page 1).
- Generations, as the report segments them: Baby Boomers (protein, calcium, vitamin D, probiotics, omega-3); Generation X (protein, collagen, omega-3s, curcumin); Millennials (protein, adaptogens, magnesium, curcumin, creatine); Generation Z (creatine, caffeine, electrolytes, ashwagandha) (page 2).
- Euromonitor data, as the report gives it: plastic packaging claims down 76%, flexible packaging up; small "shot" formats gaining; gels and creams an emerging focus (page 2) (page 3).
- Cotter: the Clarke et al. (Gut, 2014) study of 40 elite male athletes against 46 controls; correlations of 0.76 (Oscillospiraceae and creatinine) and up to 0.89 between taxa and pathways in Penney et al. 2020 (page 3) (page 4).
- minutia.ai: 20 male runners and triathletes, 8-week interventions tailored to each microbiome profile, VO2max 49±7 ml/kg/min, age 46±12 (page 5).
- Gilbert: fat-free mass was a similar share of weight lost with rapid (0.42) and moderate (0.44) loss; Susan Jebb quoted that the claim that rapid initial loss means rapid regain "is false" (page 6).
- Price: 5,000 participants, about 1,200 analytes; a USD 52 million NIH grant for a personalised healthspan optimiser; 50% of microbiome diversity variance predicted from 11 blood metabolites; 18% of circulating metabolites made or co-made by the microbiome (page 8).
- Abrahams: fewer than 5 companies offer true digital twins; generative AI nutrition companies grew from 5 (July 2024) to 20 (April 2025) (page 9).
- Chabloz: mainstream longevity buyers are 45 to 65; the report also gives "16% of customers now aged 25-35" and "60% over 45" here (page 10). In the recordings those are Biogena's buyer figures from Singer's talk, which the report repeats under Chabloz's name (page 12) (page 13).
- Nordic Mushrooms: lion's mane, chaga, reishi and cordyceps with their compounds and claimed benefits, which are the report's wording; quality standardisation and beverages as priorities (page 13) (page 14).
- Millbank: 57% of Gen Z and Millennials influenced by TikTok nutrition content; 96% of accounts studied monetised; 7 of 53 verified medical doctors; one carnivore post with 3.7 million likes against 82 million engagements for a two-year UK COVID campaign (page 14) (page 15).
- Veenstra: 80% of innovations fail, the report says through irrelevance; four consumer mindsets, need, want, solution and normal (page 15).
- White spaces and outlook: active parenting, gender-specific formulas, cellular health, AI personalisation, wearables, precision probiotics, bioavailability, upcycled ingredients and precision fermentation (page 17) (page 18) (page 20). The active parenting point echoes the editors' recap (editors-recap).
- The report ends mid-line on page 20 ("Preventive medicine: Nutrition as primary intervention") (page 20).

lessons.title: Nutrition by Algorithm
lessons.summary:
Alice Millbank, co-founder and chief scientific officer of Rooted Research Collective, asked what goes wrong when people take their nutrition advice from social media algorithms rather than from dietary guidelines.

Their starting point is that guidelines are evidence-based but rarely followed, while social media reaches far more people: one pro-carnivore post drew 3.7 million likes, against 82 million engagements for a two-year UK COVID campaign. Millbank then presented their group's study of 53 nutrition "super-spreaders" with a combined reach of over 24 million, sorted into three personas: the Doc (borrowed authority), the Rebel (counter-culture) and the Hustler (quick-fix wellness). Most had no health qualifications and nearly all had a financial incentive. Their themes were carnivore and keto diets, anti-seed-oil messages, distrust of institutions, and the demonisation of "fake meats", legumes, grains and milk alternatives.

Their conclusion for industry: this noise shapes how consumers see functional ingredients and the whole sector. Brands should simplify without denying complexity, avoid silver-bullet promises, tell the truth, use storytelling ethically and check the values and credibility of the influencers they pay.
takeaways: 57% of Gen Z and Millennials are influenced by TikTok nutrition content, and "only 2.1% aligned with public health guidelines", in the slide's words (slide 9).
One pro-carnivore post drew 3.7 million likes; a two-year UK COVID social media campaign drew 82 million post engagements (slide 10).

Of 53 super-spreader profiles, 59% had no formal health qualifications, only 7 were verified medical doctors, and 96% had clear financial incentives, many selling their own supplements or programmes (slide 14) (slide 18) (slide 19).
Doc accounts had the most followers on average (744,950), against 400,877 for Hustlers and 362,533 for Rebels; Hustlers had the highest average engagement, 43.5% (slide 15) (slide 17) (slide 18).

The spread runs on fear-mongering, joy-mongering and "sprinkling" misinformation into non-food content, framed as us versus them, shared frustrations, storytelling, and "natural" and "ancestral" as moral frames (slide 20) (slide 21).
For industry: misinformation influences behaviour and trust, "disenchants people from functional ingredients" and colours perception of the whole industry (slide 24).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: no ingredient science, but the narratives Millbank tracked attack products our customers make. "Demonisation of 'fake meats', legumes, grains, milk alternatives" (slide 12). My reading: plant protein, IsoClr: Pea included, sits inside the target of the anti-plant narrative, so our pea pitch should arm customers with plain evidence.
- Their advice to industry (slide 25) is the same discipline as our own claims rule: no silver bullets, claim strength matched to evidence. My reading: a customer's influencer partner who oversells an ingredient we supply is a reputational risk to us too.
- Read with veenstra-hmt-branding (trust and clarity at the shelf) and bucchini-essna-regulatory-update (the regulatory side of the same problem).
quotes: "Disenchants people from functional ingredients" (slide 24)
"Avoid overpromising/simple solutionism (no silver bullet)" (slide 25)
"Gauge the values and credibility of the individuals you partner with online" (slide 25)
"World Economic Forum named misinformation the #1 short-term global threat" (slide 11)
lessons.detail:
- Slide numbers are the PDF's pages (26). The opening slide shows a salt lamp sold for "ONLY £59.98" (slide 2); it carries no other text.
- Talk outline: who Millbank is, the importance of nutrition, where people go for advice, the rise of misinformation, understanding its spread, what industry can and should do (slide 4).
- Rooted Research Collective works across food, sustainability, health and international development: digging into data, uncovering facts, challenging misinformation (slide 5).
- The study was published as "Nutrition Misinformation in the Digital Age: 2024-2025"; the slide shows press coverage from May 2025 in Food Ingredients First, New Food, ConfectioneryNews, vegconomist, Green Queen, Plant Based News and VegNews. One clipping describes it as a joint analysis with the Freedom Food Alliance, read from the image (slide 6).
- Why nutrition matters: it influences maternal health, child well-being, cognition and economic productivity; overnutrition now outweighs undernutrition globally; diet is the leading preventable risk factor for non-communicable diseases (slide 7).
- An estimated 0.1% of UK adults follow the Eatwell Guide, and many UK children fall short of basic nutrition standards (slide 8).
- Personas: the Doc, 12 profiles, average engagement 37.7%, mostly fear-mongering, paid through coaching and business; the Rebel, 15 profiles, 39.9%, fear- and joy-mongering, business and affiliate income; the Hustler, 26 profiles, 43.5%, joy-mongering and sprinkling, affiliate and sponsorship income. The example posts on these slides are marked "not real posts" (slide 15) (slide 16) (slide 17).
- Misuse of authority: only 1 internist among the 7 verified MDs, and 5 of 53 held non-medical doctorates while prominently displaying "Dr" (slide 18).
- Money: one Doc-profile super-spreader "reportedly earns $100k+ per month from social media alone"; unqualified health influencers charge $100 to 250 an hour for consultations, some selling biohacking programmes worth tens of thousands (slide 19).
- Prominent themes: carnivore, keto, anti-seed oil; tallow and raw milk "promoted as silver bullet solutions"; distrust in institutions and health professionals; "natural" and "ancestral" living (slide 12).
- Consequences: in the WHO European Region 59% of adults and almost 1 in 3 children are overweight or obese; extreme, exclusionary diets; "simple solutionism" that reduces nutrition to silver bullets; tips that contradict global guidance and fuel distrust (slide 23).
- Millbank set the UK government's dietary recommendations and the Eatwell Guide against a post titled "How I lost weight in 3 simple steps" (slide 22).

lessons.title: The Vitamin Shoppe Health & Wellness Trend Report 2025
lessons.summary:
The Vitamin Shoppe, a US supplement retailer with over 635 stores, published its fourth annual trend report in 2025. Nathan filed it with this summit; whether it was presented there is not known. Its figures are the report's own: the retailer's sales and site searches, SPINS industry data, and a survey of 2,000 US adults by Talker Research in May 2025.

The report finds a proactive consumer: 69% of Americans take supplements, and 35% have used AI tools for their health. It names five trends. Protein is moving from powders into drinks, bars and snacks. NAD+ has gone mainstream for longevity. Peptides are the next frontier in sports nutrition. Formats are moving beyond pills and powders, to liquids, gummies, chews, beadlets and topicals. And shilajit is finding a new generation of buyers.

Creatine runs through two of the trends: the category has grown over 320% at the retailer since 2019, and searches for creatine gummies are up over 1,300% this year.

It closes on trust: TikTok drives curiosity, but friends, news and doctors still build credibility, and only 11% of people find influencers very trustworthy.
takeaways: Protein formats: RTD protein drinks up 20% and bars and snacks up 28% year to date, while powders fell 12%; 66% of survey respondents are trying to add protein (page 3).
NAD+: site searches up nearly 500%; the cellular health and healthy ageing category grew 91% in the first quarter, with NAD+ 90% of that growth (page 5).
Peptides: searches up over 550% in 2025, and 41% of consumers are more aware of peptides than five years ago; creatine with PeptiStrong is a top seller (page 7) (page 8).

Creatine formats: the category is up over 320% since 2019 at the retailer; "creatine gummies" searches are up over 1,300%; SPINS shows liquids, chewables and gummies growing faster than powders in creatine (page 9).
Trust: doctors (59%), family (40%) and friends (28%) are trusted most; only 11% rate influencers very trustworthy and 22% not trustworthy at all (page 12).
lessons.for_us:
- Creatine is growing fastest in non-powder formats: gummies, chews and a beadlet (page 9) (page 10). My reading: a strong prompt to show CreaWin working in gummies and chews, with stability data.
- Peptide complexes are being paired with creatine and HMB in launches (page 8). My reading: a combination angle for CreaWin and HMB with brands launching in the US.
- Clear protein drinks are a breakout RTD trend (page 3). My reading: supports a clear plant protein pitch for IsoClr: Pea, to test.
- GLP-1 companion products appear in two trends, a peptide protein and a shilajit formula (page 8) (page 11). My reading: US retail now shelves GLP-1 support as its own need.
- Relevance is high: current US retail data on creatine, protein formats and the GLP-1 shelf, though one retailer's view.
quotes: "Bars and drinks are outpacing powders for the first time in years" Jack Gayton, The Vitamin Shoppe (page 3)
"There are many more human studies on precursors versus direct NAD+ supplementation" Brittany Michels, The Vitamin Shoppe (page 6)
"Protein continues to dominate wellness routines, but RTDs have emerged as a convenient alternative to the shaker cup" Jack Gayton, The Vitamin Shoppe (page 3)
lessons.detail:
- The original is filed unchanged: files/the-vitamin-shoppe-health-wellness-trend-report-2025.pdf. Page numbers here are the file's pages; most hold a two-page printed spread.
- Sources: data from 635+ stores and vitaminshoppe.com, industry data from SPINS, and the survey: 2,000 US adults, 16 to 22 May 2025, random double-opt-in, margin of error ±2.2% at 95% confidence (page 2).
- Survey headlines: 56% are likely to try new trends; 31% feel healthier than five years ago, 35% less healthy and 30% no different; 35% have used AI for their health and 27% would consider it; AI uses include research (31%), meal planning (25%), weight-loss programmes (24%) and supplement use (21%) (page 2).
- Protein: SPINS shows the protein supplement and meal replacement category up 9.1% in 2024; "protein" searches up 81% (page 3). Clear protein RTDs are a breakout: Clean Simple Eats (20 g whey isolate a can) and RYSE (22 g a bottle) (page 3). Barebells is up 97% and the top bar of 30 brands; the David bar (28 g protein, 150 calories, 0 g sugar) is second within months; Built "Puff", with whey and collagen, reached fifth (page 3) (page 4). Protein snacks: Legendary Foods, Quest, Vaughn's (page 4).
- NAD+: the report says NAD+ levels fall by up to 50% between 40 and 60 (page 5). 75% of respondents are concerned about ageing; supplements are the top longevity activity (43%), ahead of seeing a doctor (40%) and exercise (39%) (page 6). Life Extension, with Niagen NR, grew 127% in the first quarter; Tru Niagen and Codeage liposomal NAD+ are also named (page 6).
- Peptides: 16% are a lot and 25% somewhat more aware; 30% do not know what peptides are (page 8). AN Performance Creatine + Peptide (PeptiStrong, by Nuritas) is described by the report as "clinically proven" for strength, endurance and recovery; Nuritas says three human trials show muscle benefits (page 8). PeptiStrong also appears in Force Factor's Anabolic Muscle Builder and Whole Health Rx's GLP-1 Support Protein (page 8).
- Coming peptide launches: MuscleTech creatine and DL185 dileucine products, said to give "159% greater activation of muscle protein synthesis"; BodyTech Elite products with DL185 and myHMB, VasoDrive AP, and PeptiStrong with MalTor (page 8).
- Formats: liquid vitamins up 50% year to date, MaryRuth's up 90%, New Chapter entering liquids, "liquid multivitamin" searches up 31% (page 9). Ashwagandha (KSM-66) honey sticks and a shilajit syrup (page 9). ANIMAL creatine chews up over 100%; Force Factor, Legion, Codeage and BodyTech have launched creatine chews and gummies (page 9). BodyTech Elite launched the first creatine beadlet, with Specnova's NovaQSpheres (page 10). Topicals: castor oil roll-on, magnesium spray and magnesium tape (page 10).
- Format preferences: 65% of supplement users take pills or capsules; 34% say more format variety would make supplements easier to take, and 20% that it would help consistency (page 10). The other figures on the format chart cannot be paired with labels from the text (page 9).
- Shilajit: sales up over 40% in the first quarter, searches up 52%; BetterAlt took 25% of shilajit sales within months, combining it with sea moss, ashwagandha and tongkat ali; Codeage's GLP-Harmony Companion+ includes it (page 11). Top wellness concerns: energy (49%), immunity (38%), cognitive function (37%), bone health (35%) (page 11).
- How people discover trends: friends 30%, news media 29%, other social media 28%, family 23%, adverts 21%, brands 16%, TikTok 15% (page 12).
- Related sessions: holland-barrett-fitness-generations (another retailer's view), euromonitor-sports-nutrition-trends, ostojic-creatine-lifelong-nutrition.

lessons.title: Consumer health survey: 9 countries, 6,000 people
lessons.summary:
An unnamed presenter shared results from a consumer survey run in November in nine countries with 6,000 people, covering health goals, health tech, biotics and sports nutrition. Otter heard the team as "our women and Intelligence Team"; the survey matches Lumina Intelligence's, but the company is to confirm. The presenter said they were not the data person and pointed to a colleague, Ed, for questions.

Getting better sleep was the top health goal overall. Sleep and stress lead for younger people; healthy ageing rises with age. Younger consumers track themselves: the presenter said 78 to 79% use a fitness tracker, and 91% of app users buy an app-recommended product at least once a year, mostly in physical stores.

Six percent of respondents said they regularly take GLP-1 drugs, more than the presenter expected outside the US.

On sports nutrition, 36% in Europe take none, against under 20% in the US. Protein leads everywhere. Consumers buy for muscle, but the room's guess that consumers understand creatine's benefits was wrong: they did not know, which the presenter called an opportunity. Price is the second reason for not buying in every country.

Their close: sports nutrition is broadening, consumers still think it is about muscle, and women are an underserved group who want more products.
takeaways: Better sleep was the top health goal overall; sleep and stress lead for younger people, healthy ageing and longevity rise with age [02:49].
91% of app users buy app-recommended products at least once a year: 22% monthly, 48% quarterly, 19% once a year; most buy in physical stores [02:49].
6% of respondents regularly take a GLP-1 drug [02:49].
36% in Europe take no sports nutrition supplement, against less than 20% in the US; protein leads in both [02:49] [07:57].
Consumers did not know what creatine does, which the presenter called an opportunity; 76% of creatine users surveyed were men, and women named endurance as a reason [10:41] [11:15].
Price is the number two reason for not taking sports nutrition in every country surveyed [11:15].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high: consumer data on creatine, protein and GLP-1 from a nine-country survey.
- The creatine knowledge gap is an opening [10:41]. My reading: CreaWin pitches can offer brands consumer education on what creatine does, within the evidence.
- The presenter said the US creatine market is skewing older and female, though far from 50:50 [11:15]. My reading: supports pitching CreaWin to women's and healthy-ageing brands.
- GLP-1 support is now a retail category in the US, including protein for muscle loss [02:49]. My reading: a route for IsoClr: Pea.
- Price is the second barrier everywhere [11:15]. My reading: cost-in-use belongs in our pitches.
quotes: "So if you're a brand in this space, you probably want to think about how you can partner with some of these apps" Speaker 1 [02:49]
"Yes, they did not know which I found was interesting and therefore an opportunity." Speaker 1 [10:41]
"female consumers want more sports nutrition products. It's a category that's being traditionally underserved" Speaker 1 [11:15]
lessons.detail:
- No deck was filed; every figure is as Otter heard it.
- Survey: run last November, nine countries, 6,000 people, with questions on general health and wellness, sports nutrition, biotics and the microbiome, and tech [00:31].
- A room poll guessed healthy ageing as the top goal (heard as 33%) [02:42]; the survey's answer was better sleep [02:49].
- Trackers: fitness trackers are the most used type, at 56% [02:49]. Strava is among the top four fitness apps [02:49].
- GLP-1: the presenter cited an independent source for 6% of the US population on a GLP-1 drug, "about 50 million Americans" [02:49]. GNC was the first US retailer with an in-store GLP-1 support display, covering gastrointestinal effects, nutrient deficiency, skin and muscle loss; one US retailer also offers the medications [02:49].
- Sports nutrition in the US: electrolyte hydration ranks fourth, ahead of creatine at 6%, a level similar to Europe [07:57]. In Europe creatine and hydration follow protein; the exact ranks are unclear in the recording [02:49].
- Reasons for use: muscle repair, growth, strength and soreness, then energy and endurance; younger people focus on muscle, older people on energy [07:57].
- Satisfaction: in the US 40% very and 31% somewhat satisfied, 71% in all; in Spain 33% somewhat and 13% very satisfied [07:57].
- Reasons for not using: in the US the top reason is eating a good diet (as heard); top reasons differ by country, with price second everywhere [11:15].
- Older people move less, so they need more resistance training [11:15].
- Another view of the same survey: Lumina Intelligence's Probiota 2025 deck (probiota-2025 / lumina-biotics-unleashed) gives 93% of app users buying an app-recommended product at least once a year, against 91% said here, and ranks ageing in good health first or second in five European countries, with better sleep first in France and the UK. The two figures differ; both are given.

lessons.title: From Boomers to Zoomers: Fuelling fitness across generations
lessons.summary:
Dr Mark Evans, a Senior Scientist at Holland & Barrett and a sports nutritionist by training, followed the Euromonitor overview with a retailer's view: who buys active nutrition at each age, and how to formulate and talk to each group.

Evans argued that active nutrition is now for everyone, not only athletes, and that one message does not fit all ages. Boomers want mobility and ageing well, Gen X longevity and joints, Millennials convenience and recovery, and Gen Z energy and focus. Supplement use is high in every group, but Gen Z finds products on TikTok and distrusts polished brand content.

Protein was their first example: one nutrient, told differently at each life stage, from growth to muscle repair to sarcopenia and bone health. Creatine was their second. Evans called the evidence for cognition in healthy people very preliminary, noted there is no EFSA claim for it, and showed how brands stack creatine with ingredients that do carry claims so that packs can suggest the link without stating it.

Their close: communication should be planned from the start of product development, and the science team should set efficacious doses.
takeaways: Hero ingredients shift by generation: Boomers protein, calcium, vitamin D, probiotics and omega-3; Gen X protein, collagen, omega-3 and curcumin; Millennials protein, adaptogens, magnesium, curcumin and creatine; Gen Z creatine, caffeine, electrolytes and ashwagandha (slide 11).

Supplement use is high across ages: 79% of Boomers, 78% of Gen X and 81% of Millennials (CRN 2023 survey), and 70% of Gen Z in the US and UK call TikTok their most valuable source of food recommendations (Statista 2024) (slide 9) (slide 10).

On creatine and cognition, Evans said there is "very preliminary evidence" in healthy people and that the strongest evidence is in cognitively impaired people; their slide says there are no EFSA-approved claims for creatine and cognition [00:00] (slide 13).

Their stacking table: creatine 3 to 5 g/day (no EFSA claim); L-theanine 200 to 250 mg/day with 150 mg caffeine; caffeine over 75 mg a serving; B vitamins at 20% RI; Rhodiola rosea 576 mg/day for mental energy and attention (no EFSA claim); pantothenic acid at 15% NRV for normal mental performance (slide 14).
Protein is one nutrient with many stories: growth for children, muscle repair for adults, convenient high protein, mobility, sarcopenia and bone health for older adults [00:00].
Plan communication from the start: "start with the end in mind" (slide 16) [00:00].
lessons.for_us:
- A large retailer's scientist set the bar for creatine cognition claims: preliminary in healthy people, no EFSA claim, and irresponsible to lean on studies in patients [00:00] (slide 13). My reading: CreaWin's cognition story should follow the same hedge and cite studies in healthy adults only.
- Their answer to the missing claim is stacking with ingredients that carry claims (B vitamins, pantothenic acid, caffeine) at efficacious doses (slide 14). My reading: a CreaWin plus B-vitamin concept is a pitch Holland & Barrett's own team already uses.
- Rhodiola rosea sits in their stacking table at 576 mg/day for mental energy and attention, without an EFSA claim (slide 14). My reading: a direct opening for our rhodiola in focus and pre-workout stacks; check our dose against theirs.
- Creatine appears for both Millennials and Gen Z, collagen for Gen X (slide 11). My reading: CreaWin's audience reaches beyond the gym, and the protein message for older adults (sarcopenia, bone) suits IsoClr: Pea in RTDs [00:00].
- Relevance is high: a retailer with over 1,600 stores, as introduced, set out how it judges ingredient science and claims [18:24].
quotes: "...there's very preliminary evidence to show that may have some cognitive benefits in healthy individuals. I would say that the strongest evidence for creatine in humans you would see in cognitively impaired individuals." Speaker 1 (Dr Mark Evans) [00:00]
"No EFSA approved health claims for creatine and cognition." (slide 13)
"This kind of packaging does help people to make that link of Crete into cognition without outwardly stating it." Speaker 1 (Dr Mark Evans; "Crete" is Otter's word for creatine) [00:00]
"...start with the end in mind the product communication should be part of how you're thinking about it at the very at the beginning..." Speaker 1 (Dr Mark Evans) [00:00]
lessons.detail:
- The deck is filed as received (files/holland-barrett-fitness-across-generations-deck.pdf, 17 pages); slide numbers here are the file's pages. Most slides carry the footer "Strictly confidential proprietary to Holland & Barrett International and not for onward distribution". Slides 3, 4, 7, 12, 15 and 16 are images with only a title in the file's text.
- Timestamps: [18:24] is in part 1 of the transcript (the chair's introduction); all other cites are in part 2, where Otter puts the whole talk in one turn at [00:00].
- The chair introduced Holland & Barrett as having over 1,600 stores across 19 countries; Evans said it was their third time speaking at the summit [18:24] (part 1).
- The science team: the slide says 15 scientists with nearly 150 years of combined experience (biomedical scientists, nutrition and sports scientists, registered nutritionists, pharmacists, dietitians); Evans said it was two to three people 12 to 18 months earlier and 19 on the day, with the ambition of "being known for science" (slide 2) [00:00].
- Market size: Statista's sports and active nutrition market, USD 28.4 billion in 2023 and USD 37.8 billion in 2028 (slide 6). Evans said numbers differ by source [00:00]. Euromonitor's figure in the talk before was USD 30.6 billion for 2024 (euromonitor-sports-nutrition-trends); both are kept.
- Drivers on the slide: expanding consumer base, holistic health and wellness, social media, innovation and formats, and active ageing (slide 6). Evans mentioned encapsulated ingredients and gummies growing [00:00].
- Health areas mapped to active nutrition: joint, bone and muscle; energy; immunity; stress and anxiety; sleep and relaxation; heart health; cognitive health; gut health (slide 5). Evans noted sleep ranked first as a reason to take supplements in global data but low in purchases, and asked whether consumers are underserved there [00:00].
- Generations (slide 8): Boomers (1946 to 1964) health-conscious, brand-loyal, ageing well and mobility; Gen X (1965 to 1980) time-poor, practical, holistic wellness and longevity; Millennials (1981 to 1996) digital natives, convenience, transparency; Gen Z (1997 to 2012) social-first, trend-driven, highly visual, sustainability and identity.
- Formats by generation: fortified foods and RTDs (Boomers); powders, tablets and capsules (Gen X); powders, bars and drinks (Millennials); RTDs, gummies and shots (Gen Z) (slide 11). Spoken, Evans spoke of nootropics, ashwagandha and mushrooms trending with younger groups [00:00].
- Gen Z: polished or scripted content from traditional brands gets rejected; an academic's myth-busting content for a sports nutrition brand drew comments calling it paid and scripted. Unpolished, quick myth-busting content is what holds attention [00:00]. Evans spoke of 75 to 79% of Boomers taking supplements; the slide says 79% [00:00] (slide 9).
- On creatine Evans said it is one of the most researched ingredients in the market with demonstrated safety, and thought an EFSA claim on creatine and cognition may have been submitted in the last couple of years but rejected [00:00].
- Creatine for cognition is reaching non-exercisers: a friend who does not train was taking it, having "heard all about brain health" [00:00].
- Slide 13 cites Konstantinos et al. 2018 for oral creatine possibly improving short-term memory and intelligence or reasoning in healthy individuals, with effects on other cognitive domains unclear (slide 13).
- Pack examples: a Holland & Barrett creatine pack ("Shameless plug") with creatine on front and back and "supports mental performance" tied to the B vitamins on the back; and a brand heard as "my brain co micronized creativity", which names no benefit but links creatine to the brain through its name [00:00].
- Older adults: communication may need in-store POS and education materials rather than social media [00:00].
- The Otter recording's own summary is filed as received (files/otter-summary.md).

lessons.title: From Insight to Innovation: Mapping Trends in Functional Health Ingredients
lessons.summary:
Harini Venkataraman, Associate Research Director at Lux Research, mapped where functional health ingredients are going. Lux is a research and advisory firm that tracks innovation signals such as patents and investment.

Venkataraman opened with three areas gaining momentum: phytochemicals, the gut-brain axis and small "shot" beverages. The space is crowded. Different ingredients can deliver the same benefit, so choosing between them is hard for brands and consumers, and ingredients with several benefits have an edge.

Venkataraman then took three consumer areas. Performance is mainstream: consumers agree it means building, sustaining and recovering muscle, and Lux expects strong growth over the next one to two years. Protein is table stakes, and precision fermentation may diversify protein sources over about five years, with more than 30 startups working on dairy proteins. Beauty from within is moving towards mainstream acceptance. Immune health is still at early consensus, because consumers see it as personal.

Their closing advice was to back ingredients with science and clinical evidence, solve formulation and flavour problems, partner with established ingredient players, and check what consumers mean by "performance" or "beauty" before building a product for it.
takeaways: Three momentum areas: rising phytochemicals, growing interest in the gut-brain axis, and small-volume "shot" beverages (slide 5) [02:19].
Connected impacts: different ingredients can confer the same benefit, which makes ingredient selection complex; ingredients addressing several benefits "can provide an edge" (slide 7) (slide 33).

Performance is in mainstream consensus, with strong growth expected over the next 1 to 2 years. Consumers see it as building, sustaining and recovering muscle; the ingredients they name are protein, creatine, beta-alanine, curcumin and CBD (slide 14) (slide 15).

Precision fermentation: more than 30 startups focus on dairy proteins; Perfect Day is the most mature, followed by ReMilk and Formo; DSM and Fonterra's Vivici targets beta-lactoglobulin, including for sports nutrition. Venkataraman doubted it would hit the price now; Venkataraman saw it as a path over "the next, let's say, five years or so" (slide 16) (slide 17) [02:19].

Beauty from within is moving from early consensus to mainstream acceptance; immune health stays in early consensus with steady growth expected, because consumers see it as personal (slide 20) (slide 26).

Their takeaways: back ingredients with clinical evidence that overcome formulation and flavour hurdles, collaborate with established ingredient players, and check how consumers define the category (slide 33).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: a trends map, not data on our ingredients, but it places performance as the mainstream, growing need and names creatine as a performance ingredient consumers look for (slide 14) (slide 15). My reading: support for pitching CreaWin to performance brands.
- Consumers "seek complete protein, comparing plant and animal sources" (slide 15). My reading: the IsoClr: Pea pitch should answer the completeness question directly.
- Precision-fermented dairy protein is a longer-term entrant in sports nutrition; Venkataraman did not expect it to be price-competitive yet (slide 17) [02:19]. My reading: worth watching for plant protein, not a near-term threat.
- My reading: their point on multiple benefits and consumer meaning favours pitches that state each benefit within its own evidence, in the consumer's words (slide 33).
quotes: "...if there are so many different ingredients that could confer same benefit consumer, what will he or she go after?" Speaker 1 (Harini Venkataraman) [02:19]
"...the way protein is creating table stakes. Everybody buys it." Speaker 1 (Harini Venkataraman) [02:19]
"Pro and probiotics are still leading the game." Speaker 1 (Harini Venkataraman) [21:14]
"Performance = increasing gains" (slide 13)
lessons.detail:
- Lux: founded in 2004, research hubs in Boston, Toronto, Amsterdam, Singapore and Tokyo, more than 3,000 syndicated reports a year (slide 2). Venkataraman said they lead consumer product innovation research and previously worked at DSM [00:00] [02:19].
- The bioactive "boom" (slide 6): phytochemicals and plant extracts, antioxidants (including CoQ10 and glutathione), functional proteins and peptides (collagen, casein, elastin, plant proteins, amino acids), functional sugars and HMOs, prebiotics, probiotics, vitamins and minerals, lipids (omega-3, -6, -9, DHA, phytosterols).
- Phytochemicals: extraction and processing innovations aim to improve yield, purity and bioavailability of flavonoids, terpenoids and carotenoids for metabolic health (slide 8). Venkataraman called getting them out in high quantities, formulating them and achieving bioavailability the biggest challenge [02:19].
- Other technology areas Venkataraman named: microbiome modulators, including fibres effective at lower doses; fermentation-derived ingredients (lipids, proteins), if EU regulation and scale allow; AI for microbiome profiling, where Venkataraman said earlier movers such as Day Two were not successful; encapsulation and new processing for bioavailability [02:19].
- Lux's consumer method maps conversations on a maturity curve from ideas to early consensus, mainstream acceptance and established ideas; performance shows strong consensus [02:19] (slide 14).
- Consumer voices on performance: recovery to sustain gains, and muscle and strength from training and high protein intake (slide 13). Venkataraman said protein is "probably less than $10 per kilogram" [02:19].
- Beauty from within: consumers want natural ingredients that work with the body; named ingredients are adaptogens, botanical extracts, spices (cumin, cinnamon, turmeric), collagen and ceramides, and omega-3 (slide 19) (slide 21).
- Functional mushrooms: most developers focus on lion's mane and reishi, almost all target more than two types, mainly fruiting bodies; beverages are a key application (slide 22).
- The Every Company and Landish: a protein and adaptogen coffee premix with fermentation-derived ovalbumin, 8 g protein a serving, sold direct to consumer at $49; Lux's take is that it should strengthen its B2B strategy (slide 23). The spoken price is unclear in the recording [21:14].
- Immune health consumer ingredients: probiotics, prebiotics, vitamins A, C and D, zinc and enzymes (slide 27). Venkataraman sees potential in enzymes, and said large corporates, IFF among them, are moving into postbiotics because they ease formulation, while consumers struggle to tell them apart [21:14].
- Prebiotics: immune-modulating, naturally sweet prebiotics are moving beyond gut health; Lux advises upcycled soluble fibre with several benefits (slide 28). Example: NutriLeads' BeniCaros, a carrot-derived polysaccharide described as clinically backed for immune health, distributed exclusively in the US and Canada (slide 29).
- Outlook: discovering and scaling a novel ingredient is still risky and takes years (slide 31). Venkataraman expects metabolic and digestive health to evolve further with GLP-1 [23:04].
- Marking: every slide carries "Lux Proprietary and Confidential". This is the company's own marking on a talk given at a public conference (slide 1).

lessons.title: Gut Microbiota & Sports
lessons.summary:
Silvia Barbaresi, founder and chief scientific officer of Minutia.AI, presented as one of the summit's startup award winners, followed by questions from the moderator. Minutia uses probabilistic AI to predict how individuals respond to nutrition, starting with athletes.

Their argument: the gut microbiome is a network, so single biomarkers miss the picture. The gut connects to muscle, joints, brain and blood, and may shape performance and injury risk. Minutia tests stool samples with shotgun metagenomics, adds questionnaires and blood data, and returns performance and injury indices with a tailored diet. A digital twin of the athlete's gut is the goal for the next two to three years; Barbaresi called the platform "under construction".

Barbaresi showed early pilot results. Of 20 runners and triathletes, 12 completed: six on a personalised diet with prebiotics and probiotics for eight weeks, six controls. Some blood markers moved in the intervention group, but Barbaresi said 12 people is not enough for big conclusions.

Minutia sells B2B to clinics and sports centres in several countries, is moving into longevity, and plans larger studies, transfer to the general population and partnerships with wearable makers. It does not work with brands yet but has not ruled it out.

This updates their February 2025 Probiota talk (probiota-2025 / minutia-gut-microbiota-sports).
takeaways: The thesis: the gut-muscle and gut-joint axes "play a key role" in performance and injury prevention, and interventions "are always customized" (slide 6) [06:33].
The service: stool kit, shotgun metagenomics, anamnesis, ideally blood, urine and VO2max, then a report with performance and injury indices and dietary advice (slide 7) (slide 8) [06:33].
The pilot: 20 recruited, 6 intervention and 6 control analysed, all male, VO2max 49 ± 7 ml/kg/min, age 46 ± 12, eight weeks of tailored diets with pre- and probiotics (slide 11) [06:33].

Results: Barbaresi said TIBC, total proteins, glucose and monocytes fell after the intervention [06:33]; the slide marks TIBC decreasing at adjusted p < 0.05 and shows no VO2max effect (slide 13). Barbaresi said the sample is not enough "to make big assumption" [06:33].
The digital twin is an ambition for "maybe two, three years"; the intelligent platform is under construction [06:33].
Next: the largest gut microbiota collection in sport, transfer to the general population and longevity, and wearable partnerships (slide 16) [20:02].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: sports is our core market and the talk ties gut health to performance and recovery, but none of our ingredients is named and the evidence is a pilot of 12.
- Barbaresi said performance nutrition companies are "within our range of interest" and is not ruling out working with brands [06:33] [26:21]. My reading: a personalised-advice platform could one day recommend specific ingredients; a contact to keep, not a channel yet.
- My reading: nothing here supports a claim for us; no performance effect was reported (slide 13).
quotes: "we are just 12 people, so six participants in the intervention. And we are aware that it's not enough to make big assumption, but it's still something." Speaker 3 (Silvia Barbaresi) [06:33]
"...for me, the best marketing that we can do is running a clinical trial showing that what we do make sense" Speaker 3 (Silvia Barbaresi) [28:46]
"Gut Microbiota-based interventions" (slide 6)

lessons.title: Sports Nutrition Innovation Insights

speakers.name: Luca Bucchini
speakers.role: Chair (the ESSNA title, on the deck and in the programme); introduced as an expert in food supplement regulation

lessons.summary:
A panel on the first afternoon, after the Euromonitor and Holland & Barrett talks: Nick Morgan, introduced as founder and managing director of Nutrition Integrated; Luca Bucchini, ESSNA's chair and a food supplement regulation expert; and Dr Mark Evans of Holland & Barrett. The chair is not named.

Morgan said protein and pre-workout remain the pillars of sports brands, but protein now runs through every format, and the further it spreads the simpler its message becomes. Protein waters were Morgan's model of simple innovation, and creatine Morgan's case study of an old ingredient reinvented through communication. Evans added that the science for premium protein forms over others is thin, and that sourcing quality ingredients is harder than Evans expected.

Bucchini covered regulation: claims rules differ by member state, and the Commission's coming maximum levels for vitamins and minerals look very low for several nutrients. Bucchini saw promise in botanicals but no convincing pro- or postbiotic sports products yet.

On white spaces, the panel named GLP-1 users, longevity and endurance, which Morgan said has never been unlocked. Their advice to founders: focus, believe in the product, and know the rules.
takeaways: Protein is proliferating into every format, and "all proteins are equal" in the mainstream; only powders keep the technical metrics of source, protein per serve and cost per serve [01:31] [04:33].
Newer protein bars carry less protein: iconic bars stay at 20 g, newer launches sit at 10 to 15 g, Morgan said, possibly for price or accessibility [04:33].
Evans: it is "very difficult to show any concrete data" that isolates or hydrolysed proteins beat other forms [02:45].

Bucchini expects the Commission's maximum levels for vitamins and minerals to be very low, especially for magnesium, potassium, manganese, calcium, vitamin C and vitamin B6, and claims rules to vary by member state (Germany difficult, France liberal, Italy its own rules) [13:59] [15:48].
White spaces: GLP-1 users moving into active nutrition, the shift from healthy ageing to longevity, and endurance beyond gels and summer hydration [30:23] [31:10] [32:27].
Creatine is Morgan's case study of an ingredient reinvented into new areas through communication [08:57].
lessons.for_us:
- Protein waters were singled out as simple, real innovation, with plant options and collagen both named as good fits [08:57] [11:11]. My reading: a clear RTD protein water is a format to pitch IsoClr: Pea into.
- In RTDs, Morgan said, people care less about protein source [11:11]. My reading: IsoClr: Pea wins there on taste and clarity, not on source.
- Low maximum levels for magnesium and other minerals would limit dosing across the EU [15:48]. My reading: track the proposal for any mineral we sell; bucchini-essna-regulatory-update has the detail.
- Endurance and GLP-1 users were the two open spaces [31:10] [32:27]. My reading: CreaWin and our range can be pitched to GLP-1 support and everyday fuelling stacks; Evans questioned the old 60-minute fuelling rule [34:21].
quotes: "...if you dig into the science, it's very difficult to show any concrete data that one of one of those formats is better than the other..." Speaker 3 (Dr Mark Evans) [02:45]
"Collagen, of course, makes good protein waters." Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [11:11]
"France is very liberal. Italy has its own rules, so it makes things very complicated." Speaker 4 (Luca Bucchini) [13:59]
"I still think we've never really unlocked endurance" Speaker 1 (Nick Morgan) [32:27]
lessons.detail:
- Attribution: Speaker 1 is Nick Morgan, Speaker 3 Dr Mark Evans, Speaker 4 Luca Bucchini, from who the chair addresses and what each says; the chair is Speaker 2 and others are unidentified (see to_check). The panel's introduction is part 1 of the transcript, [19:59] (from the end of the Holland & Barrett recording); all other cites are in part 2.
- Morgan: protein and pre-workout "still drive a huge amount of revenue" but, being the biggest, grow more slowly than newer niches; on protein Morgan mentioned "significant challenges" (Otter: "on the more ingredient crisis at the moment") [00:00].
- Evans: Holland & Barrett's protein work is insight-led, weighing a higher protein per serve against its cost and return [02:45].
- Launches they liked: Evans named AG1's move into sleep with an evening product (heard as "ag Zed") [07:55]; Morgan named creatine's reinvention and protein waters, and warned that the industry over-engineers products for differentiation rather than consumer need [08:57] [18:55]. Morgan also mentioned functional drinks for social, low and no alcohol occasions [08:57].
- Morgan: whey protein is the dominant source in protein waters now; there are good plant options too [11:11].
- Bucchini's three areas: one heard as "aggregation", products that "communicate benefits, but maybe less scary ... in terms of sugars", coming to Europe from the US; pro- and postbiotics for active nutrition, where Bucchini has not seen convincing products and wonders whether consumers can be convinced; and botanicals, with "a lot of potential" [12:06] [13:14]. Otter's audio here is garbled.
- Bucchini on the maximum levels: member states have long had different limits, so brands formulate to the lowest; the Commission plans a harmonising proposal; some forms may be banned in drinks, and sodium is a concern. Bucchini hopes the levels can be raised to something reasonable [15:48] [17:06].
- Evans on regulation: ashwagandha restrictions in some member states threaten products built on it as a hero ingredient [17:40].
- Competition: brands face thousands of competitors in each area across channels; to cut through now "you almost need to be a specialist", and many specialist brands in a category signal that it is taking off (Morgan) [18:55] [20:59]. Bucchini said sports nutrition is more integrated across Europe than food supplements, with more cross-border online buying and younger, more open consumers [22:29]. Evans said smaller brands are more agile and build trust in their communities faster [23:40].
- Clean label: the chair cited M&S's clean-label line dropping added vitamins [24:29]. Bucchini thinks clean label is here to stay in Europe, the challenge being functionality [25:16]. Evans said big brands risk losing high-street shoppers when a reformulation changes a product without a chance to explain it [25:58]. Morgan: products still have to taste good and stack up commercially [27:27].
- Pricing: Morgan said some brands succeed with very high prices, citing a longevity product at 800 Swiss francs, and that middle-ground premiums face a hard education job [28:44]. Morgan said they would speak on longevity the next day [28:44].
- Endurance: Morgan said participation far exceeds what endurance brands sell, and runners under an hour are not served [33:35]. Evans said they are "yet to be convinced" that fuelling every session will not help recovery, and that the link of carbohydrate to sugar is hard to overcome [34:21].
- Speaker 6 (unidentified) named muscle health as we age as lacking good solutions [31:55].
- Founder advice: get ready for regulation (unidentified); Bucchini: focus on making the idea work and be clear on the message [36:43]; Morgan: believe in the product, trust gut feeling, offer "something and not everything" [37:05].

lessons.title: Sports nutrition market: consumer trends and innovation in Europe
lessons.summary:
Aishwarya Rajpara, a Beauty and Health Consultant at Euromonitor International, opened the first day with the state of the European sports nutrition market, drawn from Euromonitor's market data, its 2025 consumer survey and its tracker of new product launches.

The global market reached USD 30.6 billion in 2024, and Europe holds 19% of it. Protein powder is still the largest category in Europe, but ready-to-drink protein grew fastest. Consumers now link health to mental wellbeing and stress, and European women report more stress than men and are turning to strength training.

Launches tell the same story. Low sugar is the feature consumers want most, convenience is their top priority, and clean-label and "free from" claims grew fastest. Sports supplements were the fastest-growing launch area, led by electrolytes and creatine, while milk protein supplement launches fell. Creatine use rose in every age group.

Rajpara closed on three trends: convenience, transparency and a holistic approach that reaches beyond protein, with women as the clearest group to grow. In questions Rajpara said consumers expect sustainability as standard rather than pay a premium for it.
takeaways: The global sports nutrition market was USD 30.6 billion in 2024; Europe holds 19% of sales, over 80% of that from Western Europe, and Europe has the second-highest two-year growth after Latin America (slide 9).
In Europe, protein powder is 43% of sports nutrition sales; protein bars grew 11% a year from 2022 to 2024 against an 8% global average, and RTD shows the highest growth (slide 12).
Sports supplement launches rose 33%, with the highest increase in electrolytes and creatine, while milk protein supplement launches fell 21% (slide 17).

The slide says creatine is "Building momentum in post-workout routine" (slide 18). Rajpara said its use rose in all age groups, and that "new studies that claim" effects beyond muscle, on cognitive function and memory, are one reason [00:00].
Low sugar is the product feature most wanted, convenience the top priority and clean label still in demand; word of mouth and web browsing drive awareness more than experts or celebrities (slide 14).
European women report 21% higher stress than men, physical activity is the first way consumers tackle stress, and more women do strength training (slide 11) [00:00].
lessons.for_us:
- Creatine is named twice in Euromonitor's data, as a top launch area and as rising use across ages (slide 17) (slide 18). My reading: this supports CreaWin as the creatine to pitch to European sports brands, including those reaching older users.
- The cognitive angle is reported as "new studies that claim" [00:00]. My reading: any CreaWin cognition story should stay at that hedge; see holland-barrett-fitness-generations on how a retailer handles it without an EFSA claim.
- Milk protein supplement launches fell 21%, and Rajpara linked the shift to "plant based" options (slide 17) [00:00]. My reading: a tailwind for IsoClr: Pea, especially in RTD, the fastest-growing protein format (slide 12).
- Electrolytes and hydration are the other launch leader (slide 17). My reading: worth checking where our range fits hydration and endurance stacks; the innovation panel the same day called endurance a white space (sports-nutrition-innovation-panel).
quotes: "There are new studies that claim to have positive effects are created on not just for muscle building, but also better support for COVID function and memory enhancement." Speaker 1 (Aishwarya Rajpara; Otter's "COVID" is probably cognitive) [00:00]
"Word of mouth and web browsing drive sports nutrition awareness in Europe; expert and celebrity influence remains limited." (slide 14)
"Creatine: Building momentum in post-workout routine" (slide 18)
"...sustainability is something that they want as a standard feature and not a trend that they really want to pay for." Speaker 1 (Aishwarya Rajpara) [17:19]
lessons.detail:
- The deck is filed as received (files/euromonitor-sports-nutrition-trends-deck.pdf, 21 pages); slide numbers here are the file's pages. Each page carries "© 2024 Euromonitor International. All rights reserved." The last slide offered a QR code to download the presentation (slide 21).
- Sources named on the slides: Euromonitor Passport Consumer Health (market sizes and shares); Voice of the Consumer: Health and Nutrition Survey, fielded February 2025 (n=21,207 overall; n=15,727 for female exercise; n=2,299 for desired product features; n=9,877 for consumption reasons; n=3,571 for creatine use); Passport Innovation, launches 2022 to 2024 across 15 countries in the UK and Europe (slides 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18).
- Passport Innovation covers 54 categories in 32 countries and over 400 attributes in 6 groups (slides 5, 6).
- Another speaker's market size: Dr Mark Evans (Holland & Barrett, holland-barrett-fitness-generations) showed Statista's sports and active nutrition market at USD 28.4 billion in 2023 and USD 37.8 billion in 2028. This talk gives Euromonitor's USD 30.6 billion for 2024 (slide 9). The two use different sources and definitions; both are kept.
- Spoken, Rajpara said the market is "doing postpartum double digit growth every year" (Otter's words) and that protein powder is "about 40%" of European sales; the deck says 43% (slide 12) [00:00]. Europe's main markets, as said: the UK, Germany, France, Spain and Italy [00:00].
- Health perception: 60% associate health with mental wellbeing and 44% recognise low stress as vital to good health (slide 10).
- Women's exercise types are compared for 2023 and 2025 (walking, at-home workouts, cycling, running, weight lifting, group classes, yoga, team sports); the chart values are not in the deck's text (slide 11). Rajpara said more women are doing weight training and cardio [00:00].
- Desired features, in the chart's order: low in sugar, ready-to-drink, bar format, clean ingredient list, portable, powder, electrolytes, caffeine, free from animal products, gel (slide 14).
- Launches: over 8,000 new and sub-brand launches in sports nutrition in Europe in 2024; clean label claims grew over 100%; health claims and flavour lead innovation (slide 15).
- Claims: sustained focus on high-protein claims, fortification rising, "no added sugar" claims up 32%, gluten-free and lactose-free gaining; natural claims drive growth, with organic and sustainable sourcing growing steadily (slide 16).
- Packaging and format: jar packaging dominates; plastic packaging claims fell 76%; flexible packaging is trending up but innovation lagged in 2024; new formats such as gels and creams (slide 17). Rajpara said new formats are "still underdeveloped" [00:00].
- Consumption reasons: performance is the key reason; beyond protein, the focus is hydration and recovery speed (slide 18). Rajpara said strength and muscle tone remain the first reason and hydration is rising [00:00].
- Their three closing trends: convenience (accessibility, flexible packaging), transparency (nutrition information, ingredient awareness, sustainability impact) and a holistic approach (broader consumption, beyond protein) (slide 20).
- Q&A: asked whether longevity interest has shifted from cardio to muscle gain, Rajpara pointed to running as the number one physical activity in the data (Otter's text is garbled) [00:00]. Asked about a sustainability premium, Rajpara pointed to beauty, where consumers pay for naturally driven formulas, as a contrast [17:19].
- The Otter recording's own summary is filed as received (files/otter-summary.md); its line that whey is 40% of sales is Otter's reading, not the speaker's or the deck's.

lessons.title: AI, Scientific Wellness and the Future of Personalised Health

speakers.name: Nathan Price
speakers.organisation: Thorne; Buck Institute for Research on Aging
speakers.role: Chief Scientific Officer, Thorne; Professor, Buck Institute for Research on Aging; Co-Director, Center for Human Healthspan

lessons.summary:
Nathan Price, Chief Scientific Officer of Thorne and a professor at the Buck Institute, argued that AI lets personalised nutrition use very deep data on one person and still give that person simple advice.

Their evidence comes from scientific wellness work on about 5,000 people, each measured for their genome, about 1,200 blood analytes, gut microbiome and self-tracking. First, genetics. A polygenic score explains about 12% of LDL cholesterol. People whose measured level sat well above their genetic prediction lowered it in a lifestyle programme; people whose genes predicted a high level did not. Price calls that gap the "Modifiability Gap", a guide to where advice is most likely to work.

Second, the microbiome. Blood metabolites predict about half the variation in gut diversity. The microbiome's gene content was the only measure that predicted weight loss once BMI was accounted for. And some gut bacteria turn phosphatidylcholine into TMAO, so a supplement taken for the brain could harm the heart in those people.

Price called for trials that test a personalisation algorithm rather than one nutrient at a time. Their conclusion: AI powered by deep phenotyping will transform personalised nutrition, and genetics are not destiny.
takeaways: Genetics predicted who lowered LDL cholesterol in a personalised programme: those measured well above their genetic prediction came down "very substantially"; those predicted high showed no significant change [00:00] (slide 11).

The "Modifiability Gap" between genetic prediction and measured value marks the people "most likely to respond"; Price would rank these gaps per person to plan advice that visibly works and keeps them engaged [00:00] (slide 12).

In the cohort, the gene content of the gut microbiome was the only predictor of weight loss independent of BMI, a correlation of about 0.3; blood metabolites, proteins and a diet questionnaire showed no signal beyond BMI [00:00] (slide 18).

Gut bacteria in some people convert phosphatidylcholine to trimethylamine, which the liver turns into TMAO, a cardiovascular risk factor; a population trial cannot show who this applies to [00:00] (slide 16).
Price wants randomised trials that test the personalisation algorithm, so each person's supplement stack differs while one thing is still tested rigorously [00:00].
The microbiome becomes more unique to each person from around age 50; their "uniqueness" score predicted all-cause mortality in people over about 80 over a four-year follow-up [00:00] (slide 17).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: a science and personalisation talk from a supplement brand's chief scientist, with one point that touches our choline group directly.
- The TMAO point is about phosphatidylcholine [00:00]. My reading: formulators may ask whether any choline source raises TMAO, so we should know what the evidence says for our choline bitartrate before a customer asks.
- Price said butyrate, made when gut microbes ferment carbohydrate, stimulates the cells that release GLP-1 [00:00]. My reading: a line worth checking against the literature for fibre in GLP-1-support products.
- Thorne's direction is algorithm-led personalised stacks [00:00] (slide 21). My reading: platforms like this will favour ingredients with responder data, not just average effects.
quotes: "So genetics are not destiny." Nathan Price [00:00]
"So you can be aiming to improve your brain health instead be poisoning your heart. That's a personalized insight." Nathan Price [00:00]
"...the only thing that predicted who would go on to lose weight in this cohort was the gene content of their microbiome" Nathan Price [00:00]
"It's just that that single thing is not a nutrient on average, it is the personalization strategy embodied by the algorithm." Nathan Price [00:00]
lessons.detail:
- The deck is marked "Proprietary & Confidential" on its title slide (slide 1). Its title slide reads "AI, Scientific Wellness, and the Future of Personalized Nutrition" (slide 1).
- Price founded Arivale about 10 years ago; it generated much of the data shown and went out of business [00:00].
- Their team has a $52 million US grant, part of which builds a "personalized health span optimizer", using large language models and agentic AI to move from pattern recognition to "deep reason" on one individual [00:00].
- Deloitte (2022): most of the $4 trillion spent on US healthcare goes on treating sickness; Deloitte forecasts a large shift towards wellness and prevention by 2040, which Price called the "$2 trillion pivot" [00:00] (slide 5).
- On Alzheimer's Price contrasted a drug costing $20,000 to $40,000 a year for a couple of months' delay with prevention giving "years, sometimes many years"; Price said 45% of dementia in the US Hispanic population is preventable by lifestyle and nutrition [00:00].
- Pioneer 5000 (PIs Nathan Price and Lee Hood; Price et al, Nature Biotechnology, 2017): whole-genome sequencing; lab tests three times (clinical chemistry 150, metabolites 700, proteins 400, about 1,200 analytes); gut microbiome three times; continual self-tracking; a database of 200 actionable possibilities (slide 6) (slide 7).
- Genetics alone captures about 12% of the variance in LDL cholesterol, enough to move someone across the clinical range (Zubair et al, Scientific Reports, 2019) [00:00] (slide 10). Price said the same holds for raising HDL cholesterol and appears to for a marker of the transition to diabetes [00:00].
- About half the variance in gut microbiome diversity can be predicted from blood metabolites, from as few as 11; the link held across conditions on the slide (abdominal pain, acid reflux, antibiotics, bloating, constipation, diarrhoea, type 2 diabetes) but broke down in extreme obesity, BMI over about 35, which Price thinks is due to inflammation (Wilmanski et al, Nature Biotechnology, 2019) [00:00] (slide 15).
- About 18% of circulating metabolites are made or co-made by the microbiome [00:00]. The slide names indole propionate, TMAO, imidazole propionate, hippurate, secondary bile acids and p-cresol sulfate as nutrients and toxins with effects in the host (slide 16).
- Weight loss: people whose microbiome breaks complex carbohydrate into simple sugars "have a really hard time losing weight"; those whose microbiome turns it more into short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate lost more in a personalised programme (Diener et al, mSystems, 2021) [00:00] (slide 18).
- Biological BMI: traditional BMI "Misclassifies up to 30% of people"; a metric built from metabolites, clinical labs and proteins "May identify metabolically unhealthy individuals who occupy a normal BMI" (Watanabe et al, Nature Medicine, 2023) (slide 19).
- Price ran their own comprehensive blood panel through ChatGPT's deep research function and called the result "probably the most informative health report I've ever gotten" [00:00].
- In questions, asked about Rob Knight's view (heard as "Rob night") that the microbiome may be destiny, Price said "it is an influence", not destiny, and that understanding the genome "gives you a roadmap" to better choices [26:54].
- Price referred to an earlier talk by a speaker heard as "Mary" and "Marion" [00:00]. My reading: probably Mariette Abrahams (abrahams-glp1-ai-personalised-nutrition), recorded the same day.
