lessons.title: Athlete Microbiome

speakers.name: Paul Cotter
speakers.organisation: Teagasc Food Research Centre, Moorepark; APC Microbiome Ireland and VistaMilk; SeqBiome Ltd
speakers.role: Head of Food Biosciences (Teagasc); Principal Investigator (APC Microbiome Ireland and VistaMilk); CTO (SeqBiome)

lessons.summary:
Paul Cotter, Head of Food Biosciences at Teagasc and a principal investigator at APC Microbiome Ireland, presented what studies of elite athletes' gut microbiomes have taught their group, and what it means for diet.

Cotter started with the gut microbiome and the many factors that shape it, from antibiotics and birth mode to diet, fibre, fermented foods, probiotics and exercise. Their group's first study compared elite rugby players with men of low and high body mass index. The athletes' microbiomes differed from both control groups, though with exceptions, and later work showed differences in what the microbes can do and the metabolites they make, including short-chain fatty acids.

Cotter then turned to diet. In a 12-week trial in 53 healthy adults, a ketogenic diet lost slightly more fat than a low-sugar diet but raised LDL cholesterol, reduced glucose tolerance and lowered bifidobacteria; cutting sugar changed the microbiome little. Cotter also showed kefirs that differed in their effect on plasma cholesterol, and work separating the effects of diet and exercise on gut microbe and host metabolism.

The deck ends with Sportgenix, a microbiome analysis programme for athletes linked to SeqBiome, the company where Cotter is CTO.
takeaways: Elite rugby players' microbiomes differed from those of low- and high-BMI controls, "though there are exceptions" (Clarke et al., Gut 2014; 40 athletes, 23 and 23 controls, men aged 18 to 37) (slide 7) (slide 8).
Athletes' microbiomes also differ in functional potential and in the metabolites they produce; short-chain fatty acids correlate with diet or microbial diversity (Barton et al., Gut 2018) (slide 9).

Ketogenic diet, 12 weeks in 53 healthy adults: 2.9 kg average fat loss against 2.1 kg on a low-sugar diet, but keto raised LDL cholesterol, reduced glucose tolerance and decreased bifidobacteria; sugar restriction did not significantly change the microbiome (slide 10) (slide 11).

Fermented foods can differ in effect: kefirs differed in their impact on total plasma cholesterol, under the heading "Fermented foods with anti-obesity impacts" (Bourrie et al., Br J Nutr 2021) (slide 12).
Diet and exercise each shape microbe and host co-metabolism, scored from urine NMR profiles against WHO healthy-eating guidelines (Penney et al., mSystems 2020) (slide 14) (slide 15).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: gut health in sport is a science story, not yet a product story; the deck names no supplement ingredient or dose. My reading: useful background for fibre and prebiotic pitches to sports brands, within each ingredient's own evidence.
- A low-carbohydrate (keto) diet decreased bifidobacteria in 12 weeks (slide 11). My reading: athletes on low-carbohydrate diets are a possible audience for prebiotic fibres; no study here tested that.
- Other microbiome talks: Minutia on gut microbiome and sport at the same event (minutia-gut-microbiome-sports), and APC colleagues Jens Walter (jens-walter-microbiome-ageing) and Siobhain O'Mahony (omahony-gut-brain-gaps). Sharon Madigan, whose SANS talk is filed (fuel-the-frame-carbohydrate-recovery-and), is among their acknowledged collaborators (slide 13).
quotes: "Dictated by types of microbes, what they do/produce and microbial diversity" (slide 3)
"The keto diet altered gut microbiome composition, notably decreasing bifidobacteria." (slide 11)
"Sugar restriction did not significantly impact the gut microbiome composition." (slide 11)
lessons.detail:
- Their roles: Head of Food Biosciences, Teagasc Food Research Centre, Moorepark; Principal Investigator, APC Microbiome Ireland and VistaMilk; CTO, SeqBiome Ltd (slide 1).
- A microbiome-in-numbers infographic opens the science (Sender et al., Cell 2016) (slide 2).
- Gut microbiota functions listed include vitamin synthesis, satiety, digestion and absorption, immune stimulation, energy harvest from food and signalling to the brain; these are "Dictated by types of microbes, what they do/produce and microbial diversity" (slide 3). Microbial products such as short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, TMA and LPS act on the heart, liver, muscle and brain (Shehata et al., Exp Physiol 2022) (slide 4).
- Factors that shape the microbiome: antibiotics, stress, birth mode, breast feeding, environment, probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, postbiotics, diet (including fibre and fermented foods) and exercise, with the consensus definitions of the four biotics (slide 5).
- Exercise influences the gut microbiota in adults, with links shown to depression and anxiety, infection, gastrointestinal permeability and inflammation (Wosinska et al., Nutrients 2019) (slide 6).
- The rugby study measured fasting blood markers, clinical bloods, diet (food frequency questionnaire), body composition (DXA and waist-to-hip) and faecal sequencing (slide 7).
- The keto trial is cited on the slide as Hengist et al., 2024, Cell Reports Medicine (slide 10): control moderate-sugar diet; low-sugar under 5% of calories from sugar; keto under 8% from carbohydrate; neither changed physical activity. The low-sugar diet "significantly reduced cholesterol in LDL particles" (slide 10).
- Kefir chart: total plasma cholesterol for five samples labelled COM, ICK, Pitch, PNY and PNL, with ICK and Pitch significantly lower than the others, read from the chart; the codes and the study population are not explained on the slide (slide 12).
- Sportgenix (sportgenix.ie) is shown as a personalised microbiome analysis programme for elite athlete performance, beside the SeqBiome logo, read from the slide images (slide 6) (slide 12).
- Collaborators acknowledged at Teagasc, UCC, the Irish Sports Institute, Imperial College London and the University of Bath, and "All athletes; elite and non" (slide 13).

lessons.title: Creatine for Lifelong Nutrition & Healthy Ageing

speakers.name: Sergej M. Ostojic
speakers.organisation: University of Agder, Kristiansand (Department of Nutrition and Public Health)

lessons.summary:
Sergej Ostojic, Professor of Nutrition and Public Health at the University of Agder in Norway, argued that creatine should be treated as a semi-essential nutrient for everyone, not only as a sports supplement.

The body turns over about 2 g of creatine a day and makes about half; the rest has to come from food, almost all of it meat and fish. Older people make less and eat less, and ageing muscle may take it up less well. In US survey data, 65.2% of adults ate less than the 1 g a day Ostojic takes as the requirement.

Ostojic then showed population studies linking low dietary creatine with more depression, heart and liver conditions, poorer cognition, cancer and earlier death, and higher creatine intake with more lean mass and grip strength. These are associations; some weakened once other factors were adjusted for. Ostojic set them beside supplementation trials in older people and the EU-authorised claim for adults over 55 who do resistance training, and called creatine safe on more than 1,000 human studies.

Their advice for older people: 1 g a day for life to prevent a shortfall, 3 to 5 g with exercise for function, and more for the brain. Ostojic wants creatine recognised as a semi-essential nutrient and added to everyday meat-free foods.
takeaways: Their frame: "Creatine appears to be a semi-essential nutrient for humans". About half of the 2 g daily turnover comes from an omnivorous diet, and older people make less, eat less and may take up less into muscle (slide 8) (slide 10) (slide 23) [00:00].

Intake is low and falling: 65.2% of NHANES adults ate less than 1.00 g a day, and dietary creatine fell significantly in infants and in children and adolescents, with a tendency in adults, across 89,161 respondents (slide 11).

Low intake is associated with worse health. Depression prevalence was 42% higher in the lowest intake quartile than the highest; older people under 1 g a day had 2.62 times the risk of angina pectoris and 2.59 times the risk of liver conditions (slide 12) (slide 13). Ostojic presented these as associations from population studies.

Higher intake is associated with more lean mass and grip strength without exercise, in children, adults and older people; Ostojic said the link weakens and is not always significant once age and sex are adjusted for (slide 16) [00:00].
The authorised claim: "Daily creatine consumption can enhance the effect of resistance training on muscle strength in adults over the age of 55" (Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/672) (slide 17).

Doses for older people: 1 g a day for life to prevent a shortfall; 3 to 5 g a day with exercise to raise stores and performance; up to 20 g a day for cognition, for 5 to 7 days and then 3 to 5 g (slide 19).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high: a leading creatine researcher makes the public-health case for creatine in healthy ageing, for people who do not train as well as those who do (slide 23) [00:00]. My reading: this supports CreaWin pitches to healthy-ageing and everyday-wellness brands, not only sports.
- The claim we can use is the EU-authorised one, for adults over 55 doing resistance training (slide 17). The population links to depression, cancer and mortality are associations, two of them from papers still in review; they are background for brands, never claims (slide 12) (slide 14) (slide 15) (slide 16).
- Their 1 g a day dose as a "Preventive strategy" and their call for "Market-driven fortification" of convenient foods point to low-dose daily formats: fortified foods, drinks and combinations (slide 19) (slide 21). My reading: a CreaWin food-fortification concept for older and meat-free consumers is worth taking to food and drink brands.
- Ostojic co-founded KRE-ALL, a Norwegian company developing creatine-enriched foods (slide 2). My reading: a possible CreaWin customer; their disclosures also list research support from several creatine suppliers.
- Other speakers agree on the move into healthy ageing: Kreider and Pasco (from-hype-to-healthspan-building-the), Nestlé Research (nutrition-to-improve-mitochondrial-functions) and the premium price of longevity creatine (nick-morgan-longevity). Mark Evans gives the same 3 to 5 g daily dose and 20 g loading (is-the-juice-worth-the-squeeze).
quotes: "Creatine appears to be a semi-essential nutrient for humans" (slide 23)
"Creatine is a promising food component for public health nutrition for healthy aging" (slide 23)
"Market-driven fortification = voluntarily enrich convenient foods with creatine" (slide 21)

"Namely, if you not are able to exercise, just getting some creative might help you to preserve your muscular mass and strength when you're older." Sergej Ostojic [00:00] (Otter's text; "creative" is creatine)
lessons.detail:
- Disclosures: member of the Scientific Advisory Board on Creatine in Health and Medicine (AlzChem LLC); co-owner of a European patent on liquid creatine supplements (WO2019150323 A1) and a US patent application on creatine for telomere lengthening; research support in the past 36 months from AlzChem GmbH, Kaneka Nutrients, ThermoLife International, Vireo Systems, a science ministry and a provincial secretariat for research; co-founder of KRE-ALL (slide 2).
- 100 years of research: a 1926 paper already suggested "Creatine may be stored as a reserve food material" (slide 4); a PubMed search shows 69,774 results (slide 5).
- Roles beyond energy: neurotransmitter, antioxidant, buffer and appetite regulator; muscle holds 120 mmol/kg of dry mass (slide 6). Ostojic said a just-completed study suggests creatine may affect appetite, submitted the week before [00:00].
- Food sources, in g/kg: herring 6.5 to 10.0, pork 5.0, beef and salmon 4.5, cod 3.0, tuna 4.0, plaice 2.0, milk 0.1; fruit, vegetables and shrimp only trace (slide 8).
- Groups at risk of a shortfall: preterm infants, inherited metabolic disorders, myopathies, multiple sclerosis, sarcopenia, vegetarians, chronic kidney disease and older people (slide 9).
- Why older people run low: less made by the body (lower AGAT and GAMT activity), less eaten, less muscle, and possibly a less effective creatine transporter (SLC6A8), which "is still under investigation" (slide 10).
- Cognition: older people eating more than 0.95 g a day (the top two quartiles) scored higher on cognitive tests (slide 13).
- Cancer: "for every additional milligram of food creatine per kilogram of body mass consumed daily, the cancer rate is reduced by approximately one percent", in US adults aged 20 and over; the slide calls this an association (slide 14).
- Mortality, from a paper in revision: survival was higher in those meeting the recommended intake (P 0.05). Hazard ratios: crude 0.85 (0.62 to 1.00); 1.03 (0.85 to 1.24) after sociodemographic factors; 0.96 (0.77 to 1.19) after lifestyle; 0.79 (0.67 to 0.94, P 0.01) after diet; 0.81 (0.69 to 0.96) after physical examination; 0.92 (0.72 to 1.17) after laboratory measures (slide 15). Ostojic spoke of 20 years of follow-up [00:00].
- Lean mass and grip, from a paper in review: lean mass excluding bone 43.5, 43.9, 46.8 and 50.2, and handgrip 58.9, 57.7, 63.9 and 71.1, from the lowest to the highest intake quartile (up to 0.21 g a day to 1.04 g or more) (slide 16). In people 65 and over the crude coefficients were 2.67 for lean mass and 3.68 for grip, both significant; in the most adjusted model shown for them, lean mass stayed significant (3.12) and grip did not (1.11) (slide 16). Ostojic spoke of 130,000 US adults [00:00].
- Supplementation in older people, as listed: less liver fat, better glycaemic control, slower tumour growth in some cancers, more strength or muscle, less bone loss, better function in knee osteoarthritis, better cognition, an antidepressant effect (slide 17). Ostojic said more than 50 studies in older people in the past 10 years [00:00].
- Safety: no risk in cross-sectional studies; no severe adverse events in long-term trials; over 1,000 human interventional studies at 0.3 to 0.8 g/kg a day for 7 days to 5 years; minor risks from RCTs: weight gain from water (?), kidney problems (?) and passing gut upset (slide 18). Ostojic said stomach upset may occur in the first 10 days [00:00].
- Open questions: no RDA or upper limit for older people; individual needs by sex, illness and microbiota; food composition data; who is at risk; interactions with other foods and medicines (slide 20).
- Fortification: eating less meat for the climate may lower creatine intake; adding creatine to meat-free foods could prevent a large-scale shortfall; first voluntary, market-driven fortification, then possibly mandated fortification (slide 21). Ostojic suggested a company could make a creatine product for older people [00:00].
- Their group in Norway built the Creatine Global Initiative (creatine.global), a library bringing together industry, scientists, regulators and consumers (slide 22) [00:00].
- Q&A: asked whether current production is environmentally friendly, Ostojic said most companies use synthetic processes, which are environmentally friendly compared with the old extraction from meat [23:44].

lessons.title: GLP-1, AI and Data for Consumer Health & Personalised Nutrition
lessons.summary:
Mariette Abrahams, founder and CEO of Qina, a data and consultancy business for personalised nutrition, described how health, food, pharma and technology are converging, and what that means for brands.

Their first trend was discovery. Consumers now move between Google, ChatGPT and reviews before they buy; "Healthy Living" rose from 75th to 10th among uses of generative AI in a year; and Shopify's link with ChatGPT lets people buy inside the chat. Wearables, AI coaches and gyms are becoming places where health advice happens, and pharma, Bayer in particular, is moving into prevention.

Their second was GLP-1. Prescriptions to adults rose 586.7% over five years, and Abrahams said Europe is two to three years behind the US. One study found GLP-1 users short of vitamin K, magnesium, choline, iron, protein and fibre, though Abrahams stressed it was small and there is much to learn. Consumers will want help while on treatment, coming off it, or instead of it.

Their advice to brands: formulate for nutrient density, smaller appetites and changing body composition; find digital partners; show clinical proof through digital experiences; and lean into AI, because a world without websites and apps may be coming.
takeaways: The number of adults prescribed a GLP-1 rose 586.7% over five years; Abrahams said about 70% are in the US and that some experts put Europe two to three years behind: "So the wave is forthcoming." [00:07] (slide 19).

In a study of people on GLP-1 treatment, intake was low in vitamin K, magnesium, choline and iron, and low in protein and fibre; Abrahams called it one study of 60 people and said "we still have an awful lot to learn" [00:07] (slide 20).
Consumers will look for solutions while on treatment, instead of it, or when coming off it, with concerns over muscle mass, lean mass and nutrient deficiency [00:07].

AI is changing discovery: on Harvard Business Review's list, healthy living rose from number 75 to number 10 among generative AI uses in a year, and Shopify's ChatGPT link lets consumers buy without visiting a website [00:07] (slide 10) (slide 12).

On Qina's tracking of features in personalised health solutions, the slide shows food logging (+20%), biomarker testing (+11%), habit tracking, and AI coaches and assistants (54%); Abrahams spoke of a rapid increase in AI coaches [00:07] (slide 14).

Their four opportunities for brands: formulate better (nutrient density, smaller appetites, body composition, holistic health), partner better, create digital experiences that show clinical proof, and lean into AI (slide 25) (slide 26) (slide 27) (slide 28).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high: the GLP-1 nutrient gaps Abrahams cited are categories we sell, and their formulation advice is the brief our customers will write.
- The gaps named were vitamin K, magnesium, choline, iron, protein and fibre (slide 20). My reading: BioK2 MK-7, our magnesium and iron bisglycinates, choline bitartrate and IsoClr: Pea together answer most of that list, for a GLP-1 companion pitch.
- "Create for smaller appetites & changes in body composition" (slide 25). My reading: low-dose, nutrient-dense formats suit us; protein that keeps lean mass on a small serving is the lead.
- The evidence base is thin, by their own words [00:07]. My reading: pitch the nutrient gaps as reported in a small study, not as a proven need.
- Discovery is moving into AI chat and agent shopping [00:07] (slide 12). My reading: our customers' brands, and our ingredient brands, need clear, citable evidence online for AI tools to find.
quotes: "...the number of adults who have been prescribed GLP one has increased by over 580% over the past five years." Mariette Abrahams [00:07]
"So the wave is forthcoming. We haven't seen anything yet." Mariette Abrahams [00:07]
"Nutrient density is going to be more and more important as we start experiencing the wave of GLP." Mariette Abrahams [00:07]
"Imagine a world without apps and" (slide 31)
lessons.detail:
- Qina combines "proprietary data, digital tools and domain expertise to help companies innovate faster and smarter" (slide 2).
- On their hype-cycle slide the technologies are agentic AI, generative AI, computer vision, natural language processing and machine learning; the trends are longevity, food as medicine, active nutrition, women's health, transparency, gut health and GLP-1 (slide 5). Abrahams said agentic AI is at the peak and GLP-1 has dipped as the drugs became widely available [00:07].
- Investment is flowing to DIY biomarker kits (vitamin D levels, for example), access to nutrition experts, smart eating and body-scan devices [00:07]. Notable 2025 investments on the slide include Bioniq, Superpower, Allora, Alba, Welltheory, Hormona, Nourish, Culina, Moom, Biohm, Epicore Biolinq, Aeon, Prenuvo and Habitual (slide 6).
- McKinsey 2025 segments: max optimizers 25% of consumers and 40% of wellness spend; confident enthusiasts 11% and 15%; health traditionalists 20% and 13%; health strugglers 24% and 20% (slide 7).
- Abrahams said younger consumers use ChatGPT as an assistant ("Shall I take my shape before exercise?"), older ones in place of Google; on Qina's data the number of solutions using generative AI had tripled by April 2025 [00:07] (slide 11).
- Partnerships: Dexcom and "aura" (as heard; glucose with sleep data), and a wearable company that pivoted into nutrition [00:07] (slide 15). Gyms are becoming places of health, with doctors, nutritionists and prescriptions inside [00:07].
- Bayer: bought a personalised supplement company for "two 50 million" and later sold it, launched a longevity offer (a genetic test, an app and a non-personalised supplement), bought an inflammatory bowel disease app, and bought top-selling Amazon supplements, which include botanicals [00:07] (slide 17).
- Levels of GLP-1 personalisation on their slide: GLP-1 companion products (food and ingredients), medical food, "phygital" products with generative or agentic AI, and digital plus biological, with digital twin technology (slide 21). Examples Abrahams gave: GLP-1-friendly labelled products, a doctor-prescribed medical food, a high-protein Abbott medical nutrition product, an agentic AI chatbot for GLP-1 users, a UK start-up selling prescription, drug and companion products together, and DNA plus microbiome tests to predict GLP-1 response [00:07].
- Abrahams said a body heard as "the American lifestyle Association" published guidance on behavioural, psychological, exercise and nutrition support for GLP-1 users, and that GLP-1 users adopt wearables and exercise more [00:07].
- Transparency: consumers scan everything, supplements and shakes included, with ingredient apps [00:07] (slide 22). Competition is shifting: consumers want simplicity and transparency, expect personalisation and demand proof of efficacy (slide 23).
- Looking ahead: virtual healthcare marketplaces where consumers upload their own data and ask what to buy, and tech companies' smart glasses pointing to "a world of no websites and no apps" [00:07] (slide 31).

lessons.title: Making Smart Choices About Longevity Supplements
lessons.summary:
Sophie Chabloz of AVEA, a Swiss longevity supplement brand, explained what longevity supplements are and how their customers choose them.

Chabloz set the biohackers aside. Bryan Johnson's 105 pills a day and Ray Kurzweil's 200 are not their market: their customers want to feel well for as long as possible, not to live to 150. No supplement has been proven to extend human lifespan, Chabloz said, but evidence for some molecules in healthy ageing grows every week. Several, such as NAD+, CoQ10 and collagen, decline with age and are hard to get from diet alone.

Their customers are mostly 45 to 65, and 70% are women. They are well read and demanding. They ask for third-party purity tests, read trials and check claims on PubMed and AI tools. They do not want tests or ingredient lists; they want their own problems solved. So AVEA tests every batch in a Swiss lab, uses evidence-based doses, runs its own studies and consumer tests, offers a broad range by need, and educates heavily.

Their closing advice was to cover the basics first: vitamin D3 and K2, omega-3, magnesium and methylated B vitamins. Without them, Chabloz said, customers will not feel the full effect of more advanced longevity supplements.
takeaways: Longevity means healthspan: "Our customers are not interested in living until 150 maybe not even until 100 what they're interested in is feeling great for as long as possible." No supplement has been proven to extend human lifespan [00:01].
Their customers are mostly 45 to 65 and 70% are women; Chabloz started AVEA because the longevity space felt "very performance, very male, driven" [00:01].

Quality is the first filter. AVEA tests each batch of each ingredient in a third-party Swiss lab for heavy metals and purity, and recently rejected a supplier's batch for mercury and went out of stock rather than use it [00:01] (slide 7).

Customers expect science: evidence-based ingredients and doses from suppliers who ran trials, then tests of the finished formula. AVEA showed a skin study in 58 people (40 women, 18 men) aged 35 to 68, with texture, hydration and elasticity improving over 12 weeks [00:01] (slide 8).

Customers buy outcomes, not tests or ingredients: most do not want a test, so a broad range by need (skin, blood glucose, joints, gut) matters more than personalisation, which Chabloz said is "not ready yet" [00:01] (slide 9).
Cover the basics first: vitamin D3 and K2, omega-3, magnesium and methylated B vitamins (especially if vegan) (slide 10) [00:01].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: a longevity brand describes its buyer and what it asks of suppliers: clinically dosed ingredients, third-party purity data and batch consistency [00:01]. My reading: purity certificates and trial-backed doses are what wins a brand like AVEA, the same lesson as the 18 of 88 creatine gummies that failed their label claim (nathan-gray-creatine-new-buyers).
- Their longevity molecules are NAD+, CoQ10 and ubiquinol, AKG, collagen and spermidine, with quercetin, NMN, fisetin, ergothioneine and resveratrol pictured (slide 4) (slide 6). Creatine is not among them; Ostojic made the healthy-ageing case for creatine the same day (ostojic-creatine-lifelong-nutrition). My reading: CreaWin can be offered to longevity brands as a molecule that declines with age and is hard to get from diet in useful amounts, within its own evidence.
- Their "cover your base first" message sells basics beside premium molecules (slide 10) (slide 13). My reading: magnesium, vitamins and omega-3 sit naturally in a longevity range; check which we supply before pitching.
- Women 45 to 65 are the buyers here [00:01]; Nick Morgan's price data put longevity products at about three times creatine's price per serving (nick-morgan-longevity).
quotes: "Our customers are not interested in living until 150 maybe not even until 100 what they're interested in is feeling great for as long as possible." Sophie Chabloz [00:01]
"And actually, there are no supplements or ingredients that have been shown to have been proven to extend human lifespan." Sophie Chabloz [00:01]
"They're not looking for tests, they're not looking for ingredients. They're just looking to solve the problem." Sophie Chabloz [00:01]
"Please cover your base first before going “fancy”" (slide 10)
lessons.detail:
- Slide 4 chart, titled as NAD+, CoQ10 and collagen naturally decreasing with age, from 100% at 20: NAD+ 50% at about 52 and 10% at 80; CoQ10 68% at about 40 and 43% at 80; collagen 85% at about 28 and 20% at 80, read from the chart; no source is given (slide 4).
- Slide 3 shows paper titles on spermidine and autophagy, AKG, glycine, NAD+ precursors, fisetin as a senotherapeutic, and an oral collagen peptide skin trial (slide 3). Slide 5 maps AVEA's Longevity Bundle onto the hallmarks of ageing (slide 5).
- Chabloz described longevity supplements as "cellular fine tuning" aimed at the hallmarks of ageing, such as DNA damage, senescent cells, impaired autophagy and nutrient sensing; not a fix for an average deficiency [00:01].
- NMN quality: the slide's headline says most NMN products tested by ChromaDex had virtually none of the active ingredient (slide 7). Chabloz also cited an NUS Singapore study and said "70 or 80%" of NMN products tested did not contain the claimed amount, adding that Chabloz could not remember the exact figure [00:01].
- Chabloz warned that protein powder, collagen and mushroom extracts can carry heavy metals, which may matter over years of daily use [00:01].
- The skin study (slide 8): average texture readings rose from about 60% to about 65%, corneometer hydration from about 36 to about 48, and cutometer elasticity from about 67 to about 70 over 12 weeks, read from the charts; the Visia evenness score (Ebenheit on the image) went from 47% to 73% in one subject after 3 months. No control group is shown. Chabloz said it should be published soon, and that AVEA patented one ingredient in the combination after cell, worm and mouse work [00:01].
- AVEA also works with contract research organisations, case studies, wearables and at-home tests to judge finished products [00:01].
- The range (slide 9): energy and focus (cellular energy via NAD+ increase), skin health, glucose control, vitamins and minerals, cellular renewal (autophagy and senescent cells), joint care, gut balance, and biological-age and epigenetic testing.
- The brand is about four years old (July 2025) with products on sale for three years; four in-house customer care staff, a fifth with a nutrition background about to join; consultations often go back to basics such as vitamin D and magnesium status [00:01].
- Supplements sit on top of a pyramid of mindset and rest, nutrition and movement (slide 11). Chabloz recommends Examine and Consensus to customers for evidence (slide 12) [00:01].
- Recap: specific longevity molecules, reliable supplements, evidence-based formulas, a routine tailored to needs, and the base of D3, K2, omega-3, magnesium and zinc (slide 13).

lessons.title: Nutrigenomics, AI & Next-Gen Supplements

speakers.name: Marimiina Pykälistö
speakers.role: Nutritionist and Consulting Advisor (programme); Certified Nutritionist (MSSc., AFMCP) on the deck

lessons.summary:
Marimiina Pykälistö, a certified nutritionist, presented nutritional genomics as the basis for a new generation of supplements. This summary comes from their deck alone; there is no recording.

Their starting point is that genes do not explain health or illness on their own: humans share 99.9% of their DNA, and lifestyle, environment and nutrition shape how genes are expressed. Pykälistö separates epigenetics, nutrigenomics (how nutrition affects gene expression) and nutrigenetics (how nutrition affects people with different genetic variations).

Food, in their framing, is information, not only calories. Cofactors are the building blocks of epigenetic change, epinutrients modulate epigenetic marks, and transcription factors control how DNA is read. Plant compounds act as epinutrients, with effects Pykälistö describes as balancing and short-lived, and they cannot replace cofactors. Common genetic variations change how much of each a person needs.

Their new generation supplements combine all three: cofactors, epinutrients and transcription-factor modulators. Their examples for metabolic health pair minerals and CoQ10 with botanicals such as berberine and cinnamon, and curcumin, vitamin D and resveratrol. Pykälistö ends on new tools for sequencing, nutrient-gene analysis and phenotyping as the future of healthcare.
takeaways: Genes alone do not explain health: humans share 99.9% of DNA, and lifestyle, environment and nutrition shape gene expression ("Genes load the gun, lifestyle pulls the trigger") (slide 2).
Nutrigenomics studies the effect of nutrition on gene expression; nutrigenetics how nutrition affects different genetic variations (slide 3).
Food as information: cofactors, epinutrients and transcription factors work together, and genetic variations change how the body benefits from nutrients (slide 5) (slide 8).
Plant compounds as epinutrients are "Multifactorial and polygenetic", "Balancing rather than one-directional" and "More short-lived than long-term", and cannot replace cofactors (slide 7).

Their metabolic example combines cofactors (chrome, zinc, ALA, CoQ10, L-carnitine), epinutrients (berberine, acacia fiber, cinnamon) and transcription factors (curcumin, vitamin D, resveratrol), sourced to the Institute for Functional Medicine (slide 10).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: a framework talk with no data on any ingredient, but it names several ingredient groups we deal in.
- My reading: pairing cofactors with epinutrients is a story a practitioner brand might use to pair minerals such as our zinc and iron forms with botanicals; the deck gives no evidence for the combinations, so we would not cite it.
- My reading: personalisation by genotype is the same direction as Nathan Price's talk (price-ai-scientific-wellness), from a practitioner rather than a cohort.
quotes: "Genes load the gun, lifestyle pulls the trigger" (slide 2)
"Food as information – not only calories" (slide 5)
"Balancing rather than one-directional" (slide 7)
lessons.detail:
- Epigenetics was "born" in 2003, when "the scientific world was shocked" that genes do not explain illness or health, sourced to Natural Therapies Clinic, 2.8.2024 (slide 2).
- DNA methylation, histone acetylation and non-coding RNA are the best-known epigenetic processes; cofactors, often enzymes, enable them, and epinutrients influence them (University of Utah) (slide 6).
- Individual variations (SNPs) affect enzyme function and change the quantity and quality of epinutrients and cofactors needed (slide 8).
- Slide 9, headed "Ex. 1 Immunity Booster" with text about metabolic health: cofactors Sod, manganese, copper, zinc, iron and sulphur; epinutrients rosemary, beetroot, pomegranate; transcription factors fatty acids and sulforaphane (source 10.1631/jzus.B1900614) (slide 9).
- Today's tools: genetic sequencing, nutrient and gene analysis, and phenotype analysis (slide 11); the final content slide is titled "The future of healthcare" (slide 12).
- The deck names no product, brand or study results of their own, and does not mention AI despite the billed title.

lessons.title: Personalised Health Panel

speakers.name: Mariette Abrahams
speakers.role: Founder and Chief Executive Officer (programme); deck in abrahams-glp1-ai-personalised-nutrition

speakers.name: Marimiina Pykälistö
speakers.role: Nutritionist and Consulting Advisor (programme); deck in pykalisto-nutrigenomics

speakers.name: Femke Hoevenaars
speakers.role: Senior Scientist Nutritional Physiology and Metabolism (programme)

lessons.summary:
A short panel on the second day, chaired by Olivia Haslam of NutraIngredients, with Mariette Abrahams (Qina), Marimiina Pykälistö (nutritionist and consulting advisor), Femke Hoevenaars (TNO) and a fourth panellist Otter does not name.

They agreed the field is moving from personalised nutrition to personalised health: lifestyle, mind and body, with tools that tell people what to do. Digital twins drew caution. Abrahams said fewer than five companies offer them and the term is used loosely; the others called them expensive, promising for research and not yet applicable.

On AI, Abrahams said it is spreading faster than the science and regulators can follow, and that advice built on unrepresentative data may not fit the individual. Weight remains the entry point, with GLP-1 users cycling on and off the drugs, but people link weight loss to energy, sleep and wider health, and a separate group wants longevity.

To build trust they called for transparency and plain explanations of why an ingredient helps. Asked for one change, Abrahams wanted proof of outcomes, Pykälistö statistics that show personalisation works, and the unnamed panellist a personal tool for health data.
takeaways: Personalised nutrition is becoming personalised health: "body of mind, soul nutrition" in Otter's words (Abrahams) and the whole lifestyle (Pykälistö) [00:42] [01:22].

Digital twins: fewer than five companies offer them in personalised health or nutrition, by Qina's tracking, and many "digital twins" are just apps (Abrahams); expensive, promising in research, not yet applicable (Pykälistö, Hoevenaars) [03:02] [04:13] [04:40].
AI is "proliferating" faster than the science and regulators; consumers love its simplicity but advice may not fit the individual (Abrahams) [06:02] [06:39].
Weight management is still the gateway, with intermittent GLP-1 use, but people now connect weight to energy, sleep and menopause symptoms; longevity seekers are a separate group [08:43] [09:19].
The missing piece is proof: "demonstrating outcomes, nutritional outcomes, behavioral" outcomes (Abrahams) [13:01].
lessons.for_us:
- Elite players valued the explanation of what is in a product and why it helps them most (Pykälistö) [10:51]. My reading: ingredient fact sheets in plain words help our brand customers more than claims we cannot make.
- Claims rules limit what supplements can say, so the panel saw social media as the channel to share the science [12:01]. My reading: consistent with Holland & Barrett's view the day before (holland-barrett-fitness-generations).
- Relevance is low: a platform and technology discussion with no ingredients named.
quotes: "What consumers are really looking for is personalized health, and that encompasses body of mind, soul nutrition" Mariette Abrahams [00:42]
"In terms of how we track the market, the number of companies offering digital twins is very small. I mean, less than five, probably." Mariette Abrahams [03:02]
"...now we are in a situation where AI is proliferating men's speed, and the science is not catching up. The regulators are not catching up." Mariette Abrahams ("men's speed" is Otter's) [06:39]
"I think we have a lot of tech, a lot of data, but demonstrating outcomes, nutritional outcomes, behavioral" Mariette Abrahams [13:01]
lessons.detail:
- Names are Otter's speaker labels; roles come from the panellists' own decks at this event (abrahams-glp1-ai-personalised-nutrition, pykalisto-nutrigenomics). The fourth panellist is Otter's Speaker 3 (see to_check).
- Pykälistö (label): referred to "my presentation"; the line about working "in France for an association" that trains professionals in epigenetics and runs genetic testing is under the Pykälistö label; the same speaker said even oncologists ask for genetic tools because patients want personalisation [01:22].
- Hoevenaars: people need a road map of what they can do themselves [02:15]; Hoevenaars had seen digital twins used in Alzheimer's research and clinical practice, "really promising" [04:40].
- Pykälistö: those most in need cannot afford digital twins; a population-level twin with simpler measurements could help healthcare [04:13].
- Abrahams: the EU AI Act came into force before other regulatory measures; Abrahams noted the Pope speaking on AI ethics [06:02] [06:39].
- Speaker 3: doctors this panellist works with use AI to look at patient data in a different way; their clients check ChatGPT answers with them by email; "We still need the human mind" [07:08] [07:45].
- Speaker 3 on weight: weight management is "the gate opener" to energy, muscle, sleep and fewer menopausal symptoms; longevity seekers "want to live until 120 years" [09:19].
- Abrahams on trust: consumers want transparency and the counterpoint to benefits, not marketing; video is "exploding" [11:30].
- Final answers: Pykälistö, inspired by "the previous talk of Nathan" (taken to be price-ai-scientific-wellness), wants statistics that show personalised recommendations work [13:18]; Speaker 3 wants a wearable or tool that gives people their own health data [13:51].
- The Otter recording's own summary is filed as received (files/otter-summary.md).

lessons.title: Propelling a Stronger Future Through Partnership

speakers.name: Jane Durga
speakers.role: Scientific Affairs and Advocacy (Dr. Jane Durga in the programme)

lessons.summary:
Jane Durga of Balchem, speaking in the female athlete session, presented Balchem's branded ingredients for active women and its sports partnerships.

Durga opened with partnership: Balchem sponsors the FC Bayern Munich women's football team, paired on their slide with its vitamin K2 brand, K2VITAL, to raise awareness of women's health and create role models. Durga then walked through the range "on the field": K2VITAL for bones, heart and muscle; VitaCholine, choline for the brain-muscle connection; and Creatine MagnaPower, a creatine-magnesium blend that Durga said improves performance where creatine monohydrate plus magnesium did not. "Off the field" came OptiMSM for recovery.

Their nutrient-gap argument ran through iron, choline and folate. Athletes lose more iron than other people and may need up to 70% more; only 7% of US adult women get enough choline from food, and falling oestrogen at menopause limits the body's own choline supply. Chelated iron and methylfolate, Durga showed, are absorbed better than the common forms.

Their conclusion: women are helping shape and expand sports nutrition, and well-absorbed minerals, choline, K2, folate and MSM serve them through every life stage.
takeaways: Only 7% of adult women in the US get enough choline from food and beverage (USDA, NHANES 2017 to March 2020) (slide 5).
Choline in one study: targeting 9% closer and 2.6 times fewer misses in a visuomotor task against placebo (Naber et al. 2015) (slide 5).
Oestrogen helps the body make choline and declines at menopause, so "For Menopausal Athletes, Ensuring Adequate Choline Intake is Important" (slide 6).
The Institute of Medicine suggests the iron requirement "is up to 70% greater for those who engage in regular exercise" (slide 9).
Absorption: Ferrochel iron bisglycinate 4.7 times higher than ferrous sulphate; L-5-MTHF 2.25 times higher plasma levels than folic acid (slide 10).
Creatine MagnaPower, in one study, improved a performance measure that creatine monohydrate plus magnesium oxide did not (Brilla et al. 2003) (slide 7).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: no new science on our own brands, but Balchem competes with much of our range in exactly the women's and active-ageing positioning our customers are chasing.
- My reading, the overlap: K2VITAL against the BioK2 MK-7 we sell; Creatine MagnaPower against CreaWin; VitaCholine against our choline bitartrate; OptiMSM against our MSM; Ferrochel against our iron and magnesium bisglycinates; and L-5-MTHF against Advifolate.
- Their pitch is a nutrient gap plus a life stage plus a better-absorbed form (slide 6) (slide 10) (slide 11). My reading: the same structure works for our bisglycinates, choline and K2 in women's active nutrition, provided the claims are ones our customers can use in the EU; Balchem's own deck warns its claims may not suit marketing (slide 12).
- The team-sponsorship model (slide 3) is beyond our size; my reading, co-marketing with a customer's athlete partner is the realistic version.
- Related: the same female athlete session (women-in-sports-nutrition) and ostojic-creatine-lifelong-nutrition for creatine in women and ageing; Balchem's OptiMSM was also presented at Remedy CDMO 2026 (remedy-cdmo-2026/novosol-optimsm).
quotes: "We need to champion women, listen to their voices with greater intent." (slide 3)
"Choline transforms potential into performance as the champion of the mind -body connection." (slide 5)
"Women are helping shape and expand the sport nutrition category." (slide 11)
"MSM delivers recovery benefits – an overlooked aspect of performance nutrition." (slide 11)
lessons.detail:
- Slide numbers are the PDF's pages (12). The title slide names Durga and "Women’s Health" (slide 1). The closing slide says the information is for industry professionals, not consumers, that explicit or implied claims in it "may not necessarily be appropriate for marketing purposes", and is copyright 2024 Balchem (slide 12).
- K2VITAL, with the slide's hedges: MK-7 "may help trained athletes maintain maximal cardiac output during aerobic exercise"; K2 "supports ATP production"; K2 MK-7 "supports calcium uptake for strong bones and plays a role in the maintenance of bone mineral density" (slide 4). Slide 2 pairs K2VITAL with FC Bayern Munich Women as "The Perfect Pair" (slide 2).
- Choline is a component of cell membranes and of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, "critical for the connection between your brain and muscles"; it is found mainly in animal foods such as eggs and beef, and the body makes some but not enough (slide 5) (slide 6).
- Creatine MagnaPower: "a unique blend of creatine and magnesium" with "no loading phase required"; claims of improved cellular swelling and anabolic signalling, muscle power and torque, sprinting and bench press work capacity. The chart compares placebo, MgO plus creatine and Creatine MagnaPower before and after, with only Creatine MagnaPower significantly different from baseline; its y-axis is not labelled (slide 7).
- OptiMSM is "a source of sulfur", a component of glutathione; MSM supplementation "has been shown to" reduce oxidative stress after exercise, post-exercise pain and muscle damage, and improve the antioxidant response. The charts show lower pain change at 2 hours and lower exercise-related pain after leg extensions with OptiMSM 3,000 mg a day for 14 weeks (N=24, mean age 25.5) (slide 8).
- Athletes experience greater daily iron loss than the general population, especially in endurance sports such as running, rowing, HIIT, cycling and basketball; younger athletes need iron too (slide 9).
- Their five closing takeaways also include chelated minerals for "a time of lower micronutrient intake", choline for "cognition and active aging", and K2 and folate in "high quality, pure, stable forms"; Balchem names the NY Jets and FC Bayern Munich as team partners (slide 11).

lessons.title: Weight Loss & Long Term Outcomes

speakers.name: Mark Gilbert
speakers.organisation: The 1:1 Diet by Cambridge Weight Plan
speakers.role: Commercial Nutritionist (programme); Nutritionist in the deck's disclosures, also on the Science Committee of TDMR Europe

lessons.summary:
Mark Gilbert, a nutritionist at The 1:1 Diet by Cambridge Weight Plan and former ESSNA vice chair, challenged two established views about rapid weight loss with total diet replacement (TDR): that it costs disproportionately more lean body mass, and that the weight comes back faster.

On lean mass, Gilbert showed that weight loss of any kind removes fat and lean mass in proportion to how much is lost, with or without exercise, and after bariatric surgery too. Exercise adds little to diet for weight or lean mass. Every study Gilbert found comparing rapid TDR with slower dieting seemed, Gilbert said, to show no greater loss of lean mass.

On regain, Gilbert cited the DROPLET trial and Susan Jebb: faster early loss did not lead to faster regain, and those who lost fast were more likely to reach their target. A Copenhagen study kept all of a 10 kg loss over three years of maintenance with meal replacements.

Gilbert closed by asking what lean mass is. Only about 40% is muscle; organs also shrink with weight loss, and that may be healthy. Calorie restriction also triggers autophagy, a cellular clean-up linked to longer lifespan in research from yeast to primates.
takeaways: Weight loss reduces both fat and lean body mass "in proportion to degree of weight loss", usually even with exercise, and bariatric surgery does the same (slide 6).
Their conclusion on lean mass: "all of the comparator studies I found seem to disprove the idea that rapid, substantial weight loss (with TDR) causes greater LBM loss" (slide 16).

In the TEMPO trial (101 postmenopausal women with obesity), severe restriction for 4 months gave twice the weight and fat loss of moderate restriction for 12 months, about 1.5 times as much lean mass loss, and no greater adverse effect on relative lean mass or grip strength (slide 12).

On regain, Gilbert said experts now believe the idea that fast loss means fast regain "is a myth", citing DROPLET and Susan Jebb: the rapid group "were more likely to achieve their target weight loss and more likely to stick with the programme" (slide 18) (slide 19).
Only about 40% of lean body mass is muscle; other organs shrink with weight loss, and "it may be healthy for these other organs to shrink" (slide 22).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: TDR and meal replacement products are a protein-led format, and their argument answers the muscle-loss worry that drives much of the weight-management protein story (slide 16). My reading: their data are a counterpoint brands will hear.
- Their view differs from the muscle-protection message heard elsewhere: GLP-1 users' named need is protecting muscle (beyond-the-glp-1-boom-nutrition, from-hype-to-healthspan-building-the). Both are valid; Gilbert argues lean mass loss is proportionate and partly not muscle, and does not discuss GLP-1 medicines (slide 22). My reading: pitch protein and creatine for muscle on its own evidence, not on a claim that rapid weight loss uniquely wastes muscle.
- Cambridge Weight Plan's 1:1 Diet is a TDR brand (slide 2). My reading: a possible customer for proteins and other meal-replacement ingredients.
quotes: "Research “shows clearly that the common claim that more rapid initial weight loss is associated with more rapid regain is false…" Susan Jebb, as quoted on Gilbert's slide (slide 19)
"Experts now believe this is a myth" (slide 18)
"Furthermore, it may be healthy for these other organs to shrink…" (slide 22)
lessons.detail:
- Their roles: nutritionist at The 1:1 Diet by Cambridge Weight Plan; Science Committee at TDMR Europe; BASc (Nutrition), RNutr, CISSN; sports nutrition consultant on formulas, labels and regulation; pharma and clinical nutrition; former ESSNA vice chair; advisory board and columnist for M&F, Flex and Muscle Insider; co-founder of Fitness Genes and GoMetabolic (slide 2).
- Why lean mass matters: it is associated with healthy ageing, mobility, avoiding falls, survival and a higher metabolic rate, "BUT…Muscle is only one component of LBM" (slide 5).
- Exercise: used for weight loss it usually reduces lean mass; with diet it adds small, often insignificant effects; sustained supervised exercise gives about 2 kg loss (Wing, 1999) (slide 7).
- Weinheimer 2010 review: with diet, 75% of groups lost 5 to 10 kg; diet and exercise both left over 75% of groups losing 0 to 40% of fat-free mass; exercise gave under 5% loss in 94% of studies and 15% gained fat-free mass (slide 8) (slide 9).
- Bariatric surgery: 25 to 33% of loss as lean mass just over a year after surgery (Zalesin, 2010), rising with greater weight loss; up to at least 35% (Haghighat, 2021) (slide 10).
- Coxon 1989: women losing 1.9 kg a week against 1.1 kg a week over 8 weeks lost 0.42 and 0.44 of their weight as fat-free mass (slide 13).
- Coutinho 2018: 35 adults with obesity, 550 kcal TDR for 4 weeks against 1,200 to 1,500 kcal for 8 weeks; both lost about 9% of weight, with similar fat and fat-free mass loss, at 2.2 and 1.2 kg a week; in a one-month maintenance phase the rapid group significantly increased fat-free mass (slide 14).
- Ard 2016: 28 older adults with BMI over 35, 500 kcal deficit against 960 kcal TDR; total lean mass loss did not differ significantly (slide 15).
- DROPLET (University of Oxford, The BMJ): doctor referral of people with overweight to low-energy TDR (slide 18).
- Copenhagen study in people with knee osteoarthritis: intensive 800 kcal weight loss of 10 kg at 1 year, then 3 years of maintenance in 109 people with meal replacements or intermittent use; "Maintained 100% of weight loss – most successful LT weight maintenance study?" (slide 20). The chart shows mean body weight over 156 weeks (slide 21).
- Organ loss: DEXA, MRI and four-compartment research shows several organs beyond muscle shrink with weight loss of 9.5 kg (Bosy-Westphal, 2009) (slide 22).
- Autophagy: calorie restriction triggers it, and research on fasting and calorie restriction shows it "can help incr lifespan of everything from yeast & flies to primates" (Madeo 2015; Balasubramanian 2017) (slide 23).

lessons.title: Women in Sports Nutrition

speakers.name: Steffen Oesser
speakers.role: Director (programme); spoke on collagen peptide studies

speakers.name: Nicky Keay
speakers.role: Honorary Clinical Lecturer (programme); a medical doctor (as said)

lessons.summary:
A panel in the second day's Female Athlete session on nutrition for active women. The recording starts after the introductions; matched to the programme, the panel was Steffen Oesser (CRI), on collagen peptide studies; James Morton (SiS); the sports dietitian Renee McGregor; and the doctor Nicky Keay (UCL). The chair is not named.

The panel agreed that the old rigid rules for each day of the menstrual cycle have no evidence behind them. Recent studies, Morton said, largely show no difference in substrate use across the cycle, so the advice is back to fundamentals: fuel consistently, treat each woman as an individual, and coach rather than instruct. McGregor's main message was to stop demonising carbohydrates; Keay called a regular period "a free monthly medical check" and warned that missing ovulation can hide behind normal-looking cycles.

Oesser said research in women is growing and described studies of specific collagen peptides on tendons and ligaments, body composition, endurance in women and bone density in women, with results Oesser called outstanding and very promising.

Asked for one nutrient, Keay chose vitamin D across the lifespan, Morton iron for athletes, and McGregor none: needs come first.
takeaways: Recent studies largely show no difference in substrate metabolism across the menstrual cycle, Morton said; day-by-day cycle rules have no evidence, so fuel consistently [01:22] [13:50].

Oesser described studies of specific collagen peptides on ligaments and tendons (with a men-and-women analysis), on body composition alongside training, and on endurance in women only, with an "extra benefit" over placebo when combined with training [09:55].

Oesser also described a published study on bone density in women: one controlled year, then open-label follow-up to four years, where loss stopped and density rose; a second study with two controlled years is "very promising", final results awaited [22:45].

Keay: in the luteal phase progesterone slightly raises metabolic rate, so women may need a little more food; in a year-long study of dancers, many with periods were not ovulating or made too little progesterone [14:59] [20:48].
One nutrient each: vitamin D throughout the lifespan (Keay), iron especially for endurance athletes (Morton), none without a needs analysis (McGregor) [25:05] [26:44] [27:46].
lessons.for_us:
- Collagen peptide research in women is cited for tendons, body composition, endurance and bone [09:55] [22:45]. My reading: collagen for active women has a science story, though the product and the studies are not named in the recording (Oesser directs CRI, the Collagen Research Institute, per the programme); find them before using any of it.
- Vitamin D and iron were the two nutrients panellists would recommend [26:44] [27:46]. My reading: pair them with protein or collagen in women's active formats.
- The experts' message is fundamentals and individual needs, not cycle-syncing products [01:22] [25:05]. My reading: avoid pitching menstrual-phase claims to brands; they are the myths this panel set out to bust.
- Relevance is medium: women's sports nutrition is the growth group Euromonitor named the day before (euromonitor-sports-nutrition-trends), but the panel spoke little about ingredients we sell.
quotes: "...we have to stop demonizing carbohydrates." Speaker 2 (Renee McGregor, as matched to the programme) [25:28]
"...it's a free monthly medical check." Speaker 3 (Nicky Keay, as matched to the programme) [20:48]

"Actually, the only absolute supplement is vitamin D throughout the lifespan, because not only is it good for your well being, but it's also good for your bone health, also good for muscle recovery..." Speaker 3 (Nicky Keay, as matched to the programme) [26:44]
"And probably we're not getting enough iron, especially endurance athletes." Speaker 4 (James Morton) [27:46]
lessons.detail:
- Attribution: Speaker 1 is "Stefan" and Speaker 4 is "James", from how the chair and panel address them; Speaker 2 (the sports dietitian) mentions "Nikki" and Speaker 3 (the doctor) mentions "Rene" and "Greg". Matched to the programme's Female Athlete speakers, they are Oesser, Morton, McGregor and Keay; the chair is Speaker 5 (see to_check). Much of Oesser's audio is garbled in Otter, so Oesser's figures are not given here.
- Oesser said that in the past most studies were in men because a simple model avoids hormonal changes, and that this "now seems to switch", with more research focused on women in the pipeline [00:00] [09:55].
- Oesser's collagen peptide study on ligaments and tendons: "high effect size" and a benefit for professional athletes and "weekend warriors" (Otter's words) [09:55]. On body composition: "it's not enough to take this ingredient and sit on the couch"; training is needed [09:55].
- The bone study, as Oesser said it: progressive bone loss "stopped. It goes in the other direction"; not "turning the clock back to zero"; Oesser suggested it may delay the problems of bone loss by years (Otter's figure is garbled) [22:45].
- McGregor: women need equity, not only equality, in protocols [00:12]; practitioners need nuance, and social media spreads misinformation [03:13]; understand why an athlete fears carbohydrates or body changes [07:37]; every cycle differs with stress and travel, and knowing your own body is "the biggest gift we can give women" [17:35]; maintain carbohydrate availability, liquid or real food, for steadier performance [19:31]; too much monitoring is "creating more health anxiety" [25:28].
- Morton: change the people around an athlete, not only the athlete; "We're coaches" [05:21]. Morton's group surveyed about 600 female athletes; the biggest symptom was cramps (Otter: "crabs"), and low-fibre carbohydrate can keep fuelling on bad days [13:50]. Morton was surprised how little athletes knew about female physiology [19:09].
- Keay: hormonal contraception largely flattens the cycle's hormones, which many women do not realise [14:59]; loss of periods (functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea, heard as "FHA function, hyper NRA") is a "big red flag" for low energy availability [20:48].
- McGregor said national bodies refer players out to McGregor and a colleague heard as "Nikki" (taken as Keay) when in-house communication fails [07:37].
- The Otter recording's own summary is filed as received (files/otter-summary.md).

lessons.title: Branding that moves the right consumer in Active Nutrition
lessons.summary:
Marit Veenstra, a brand and innovation strategist at HMT, the Healthy Marketing Team, argued that active nutrition brands lose sales to confusion, not to weak science. Shoppers face too many options and unclear benefits, and many walk away without buying. Most launches fail, Veenstra said, because no one understood, trusted or felt anything for them.

Their answer is HMT's FourFactors: a consumer must see who needs the product, accept the ingredient, understand the benefit and trust the brand. The factors sit on an adoption curve that runs from technology and lifestyle buyers to the early mass market and the mass market. Niche trends start with low awareness; embedded trends are familiar to everyone.

Veenstra then split active consumers into four mindsets: professional athletes driven by need and proof, fitness influencers driven by beliefs and novelty, recreational sportspeople who want easy solutions, and "daily strollers" who want what is normal and familiar. Each needs its own message and its own kind of proof. Their examples were Upfront's protein matcha, sold in Dutch-language packs, and Heinz's lycopene drink.

Their conclusion: know where to play and how to win, and translate the message as a product moves from medical to trend to mass market.
takeaways: Shoppers are confused: 73% feel overwhelmed by too many choices, 72% are confused by how benefits are explained, and 74% have walked away without buying (Consumer Pulse Survey 2024, Waitrose 2024) (slide 6).
80% of new launches fail within 12 months, Veenstra said, not for weak science but because no one understood, trusted or felt anything for them (slide 8).
The FourFactors test for a concept: who needs it, is the ingredient accepted, is the benefit understood, is the brand trusted (slide 11) (slide 34).
There is not one active consumer but four mindsets, Need, Want, Solution and Normal, each with its own message and trust strategy (slide 19) (slide 35).
The professional athlete wants scientific proof, health claims and rational branding; the daily stroller wants taste, no change in habit and a mass-price brand (slide 20) (slide 23).
Crossing from medical to trend to mass market needs different messages, benefits and proof at each step (slide 35).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: a marketing framework, not ingredient science, but it is the lens our customers' brand teams use to judge an ingredient. Factor 2, "accept the ingredient", is where we sit (slide 11). My reading: our pitch decks should say which mindset an ingredient serves, with proof matched to it.
- Their Upfront example pairs 20g protein with matcha for "natural caffeine + L-theanine" energy and clarity, and Upfront also sells creatine tabs (slide 25) (slide 26). My reading: we sell matcha and creatine (CreaWin); Upfront is worth checking as a customer, starting with the creatine in its tabs.
- Their Heinz case puts lycopene in a fruit drink under a trusted food brand (slide 29). My reading: we sell lycopene (LycoLex); their point is that a familiar brand carries an unfamiliar ingredient into the mass market.
- HMT also presented on the probiotics category at Remedy CDMO 2026, the same speaker, as Nathan confirmed (remedy-cdmo-2026/hmt-probiotic-market); the misinformation side of this summit's marketing theme is millbank-nutrition-by-algorithm, and the regulatory side bucchini-essna-regulatory-update.
quotes: "Not because the science was wrong." (slide 8)
"I don’t care about hype — I need products that are proven, precise, and built to support my performance." (slide 20)
"I like what I know. I just want something that fits into my day without changing anything" (slide 23)
"Technology without storytelling stays invisible" (slide 35)
lessons.detail:
- Slide numbers are the PDF's pages (36). Small print on the framework images reads "Confidential © 2026 All rights reserved to HMT" and credits "Wennström's FourFactors® Brand Acceleration System ©2008", read from the images (slide 14) (slide 16).
- HMT says it has worked with over 500 brands in 60+ markets, and offers insights, strategy and positioning, brand building, and design (slide 2) (slide 3).
- Why confusion stops a purchase: trade-off stress, mental fatigue that leads people to default to the familiar "or nothing at all", and preference uncertainty (slide 7).
- The 80% failure figure is sourced to Richard Howells, Forbes, July 2011 (slide 8).
- The purchase decision is made "in a few seconds" at the shelf (slide 10). Factors 1 and 3 are "factors of motivation", factors 2 and 4 "factors of permission" (slide 11).
- The adoption chart has three lines: consumer awareness and volume (rising, then falling in the mass market), price and margin (falling over time), and a flat line for an innovation consumers do not pick up. Its strategy row reads NC, NSC, WCS, LHNA and FFMO, not spelled out on the slides (slide 14) (slide 16).
- Trends: niche trends enter with low awareness, emerging trends head towards the early mass market, embedded trends are familiar to all in the mass market (slide 16). The sticky notes on their title image read "individual health", "protein shift" and "gut health" (slide 13).
- Fitness influencers want products that fit them, match their values, are trendy, inspire them and make them feel special; recreational sportspeople want familiar, convenient, tasty products that fit their routines (slide 21) (slide 22).
- Upfront's FourFactors: need shown by an active young woman, the ingredient matcha, the benefits "20g protein = supports muscle maintenance" and matcha for "sustained energy + mental clarity", and trust in the Upfront brand. Veenstra placed the product among technology stakeholders on the curve (slide 26) (slide 27).
- Heinz: the Sunshine drink rests on lycopene and the Heinz Tomato Ketchup brand; Veenstra asked where it sits on the curve, then showed what works for ketchup: renovations, convenience, and a no-added-sugar-and-salt version with "NO compromise on taste" (slide 29) (slide 30) (slide 31).

lessons.title: Cognitive Health

speakers.name: Kristiina Singer
speakers.role: Clinical nutritionist (as introduced in the recording); Scientific Expert in Clinical Nutrition and Supplements (programme)

lessons.summary:
Kristiina Singer, a clinical nutritionist who has worked for Biogena for over ten years, opened the summit's last day with the case for natural cognitive support. Biogena is an Austrian family company that makes its own supplements near Salzburg and runs a flagship store in Vienna.

Their argument started with demand. Cognitive health is no longer only a concern of older people: in US data Singer showed, memory loss is the health problem adults under 40 fear most, and in Germany dementia is feared second only to cancer. Dementia cases are expected to reach 75 million worldwide by 2030 and roughly double by 2050.

Singer then turned to diet. The MIND diet, built on the Mediterranean and DASH diets and rich in berries and leafy greens, was linked in one study to a cognitive age 7.5 years younger. Polyphenols, and anthocyanins in particular, may help through new neurons, synaptic plasticity and protection against oxidative stress. Citicoline, a precursor of acetylcholine that crosses the blood-brain barrier, showed memory and attention effects in old and young people.

Biogena combines both, with activated B vitamins, in one product. Its sales are growing; over 60% of buyers are over 45, and about 16% are aged 25 to 35.
takeaways: Cognitive health is a concern for younger adults too: in US data from 2022, memory loss is the health problem people under 40 fear most [00:50].
A high MIND diet score was associated in one study with a cognitive age 7.5 years younger; Singer framed polyphenols as central to the diet [00:50].

Polyphenol studies Singer showed: 12 weeks of a blueberry powder standardised to 302 mg anthocyanins in 61 people over 65 improved flow-mediated dilation, systolic blood pressure and immediate recall; a single 600 mg dose of a polyphenol-rich extract in 30 students aged 18 to 25 gave more correct answers and fewer errors than placebo [00:50].

Citicoline studies Singer showed: brain ATP up 13.6% and membrane turnover up 26% in one study; better attention and psychomotor speed and less impulsivity in 75 healthy males aged 13 to 18; better overall and episodic memory in older adults [00:50].
Biogena's citicoline, polyphenol and activated-B-vitamin product is its fastest-growing: over 60% of buyers are over 45, and about 16% are 25 to 35 [00:50].
lessons.for_us:
- Citicoline was one of two ingredients a brand chose to build a cognitive product on, with study results quoted for teenagers as well as older adults [00:50]. My reading: support for pitching CogniWin to brands beyond the healthy-ageing shelf, including gaming and study occasions.
- The buyer data says cognition is reaching 25 to 35 year olds [00:50]. My reading: a combination with polyphenols, as Biogena makes, is a ready formulation idea for CogniWin.
- Biogena makes its own products in Austria and builds combinations from single-ingredient research [00:50]. My reading: a possible customer for citicoline and other range ingredients.
quotes: "...younger people under 40 years the memory loss is the number one health problem that they fear" Kristiina Singer [00:50]
"We research the effects of single substances, and then we make combinations which make sense." Kristiina Singer [00:50]
"The biggest group of buyers is 45 plus years is also, of course, here, over 60% of the consumers are over 45 years." Kristiina Singer [00:50]
lessons.detail:
- Biogena, as Singer described it: an Austrian family business for 20 years, production near Salzburg, over 300 products, a scientific team of 20, every batch checked by a third-party laboratory in Germany, and a focus on avoiding technical additives and raising bioavailability. The Vienna flagship store near the State Opera also offers diagnostics with doctors, laboratory tests, infusions and a biohacking area (cryotherapy, bone density checks, altitude training, light therapy) [00:50].
- An audience poll on what Germans fear most: the room put Alzheimer's and dementia first; the data Singer showed puts cancer first and Alzheimer's and dementia second, ahead of stroke and heart attack [00:50].
- Dementia cases worldwide: 75 million expected by 2030, with newer data saying over 82 million; 135 million by 2050, with a newer, higher figure Otter did not catch clearly [00:50].
- A review found the Mediterranean, DASH and MIND diets can reduce the risk of dementia and Alzheimer's disease; a 2024 Nature Medicine article said the MIND diet modifies risk factors such as hypertension, obesity and type 2 diabetes, which "could delay" dementia [00:50].
- Long-term berry and plant intake over 10 to 13 years has been associated with slower cognitive decline [00:50].
- The student study measured raised plasma flavonoids after the extract; Singer called it a safe way to acutely improve working memory and attention in healthy young people [00:50].
- Citicoline has been used as a neuroprotective drug since the 1970s and 1980s; Singer said it has good bioavailability and stabilises neuron membranes [00:50].
- Q&A: on dietary silica and aluminium, Singer said studies show an impact of aluminium and mercury but had no data to hand [28:19]. On mood, Singer treats it separately; Biogena has other products for mood and stress, one with 5-HTP [29:16]. The MIND diet limits fruit relative to vegetables partly because of sugar and fructose [29:16].
- The overview report attributes the 60% and 16% buyer figures both to this talk and to the Avea longevity talk (summit-overview-report, chabloz-avea-longevity-supplements).
- Related sessions: nordic-mushrooms-functional-mushrooms (lion's mane and cognition), ostojic-creatine-lifelong-nutrition (creatine and brain energy).

lessons.title: Editors' Recap
lessons.summary:
Two NutraIngredients hosts, Lauren Nicolle and Olivia Haslam, closed the summit with a six-minute run through what they had heard over three days.

They went through the programme roughly in order. Protein is still big, with hydration supplements rising in the US. There is a gap between how worried people are about sleep and how many buy sleep products. GLP-1 remains a major topic, with brands labelling products as supporting GLP-1 and the question of whether they have the right to make that claim.

From the female athlete session they took the culture of carbohydrate fear and a finding that the menstrual cycle may matter less than thought. Gut health and performance, personalisation, wearables that could mean fewer doctor visits, and a move from "healthy ageing" to "ageless" language followed. Cellular health, beauty from within and recovery were rising. Creatine as a possible semi-essential nutrient, regulation that makes it hard for brands to say what they want, and functional mushrooms rounded it off.

Haslam named active parenting as a space to watch; Nicolle suggested it for next year.
takeaways: Protein remains the biggest topic, and hydration supplements are rising in the US [00:00].
GLP-1: brands now label products as supporting GLP-1, and whether they may make that claim is an open question [00:51].
Female athletes: a culture of carbohydrate fear, and a finding that the menstrual cycle did not change what athletes need, which opens research questions [00:51] [02:35].
Ageless consumption: cellular health, beauty from within and recovery are coming to the fore [03:31] [04:19].
Regulation is convoluted, and many brands struggle to communicate what they want; how some get around it raises ethical questions [04:51].
lessons.for_us:
- Creatine was named among the summit's lasting topics, as a possible semi-essential nutrient [04:51]. My reading: confirms creatine's move beyond sport, the theme of ostojic-creatine-lifelong-nutrition, and supports CreaWin's wider pitch.
- Brands claiming GLP-1 support [00:51]. My reading: our GLP-1 companion pitches must stay within claims we can support.
- Relevance is low: a hosts' recap, not new data; the talks themselves carry the figures.

"it's interesting to see that there's little brands labeling their products with, you know, that they support GLP one, and whether they sort of have the right to make those claims" Olivia [00:51]
"how so many brands still have problems communicating the messages that they want to convey because of these strict regulations" Lauren [04:51]

lessons.title: Fireside with Tonic Health
lessons.summary:
Sunna Van Kampen, founder and CEO of Tonic Health, a UK supplement brand, talked with Olivia Haslam of NutraIngredients about building a brand almost entirely on social media.

Van Kampen started the business during COVID after finding that most supermarket supplements were dosed too low to correct deficiencies. Their products use what they called the right doses, without sugar, sweeteners or additives. Science-heavy podcasts and newsletters did not work: focus groups showed customers had no time for them. What did work was short videos, under 60 seconds, telling people to swap one product for another and why. After 10 to 15 TikTok posts, one reached 250,000 views; the brand now gets 50 million views a month.

Their case is that consumers buy supplements on trust and awareness, so click-through rates per post miss the point; they credit the brand's growth entirely to social media. They never make medical claims, but argue the ASA holds back science, and that regulators should focus on safety and fake products, such as a creatine brand found to contain no creatine.

Next come recipe content and a podcast with Channel Four.
takeaways: The brand's origin: most supermarket supplements were "such low dose" that they did little; Tonic set out to give "the right doses" without sugar, sweeteners and additives [01:11].
Science content did not reach consumers; under-60-second "swap this for this" videos did, starting on TikTok [02:43] [04:41].
They do not promote their own products on social media: it is now entertainment media, where the best content wins regardless of followers [05:22].
Supplements are bought on trust and awareness, so per-post sales tracking is "a big waste of time"; a team of six grew the brand on social media alone [06:42].
Regulation should target safety and fraud: they cited 75% of mushroom brands on Amazon not containing the mushroom, and a creatine brand with about 10 million in sales and no creatine in it [13:06].
lessons.for_us:
- Their pitch rests on proper doses against under-dosed supermarket products [01:11]. My reading: brands like this need ingredients they can dose at study levels and explain simply.
- The creatine fraud example [13:06]. My reading: tested, traceable creatine with a certificate of analysis per batch is a selling point for CreaWin with brands worried about their reputation.
- Social media brands are held to account by their audience on formulation and claims [08:11]. My reading: clean labels and claims we can support protect our customers as well as us.
quotes: "Now it's really not social media anymore. It's entertainment media" Sunna [05:22]
"Consumers shop in supplements. According to the data I have from Intel in the UK, they shop on trust often and awareness" Sunna [06:42]
"there was a creatine brand that got to about 10 million sales before anyone tested their product" Sunna [13:06]
lessons.detail:
- The first viral video came after "maybe 1015 posts" (10 to 15) on TikTok, with about 250,000 views; they were early to TikTok as social media moved from pictures to video [04:41].
- They said social media is now the number one source of news globally, bigger than TV, and the only channel that lets a brand grow without millions to spend on TV [08:11].
- Risks: a competitor (Otter heard "fuel") paid influencers for take-down posts of the brand; audiences call out formulations and untrue claims [08:11].
- Regulation: other supplement websites link products to autism and ADHD without data; they never make medical claims but will "push the ASA" where science is ahead of the rules, and asked "Who is the ASA?" They called UK health "a mess" [10:53].
- The mushroom figure refers to an earlier talk that morning (nordic-mushrooms-functional-mushrooms) [13:06].
- They argued that factory farming and ultra-processed food reduce the nutrition people get, so more supplements will be needed [14:07].
- Next: recipe content showing how easy it is to eat whole foods, and a podcast launching "next week, Friday" with Channel Four, with celebrity guests; an earlier podcast failed for lack of distribution [14:07] [17:13].
- On criticism: they do not argue in comment sections; debate belongs on the podcast. They commended a protein brand for moving to stevia while disagreeing with it, and used baked versus fried crisps to show health is a step-by-step journey [18:28] [19:55].
- Early posts about the brand itself did not work; supermarket content about bread, wine and yoghurt reached the mass market [21:47].
- An in-house nutritionist answers every direct message, hundreds a day [22:56].
- Related sessions: millbank-nutrition-by-algorithm (nutrition misinformation on social media), bucchini-essna-regulatory-update (claims regulation), veenstra-hmt-branding (branding), editors-recap.
