lessons.title: Functional Mushrooms
lessons.summary:
Eric Puro, co-founder and CEO of Nordic Mushrooms, which makes mushroom extracts in Finland, made the case for functional mushrooms in brain health and then warned that much of the market does not contain what its labels say.

Puro opened with growth: their slides put the global functional mushroom market on course for $65B by 2030. Their lead example was lion's mane for the brain: Puro presented nerve growth factor and BDNF as the mechanism, and their company's human trial in healthy adults, which their slide says showed better working memory, complex attention and reaction time, with effects building week on week where caffeine's fade.

Then the problem. In an Italian study, 13 of 19 mushroom supplements did not contain the listed mushroom; in a US study, 74% of reishi supplements did not contain the listed ingredients. Puro named poor-quality material from China as the industry's biggest risk, and argued that the usual quality markers, polysaccharides and beta-glucans, are not what delivers the benefits. Each species should be specified on its own compounds: hericenones and hericenes for lion's mane, cordycepin for cordyceps, ganoderic and lucidenic acids for reishi, inotodiol for chaga.

Puro closed with their NordRelease extraction, which their slide credits with 92% bioavailability, and trials under way on lion's mane and chaga.
takeaways: Market: from $25B to $65B "in ten years" on one slide, and $31B growing to $65B by 2030 at 11% CAGR on another, both credited to Horizon Grand View Research; growth of 31% in 2023, credited to the American Botanical Council (slide 3) (slide 4) (slide 5).

Their company's lion's mane trial: healthy adults, four weeks, 50 participants, lion's mane extract against caffeine and placebo (La Monica et al. 2023); their slide says lion's mane "improves cognitive performance, enhancing working memory, complex attention, and reaction time" (slide 11) (slide 12).

Quality failures: 13 of 19 Italian mushroom supplements did not contain the listed mushroom; 74% of US reishi supplements did not contain the listed ingredients, 58% showed no reishi triterpenes, and a key reishi polysaccharide was found in only 26.3% (slide 16) (slide 18).
"The biggest industry risk is poor quality material from China." (slide 19)
Polysaccharides and beta-glucans are, Puro said, not responsible for the benefits people want; quality should be specified on each species' own compounds (slide 21) (slide 22) (slide 23).
Extraction, as their slide puts it: water 5% bioavailability, dual alcohol-and-water extraction 50% and flagged as "Novel non EU approved extraction technology", NordRelease 92% (slide 25).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high: we sell lion's mane, reishi, chaga and cordyceps extracts and a mushroom blend, and our specs lead with polysaccharides and beta-glucans, the markers Puro called the wrong ones (slide 21). My reading: expect customers who heard this to ask for hericenone and hericene, cordycepin, triterpene and inotodiol content; one of our lion's mane extracts already states 1% hericenone.
- Their adulteration evidence and their warning about Chinese material (slide 16) (slide 18) (slide 19). My reading: identity testing and origin for each mushroom SKU should be ready before a customer asks.
- Their slide calls dual extraction a novel technology not approved in the EU (slide 25). My reading: check how each of our mushroom extracts is made and its Novel Food status before selling into the EU; this is their claim and needs checking against the Novel Food catalogue.
- Nordic Mushrooms is a possible supplier or partner for a Finnish, compound-specified range; my reading, not a lead yet.
- Related: the mind-health session's other speakers, e.g. singer-biogena-cognitive-health; caffeine as the comparator ties to the energy positioning in veenstra-hmt-branding.
quotes: "13 out of 19 products tested did not contain the actual listed mushroom." (slide 16)
"74% of reishi mushroom supplements did not contain the ingredients listed on the product." (slide 18)
"The biggest industry risk is poor quality material from China." (slide 19)
"It’s important to align the needs of consumers with the compounds per species." (slide 23)
lessons.detail:
- Slide numbers are the PDF's pages (28). The title slide reads "Honest and potent mushroom extracts from Finland"; several slides are headed "KÄÄPÄ Mushrooms", and their contact and the NordRelease news link are at Kääpä Biotech (slide 1) (slide 9) (slide 25) (slide 28).
- The market chart is in US$M, 2018 to 2030, with bars from about 20,000 in 2018 to about 65,000 in 2030, read from the chart; its two headline figures differ, $25B as the 2020 start on one slide and $31B as today's market on another (slide 3) (slide 5). Slide 4 carries both a Grand View label and the American Botanical Council Market Report Issue 141 as sources for the 31% figure (slide 4).
- A large market means a large body of research: "1586 results for Reishi alone" (slide 6).
- Lion's mane, as their slides put it: nerve growth factor stimulation, BDNF, "reduction of amyloid beta plaque build-up", neuroprotective and neurocognitive benefits, gastroprotective effects; primary compounds hericenones and hericenes. The problem slide reads "Loss of NGF", and a footnote says depression correlates with significantly lower NGF levels (Chen et al. 2015) (slide 7) (slide 9) (slide 10).
- The paper shown is La Monica et al., "Acute Effects of Naturally Occurring Guayusa Tea and Nordic Lion's Mane Extracts on Cognitive Performance", Nutrients 2023; 15(24): 5018. The slide calls it the "first human clinical research with healthy adults" (slide 11).
- Their slide's further points on the trial: "Results steadily growing weekly", a "stacking effect" of neuroregeneration in which "the impact on mood and cognition effectively gets better every time", and caffeine's effect diminishing over time "because the body builds tolerance" (slide 12).
- Myelin: quoted findings that H. erinaceus extract and its compounds HeA and HeS "display promising functional effects and promote OL maturation", and a regulatory effect on myelin genesis in vitro, under the heading "Potential for myelin regeneration" (slide 13).
- The Italian study is Risoli et al., "Mushroom-Based Supplements in Italy: Let's Open Pandora's Box" (PubMed 36771482): most facilities lacked internationally recognised GMP and some products had contaminants above legal limits (slide 15) (slide 16).
- The US study is Wu et al., "Evaluation on Quality Consistency of Ganoderma Lucidum (Reishi) Dietary Supplements Collected in the United States", Scientific Reports 2017; it concluded quality consistency "was poor" (slide 17) (slide 18).
- Quality markers Puro showed as current: beta-glucans (a Nammex white paper), polysaccharides (Chinese products); their alternative is "bioactive compounds (beyond beta glucans)" (slide 22).
- Compounds and benefits by species: chaga, inotodiol, for longevity and antioxidants; reishi, ganoderic and lucidenic acids, for calmness and sleep; lion's mane, hericenones and hericenes, for brain health and focus; cordyceps, cordycepin and adenosine, for energy and endurance (slide 23).
- History: Ötzi the Iceman (3230 BC) carried two polypores, one probably used medicinally; mushrooms in Han Dynasty medicine (202 to 220 AD); NordRelease introduced in 2019, with a linked news item titled as an EU approval of Kääpä Biotech's NordRelease extract powders (slide 25).
- Trials under way: lion's mane and neurogenesis over 3 months; chaga and stem cell regeneration in healthy ageing; chaga and mitochondrial function and longevity (slide 27).

lessons.title: Regulatory Updates, Challenges & Opportunities in Active Nutrition
lessons.summary:
Luca Bucchini, Chair of ESSNA, the European trade association for sports and active nutrition, set out the regulatory issues facing the sector in Europe.

The biggest is maximum amounts of vitamins and minerals. Limits differ between member states today, so a product legal in Belgium may not be legal in Italy. The European Commission has restarted work to harmonise them, and a leaked working document suggested very restrictive limits: sodium might not be allowed in electrolyte drinks without added sugars, and vitamin B6 or potassium might not be allowed in drinks. Bucchini said the real cost is lost functionality and lost health claims, not one-off reformulation. Yet harmonisation matters: if it fails, France and perhaps Germany may set even tighter limits.

Bucchini then covered health claims, where approvals have dried up and botanical claims remain on hold; novel foods, where the scope has grown and approval is slow and costly; the Green Claims Directive; ultra-processed foods, whose definition could catch sports products; and influencers normalising steroids for Gen Z.

Their conclusion: after many years of regulatory certainty, the sector faces a new wave of concern. If the maximum levels are set right, they could open markets.
takeaways: The European Commission plans EU-wide maximum amounts for vitamins and minerals in supplements and fortified foods; details "may change", but "very restrictive" limits may come, for example no sodium in electrolyte drinks without added sugars [00:00] (slide 7).
Bucchini said the real loss would be functionality and the ability to make authorised health claims, not one-off reformulation costs [00:00] (slide 8).
Harmonisation still matters: if it fails, "France (and potentially Germany)" appear poised to propose even more restrictive maximum amounts [00:00] (slide 8).

Health claims: valid claims have been rejected, "on hold" botanical claims fragment the market, approvals have stopped and applications have fallen to zero; new sports probiotics cannot communicate their benefits [00:00] (slide 9).
Novel foods: the regulation's scope has expanded and approval is "expensive, lengthy and complex"; the EFSA performance review may be a chance to streamline it [00:00] (slide 10).

Influencers are making steroid use look normal to Gen Z; ESSNA is working with authorities, Europol included, and calls on the industry to explain what safe sports nutrition is [00:00] [14:58] (slide 13).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance high: EU maximum amounts, health claims and novel food rules decide what our customers can formulate and say with our ingredients.
- Our vitamin and mineral ingredients (the iron and magnesium bisglycinates, BioK2 MK-7, Advifolate) sit inside the maximum-amounts work (slide 7). My reading: follow ESSNA's position and the Commission's draft so we can tell customers early if a dose they use is at risk.
- Botanical claims stay on hold (slide 9). My reading: for botanicals we sell, such as KSM-66 ashwagandha, pitches rest on the science, not on an EU claim, and that will not change soon.
- Novel food approval is slow and costly (slide 10). My reading: any new ingredient we bring to the EU should have its novel food status settled before launch plans.
quotes: "...the real problem is that we lose functionality. We lose ability to communicate, in some cases, sodium." Luca Bucchini [00:00]
"So it's a difficult balancing act, we still hope." Luca Bucchini [00:00]
"So it's very difficult to do innovation." Luca Bucchini [00:00]
"Ultra-Processed Foods should not be our concern," (slide 14)
lessons.detail:
- ESSNA was created in 2003 "to prevent the introduction of EU legislation which could have been damaging to the industry"; it represents the whole supply chain to national and European policy-makers (slide 4). Its objectives include EU-UK regulatory divergence and "Tackling inadvertent doping, non-compliance and unscrupulous online vendors" (slide 5).
- Their example of today's patchwork: a 2 g vitamin C capsule, one a day, cannot be sold in France or Italy [00:00]. The Commission first tried to harmonise about five years ago, and has restarted; the work covers supplements and foods such as protein bars and drinks [00:00].
- Bucchini heard of the leaked working document through a member's call about sodium a few months before; ESSNA is engaging member states and the Commission so sports nutrition's needs are considered [00:00] (slide 8).
- The claims system was meant to reward companies that spend millions on trials; Bucchini showed a chart of rejected and approved claims and said approvals stopped long ago and applicants have lost trust [00:00]. The slide asks for "A more flexible approach for structure-function claims for sports benefits" (slide 9).
- Novel food: an officer from a German-speaking country told them a mango smoothie nobody had made before 1997 would be a novel food [00:00].
- Green Claims Directive: the slide says European institutions are negotiating the final text (slide 11); in the talk Bucchini said the Commission had decided to pull the proposal after a political backlash [00:00]. The two differ; the deck predates the talk.
- Ultra-processed foods: the definition is not consistent and sports nutrition products may fit it "at least from a formal standpoint"; reviews are under way in the UK and EU, and ESSNA is monitoring the definitions (slide 12). Bucchini said the mechanism behind the epidemiology is not known [00:00].
- Social media: Bucchini told Europol's annual meeting about the problem; brands are being built on steroids and other substances, injectable and in pills, and a German customs officer linked seized products to an influencer-promoted brand [00:00] [14:58] (slide 13).
- The deck is dated 23.6.2025 on most slides; some carry a template date "2x.6.2025" (slide 4) (slide 5).

lessons.title: Biotics Unleashed: How microbiome science and health tech transform consumer choices
lessons.summary:
Ewa Hudson of Lumina Intelligence presented consumer survey data on biotics and health tech. The deck is the short version released for distribution. Their question: how changing health goals, medicines such as GLP-1 drugs and technology shape what consumers buy for their microbiome.

The data come from Lumina's Global Nutrition Research for NutraIngredients, November 2024, with 6,000 respondents. In the five European countries shown, ageing in good health and better sleep are the top two health goals. Sleep, stress and mental health lead for younger adults; longevity enters the top three at 45 to 54 and leads from 55.

Europeans who take biotics do so mainly for the gut microbiome, general wellbeing and immunity. Few take them for sleep or mood, or alongside antibiotics. Hudson set this against two numbers: 84% think they lead a healthy life, yet 70% took antibiotics, GLP-1 drugs, laxatives, metformin or proton-pump inhibitors in the past two years.

Their close was technology. Over half use health or fitness apps, and almost all of those buy a product an app recommends at least once a year. Their message: tech is changing behaviour, so build new habits on it.
takeaways: Ageing in good health and longevity ranks first or second as a health goal in all five countries; better sleep ranks first in France and the UK; mood and mental health ranks first in Spain (slide 5).
By age, sleep, stress and mental health are the top three goals from 18 to 44; longevity joins at 45 to 54 and leads at 55 to 64 and 65 plus, with sleep and weight, read from the chart (slide 6).

Why Europeans take biotic supplements, food and beverages: to improve the gut microbiome 15%, general wellbeing 14%, immunity 14%, digestive issues 10%, energy 8%, sleep 6%; alongside antibiotics only 4% (slide 7).

84% believe they lead a very or fairly healthy life, but 70% took antibiotics, GLP-1 drugs, laxatives, metformin or proton-pump inhibitors in the past two years; regular users: antibiotics 7%, GLP-1 receptor agonists 5%, laxatives 8% (slide 8).

54% use health or fitness apps or trackers, and 93% of them buy an app-recommended supplement, sports nutrition product or meal plan at least once a year: 26% monthly, 52% quarterly, 22% once a year (slide 9).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: consumer data on health goals and buying, not on our ingredients. It touches us through fitness, energy and healthy ageing, and through apps as a route to sports nutrition buyers.
- Optimising fitness and performance ranks third in Germany, fourth in France, fifth in Spain, sixth in Italy and tenth in the UK; energy ranks fourth in Spain and the UK (slide 5). My reading: performance is a mid-table goal in Europe; healthy ageing leads, which supports pitching CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea to healthy-ageing brands within each ingredient's own evidence.
- 93% of app users buy an app-recommended supplement, sports nutrition product or meal plan at least once a year (slide 9). My reading: fitness apps are a recommendation channel our sports nutrition customers could use; a lead for their marketing, not ours.
- Their November 2026 talk at the Nutra Healthspan Summit, on a newer survey (July 2026, 10,500 people, nine countries), also put energy and strength among the top three ageing concerns in every age band (lumina-new-longevity-consumer). The two surveys ask different questions; both are given.
quotes: "Ageing in good health and improving sleep are key health concerns in Europe" (slide 5)
"Let’s adapt Maslow’s Pyramid of Needs to the evolving Health Needs with AGE" (slide 6)
"Tech is transforming consumer behaviours, let’s create new habits" (slide 9)
lessons.detail:
- The deck is the "for distribution" short version; slide 2 says Hudson examined how changing health goals and medication use, "particularly GLP-1 agonists", influence microbiome health and buying, and offers the full version for download (slide 2). The link is not in the PDF.
- Survey base: Global Nutrition Research (Nov 2024), 29 questions, 6,000 respondents, 9 countries (China, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, South Korea, Spain, the UK, the USA), in four parts: general wellness, health tech, biotics, sports and active (slide 4). The charts on slides 5 to 9 are sourced to 5 European countries (France, Italy, Germany, Spain, UK), still marked n=6,000 (slide 5). Which base each chart uses is to confirm.
- Health goal ranks, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, UK: ageing in good health and longevity 2, 1, 1, 2, 2; better sleep 1, 2, 2, 3, 1; mood and mental health 5, 5, 5, 1, 6; managing stress 3, 7, 3, 7, 5; healthier weight 6, 4, 8, 5, 3; fitness and performance 4, 3, 6, 5, 10; energy 7, 8, 7, 4, 4; immunity 8, 6, 4, 10, 7; digestive health 9, 10, 9, 8, 8; skin 10, 9, 10, 9, 9. Hunger and insulin peaks, hormonal health and fertility, and menopause rank 11 to 13 everywhere (slide 5).
- The bottom three goals at every age are fertility and hormonal health, hunger and menopause, in shifting order, read from the chart (slide 6).
- Other reasons for taking biotics: heart health 5%; mood, anxiety, depression and stress 5%; reducing side effects of drugs other than antibiotics 5%; skin 5%; weight loss or preventing obesity 4%; women's health 3%; men's health 2%; first 1,000 days 1% (slide 7).
- Healthy life: very healthy 15%, fairly healthy 73%, not very healthy 11% (slide 8). The slide's headline adds "5% of regulars and 8% of irregular users in Europe"; it does not say of what (slide 8).
- App users by purpose, read from the chart: diets 19%, fertility 10%, fitness 33%, mind and mood about 14%, overall health about 18%, menopause and pregnancy small (slide 9).
- Slide 3 describes Lumina Intelligence as consumer research for ingredient suppliers, brand owners and retailers (slide 3). Lumina is part of the William Reed group, which runs NutraIngredients (lumina-new-longevity-consumer).
- Figures are from a November 2024 survey, presented in February 2025. No slide is marked Confidential.
- Cross-reference with their November 2026 talk (lumina-new-longevity-consumer): there, 22% named probiotics among the categories most helpful for healthspan, and 6.1% of UK adults currently used GLP-1 drugs. Here, 5% of Europeans are regular GLP-1 users (slide 8). Different surveys, dates and questions; both are given.

lessons.title: Alba Health (Probiota Pioneers 2025)
lessons.summary:
Nora Cavani, co-founder of Alba Health, pitched as one of NutraIngredients' Probiota Pioneers for 2025. Alba Health, based in Sweden, sells a gut microbiome test for children aged nought to two, with a diet plan and probiotic recommendations.

Cavani started the company after their own eczema. Their argument is that how microbes settle in a baby's gut in the first years is linked to later asthma, obesity, eczema and allergies, and to everyday symptoms such as colic and constipation that have no good answer today. Testing early could spot imbalances and correct them with diet, lifestyle and possibly probiotics.

Their edge is data: a partnership with a University of Helsinki study that followed 1,000 children for over six years, and its own Swedish cohort of 300 children. Customers report their children's eczema or constipation easing, though no trial was presented.

In the panel Cavani said their biggest hurdle is consumer education. Alba Health sells no probiotics of its own and recommends other companies' products with clinical evidence; Cavani said most customers buy the one recommended. Given money for one thing, Cavani would spend it on marketing.
takeaways: The product: "a gut microbiome test specifically developed for children, zero to two years old", used to detect imbalances early, restore them with diet and possibly probiotics, and track development [14:42].

Evidence claimed is the partner cohort: 1,000 children followed for over six years, over 10,000 samples, over 50,000 data points on diet and health; Cavani said a 2024 paper showed an early-life test predicts later allergies, coughs, colds and crying [14:42].
Results so far are customer reports: "a lot of our users and customers tell us that their children's eczema or constipation significantly reduced" [14:42].
Alba Health recommends existing probiotics from other companies and takes no profit on them; "most of our customers buy the probiotic we recommend" [49:19].
Trust comes from a scientific advisory board with doctors from each market, and simple messages through social media and podcasts [47:04].
90% of customers opt into research [14:42] [51:58].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: a test for infants, outside our sports and healthy-ageing markets and our range.
- My reading: an independent recommender that sells nothing itself can drive which branded probiotic a parent buys. That is a channel worth knowing for any partner with a clinically backed strain.
- My reading: the panel's shared lesson, that education is the hurdle and that a neutral expert voice beats ads, applies to how we pitch evidence-based ingredients to brands.
quotes: "the gut microbiome in early life is both linked to here and now, symptoms that have no solution today, but also to health later life" [14:42]
"when people see ads, they're so used to just filtering them out as ads" [49:19]
"we every time we deliver our results, we do that with a certified nutrition and health coach" [55:45]
lessons.detail:
- Figures Cavani gave: one in three people in the US has an allergic disease and almost two in three a chronic disease; the UN puts chronic diseases' cost at $47 trillion by 2030; 40% of US children have at least one chronic disease; over 50% of babies have unresolved symptoms such as colic and constipation [14:42].
- Cavani tied this to diet: a Swedish public health warning, two days earlier, that children eat more processed food and little fibre [14:42].
- Own cohort: 300 children, over 1,000 samples, over 300,000 health data points, with universities in Sweden, Denmark and Belgium [14:42].
- Company: started three years earlier with a professor co-founder; 2.6 million raised in pre-seed in the past year; "well over 1000 tests since the fall"; a market opportunity Cavani put at 80 billion; publications in microbiome science rose to 20,000 a year in 2024 [14:42].
- Each sample carries answers to over 300 questions on diet, probiotic and formula use; Alba Health complies with GDPR and uses a consent form [51:58].
- On whether testing makes parents of healthy children anxious: Cavani said they have not seen it; results are delivered on a call with a nutrition and health coach, with doctors for children with symptoms [55:45].
- Their differentiator: scientific credibility with universities and doctors plus very simple explanations, both in-house [51:58].
- The moderator described Alba Health as a Danish-Swedish company using machine learning and metagenomics [13:38]. Figures date from February 2025.

lessons.title: DynaMAP – Precision metagenomics beyond sequencing
lessons.summary:
Arno Bouwens, R&D Director at Perseus Biomics, one of NutraIngredients' Probiota Pioneers for 2025, presented DynaMAP, the company's way of profiling a microbiome without sequencing. Their problem: benefits are strain-specific and labels must name the strain, but today's methods have low resolution and sensitivity.

DynaMAP labels long strands of native DNA with fluorescent dye at a short sequence motif, stretches and images them, and matches each pattern of dots to a reference database. Because it reads genome structure, Bouwens said it can tell apart strains almost identical in sequence, without PCR amplification.

Their evidence is the company's own preprint. In a standard mock community all strains were found, spikes down to 0.1% were detected, and strains up to 99.9% identical were told apart. On a stool sample, results matched shotgun sequencing closely.

Bouwens closed with the roadmap: a profiling service from the company's lab in Belgium with under five days' turnaround, available now, and a benchtop device from the second quarter of 2025.

In the panel Bouwens said customers had failed to find their own probiotic in samples with amplification-based methods. Their customers are experts, so the hurdle is conservatism, not education; new money would go on marketing.
takeaways: The pitch: strain specificity drives benefit, and labels must declare genus, species and strain, yet current methods face low resolution, sensitivity issues and noise (slide 2).

The method reads 100,000+ long native DNA molecules per sample in under 20 minutes; the label pattern on each is a taxonomic barcode "down to strain level" (slide 4). Strains with average nucleotide identity (ANI) above 99.5% were told apart, and up to 99.9% in the mock community (slide 7) (slide 8).

In the Zymo D6300 mock community it had a 100% recall rate, no significant Gram-positive against Gram-negative bias, a limit of detection better than 0.1%, and no false positives above 0.05% (slide 6).
On one healthy adult's stool sample, profiles correlated 70 to 80% (log-log) with shotgun metagenomic sequencing, with equivalent reproducibility (slide 9).
In the panel: customers came to Perseus after failing to detect their probiotic in samples, "most likely because of amplification bias"; shotgun sequencing and DynaMAP found it [54:50].
Roadmap: a service from an EU-based central lab, under 5 business days, available now; a fully automated benchtop device with a 6-hour turnaround, from Q2 2025 (slide 10).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: a microbiome testing technology for probiotic makers and researchers; it touches none of our ingredients or our sports and healthy-ageing markets.
- My reading: strain-level identity checks matter to probiotic brands and their quality control, the same proof-of-identity question buyers ask of any branded ingredient. Background only.
quotes: "Strains specificity maximizes therapeutic benefits…" (slide 2)
"DynaMAP measures strain-level resolved microbiome profiles" (slide 5)
"Strains with ANI higher than 99.5% can be differentiated with DynaMAP!" (slide 7)
"amplification bias can be so strong that it altogether misses some species" [54:50]
lessons.detail:
- Slide 2 reproduces a figure from Spacova et al., Frontiers in Microbiology 2023: probiotic foods and probiotic supplements, the claims generally possible (structure-function, nutrient, general or strain-specific health claims and disease risk reduction, requiring pre-approval), and the labelling of genus, species, subspecies and strain (slide 2).
- Five steps and times: high-molecular-weight DNA extraction; fluorescent labelling (about 60 minutes); molecular combing (about 10 minutes); optical mapping (about 20 minutes); matching to a reference database (about 30 minutes) (slide 3).
- Strains can share over 99% ANI yet differ in genome structure; DynaMAP labels a site such as "TCGA" on fragments over 30 kbp and reads native DNA without amplification (slide 5).
- Mock community: eight bacteria at 12.5% each, three easy-to-lyse Gram-negative and five tough-to-lyse Gram-positive; spike-ins at 1%, 0.1% and 0.01%; the 1% and 0.1% spikes were reliably detected by both DynaMAP and sequencing (slide 6).
- Strain test: the reference database held all complete NCBI genomes over 200 kb; for Enterococcus faecalis the true strain was identified and the nearest false positives had ANI over 99.9% (slide 7). The slide's own definition puts the strain threshold at ANI 99.5% to 99.9% (slide 8).
- Stool test: five aliquots of one sample, compared with Kraken classification of sequencing on the same reference database, GTDB taxonomy (slide 9).
- Spoken: the central lab is "based in Belgium", turnaround "less than five days", and the device for use in a customer's own lab is being introduced "this year" [31:35].
- The shotgun comparison used about 10 gigabases of sequencing [43:01].
- Cost: "we were able to reach the same level as 60 this" (Otter; the method compared is unclear), including sample preparation and bioinformatics; a relative abundance profile is delivered [43:21].
- Customers hold their data and can reprocess it, under the FAIR principles [50:35]. What makes a microbiome start-up stand out, Bouwens said, is data quality, comparable across technologies [53:58].
- All performance data are the company's own, from its preprint (bioRxiv, December 2024) (slide 6). Figures and the roadmap date from February 2025; whether the benchtop device launched is not known. No slide is marked Confidential.

lessons.title: Gut-brain axis panel discussion

speakers.name: Dr Siobhain O'Mahony
speakers.organisation: APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork

lessons.summary:
Stephen Daniells of NutraIngredients chaired the Day 1 gut-brain panel after the break. Siobhain O'Mahony of APC Microbiome Ireland and Julia Rode of Örebro University had spoken before it; Katie Guzzetta of ETH Zurich and Emily Prpa, head of science at Yakult UK and Ireland, joined them. Daniells's question: how far does the science on gut microbes and the brain really go?

The panel agreed it is early. Most human evidence comes from clinical groups, such as people with depression, where probiotics helped as an add-on to treatment rather than on their own. Data on cognition in humans are sparse, and trials in healthy people are few, short and measure small shifts on subjective scales. Prpa said nutritional psychiatry is only about 50 years old and that probiotics are food, not medicine.

On products, nobody could say whether single strains or blends work better, and O'Mahony said formulators are limited to the few strains that are stable and safe. Prebiotics may need the right bacteria present first, which points to synbiotics.

Guzzetta brought mouse work: faecal transplants from young to old mice improved memory, and gut-made acetate reached the brain. Guzzetta warned that gut-made serotonin or GABA probably does not reach the brain. The recording ends as the panel turned to athletes' microbiomes.
takeaways: Most of the evidence is in clinical populations, with only a handful of studies in healthy people, and what counts as a good enough outcome in a healthy person is still unclear (Emily Prpa) [1:03:46].

In bipolar and major depressive disorder, probiotics "can be well effective when used as an adjunct, not when administered on their own"; Prpa said translating that to the everyday person is not there yet, and randomised trials run about 12 weeks at most [1:08:40].

Cognition in humans has little data; probiotics are the best studied, "But also there, it's quite sparse", and repeat testing makes change hard to capture (Julia Rode) [1:06:34] [1:07:09]. The panel asked whether prevention, before disease, is the window to act [1:07:33] [1:08:00].

Single strain or multi-strain cannot be called: the studies differ in products, doses and durations (Rode) [1:11:44]; O'Mahony finds the single-strain evidence compelling but says formulators can only use the few strains that are stable and safe [1:12:47].

A single prebiotic such as inulin may fail in depressed people whose gut lacks the bacteria to make short-chain fatty acids; Prpa suggested the gut may need conditioning first [1:15:27]. Guzzetta said a synbiotic may be needed [1:14:52].
Mechanisms remain open: gut-made neurotransmitters probably do not reach the brain (Guzzetta) [1:19:11], and the effect is "definitely not only inflammation" (Rode) [1:26:21].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: we sell no probiotics, and the panel was academic. My reading: its value is as a check on how far gut-brain and mood claims can go.
- My reading: the panel's own view is that the healthy-person evidence is thin and effects on subjective scales are small; a customer pairing a gut-brain ingredient with ours should keep mood and cognition wording at the level of that ingredient's own trials.
- O'Mahony floated a possible overlap between "the elite athlete strain" and psychobiotic strains, and Daniells recalled a study suggesting gut microbes may affect the motivation to exercise [1:28:43] [1:28:59]. My reading: a sports angle for gut-brain products is speculative at this stage.
- The calls for sex-specific research and prevention-stage trials [1:02:53] [1:07:33] match O'Mahony's talk (omahony-gut-brain-gaps).
quotes: "I don't believe food is medicine." (Emily Prpa) [1:08:00]
"...we are really limited by what we can put into a supplement, what's stable, what's safe for people" (Siobhain O'Mahony) [1:12:47]
"...as scientists, we're really good at measuring what we can ignore everything that we can't measure." (Emily Prpa) [1:17:57]
"I think it's definitely not only inflammation." (Julia Rode) [1:26:21]
lessons.detail:
- Sex differences are under-studied, even in animals; Guzzetta called this "really, really critical", and O'Mahony said it would help male-based therapies too [1:02:53] [1:03:32].
- In rodents there is a decent amount of data linking microbes to memory; in humans, O'Mahony said longitudinal studies going back to the years before symptoms are needed [1:05:06].
- Prpa: nutritional psychiatry, food or supplements as an adjunct or alternative to treatments such as antidepressants, is "like 50 years young"; a one-point drop on a subjective stress scale may be statistically significant but not felt [1:08:40].
- O'Mahony said they are developing a women's health supplement; half the strains first chosen were not stable or possible to put into a capsule, so fibres are used to support the bacteria wanted [1:14:15].
- Prpa: probiotics show strength in depression; for cognition there is "some interesting data out there" on relational memory; prebiotics show their strength in cognition and memory [1:15:27].
- Guzzetta: preclinical work in mice found that phages isolated from faeces and given back after stress reverted the stress response, so the virome may also be a target [1:16:54].
- Guzzetta: about 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut but probably does not change systemic levels; whether tryptophan- or serotonin-producing bacteria act through those metabolites is unclear [1:19:11].
- Guzzetta: a 2021 mouse study traced carbon-13 labelled acetate from the gut to the brain, where it entered microglia [1:21:23].
- Guzzetta's own study: faecal transplants from young to aged mice improved long-term memory and changed 35 metabolites in the hippocampus; Guzzetta pointed to Sean Gibbons's talk the next day on ageing trajectories (sean-gibbons-ageing-gut-microbiome) [1:22:59].
- Two case studies in Alzheimer's patients reported improved scores after faecal transplants, with follow-up to 12 weeks in one; Guzzetta noted the risks, and that many transplant trials were halted [1:24:41] [1:25:40].
- Rode and Guzzetta: short-chain fatty acids may affect blood-brain barrier permeability in cell culture, and act through immune cells that reach the brain [1:26:21] [1:27:00].
- Daniells asked whether, as with elite athletes and centenarians, special strains could be mined for psychobiotics [1:27:13].

lessons.title: Postbiotics panel
lessons.summary:
Stephen Daniells of NutraIngredients chaired the panel that closed the opening postbiotics session. Maria Rescigno and Simone Guglielmetti, the two speakers, were joined by Richard Day of ADM, Hongwei Wang of Biogrowing and Marco Pane.

Asked why postbiotics opened a probiotics event, Rescigno called them a possible next generation that acts without depending on the host. Guglielmetti said every probiotic product already holds postbiotics. On safety, Guglielmetti said yes, they are safer, from a 2023 review of trials. Wang and Pane said it must be measured, not assumed.

On efficacy, Day said ADM's heat-treated ES1 strain matched its live form in one trial in adults with diarrhoea-predominant IBS. With its BPL1 strain the two forms differed in metabolic effects. Guglielmetti stressed that the way cells are killed changes the product. Pane favoured flow cytometry for counting cells.

On regulation, George of the IPA said no government is yet ready to regulate postbiotics; some call them marketing. Wang described China's stepwise route. Pane warned against a health-benefit definition, citing the EU's claims experience, and saw new formats such as shelf-stable juices and cosmetics. Audience questions covered mechanism and the microbiome; Rescigno and Day reported clinical effects with little change in microbiome composition.
takeaways: Guglielmetti: "it's not possible to have a probiotic product without postbiotic inside", and postbiotics are sometimes the real reason probiotics work [04:48].

Safety is split: Guglielmetti cites a 2023 review of about 52 trial papers, including preterm infants, with extremely low side effects; Wang says it cannot be generally claimed, and Pane says postbiotics "may be safer" but it must be measured [06:22] [07:48] [08:55].

ADM (Day): ES1 as heat-treated whole cells and as a live probiotic gave "pretty much identical" results in a published trial in adults with diarrhoea-predominant IBS; for BPL1, the postbiotic had a more pronounced effect on glucose control and the probiotic on BMI [11:29].

How cells are inactivated matters: gamma-irradiated biomass kept membrane integrity and enzyme activity over 18 months of storage, and differed from the same biomass heat-treated; Guglielmetti was unsure gamma irradiation is allowed in EU food [14:49].

Regulation: George of the IPA says some governments call postbiotics marketing and none is ready to put forward a regulation yet [28:56]; Biogrowing is helping lead a postbiotics standard with the Chinese Nutrition Society [25:18].
Pane sees formats beyond capsules: no live-cell stability problem, so juices that keep longer and cosmetics become possible [31:55].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: postbiotics are outside our range, and none of creatine, clear pea protein or Oxystorm comes up.
- My reading: Pane's format point is the one that touches us. Shelf-stable postbiotics could appear in drinks and powders next to our ingredients, as co-actives rather than competitors.
- My reading: Pane's warning about defining a category by health benefit, after the EU's claims experience, matches what our own ingredients face under EU health-claim rules.
- ADM's ES1 and BPL1 figures are ADM's own, from its published trials as Day described them; we have not checked them.
quotes: "postbiotics are sometimes the real reason why probiotics work" [04:48]
"So in principle, os biotics mean, may be safer, but it's something that has to be measured" [08:55]
"So some governments tell me it's marketing." [28:56]
"you don't have to care about stability in the classic thermal viability of the cells" [31:55]
lessons.detail:
- Rescigno is developing a product Otter renders "postbiotics, mood", to be tested on zonulin and other leakiness markers plus a questionnaire, starting with people with anxiety and depression [00:46]. Day says ADM is running a trial in adults with Parkinson's [01:39].
- Rescigno says the production set-up took almost 10 years and makes metabolites without culture medium, under patent [02:24].
- Rescigno: postbiotics act fast and are host-independent, whereas a probiotic must survive the stomach, compete in the gut and depends on diet [03:41].
- Guglielmetti's theoretical risks: antibiotic-resistance genes surviving in the DNA, and residual enzyme activity, neither shown to cause harm [06:22].
- Pane: healthy people lack safety guidelines; in principle, a gram-negative postbiotic carrying lipopolysaccharide is less safe than live gram-positive bacteria; smaller molecules are likelier to spread through the body [08:55].
- Day: ADM has worked on postbiotics for about 10 years, is moving into dogs, and has linked BPL1's metabolic effect to its lipoteichoic acid [11:29].
- Rescigno sees less variability between people with postbiotics, as the end products act directly; Rescigno and Guglielmetti stress starting from a safe or approved strain [17:04] [18:15].
- Day: depending on the definition, over 80% responded to both the probiotic and the postbiotic in the IBS trial; Day says postbiotic research is at an early stage [18:46]. Wang sees effects that may be strain-specific [20:36].
- Pane wants dose, quantity and validated methods behind any efficacy claim; Pane cites a number needed to treat of 67 for aspirin [21:16].
- Pane: flow cytometry is best for counting inactivated cells, and was the basis of the Akkermansia approval [23:40].
- Day wants large, well-designed randomised controlled trials; Guglielmetti sees communication with regulators, through bodies like the IPA, as the main problem [26:46] [27:42].
- Pane links the boom partly to probiotic market saturation and the search for new space [31:55]. Rescigno adds gynaecological uses and other mucosae [34:46].
- To a questioner from what Otter renders "Dan on" (possibly Danone): Pane would use live cells for a metabolic outcome and inactivated cells for an immune one, testing both where possible; Rescigno says they have identified the metabolite behind each activity [35:52] [37:49].
- To a questioner from DSM: Rescigno saw the postbiotic stabilise the microbiota in the cancer patients rather than change it; Day saw only modest taxonomic changes despite a large clinical effect in the IBS trial; Guglielmetti says exopolysaccharides can act as prebiotics; Pane does not trust microbiome composition as a marker of efficacy [39:48] [40:24] [41:27] [42:16].
- The regulatory route in the EU is covered in more depth by the UCAM talk later in the event (ucam-postbiotics-new-frontier).

lessons.title: Postbiotics, the gut barrier and the leaky gut
lessons.summary:
Professor Maria Rescigno of Humanitas University spoke second, on why their group works with postbiotics. The gut keeps its microbes behind a two-layer mucus wall, the epithelium and a gut vascular barrier that their group described. Postbiotics, Rescigno argues, are small enough to cross all three, so they are "the mediators" of a probiotic's benefit.

Their postbiotics are metabolites made by fermenting a fibre with a Lactobacillus paracasei strain, in a patented process that also removes the gas. In their lab work the postbiotic, not the live bacteria, damped inflammatory signals in immune cells and in gut tissue from patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Live probiotics made that tissue worse.

Rescigno then linked a leaky gut to liver disease and, through a second barrier in the brain, to anxiety and depression. In mice, pre-treatment with the postbiotic protected the gut barrier against Salmonella. In a trial at Humanitas in women with breast cancer on a CDK4/6 inhibitor, no patient taking the postbiotic had grade 3 diarrhoea or had to cut or stop treatment in the first cycle. In mice it also made immunotherapy work better. Rescigno closed on personalised use.
takeaways: Postbiotics can cross the inner mucus layer, the epithelium and the gut vascular barrier, so Rescigno calls them the mediators of a probiotic's benefit [01:59].
Their postbiotics are metabolites of Lactobacillus paracasei fermenting a fibre, separated from the bacteria; the patented process removes the gas that fibre can cause [01:59].
In tissue from patients with inflammatory bowel disease, the probiotics tested worsened inflammation while the postbiotic reduced it [01:59].
In mice, one week of a high-fat diet opened the gut vascular barrier and let bacteria reach the liver; pre-treatment with the postbiotic protected the barrier against Salmonella [01:59].

In a Humanitas trial in women with breast cancer on a CDK4/6 inhibitor, grade 3 diarrhoea was avoided and no dose was cut or stopped while patients took the postbiotic; it returned when they stopped [01:59].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: postbiotics are outside our range, and none of creatine, clear pea protein or Oxystorm comes up.
- My reading: the claims are clinical and mechanistic (inflammatory bowel disease, cancer therapy), far from the healthy-consumer supplement claims our customers can make.
- My reading: their process, a probiotic fermenting a fibre, ties the prebiotic and postbiotic stories together; fibre suppliers may pitch this.
quotes: "they are, they are the mediators of the benefits of having a probiotic" [01:59]
"So by pre treating the mice, the mice with postbiotic, we are avoiding the formation of the leaky gut." [01:59]
"we think that postbiotics can be used as a in a personalized way" [01:59]
lessons.detail:
- The mucus has an outer layer the microbes colonise and a firm inner layer they cannot cross [00:00].
- The gut vascular barrier works like the blood-brain barrier, protecting the liver and brain from large molecules and bacteria [01:59].
- Two postbiotics from the same strain with different substrates and processes; batches of each cluster together on metabolomics, which Rescigno presents as reproducible [01:59].
- Dendritic cells given Salmonella: adding the postbiotic, not the live probiotic, reduced the inflammatory cytokine IL-12 (Otter: "L 2070") [01:59].
- In tissue from patients with inflammatory bowel disease, the postbiotic moved NF-kappa B out of the cell nucleus and reduced several inflammatory cytokines [01:59].
- Rescigno says 40% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease suffer from depression in a phase of the disease (Otter: "blue phase"); their group found a choroid plexus barrier in the brain that closes when gut inflammation rises, linked to anxiety and depression, with evidence now in autism spectrum disorder [01:59].
- Mice were pre-treated for "10 days, I think it was" before Salmonella; the postbiotic kept the mucus, kept the barrier marker PV1 down and limited spread to the liver [01:59].
- The trial gave the postbiotic for a week before and through the first treatment cycle, with a comparison group without it; the number of patients is not given [01:59].
- In mice with triple-negative breast cancer on anti-PD-1, the postbiotic increased the treatment's effect, with more immune cells in the tumour and more MHC class I [01:59].
- The recording ends before questions; their answers in the panel that followed are in postbiotics-panel [18:48].

lessons.title: Postbiotics: a classification for industry and regulators

speakers.name: Simone Guglielmetti
speakers.role: presenting the IPA-coordinated postbiotics roadmap paper

lessons.summary:
Simone Guglielmetti opened the first day with the postbiotics roadmap that the International Probiotics Association (IPA) has coordinated. Their starting point is confusion. Academic definitions disagree, and products sold as postbiotics range from heat-killed cells to metabolites and even sodium butyrate. For the talk Guglielmetti used a broad working definition: any non-viable agent of microbial origin that confers a physiological benefit.

The roadmap is meant for commercial and regulatory use, which academic definitions do not address. It was reworked after about 400 stakeholder comments received in July. Its decision tree asks, in order: is it alive, was it inactivated on purpose, is it meant for food and supplements rather than disease, and is the parent microbe safe or approved? Purified molecules are now left out. What remains falls into four groups: microbial metabolites, intact cells, fragmented cells and complex mixtures. Guglielmetti placed real products in each, with pasteurised Akkermansia as the intact-cell case.

Their aim is to stop postbiotics being seen as a marketing gimmick. The paper was in draft. In questions Guglielmetti said the IPA kept the word "postbiotic" because the market uses it, that yeast extract would count, and that the evidence needed for a benefit depends on each regulator.
takeaways: Definitions clash: the academic one Guglielmetti cites covers inactivated cells and fragments but excludes metabolites, while products sold online use the word for metabolites, sodium butyrate and heat-killed cells [00:00].
The IPA-coordinated roadmap was revised after "around 400 different specific comments from stakeholders", mostly companies, received in July [00:00].

The decision tree's gates: not alive (probiotics and phages are out), intentional and reproducible inactivation, food or supplement use rather than treating disease, and a safe or approved parent microbe [00:00].
Purified molecules (a metabolite, an enzyme, butyrate, beta-glucans) are now outside the category, one of the biggest changes made [00:00].
Four groups remain: microbial metabolites (MM), intact cells (IC), fragmented cells (FC) and complex (CX), with combinations counted as complex [00:00].
In questions Guglielmetti said the word "postbiotic" was reinstated because companies use it widely, and that excluding metabolites would mostly create confusion [17:15].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: postbiotics are outside our range, and none of creatine, clear pea protein or Oxystorm comes up.
- My reading: the decision tree is a useful model for how an industry body tidies a loose ingredient term before regulators do it; the same pressure could reach other loosely used category names.
- My reading: the gate on a safe or approved parent microbe mirrors the novel-food and QPS logic in the UCAM postbiotics-regulation talk at the same event (ucam-postbiotics-new-frontier).
quotes: "the word postbiotics is used to indicate any non viable agents of microbial origin that is conferring beneficial physiological effects" [00:00]
"The inactivation must be intentional." [00:00]
"trying to avoid that the whole category of post bionics can be perceived as a commercial marketing gimmick" [00:00]
lessons.detail:
- Their examples from an e-commerce search: metabolites produced by probiotics, sodium butyrate, heat-killed cells, and metabolites made by probiotics grown on prebiotics [00:00].
- The work began two to three years earlier (Guglielmetti gives both), was first shown in June at what Otter renders as the "IPC" probiotic conference, and drew on IPA members, regulators and governments' views [00:00].
- A parent microbe without a long history of safe use (not on the EU QPS list) can still be used once the final ingredient is approved by a competent authority [00:00].
- Akkermansia example: a product with pasteurised Akkermansia at 30 million units counted by flow cytometry; Guglielmetti says the live microbe had a negative QPS opinion in 2020 and a positive EFSA novel-food opinion a year later. Intact-cell group [00:00].
- Other examples: a lysate of lactic acid bacteria and bifidobacteria (fragmented cells); a fermented skim milk ingredient, heat-treated, with no separation from the medium (complex); hyaluronic acid purified from a non-food microbe (not a postbiotic); a cell-free product fermented by a paracasei strain (microbial metabolites) [00:00].
- All the groups still need notification or approval for efficacy; Guglielmetti did not cover efficacy [00:00].
- The roadmap paper was being finalised for publication [00:00].
- Yeast extract made in a standardised, reproducible way with a shown health benefit would, in their opinion, be a fragmented-cell postbiotic [18:50].
- On the burden of evidence Guglielmetti said they could not answer; it depends on regulators, and Europe's health-claim rules make it complex [19:32].
- Unfiltered beer with dead yeast could, in their opinion, be a food containing a postbiotic if standardised and a benefit shown, though it contains alcohol [20:12].

lessons.title: Psychobiotic B. longum 1714 for mental wellness
lessons.summary:
Louis Koeninger of Novonesis presented the company's psychobiotic strain, Bifidobacterium longum 1714, in the Day 1 gut-brain session. Their question: people want better mental wellness but do not know how to get it; can a bacterium help?

Koeninger opened with consumer data: 65% of people rank mental wellness as the most important health topic, and 80% say they need to do more for it. Poor sleep and stress are the main obstacles. A psychobiotic, Koeninger said, is a probiotic whose benefit is for brain or mental health, and not all probiotics are psychobiotics.

The strain was found at APC in Cork in 2008. Koeninger described two routes of action: making tryptophan, and a strain-specific exopolysaccharide that Koeninger said shifts tryptophan metabolism towards a neuroprotective pathway. Much of that data is still unpublished.

Two trials carried the talk. In 22 healthy adults, the strain reduced the cortisol response to a cold-water hand test, with lower anxiety and perceived stress. In 89 poor sleepers over eight weeks, it improved sleep quality and daytime function, energy and vitality. An Antarctica trial is still being written up. Every trial was in healthy people.

In the Q&A Koeninger said brands cannot claim mental health benefits on pack in Europe; they can add ingredients that carry authorised claims.
takeaways: Demand: 65% of people consider mental wellness the most important health topic, 80% say they need to do more for their mental well-being, and poor sleep and stress are named as the major obstacles [00:00].

Acute stress (Allen and colleagues, as Otter hears "Ellen" and "Alan", 2016; 22 healthy adults, repeated-measures, placebo-controlled, cold pressor test): a reduced cortisol peak and a significantly lower total cortisol output against placebo, plus lower state anxiety and perceived stress. Koeninger presents this as helping manage the response to everyday stress [00:00].

Sleep (published 2024 by their account; 89 healthy adults with a sleep quality index above 5, eight weeks): a sleep quality component improved significantly from four weeks, daytime dysfunction at eight weeks, and energy, vitality and social functioning scores rose against placebo [00:00].

Mechanism as Koeninger gave it: the strain produces tryptophan, a precursor of serotonin and melatonin, and a unique exopolysaccharide that Koeninger says moves tryptophan metabolism to the neuroprotective pathway; the plasma data on both were "out soon" or in revision, not shown [00:00].
Claims: asked what brands can claim on pack, "You cannot claim it, not in Europe"; the route is to add ingredients with granted health claims [17:44].

On clinical relevance in healthy people: "It's not that easy to answer"; Koeninger expects stronger effects under more stressful conditions and points to real-world evidence studies with a significant effect [16:23].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: Novonesis is one of the biggest biotics suppliers, and its strain is aimed at the stress and sleep shelf where adaptogens we sell, such as KSM-66 ashwagandha, also compete.
- My reading: their answer on claims is the opening for us. A 1714 product cannot say "mental health" on pack in Europe, so a brand building a stress or sleep formula needs a partner ingredient carrying an authorised claim (for example a vitamin or mineral); the same EU limit applies to our own botanicals.
- My reading: "all our studies were conducted in healthy people" is their selling point for a general consumer product; trials in healthy adults are what a stress or sleep pitch for our ingredients would need too.
- The figures are theirs and date from February 2025; the consumer figures have no named source in the recording.
quotes: "not all probiotics are psychobiotics, and not all psychobiotics are equal" Louis Koeninger [00:00]
"this shows that 1714 helped to manage what we call, what we call psychological or the managed psychological response to everyday stress" Louis Koeninger [00:00]
"You cannot claim it, not in Europe. But of course, it's possible to add some ingredients that have health claims granted" Louis Koeninger [17:44]
lessons.detail:
- Mental wellness is defined from the Global Wellness Institute ("an internal resource" for resilience, growth and flourishing) and the WHO definition of mental health; country quotes from Germany and the US show people describe it the same way [00:00].
- The "vicious circle" consumers know: poor gut health can lead to stress and stress to poor gut health, then anxiety and poor mental wellness; "what people do not know is how to break the vicious circle" [00:00].
- The term psychobiotic is credited to Ted Dinan and John Cryan of Cork (Otter "John crying") [00:00].
- The strain was isolated from a mucosal biopsy of the colon of a 61-year-old; Koeninger presents it as a natural resident of the human gut [00:00].
- Their claim: it is "the only psychobiotic solution clinically studied" across several aspects of mental wellness; this is the company's claim, not checked [00:00].
- Programme history as Koeninger gave it: discovered 2008 at APC, Cork; more than 15 years of research; acute stress trial 2016; a second trial published in 2019 as part of a colleague's PhD (the subject is garbled in Otter); the sleep study last year; a mode-of-action manuscript in revision [00:00].
- Sleep scoring: the component score runs from 0 (best) to 3 (worst); participants started at about 1, "fairly good", and still improved [00:00].
- Antarctica: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 32 healthy adults at Concordia Station, led by a professor at the University of Tübingen; manuscript in preparation; no results given [00:00].
- Asked about a non-viable (postbiotic) form: not studied clinically, because the mechanism depends on the exopolysaccharide [17:18].
- The chair asked, as a joke, whether it works for jet lag; there was no answer [16:02].
- No slides were filed; the trial figures are as spoken.

lessons.title: Postbiotics for Glycemic Control: Insights into the Efficacy of Pediococcus acidilactici pA1c®HI
lessons.summary:
Dr Deyan Yavorov Dayliev of Genbioma Aplicaciones presented its postbiotic, a heat-treated strain of Pediococcus acidilactici called pA1c®HI. The aim is to position it as a food supplement for blood sugar control in people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

Dayliev worked up from worms to mice to people. In worms it reversed the effect of glucose on insulin signalling, and kept working after ultra-high-temperature treatment. In mice on a high-fat diet it cut fasting blood glucose by almost half against controls, lowered leptin and raised GLP-1 in the colon.

In a 12-week pilot in 17 people with obesity, HbA1c fell 0.22% against placebo. In a small subgroup with prediabetes there were trends in insulin and weight, and fat mass fell 2.16 kg against placebo. In seven people with type 2 diabetes, with no placebo group, HbA1c fell 0.27% and LDL cholesterol fell too.

Dayliev concluded the postbiotic improves short- and long-term blood sugar control and is a stable option for preventing type 2 diabetes. In questions Dayliev said its effect beside GLP-1 drugs has not been studied, and that three trials at a lower dose were running, with results expected before summer 2025.
takeaways: The pitch for postbiotics over probiotics: no need for live cells, so stable at ultra-high temperatures and in storage; the deck says few postbiotics have been studied for blood sugar (slide 2).
In mice on a high-fat diet, the postbiotic cut fasting blood glucose by almost 50% against control mice, lowered leptin and raised GLP-1 in the colon (slide 5) (slide 6).

The human pilot was small: randomised, double-blind and placebo-controlled, 17 people with obesity, one capsule a day of 10^10 cells for 12 weeks; HbA1c fell 0.22% against placebo (p=0.018) (slide 7) (slide 8).

The prediabetes results are a post-hoc split of 6 on the postbiotic against 3 on placebo; most are tendencies that did not reach significance, though fat mass fell 2.16 kg against placebo (p=0.04) (slide 9) (slide 12).

In 7 people with type 2 diabetes, each their own control, two capsules a day (5x10^10 cells): HbA1c down 0.27% (p=0.03), total cholesterol down 16.7 mg/dL and LDL down 14.2 mg/dL (slide 13) (slide 14).
Asked about use beside GLP-1 medication: "this is the next step that we have to further investigate", as GLP-1 was measured only in preclinical models [11:23].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: a postbiotic for blood sugar is outside our range and our sports and healthy-ageing pitches.
- My reading: it shows how ingredient firms are reaching for the GLP-1 and blood sugar story with gut ingredients. The human data here are small and early, which is the evidence bar our own GLP-1 positioning will be compared against.
- My reading: Genbioma names its strain after the HbA1c marker ("A1c"); the chair asked whether that drew regulatory scrutiny, and the answer was lost in the recording [10:47].
quotes: "now we are conducting another three clinical trials with low dose" [12:35]
"Because was the first study, and we wanted to see the results." [12:35]
"We only have measured GLP one in pre clinical models." [11:23]
lessons.detail:
- Worms (C. elegans) in a glucose-loaded medium: the postbiotic reversed the glucose-driven fat build-up (p<0.001); heat-treated versions (121 and 135 °C) worked the same as untreated (slide 4). It halved daf-2 expression (the insulin receptor gene in worms) and raised daf-16 20-fold; in mutants without both genes it had no effect, so it needs the insulin signalling pathway (slide 4).
- Mice: high-fat diet, three groups (control, live probiotic at 10^10 CFU a day, postbiotic at 10^10 cells a day); spoken as 30 males, fasting glucose checked every two weeks, to week 15 [00:01] (slide 5).
- Mouse gut: more Pediococcus and less Fusibacter and Clostridium cluster XVIII, which the deck says are associated with diabetes (slide 6).
- Pilot site: the University Hospital of Vinalopó, overseen by Bioithas, with ethics approval (slide 7). Fasting glucose rose 3.2 mg/dL on the postbiotic against 7.29 on placebo, not significant (p=0.43) (slide 8).
- Prediabetes subgroup: HOMA-IR "tendency" to fall 25.6% at 6 weeks and 60.3% at 12 weeks against placebo (p=0.18); insulin down 9.74 μU/mL (50.2%, p=0.22); weight down 1.55 kg and BMI down 0.59 against baseline (p=0.04); against placebo, weight and BMI were trends only (p=0.08, p=0.06) (slide 11) (slide 12).
- Type 2 diabetes series at the Public University of Navarra: fasting glucose down 15 mg/dL, a tendency only (slide 13) (slide 14).
- The postbiotic still contains a small residue of live cells, which Dayliev suggested may explain the Pediococcus seen in the gut analysis [11:58].
- The deck closes that the postbiotic holds promise as an innovative tool for blood sugar control in type 2 diabetes, and that it reduces BMI, body fat mass and cholesterol (slide 15). Figures date from February 2025. No slide is marked Confidential.

lessons.title: The Gut-Mitochondria Connection – A new way to optimize health through the gut
lessons.summary:
Mads Bjørnhof, Chief Commercial Officer of Migalis, a Danish supplement start-up, pitched as one of NutraIngredients' Probiota Pioneers for 2025. Migalis sells a blend of human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) and pomegranate extract. The idea, which it calls "Mitobiotics", is to improve health through the link between gut bacteria and mitochondria, the parts of the cell that make most of its energy.

The HMOs feed good bacteria. Pomegranate supplies compounds that some gut bacteria turn into urolithin A, and many people lack those bacteria. Urolithin A is said to support the clearing out and renewal of worn mitochondria.

The evidence shown is one chart: urolithin A at about 4.9 mg/L with the blend, against about 1 with pomegranate alone, with no test type given. On stage Bjørnhof said the effect was confirmed in a lab gut simulation and a very small study, with clinical trials ahead. The focus is endurance athletes, for gut trouble, recovery and muscle fatigue; the product has soft-launched in Denmark.

In the panel Bjørnhof said it is not a rival to taking urolithin A directly, and that which gut bacteria do the work is not yet known. Bjørnhof would put new money into research first.
takeaways: The company's claim: urolithin A is a "metabolite that supports mitochondrial health through mitophagy", and many people lack the gut bacteria to make it; the blend "aims to support gut health and promote the production of urolithin A" (slide 4) (slide 2).
One chart shows urolithin A at about 0.35 mg/L (blank), 0.27 (HMO), 1.0 (pomegranate) and 4.9 (HMO plus pomegranate), read from the chart; no study design, source or sample is given (slide 4).
Target areas: brain, longevity and muscle, with endurance sport first: "Athletes struggle with GI challenges, recovery and muscle fatigue" (slide 6).

Human clinical trials are listed as a next step (slide 8); on stage Bjørnhof said the effect was confirmed "in in vitro gut simulation study as well as in very small" study, as Otter heard it, with "lots of trials ahead of us" [22:40].
Asked why not supplement urolithin A directly, Bjørnhof said "it's not sort of a competition", the aim being the natural process plus general gut health [40:38].
Which strain converts pomegranate to urolithin A is not known: "We just know that with HMOs, it works" [57:06].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: not our ingredients, but pitched to the buyers we sell to, endurance athletes and longevity, on muscle energy. It touches us indirectly.
- My reading: creatine works on cell energy too, through a different route (the phosphocreatine system that restores ATP in muscle); the deck does not mention creatine. Mitochondria and energy are becoming a shared healthy-ageing story, so CreaWin can be pitched beside urolithin A rather than against it, within CreaWin's own evidence. At the Nutra Healthspan Summit in November 2026, Philipp Gut of Nestlé Research listed creatine first and urolithin A third among supplements to improve mitochondrial function (nutrition-to-improve-mitochondrial-functions).
- My reading: athletes' gut trouble on long runs (slide 7) is a real problem for endurance brands; a gut product could sit beside Oxystorm or CreaWin in an endurance stack. Their evidence is testimonials so far, not trials.
- My reading: a small Danish company whose founders include a former Glycom CEO (slide 9); a possible formulation partner for endurance or healthy-ageing concepts, not a buyer of our range.
quotes: "Gut issues often pose a real challenge during the extra long-distance runs" (slide 7)
"Mitochondria create 90% of the energy we need to sustain our lives" (slide 3)
"Many people lack the gut microbiota to produce urolithin A" (slide 4)
"it's the first step is not to fall too much in love in your technology" [45:09]
lessons.detail:
- The four-step model: gut profile optimisation, urolithin A production, mitophagy activation, improved cell function, drawn as more ATP energy in muscle (slide 5).
- The company: a "Danish science-based nutrition and health company" making supplements that "harness the power of the gut microbiome to enhance health and performance" (slide 2). The packs shown read "POMHMO 2'FL" and "POMHMO Granatæble" (pomegranate), read from the photo (slide 2).
- "Mitobiotics: Support gut synergies by influencing the gut bacteria–mitochondria relationships"; the deck gives 100 trillion microbes in the gut, 35 trillion human cells and "quadrillions of mitochondria", assuming 1,000 per cell; target organs drawn are brain, immune, skin, muscle, bone and eye (slide 3).
- The pathway drawn: ellagic acid to urolithins D, C, A, iso-urolithin A and B; mitophagy is defined as "Mitochondrial renewal and biogenesis" (slide 4) (slide 5).
- Brain and longevity are tied to mitochondrial dysfunction "in brain cells" and in "functional performance of tissue and organs" (slide 6).
- Testimonials, the athletes' own words: ultrarunner Danni Møller; extreme hiker Kevin Lyngvold Rubiano; ultrarunner and coach Morten Klingenberg, who says "99% of all long-distance runners have experienced that the gut fails them before the mind or legs"; triathlete Lillan Sindahl Glümer, who reports a calmer gut and no loose stools after taking the product (slide 7). These are testimonials, not study results.
- Status as drawn: studies, IP, user validation, product and commercialisation ticked; next, human clinical trials, target consumer testing, new formats and geographical expansion (slide 8).
- Team: Ina Giversen, PhD, CEO and co-founder (also CEO and co-founder of Nerthus ApS, inventor of Punalpin, a supplement for reduced sperm quality); Leif Helth Jensen, MSc, co-founder (former CEO of Glycom A/S, now dsm-firmenich); Kasper Kemp Hansen, MSc, chairman (Paxstone Capital) (slide 9).
- Spoken: "We have soft launched the first version of the product here in Denmark"; next, stronger clinical evidence, a targeted focus on endurance athletes, then markets beyond Denmark [22:40].
- Spoken: the primary focus is "the gut mitochondria muscle axis"; brain health, longevity and healthy ageing are named as further potential [22:40].
- Pomegranate came from a founder's history with the extract, not from screening many extracts [57:06].
- Marketing: work with athletes who are willing to learn, find the consumer's language with users, and educate "with the very small spoons" once they use the product [45:09] [48:12].
- Data: product testing data are anonymous and owned by users, and feed an innovation engine [50:54].
- The deck's file name carries "Day 1 12.22" and "21.01.2025". Figures date from February 2025. No slide is marked Confidential.
- Urolithin A elsewhere in these notes: Euromonitor's Nick Stene gave US share growth of 17% and a price index of 1.37 for urolithin A in 2026 (euromonitor-who-is-winning-healthspan).

lessons.title: Highlighting Gaps & Opportunities in the Microbiome-Gut-Brain Axis Field

speakers.name: Dr Siobhain O'Mahony
speakers.organisation: APC Microbiome Ireland, University College Cork

lessons.summary:
Dr Siobhain O'Mahony of APC Microbiome Ireland at University College Cork opened the Day 1 gut-brain session with a map of what is known and what is not. Their question: where are the gaps, and where are the openings for research and business?

On the slides O'Mahony starts with the market: the human microbiome market is put at $814.6 million in 2024, rising to $4.2 billion by 2030. In the room O'Mahony began with their own field, sex and hormone differences in the gut microbiome over life. Most of the evidence comes from rodents, which O'Mahony would rather call proof-of-concept tools than models of disease, and how far it carries over to people is largely unclear.

O'Mahony then turned to three groups. In ageing, cognitive decline goes with fewer bacteria that make butyrate, but O'Mahony does not suggest giving butyrate to everyone; prevention across life matters more. In women, dementia risk is higher and mood and memory change around the menopause. In athletes, about 35% of elite athletes have mental health concerns, sports anxiety is rising, and O'Mahony sees room for microbiome products against it.

Their close: the gut microbiome changes over life and between the sexes, and diet and lifestyle can change it. That leaves large gaps for research and companies. Questions were held for the panel.
takeaways: The animal evidence is strong but its translation is not: animal models show "profound contributions" of gut bacteria to brain activity and behaviour, yet how far these carry over to humans is "largely unclear" (slide 4). Spoken, O'Mahony would call rodents "proof of concept" rather than "models of disease", and said animal work is getting harder to justify in Europe [00:00].

Ageing: cognitive decline goes with lower diversity and fewer short-chain-fatty-acid makers such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii (less butyrate); longevity "may" also mean a more flexible, stable microbiome (slide 8). O'Mahony is "not suggesting" butyrate for everyone as they age; lifelong prevention is the target [00:00].

Women: higher risk of Alzheimer's disease and dementia than men; cognition and mood change before, during and after the menopause; about 1.2 billion postmenopausal women by 2030, a stage O'Mahony puts at about a third of a woman's life (slide 10) [00:00].

Athletes: about 35% of elite athletes have mental health concerns (slide 12); spoken, O'Mahony put sports performance anxiety at about 35% of elite athletes [00:00]. Female athletes report it more often, and O'Mahony sees "potential, possibly" for microbiome interventions to reduce it and improve performance (slide 12) [00:00].

Gaps O'Mahony lists: a meta-database and new algorithms, blood tests of "microbiome function" (accurate today but not cheap), organoids, high-throughput culturing, microfluidics and AI, and condition- and sex-specific choice of intervention, with cost-effectiveness still to analyse (slide 14) [21:19].
On mechanism O'Mahony accepts "we may never have mechanistic insights into some of this, and that's okay", as long as the links justify modulating the microbiome [00:00].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: the talk touches us only indirectly. It names no ingredient of ours and no product category we sell.
- My reading: their two growth groups, ageing brains and athletes under mental strain, are the same buyers our range serves in healthy-ageing and sports nutrition. Creatine for cognition is a known adjacent angle; their slide on brain health across the lifespan lists physical exercise and diet among protective factors (slide 6), which leaves room for that story without naming it.
- My reading: their sports-anxiety slide points at a mental side of sports nutrition that brands may want to address; nothing in the deck ties it to creatine, protein or nitrate.
- The market figure ($4.2 billion by 2030) is for the human microbiome market, not supplements, and dates from February 2025 (slide 2).
quotes: "Yet exactly how the microbiome plays a role in these is not fully known" (slide 5)
"Female athletes tend to report sports anxiety more frequently" (slide 12)
"is key to the health of our body and brain" (slide 15)
"this could be something that we might have to resign to and say we may never have mechanistic insights into some of this, and that's okay" [00:00]
lessons.detail:
- Market: human microbiome market $814.6 million in 2024 to $4.2 billion in 2030, 31.5% a year; no source is named on the slide. Figures date from February 2025 (slide 2).
- The infographic on the same slide claims "up to 90%" of all disease can be traced in some way to the gut and the microbiome, over 10,000 microbial species identified in the body, and 3.3 million non-redundant genes in the gut microbiome; humans are 99.9% alike in their genome but 80 to 90% different in their microbiome (slide 2, read from the image; attributed to Femmebiome.com).
- Their own work on the lifespan and sex slide: sex-specific gut microbiota signatures after early life stress (Neurobiology of Stress, 2024) and sex, pain and the microbiome (Brain, Behavior, and Immunity, 2022); open questions are volatility over time and hormone-driven differences (slide 3).
- Brain diseases linked to the microbiome: cerebrovascular (stroke, multiple sclerosis), neuropsychiatric (cognitive dysfunction, anxiety and depression, autism) and neurodegenerative (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS); how the microbiome plays a role "is not fully known" (Zhu et al., 2020) (slide 5).
- Brain health across the lifespan is called "a multi-billion-dollar industry"; the chart of factors places the microbiome beside healthy diet, physical exercise and cognitive activity on the protective side (Glow, 2021; read from the chart) (slide 6).
- "Global aging" raises memory loss and cognitive decline from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease, with "interest in identifying lifestyle-related factors" to prevent them (slide 7).
- Athletes: a review figure (Clauss et al., 2021) lists probiotic effects reported in athletes: fewer and shorter upper respiratory infections, better immune and antioxidant markers, longer run time to fatigue, better recovery after muscle-damaging exercise and lower body fat (slide 11, read from the figure).
- The Human Microbiome Compendium: over 160,000 samples from 68 nations, meant to fill gaps left by studies dominated by high-income countries (slide 13).
- Closing slide shows "the gut brain axis diet": Mediterranean-style eating, avoid processed foods, elimination diet for sensitivities, supplements and herbs "when needed" (slide 15, read from the image).
- Spoken, not on the slides: in a rat model of early life stress, sex-specific microbiota differences predicted which animals would be resilient or vulnerable; in a small human pain study there were sex differences in pain but minimal microbiota differences, and the female microbiome responded more to induced pain [00:00].
- O'Mahony said the gut microbiome produces every neurotransmitter the central nervous system produces, and named three routes to the brain: the stress (hormonal) system, the immune system and the vagus nerve and spinal cord [00:00].
- A University College Cork study transferred faecal microbiota from people with Alzheimer's disease to mice and transferred some memory loss and amyloid plaques, as O'Mahony described it [00:00].
- The brain stays plastic as we age; O'Mahony named a new diet, a new exercise regime or a probiotic as possible inputs in mild cognitive impairment [00:00].
- Sports anxiety drivers O'Mahony named: performance pressure, injury, overtraining, keeping peak physical health, and media and social presence [00:00].
- The large public database O'Mahony showed is the Human Microbiome Compendium (Otter "Pentium") [00:00].
- No slide is marked "Confidential". The deck carries APC Microbiome Ireland copyright marks.
