lessons.title: Neuropsychobiological effects of pro- and prebiotics
lessons.summary:
Julia Rode, Associate Senior Lecturer at Örebro University, asked what pro- and prebiotics do for the mind, and how we could measure it better. Rode spoke straight after Novonesis's psychobiotic talk and set out the academic view.

Rode began with the meta-analyses. Pooled trials show probiotics reducing depressive symptoms, in people with and without depression. In patients with depression the effect held regardless of severity or the number of strains, and lasted to follow-up, but only when probiotics were added to antidepressants. Probiotics reduced psychiatric distress but did not significantly reduce anxiety.

Their critique: almost all of this rests on self-reported scales, and few studies look at behaviour, mood, cognition and brain function together. Their answer is neuroimaging. Their group's unpublished review finds a small, mixed set of trials, mostly in healthy adults, over 4 to 24 weeks. Across them, probiotics changed resting brain activity, damped the response to negative emotions and improved sleep quality, and scans and symptom scores often moved together.

Rode ended by saying scanning may pick up subtle effects that symptom scores miss, and the field needs standard protocols. In the Q&A Rode said no one has yet compared strains in the imaging trials, longer intake is probably better, and an hour of scanning costs about €1,000 at their institute.
takeaways: In patients with depression, probiotics reduced depressive symptoms overall (SMD -0.34, -0.46 to -0.22, read from the chart), whatever the severity or the number of strains, and the effect lasted to follow-up (Zhang et al. 2023) (slide 8) (slide 9) (slide 10) (slide 12).

On their own, probiotics did not affect depressive symptoms (SMD -0.13, -0.49 to 0.24); added to antidepressant medication, they reduced them (SMD -0.36, -0.49 to -0.24) (slide 11, read from the chart).

Probiotics did not significantly affect anxiety (SMD -0.30, -0.60 to 0.01, p=0.06) but did reduce psychiatric distress (SMD -0.33, -0.53 to -0.13, p=0.001) (Le Morvan de Sequeira et al. 2022) (slide 6) (slide 7, read from the charts).

The evidence rests on self-reported rating scales; neuroimaging trials of probiotics are few and mixed but mostly high quality, and they report changed resting brain connectivity, less brain involvement under negative emotional stimuli and better sleep quality (Hutchinson et al., unpublished) (slide 13) (slide 15) (slide 19).

Q&A: the imaging trials cannot yet be stratified by strain, as only two used the same probiotic; Rode believes longer intake gives "more resilient results" but there is no evidence-based sweet spot, since most trials ran 4 to 6 weeks and a few 24 [38:23] [39:43] [41:16].
Their take-home: imaging "may be more sensitive" than symptom scores and cognitive tests for subtle effects of mild, short interventions, and the field needs standardised protocols (slide 23).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: the talk touches us only indirectly. It is about probiotics and prebiotics for mood, not about any ingredient we sell.
- Their Q&A puts a price on objective brain data: about €1,000 an hour of scanning at their institute, given as a rough guess [39:43].
- My reading: their method point carries over. Brain claims built on self-reported scales are the weak spot Rode names; if we ever pitch creatine for cognition, brain-imaging or objective test data would be the stronger evidence to look for.
- My reading: their sleep-quality finding and the mood results sit in the brain, mood and sleep market where healthy-ageing customers buy, but nothing here links to creatine, pea protein or nitrate.
quotes: "Evidence from self-reported rating scales" (slide 13)
"Relatively small number of studies with considerable heterogeneity" (slide 15)
"Effects on neuroimaging outcomes and clinical symptom ratings" (slide 22)
"I'm an academic. I don't have a commercial interest." Julie Rode (Otter's spelling) [18:34]
lessons.detail:
- Prebiotics reduced depressive symptoms in people with depression (SMD 0.39, 0.04 to 0.73 in favour) but not in people without it (0.13, -0.23 to 0.48) (Hofmeister et al. 2021) (slide 5, read from the chart).
- The gut-brain axis diagram is Robert Brummer's (2014) (slide 2).
- No "healthy" microbiota has been defined, but it is marked by high diversity; IBS, depression, anxiety, autism, ADHD and dementia are named as conditions with neuropsychological parts linked to dysbiosis (slide 3).
- Hofmeister et al. 2021 (PMID 34933877): in populations without depression, probiotics favoured the intervention (SMD 0.31, 0.15 to 0.46, 34 trials); in populations with depression 0.78 (0.19 to 1.37); synbiotics without depression 0.68 (0.36 to 1.00); one synbiotic trial in depression and one faecal transplant trial showed no clear effect (slide 4) (slide 5, read from the charts).
- Le Morvan de Sequeira et al. 2022 (PMID 35276981): the anxiety analysis pooled 17 trials (728 on probiotics, 650 on placebo) with high heterogeneity (I² 86%); the psychiatric distress analysis pooled 8 trials (360 against 320) (slide 6) (slide 7, read from the charts).
- Zhang et al. 2023 (PMID 37386630): subgroups read from the charts: moderate depression -0.39, mild -0.38; multi-strain -0.27, single-strain -0.42; at the end of intervention -0.33, at follow-up -0.42 (slide 9) (slide 10) (slide 12).
- The neuroimaging review takes randomised placebo-controlled trials of oral probiotics in adults 18 and over, healthy or ill, with brain imaging or electrophysiology outcomes; fMRI and EEG are the most used tools (slide 14) (slide 15).
- fMRI: 2 to 3 mm spatial resolution, a few seconds' temporal resolution, non-invasive and repeatable in healthy people; resting-state and task-based versions (slide 16) (slide 17).
- Their own example (Rode et al. 2022, PMID 36139496 and 35571902): brain responses to emotional tasks changed on a probiotic, and total HADS and HADS depression scores fell against placebo over 4 weeks (slide 20, read from the charts).
- A figure from Crocetta et al. 2024 (PMID 39360283) maps brain regions changed by probiotics in healthy people across task-based and resting-state fMRI studies (slide 21).
- Most neuroimaging studies of probiotics were published in the last 5 years (slide 23). Figures date from February 2025.
- Spoken: in healthy populations, "similar as the studies that Louis just presented", probiotics reduced depressive symptoms; whether such effects matter when people already feel well is "very hard to say" [18:34].
- Spoken: the anxiety evidence is thinner than for depression, so "this might be an outcome subject to change" [18:34].
- Resting-state fMRI protocols vary across gut-brain studies (5 or 10 minutes, eyes open or closed); the wider field is becoming more standardised [42:03].
- A questioner from DSM-Firmenich (Otter "DSM Fermi") asked about duration and the cost of imaging in an 80-subject trial [39:04].
- No slide is marked "Confidential".

lessons.title: Bifidobacterium breve MCC1274: The Unique Probiotics in Cognitive Health. Deep dive into Gut-Brain Axis
lessons.summary:
Asuka Tada, commercial manager at MILEI, the European arm of Morinaga Milk Industry, pitched Morinaga's probiotic strain B. breve MCC1274 for memory in older adults. The studies shown are Morinaga's own.

Tada set the scene with ageing and dementia. Dementia cases are expected to rise from 46.8 million in 2015 to 131.5 million by 2050. Because amyloid-β builds up about 20 years before Alzheimer's disease, Tada argued the time to act is mild cognitive impairment, the stage between healthy and dementia. People with Alzheimer's disease have less diverse gut bacteria and fewer bifidobacteria, which is why Morinaga chose a bifidobacterium.

The evidence is three human studies at 20 billion CFU a day. In an open pilot without placebo, MMSE scores rose into the normal range. In a 16-week placebo-controlled trial of 80 adults with suspected mild impairment, total, memory and visuospatial scores improved. In a 24-week trial in older adults, MRI showed less brain atrophy than on placebo.

Tada closed on credentials: 16 published papers, a Japanese functional claim, US GRAS status and a memory supplement sold in Japan.

In questions from the chair, Stephen Daniells of NutraIngredients, Tada said Morinaga has no data yet on pairing the strain with a prebiotic, and that its strain-specific mechanism data are especially on indole-3-lactic acid.
takeaways: Positioning: act at the stage of mild cognitive impairment, where cognition can "recover", "maintain" or "decline", because amyloid-β accumulates about 20 years before Alzheimer's disease (slide 11) (slide 12).

Open pilot (single arm, no placebo): 24 weeks at 20 billion CFU a day in older people with mild cognitive impairment raised mean MMSE from 24.3 to 27.0; the slide says the strain "improved cognitive function in participants with MCI to be normal score" (Kobayashi et al., 2018) (slide 19, figures read from the chart).

Trial 1 (randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled; 80 adults aged 50 to 79 with suspected mild impairment; 16 weeks): RBANS total, immediate memory, visuospatial and delayed memory improved against placebo (P<0.0001 each); language (P=0.064) and attention (P=0.740) did not (Xiao et al., 2020) (slide 20) (slide 22, read from the charts).

Trial 2 (randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled; 24 weeks; MRI analysis 42 on the strain, 47 on placebo): whole-brain atrophy was lower on the strain (P=0.0134), and the orientation score moved better; on the chart the total ADAS-Jcog lines of the two groups overlap (Asaoka et al., 2022) (slide 23) (slide 24, read from the charts).

Credentials: patents for brain function, Food with Function Claims in Japan (2021), US FDA GRAS for foods (2022), 16 scientific studies as of September 2024 (slide 17) (slide 18); on stage Tada said "we have published 16 papers so far on this string" [00:00].

Q&A: on pairing the strain with a prebiotic, "at this moment, we don't have any data" [17:01]; on mechanism, Morinaga has data specific to this strain, "especially for ILA production" (indole-3-lactic acid) [17:57].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: it is a competitor's playbook for the shelf a creatine-for-cognition pitch would go to. Morinaga targets the same healthy-ageing buyer with memory claims built on its own trials.
- My reading: the route they took, MCI-stage trials, standard cognitive batteries (RBANS, MMSE), MRI as a secondary outcome, a Japanese functional claim and GRAS, is a template for what a cognition claim for CreaWin would need to show.
- My reading: a probiotic for memory and creatine for brain energy are different mechanisms; a combined healthy-ageing brain product is possible, but the deck says nothing about combinations.
- The market and population figures date from February 2025 or earlier (the dementia figures are from 2015 sources).
quotes: "Gut might modify your mind" (slide 14)
"B. breve MCC1274 improved cognitive function in participants with MCI to be normal score." (slide 19)
"Reaching the gut, working on the brain" (slide 27)
"...this is a quite simple study, and yeah, but the result was extremely impactful for us" (Asuka Tada, on the open pilot) [00:00]
lessons.detail:
- Morinaga history: founded 1917 as Nippon Rennyu, launched Morinaga Dry Milk in 1921, discovered its flagship strain B. longum BB536 in 1969 (slide 2).
- Bifidobacteria levels peak in early life and fall in old age (Arboleya et al., 2016); Morinaga calls strains native to the human gut "Human-Residential Bifidobacteria", with B. breve as an infant type (slide 3) (slide 4).
- MCC1274 was isolated from an infant in 2002 and is aimed mainly at adults; certifications FSSC22000, Halal and Kosher; described as stable in "numerous innovative applications"; patents WO2017209156A1 and WO2021256077A1 (slide 17).
- Population: people over 60 about 1 billion in 2019, about 1.4 billion in 2030 and about 2.1 billion in 2050 (WHO; read from the chart) (slide 6). A UN chart shows Europe and Northern America with the highest old-age ratios (slide 7).
- Consumers: 35% say they suffer general forgetfulness and 31% periods of memory loss at least some of the time (FMCG Gurus) (slide 8).
- Dementia: in Japan, 5.3 million over-65s (16%) in 2015, 8.3 million (23%) in 2030 and 10.2 million (27%) in 2050 (Cabinet Office 2017; read from the chart) (slide 8). Worldwide 46.8 million in 2015, 74.7 million in 2030 and 131.5 million in 2050; Europe 10.5, 13.4 and 18.7 million (World Alzheimer Report 2015) (slide 9).
- Alzheimer's disease accounts for over 60% of dementias (63% on the chart) (slide 10).
- PubMed studies on the "gut brain axis" rose from under 200 a year in 2014 to about 1,700 in 2023 (read from the chart) (slide 13).
- Alzheimer's patients had lower gut diversity and less Bifidobacterium than controls (Vogt et al., 2017); the slide says probiotics, "especially bifidobacteria, may be effective" for cognition (slide 16).
- The deck's numbers for its trials differ between slides: trial 1 is "50 - 79 years old" on slide 20 and "Age 50 to 80" on slide 22; trial 2 is "130 patients aged from 65 to 88" on slide 23 and "Age 65 to 90, 89 people" on slide 24 (the MRI subset, 47 and 42) (slide 20) (slide 22) (slide 23) (slide 24). Trial 2's full analysis set was 55 on the strain and 60 on placebo (slide 23, read from the flow chart).
- Suggested mechanism (Microbiome Science, July 2024): metabolites such as acetic acid and indole-3-lactic acid, lower amyloid-β, less microglial activation and inflammatory cytokines, and more synaptic proteins via the vagus nerve; the slide calls it "suggested" (slide 25, read from the figure).
- Claimed firsts: the only probiotic introduced on the ALZFORUM website, and the "world's first" bifidobacterium shown to maintain memory as a single strain; NutraIngredients-Asia Award 2023 for cognitive function and a 2023 Japanese wellness award (slide 26).
- On stage Tada said about 5% to 15% of people with mild cognitive impairment progress to dementia within a year, and that some recover to healthy status within a year (Otter heard "16% to 14%"); the deck does not give these figures [00:00].
- Tada described RBANS as usable from healthy people to moderate dementia, with two equivalent forms to avoid a learning effect, which is why Morinaga chose it for the second study [00:00].
- Tada said the strain also converts soy isoflavones to the aglycone form, as part of the suggested mechanism [00:00]; in Q&A Tada said the acetic acid point is more general to bifidobacteria [17:57].
- The finished product: a Japanese supplement at 20 billion CFU per two capsules, "reported to help maintain memory and spatial awareness" in healthy middle-aged and older people (slide 27).
- No slide is marked "Confidential". Every slide carries Morinaga's copyright.

lessons.title: Clinical outcome of registered trials with probiotics

speakers.name: Ger T Rijkers
speakers.organisation: Department of Science, University College Roosevelt, Middelburg, The Netherlands

speakers.name: Samuel Varga
speakers.organisation: Department of Science, University College Roosevelt, Middelburg, The Netherlands

speakers.name: Tiara Dusselier
speakers.organisation: Department of Science, University College Roosevelt, Middelburg, The Netherlands

lessons.summary:
Ger Rijkers of University College Roosevelt in Middelburg, the Netherlands, presented a review of probiotic trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, with co-authors Samuel Varga and Tiara Dusselier. Rijkers declared grant support and lecture fees from the IPA.

The question is whether registered probiotic trials show a clinical benefit. The team found 504 publications from registered trials. Gastrointestinal conditions led with 148 studies, then infants with 49 and metabolic disorders with 40.

Those studies used 405 different outcome measures. The team set a strict bar for benefit: a significant improvement in a predefined clinical measure and also in the patient's own reported quality of life.

The deck then charts the overall clinical benefit, compares metabolic with gastrointestinal trials and single-strain with multi-strain products, and looks at trends over time. Those results are in charts with no values in the deck's text. The most studied strains are LGG and BB-12, from Rijkers's group's earlier global analysis published in 2020.
takeaways: Source: probiotic trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, leading to 504 publications (slide 5) (slide 7).

By area: gastrointestinal 148, infant 49, metabolic disorders 40, dental 38, multiple 33, respiratory 29, obstetrics and gynaecology 27, neurological and cognitive 21, mood 14, dermatology 13, renal 13, hepatic 10, general 9, others 60 (slide 8).
The trials used 405 different outcome measures, (slide 9); that this makes them hard to compare is my reading.
Benefit was judged as a significant improvement in a predefined clinical measure and in patient-reported quality of life, both together (slide 10).
The most studied species are LGG and BB-12, citing Dronkers, Ouwehand and Rijkers, Global analysis of clinical trials with probiotics, Heliyon 2020 (slide 19).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: probiotics are outside our range.
- My reading: the double test, a clinical measure plus quality of life, is a high bar that buyers and regulators may come to expect of any health ingredient. Our evidence packs could say which of our studies meet both.
- My reading: 405 outcome measures across 504 studies shows why a consistent outcome set makes evidence easier to sell.
quotes: "Healthy: Longer (and more) healthy" (slide 4)
"Disease: Reduce disease burden" (slide 4)
"Most studied species: LGG and BB-12" (slide 19)
lessons.detail:
- Disclosure: grant support and lecture fees from the IPA; most of the work presented was done by Rijkers's students and PhD students (slide 2).
- Probiotics are defined as "live microorganisms that, when administered in adequate amounts, confer a health benefit on the host" (slide 3).
- The search used is ClinicalTrials.gov with the term "probiotics" (slide 5).
- Charts without text values: the clinical outcome measures, the overall clinical benefit of probiotics, metabolic against gastrointestinal, and single against multi-species or multi-strain products (slide 13) (slide 14) (slide 15) (slide 16) (slide 18).
- An in vitro chart shows Lactobacillus acidophilus counts during simulated passage through the gut over six hours (slide 17).
- From the 2020 analysis: a chart split into single, dual and multi-strain products, each by positive primary, positive secondary or not significant outcome, with "70%" beside "Single" in the text (slide 19).
- A chart of trends over time in positive primary and secondary outcomes (slide 20). Figures date from February 2025. No slide is marked Confidential.

lessons.title: Tinder for microbes: The Gut Stuff
lessons.summary:
Alana MacFarlane Kempner, founder of The Gut Stuff, a UK gut health brand, made the case for partnerships between brands, ingredient makers and educators. The Gut Stuff began as an education business and grew into products, an app, a podcast and a Channel 4 TV series.

Their starting point is that gut health matters to almost everyone but information is complex and products are confusing and expensive. Their market figures: 80% of UK consumers consider gut health important, and in July 2024 searches for "gut health" edged ahead of "weight loss diet". Yet only 40% are confident they know what a healthy gut should feel like.

MacFarlane Kempner then set out why probiotics disappoint. Customers expect quick results, with 19% expecting changes within a day, though the British Dietetic Association advises at least four weeks. They forget doses, do not track symptoms and do not know which product to trust. Brands lack data on who their customers are and whether the product helps.

Their answer is the partnership with Novonesis and PrecisionBiotics. Customers on a 12-week plan get free access to The Gut Stuff app, with education, tracking and reminders, and their consented data become real-world evidence. MacFarlane Kempner closed on shared responsibility: emerging categories need collective voices.
takeaways: Consumers care but are unsure: 96% know gut health affects their quality of life, yet only 40% are confident they know what a healthy gut should feel like, 33% are unsure and 27% have no idea (PrecisionBiotics research, 2024) (slide 6).
Probiotic problem: 19% of consumers expect changes within a day and 18% within a week, against the British Dietetic Association's advice of at least four weeks (slide 11).
Users do not track symptoms, forget daily doses and do not know which probiotic to trust; companies lack data on whether the product helps (slide 11).

The real-world evidence pilot: PrecisionBiotics 12-Week Plan customers get free app access with a "hack your gut health" programme, diet, lifestyle and symptom tracking, and push reminders to take the product (slide 12).
Consented app data will be analysed for usage, motivations, health needs and perceived outcomes, to refine products, improve engagement and add to science (slide 13).
Reach claimed: over 250,000 across email and social media, 25,000 organic website users a month, 140+ pieces of coverage last year and a Channel 4 series now in Germany and Belgium (slide 3).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: not our ingredients, but a working model of an ingredient maker paying for consumer education and real-world data through a brand partner.
- My reading: the adherence problem is general. Any ingredient that needs weeks of daily use faces customers who expect results in days; an app or plan that reminds and tracks could support our brand customers' launches.
- My reading: real-world evidence from consenting users is a cheaper complement to trials for supporting a branded ingredient's story, though it is perceived outcomes, not clinical proof.
quotes: "everyone in the space shares a social responsibility" (slide 6)
"emerging categories need collective voices" (slide 7)
"Customers expect immediate results" (slide 11)
lessons.detail:
- History on the timeline: TwinsUK research with Tim Spector; a business founded to educate, through websites, social channels, supper clubs, road shows and pop-ups; workplace wellness talks from 2017; a give-back pledge from 2020; products and an app from 2021 (slide 2).
- In workplaces, 1 in 5 take time off work for digestive issues, the deck says; The Gut Stuff sits on the NHS food review board and piloted a module for the UK school curriculum (slide 2).
- Media: "we’ve made science pop culture to make it mass market"; 45 million in circulation; 60% organic search; a brand for younger shoppers (slide 3).
- Context figures cited: 1 in 4 people have digestive issues; more NHS admissions for digestive diseases than anything else (NHS 2021-2022); 8 million people with an anxiety disorder at any one time (slide 4). Over 80% admit gut health issues (The Grocer, May 2021); GPs spend 10% of their time on digestive issues, yet 41% with symptoms never seek advice (Guts UK); 28% of bowel cancer cases are caused by too little fibre (Cancer Research, 2015) (slide 6).
- Market sources cited: Food Navigator 2024, McKinsey 2024 and Really Good Culture 2024; consumers will keep spending on health, nutrition, appearance, sleep and mindfulness (slide 5).
- With Novonesis, "A 360 partnership": the PrecisionBiotics partner conference, consumer campaigns and educational videos on the strains for health professionals and consumers (slide 8) (slide 9).
- Podcast: #3 in Nutrition on Apple Podcasts, presented by Lisa and Alana (slide 10).
- Why partner: large and small businesses bring different things; front-facing education empowers consumers and gives businesses better insights (slide 7). Figures date from February 2025. No slide is marked Confidential.

lessons.title: Bifidobacterium longum subsp. iuvenis thrives around weaning and is adapted to transition from milk to solid diets

speakers.name: Olga Sakwinska, PhD
speakers.organisation: Nestlé Institute of Health Sciences, Nestlé Research (Lausanne)

lessons.summary:
Olga Sakwinska of Nestlé Research presented the discovery of a new subspecies of a common infant gut bacterium. Their starting point: the gut microbiome of early life shapes later health, from growth and metabolism to infections and vaccine response.

Bifidobacteria dominate the infant gut, and one subspecies, B. longum subsp. infantis, is built to feed on the sugars in breast milk. Nestlé followed 220 infants in Dhaka, Bangladesh, from birth to two years, with stool samples and metagenomic data. In that data a third group of B. longum turned up that was neither the infant nor the adult type. It peaked between about 10 and 24 months, in children eating both breast milk and solid food.

The group was common in Bangladesh, at about 61%, and rare elsewhere. Nestlé isolated five strains, read their genomes and found they can digest both breast-milk sugars and food glycans. The group was named a new subspecies, B. longum subsp. iuvenis, in 2023.

Their conclusion: B. l. iuvenis thrives around weaning and is adapted to the move from milk to solid food. The deck shows no product and no human trial of the strain.
takeaways: A transitional clade of B. longum, distinct from the infant (infantis) and adult (longum) types, was found in the metagenomes of infants in a Nestlé cohort in Bangladesh (slide 8).
It is associated with partial breastfeeding, a diet "combining human milk and solid foods" (slide 9).
It was present at 61.21% in Bangladesh (n=1,606) but at 0% to 18.18% in eight other countries' cohorts, including 0.50% in the USA (n=400) (slide 10).
Its five sequenced strains carry enzymes for both breast-milk sugars (fucosylated HMOs) and diet-derived glycans (slide 11) (slide 12).
Named a new subspecies in 2023, B. longum subsp. iuvenis, type strain NCC 5000T; isolates come from Asia and Africa (Modesto et al., 2023) (slide 13).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: infant and toddler gut science, with no tie to creatine, clear pea protein or Oxystorm, or to sports and healthy-ageing nutrition.
- My reading: Nestlé owns the type strain (NCC 5000T) (slide 13). A weaning-stage probiotic or synbiotic for young-child nutrition looks a likely next step, but the deck does not say so.
- My reading: the talk shows Nestlé using metagenomics to find strains in under-studied populations; that is background on how probiotic pipelines are built, not a lead for us.
quotes: "Transitional B. longum is prevalent in Bangladesh but rare globally" (slide 10)
"…and where present, remained unnoticed" (slide 10)
"Harbors fucosylated HMO utilization gene cluster" (slide 13)
lessons.detail:
- Early-life microbiome and health, four papers cited: lasting effects on health (Tamburini et al., Nature Medicine 2016), paediatric metabolic disorders (Jian et al., EBioMedicine 2021), undernutrition (Barratt et al., Cell Host & Microbe 2022) and vaccine response (Jordan et al., Lancet Microbe 2022) (slide 2).
- HMOs: more than 160 structures, 20 of them over 80% of the total; mostly not digested or absorbed; far more concentrated and varied in human milk than in farm animals' or pets' milk (slide 3).
- The cohort: Nestlé Microbiota and Health study, Dhaka, Bangladesh, 2013 to 2016 (NCT02361164), with icddr,b and the Broad Institute; n=220; growth, diarrhoea and respiratory infections, medicines and breastfeeding recorded; stool and nasopharynx samples at visits from birth to 24 months (slide 5).
- In the cohort most infants were breastfed and 25% were born by caesarean section; exclusive breastfeeding gave way to partial breastfeeding by about four months, and infection rates peaked between about 4 and 12 months, read from the chart (slide 6).
- Microbial diversity rose from birth to 24 months, and Bifidobacterium dominated absolute abundance from 2 to 15 months before Prevotella and others grew, read from the chart (Vatanen et al., Cell 2022) (slide 7).
- Relative to all B. longum, infantis was near 100% at 2 to 6 months and fell to near zero by 24 months; the transitional clade rose from about 10 months, with a median near 60% at 18 months, read from the chart (slide 8).
- Prevalence by cohort: Bangladesh 61.21%, China 18.18% (n=11), Italy 9.49%, Russia 5.19%, Estonia 3.61%, Sweden 1.33%, New Zealand 1.08%, USA 0.50%, Finland 0.00% (slide 10).
- Isolation: metagenomics flagged samples rich in the clade; 77 Bifidobacterium isolates were taken, 54 of them B. longum, 9 transitional; complete genomes gave 5 unique transitional strains (slide 11).
- In vitro, B. l. iuvenis and B. l. infantis grew on 2'-FL, 3-FL, diFL and LNT; B. l. longum and B. l. suis did not, read from the chart (Modesto et al., 2023) (slide 14).
- Like infantis, and unlike suis, B. l. iuvenis carries an operon to make riboflavin (slide 13).
- All figures are as presented in February 2025; the papers behind them date from 2016 to 2023. No slide is marked Confidential.

lessons.title: Longevity panel: the microbiome and healthspan

speakers.name: Sean M. Gibbons, PhD
speakers.organisation: Institute for Systems Biology (ISB); University of Washington
speakers.role: Associate Professor, Institute for Systems Biology

lessons.summary:
Stephen Daniells of NutraIngredients chaired the Day 2 closing panel with three start-ups and one academic: Caitlin Hill of Myota (prebiotic fibre blends), Patrick Guye of Trilliome (upcycled plant fractions), Bruno Balen of AniBiome, and Sean Gibbons of the Institute for Systems Biology, back from their own talk.

Each first set out an approach to longevity. Hill argued that people ferment fibres so differently that single-fibre trials are flawed, so Myota uses a blend and measures inflammation, blood sugar, lipids and cognition. Guye said life expectancy has risen by about 20 years in 60 years while the share of life spent in good health has not.

The panel then rejected the idea that a younger microbiome is better. Gibbons warned against banking your own young stool and preferred raising the microbes that fall with age. Balen wanted measured end points, such as grip strength, over any ideal microbiome.

On centenarians, Gibbons said lifestyle can get you to 85 or 90 and genetics does the rest. On diet, Gibbons said high-protein diets can harm glucose control in young people but have been shown to prevent frailty in older people, with plant protein a little better than animal.

Asked for a $5 million trial, each named one: cognitive decline, windows of vulnerability, precision prebiotics, and a carnivore-diet comparison.
takeaways: Gibbons on protein: in young people, high-protein diets "does kind of promote loss of glucose control and type two diabetes. It can, at least", and shift gut fermentation towards protein by-products Gibbons called uremic or liver toxins; in older people a high-protein diet "has been shown to prevent frail" (Otter's words; frailty) [21:41].

Gibbons added that plant-based proteins are "a little better" than animal protein, and that at older age an animal-type protein mix "seems to be maybe protective" against frailty (Otter: "Braille") [25:10] [26:08].

Young is not automatically better: Gibbons cautioned against "baking your 20 year old poo and putting in yourself when you're 80", and preferred promoting the microbes that decline with age (Bifidobacterium, Akkermansia) over "the sledge hammer of fecal transplant" [06:35] [08:38].

Hill (Myota): single-ingredient prebiotic trials are "quite flawed" because individuals ferment fibres very differently; Myota's blend is meant to work across microbiomes and is tested on IL-6, CRP, TNF-alpha, HbA1c, insulin sensitivity, lipids and cognition [00:10].

Guye (Trilliome): in the past 60 years average life expectancy rose by 20 years but the share of life in good health "hasn't changed": about 50% in good health, 34 to 35% moderate and 14 to 15% bad [03:23].
Outcomes over composition: Balen and Guye both named grip strength as a measure that matters, Guye calling hand force "one of the biggest predictors of health and age" [11:57] [27:22].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: the only protein discussion in this session, from an ISB scientist, and it splits by age. My reading: it supports protein for older adults against frailty, where we pitch IsoClr: Pea, and Gibbons's view that plant protein is a little better than animal helps a pea pitch; the warning on high protein in young people is hedged ("It can, at least") and worth knowing if a customer raises it [21:41] [25:10].
- My reading: grip strength and gait keep coming up as the healthspan end points that matter, the same physical-function outcomes we use for CreaWin and protein in older adults [27:22].
- My reading: Myota (fibre in a bread-type product for over-60s) and Trilliome (plant fractions) are small healthspan brands that could want protein or creatine partners for a combined ageing product; neither said so [02:35] [03:23].
quotes: "prebiotics will not let you live until 150 years old. But how can we improve our health span, rather than lifespan?" [00:10]
"I would caution against baking your 20 year old poo and putting in yourself when you're 80." [06:35]
"I think that the advice you would give to someone in terms of nutrition may change throughout the lifespan" [21:41]
"Plant based proteins, a little better than analytical protein." [25:10]
lessons.detail:
- In the first recording ("Probiota 2"), the chair introduced Hill as from Myota and Guye as "co founder and CEO of Trillium" (Trilliome), which Guye said had been "pretty much under the radar until right now" [18:27].
- Also in that recording, Hill opened by noting that in 2022, in Copenhagen, ageing experts added the microbiome as a pillar of ageing, and that inflammation belongs alongside it [18:59].
- Hill: Myota sells direct to consumers and as an ingredient in functional products; its cognitive trial gives people over 60 a product (Otter: "brand role") with 10 grams of prebiotic fibre, against average UK intake of 18 grams, aiming at mild cognitive impairment before it progresses [02:35].
- Guye: Trilliome makes supplements that modulate the gut microbiome and, later, the skin's, from upcycled plant parts split into many fractions (polyphenols, flavonoids, small-molecule combinations); its current product "can massively boost a few species" linked to brain protection, which are obligate anaerobes hard to sell as probiotics [03:23].
- Gibbons: traits of youth are often anti-correlated with longevity, and a falling metabolic rate with age could protect against damage; banked young stool carries opportunistic pathogens that could harm someone later immunocompromised, so screened donors are better [06:35].
- Gibbons: a transplant from a 20-year-old to a 45 or 50-year-old "you'd probably be okay"; people usually lose Bifidobacterium by their 70s or 80s, and Lactobacillus [08:38].
- Balen: stool should be analysed by metabolomics rather than transplanted blind; live bacteria in transplants "don't survive", so what acts is metabolites; Balen's target is an "in silico projection of our best self" [09:17].
- Hill: we do not know the perfect microbiome; for women, putting a pre-menopausal microbiome into a post-menopausal body "would be potentially ineffective" [11:14].
- Balen said they personally eat "zero fiber" and earlier ate a lot of fibre as a vegetarian; Balen cares about systemic effects that can be measured [11:57].
- Guye: much of the evidence that a young microbiome is better is mouse transplant work; it needs experiments such as clearing the microbiome with antibiotics and restoring a defined consortium [13:06].
- Gibbons: exercise first, then a mostly plant-based diet, are the biggest levers; past 100, genetics dominates and centenarian studies risk survivor bias [15:00].
- Guye: ageing starts early and symptoms appear at 40 to 60, so the trajectory matters more than centenarians; Trilliome works with a longevity centre in Okinawa (Otter: "center longevity Okinawa") [17:19] [19:12].
- Hill: lifestyle signals up to 80 to 85 are clear (diet, exercise, social inclusion); the Blue Zones study is "slightly flawed" [18:26].
- Balen cited a Stanford study (Otter: "Dr zelenberg") in which another diet "was superior to high fiber diet"; Hill replied that its fibre arm was not personalised; Balen agreed fibre should be personalised [20:12] [20:21] [20:30].
- Gibbons: high-protein studies include Atkins-style diets, plant-only and animal-only protein, and liquid amino acid mixtures matching animal or plant protein; the animal-type mixture in excess "can drive some some issues with your metabolism" [26:08].
- The $5 million trials: Guye, about 250 people in early old age with first signs of cognitive decline, given defined strain mixes and perhaps prebiotics for one to two years, tracking inflammation, hand force and gait [27:22]; Hill, intervening in windows of vulnerability such as perimenopause and mild cognitive impairment [28:27]; Gibbons, precision prebiotic cocktails from community metabolic models to maximise engraftment of the microbes that fall with age, for which Gibbons was writing a grant [29:17]; Balen, healthy carnivore cohorts tested with interventions such as GLP-1 drugs (Otter: "GFP, one") or psychedelics [30:10].
- Gibbons's own talk, with the slides behind the remarks, is in sean-gibbons-ageing-gut-microbiome (my reading: the panel extends the talk's conclusion that a young microbiome is not automatically better).

lessons.title: The Pantryome Paradigm: Framing the Microbial-Human Health Interface

speakers.name: Jeremy P. Burton
speakers.organisation: Lawson Research Institute and Western University, Canada
speakers.role: Departments of Surgery, Microbiology and Immunology

lessons.summary:
Jeremy Burton of the Lawson Research Institute and Western University in London, Canada, set out a new way to think about the gut microbiome. Their group runs microbial therapy studies and kept finding molecules from energy pathways in its results.

Their idea, the "pantryome", is that gut microbes share the parts they need to make energy outside their cells: B vitamins, haem, vitamin K2 and short-chain fatty acids such as acetate. A healthy gut keeps this shared pantry well stocked, and the host uses it too. Burton suggests disease may come with a poorly stocked pantry, citing kidney stone patients, whose gut microbes were less diverse than healthy controls'.

Supplementing these molecules directly mostly helps the host, not the microbes, because many are absorbed in the small intestine before reaching the colon. Free acetate is absorbed within 20 minutes. Their group therefore focused on getting acetate to the colon. A prostate cancer drug that carries acetate deep into the gut raised Akkermansia about fivefold in patients. They then put apple cider vinegar capsules inside delayed-release capsules.

In a small, early pilot in young adults gaining weight on psychiatric drugs, the delayed-release vinegar changed the gut microbiota, with some markers trending better. Burton sees delayed release as a way to make probiotics, prebiotics and faecal transplants work better.
takeaways: The pantryome: microbes build "interconnected and interdependent electron transport chains" that rely on sharing energy components outside the cell, used by microbes and host; "The performance of this environment links to the health of the host" (slide 68).
Shared nutrients include amino acids, B vitamins, haems and menaquinones (vitamin K2), mapped across the 75 most common gut genera in the PREDICT 1 cohort of 1,098 healthy volunteers (slide 24).

The delivery problem: many helpful molecules are absorbed in the small intestine, and free acetate reaches the bloodstream within 20 minutes; supplementing the host may "temporarily help the host but not the microbiota" (slide 36) (slide 42).

Abiraterone acetate, a poorly absorbed prostate cancer drug, carried acetate deeper into the gut: Akkermansia was about 5 times higher in treated patients, and rose over 1,000-fold in a host-free model (slide 46) (slide 47) (slide 49).
A 500 mg apple cider vinegar capsule held 25 mg acetate, and many vinegar powders tested held no acetate; six capsules match the acetate in the drug's daily dose (slide 57).

Pilot: people aged 16 to 35 gaining weight on stable psychiatric medication took three delayed-release vinegar capsules twice daily for three months, in an N-of-1 design; results are "Preliminary results only", with weight, lipid and cholesterol markers trending better and the gut microbiota changed (slide 61) (slide 62) (slide 63).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: microbiome research, outside our range and our sports and healthy-ageing pitches.
- My reading: the delivery point applies to any gut-targeted ingredient. Delayed-release capsules that open lower in the gut are a format idea for brands, though their data here are early.
- My reading: Burton lists vitamin K2 as a shared nutrient with roles in both microbes and host, a link brands with K2 may use; it is their hypothesis, not a claim.
quotes: "Call it what you will, but microbes must constantly cross-feed to make energy and build." (slide 67)
"It would be better to support the microbiota to produce them" (slide 37)
"Free acetate is absorbed into the bloodstream within 20 minutes" (slide 42)
lessons.detail:
- Their group's studies in London, Canada cover rheumatoid arthritis, immune therapy, melanoma, pancreatic and renal cancer, NAFLD, HIV, multiple sclerosis, bladder and kidney transplant, cranberry, urinary infections and vaginosis, recurrent C. difficile, atherosclerosis, medication-induced weight gain and anorexia, using faecal transplants, prebiotics, probiotics, phage and fermented food (slide 2).
- "Dysbiosis" has no agreed definition; Burton lists five in use, and says the microbiome's complexity makes biomarkers hard to find (slide 4). A cited study found the gut microbiota of 1,000 very healthy Chinese people similar to that of healthy young people (slide 5).
- Their group's 2021 Cell Reports review posits a well-stocked pantryome in a healthy microbiome and a deficit of shared resources in diseased ones, especially in metabolic disease; dysbiosis "might be more appropriately referred to as bioenergetic failure" (slide 17) (slide 20).
- Lactobacillus crispatus was found to release ATP, which may act on the bladder through purinergic receptors (slide 12) (slide 13).
- Kidney stones affect about 5% of people in Canada, with a lifetime risk of about 10%; half recur within 5 to 7 years; most are calcium oxalate (slide 29). A study of 83 stone patients and 30 healthy controls found lower gut microbial diversity in stone formers (slide 31) (slide 32).
- In the drug study, Akkermansia gains came with more microbial vitamin K2 production; acetate is "likely partially responsible" for the drug's efficacy, the deck says (slide 47) (slide 51).
- Acetate food additives are listed with their FDA and Health Canada status; most are GRAS (slide 54). Compounds screened included calcium, magnesium, manganese, potassium, sodium and zinc acetate, ethyl acetate, triacetin and apple cider vinegar (slide 56).
- Delayed-release capsule study cited: eight people, gamma scintigraphy, capsules opening in the stomach or small intestine (slide 58). A slide imaging an ingested probiotic (E. coli Nissle 1917) in a pig, marked preliminary and unpublished, notes small-intestine transit of about 4 to 6 hours and colon transit of about 24 to 48 hours (slide 41).
- Faecal transplants are costly: screening donors cost $15,180 for one enrolled donor out of 46 prescreened; capsules are now 30 to 40 per stool; Burton proposes acetate as an add-on to lower doses (slide 65) (slide 66).
- Figures date from February 2025. No slide is marked Confidential.

lessons.title: healthy aging and the human gut microbiome

speakers.name: Sean M. Gibbons, PhD
speakers.organisation: Institute for Systems Biology (ISB); University of Washington
speakers.role: Associate Professor, Institute for Systems Biology; Affiliate Associate Professor, Departments of Bioengineering and Genome Sciences, University of Washington; Data Science Fellow, eScience Institute

lessons.summary:
Sean Gibbons, an associate professor at the Institute for Systems Biology in Seattle, asked whether the changes in the gut that come with age are a decline to manage or a sign of healthy ageing. Their answer, from their group's published work, leans to the second.

In more than 4,500 adults, each person's gut grows more "unique" with age and Bacteroides falls. In men over 78, a more unique gut went with better health, such as faster walking, and in men aged 85 and over, high Bacteroides went with a higher risk of death over four years.

Gibbons then turned to statins. How well statins worked, and how far they disturbed blood sugar, varied with the make-up of the gut, and the pattern held in a separate European cohort. Gibbons suggests that probiotics targeting butyrate producers and Akkermansia could be useful.

Their conclusion is cautious. Some ageing changes may be protective: an 80-year-old probably does not want a 20-year-old's microbiome, so faecal transplants from young to old are premature. Targeted approaches and better frailty markers are needed. Questions were held over to the panel at the end of the session. The talk is from February 2025, so its figures may be dated.
takeaways: The gut microbiome becomes more unique with age, and uniqueness rises as Bacteroides falls (Spearman rho -0.73); seen in two Arivale datasets and American Gut (slide 5) (slide 8).

In older men (MrOS, aged 78 to 98), higher uniqueness went with better health: high walk speed, excellent self-rated health, fewer medicines and a composite healthy group, in discovery and validation sets (read from the chart) (slide 8).

Over a four-year follow-up of community-dwelling men aged 85 and over (N=257), high Bacteroides went with higher mortality (adjusted HR 1.90, 95% CI 1.37 to 2.64) and high uniqueness with lower mortality (HR 0.70, 0.50 to 0.99); across all ages only Bacteroides reached significance (read from the table) (slide 9).

Statin response tracked gut make-up: higher diversity went with a weaker effect, and one Bacteroides-dominant enterotype had the largest LDL drop but also more insulin resistance; the results replicated in the European MetaCardis cohort (slide 16) (slide 18) (slide 19).

Their suggestion, hedged: probiotics like A. muciniphila and butyrate producers like F. prausnitzii "could help mitigate" statins' metabolic side-effects and improve metabolic health with age (slide 20).

The closing view: some ageing changes may be protective, and targeted interventions are "probably better" (slide 21); as spoken, an older microbiome may be adapted to an older body (thinner mucus layer, less food, slower transit), so young-to-old faecal transplants are "too early" with "not enough evidence" [00:00].
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: a probiotics and microbiome science talk with nothing on protein, creatine, nitrate or muscle. It touches our healthy-ageing pitch only indirectly. Their remarks on high-protein diets came in the panel (longevity-panel-microbiome-healthspan).
- My reading: the outcome Gibbons wants for healthy ageing is function (walk speed, frailty metrics), the same physical-function language we use for CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea in older adults (slide 8) (slide 21).
- My reading: their warning against a "young is better" model is a useful caution for healthy-ageing marketing that promises to restore youth; Gibbons frames ageing changes as possibly protective (slide 21).
quotes: "Some aging-associated processes in the body may be protective (e.g., decline in Bacteroides)." (slide 21)
"Maybe we shouldn’t give FMTs from younger to older individuals?" (slide 21)
"You probably, if you're 80, you probably don't want a 20 year old microbiome that might not be good for you." [00:00]
"Targeted interventions, based on mechanistic knowledge, are probably better (e.g., probiotics, prebiotics, postbiotics, drugs, and diet)." (slide 21)
lessons.detail:
- Two schools of thought: ageing changes in the gut as "managing the decline" (older people in assisted living) or as healthy ageing (community-dwelling people and centenarians) (slide 2).
- Cohorts: Arivale, N=3,653, aged 18 to 87, two sequencing vendors (2,539 and 1,114); MrOS, N=907 men aged 78 to 98, split into discovery (599) and validation (308); American Gut as a further check (Wilmanski et al., Nature Metabolism 2021) (slide 4).
- Uniqueness is each person's distance from their nearest neighbour; it rose step by step across age bands in both Arivale datasets and in American Gut (read from the chart) (slide 5).
- The genera most tied to uniqueness: Bacteroides and Prevotella plus Bacteroides fall (rho about -0.8 in Arivale and MrOS); several Ruminococcaceae, Christensenellaceae, Methanobrevibacter and Desulfovibrio rise (read from the chart) (slide 6).
- Uniqueness shows in the blood: microbe-derived metabolites phenylacetylglutamine, p-cresol sulfate, p-cresol glucuronide, indoleacetate and 3-indoxyl sulfate rise with it (rho up to about 0.30, read from the chart) (slide 7).
- Survival in all community-dwelling men (N=706): Bacteroides adjusted HR 1.28 (1.00 to 1.64); uniqueness HR 1.11 (0.87 to 1.42), not significant; Kaplan-Meier p=0.0026 for high against low Bacteroides (read from the table) (slide 9).
- Preliminary follow-up: uniqueness tracks a complement-inactivating C5a peptidase gene (rho 0.51), falls with a host-glycan-degrading fucosidase (rho -0.42), and rises with predicted butyrate production (r=0.53, MICOM model) (slide 10).
- Statin background: LDL response varies widely between people; in 7,856 observations some had no fall or a rise, and event rates were 11.2 per 1,000 person-years on placebo against 4.8 with a 50% or greater LDL fall (Ridiker et al., Eur Heart J 2016, as on the slide; read from the chart) (slide 12).
- Arivale statin work: 244 statin users among 1,848 with medication data; plasma HMG used as a blood marker of statin effect; it rose with dose (P=1.1e-22) and with an APOE variant linked to statin efficacy (Wilmanski et al., Med 2022) (slide 13) (slide 14) (slide 15).
- Diversity: statin users in the lowest Shannon diversity tertile had the highest HMG, that is the strongest statin effect (interaction P=0.0014) (slide 16).
- Enterotypes: LDL fell about 33% against non-users in the Bac.2 enterotype against about 16 to 20% in the others (read from the chart); Bac.1 and Bac.2 statin users also had higher HOMA-IR (P=7.2e-07 and P=1.2e-04) (slide 18).
- Implications slide: more than 2,800 people across both cohorts, 22% on statins; high Bacteroides dominance with fewer butyrate-producing clostridia and less A. muciniphila "is associated with" poorer metabolic health in statin users (slide 20).
- An extra slide after the acknowledgements: in mice, NMN supplementation raised Anaerotruncus colihominis, which in females fell as frailty rose (not significant in males); labelled "unpublished data" (read from the chart) (slide 23).
- The recording starts part-way through the talk, at the uniqueness and butyrate slide; the cohort and survival slides before it were not recorded [00:00].
- Spoken on statins: in the JUPITER trial everyone had the same dose of rosuvastatin (Otter: "Azula statin"); LDL fell 50% on average, but "for more than half of the population, they fail to achieve that clinical target" and some saw a rise [00:00].
- Spoken: "something like 22% of every American adult is on a statin"; the slide gives 22% on statins across their two cohorts. The two figures describe different groups [00:00] (slide 20).
- Spoken: about 240 statin users out of roughly 1,600 people with medication data, against 244 of 1,848 on the slide; Gibbons gave the figures from memory [00:00] (slide 13).
- Spoken: the Ruminococcaceae-type group "seems to be protected" from the metabolic side-effects, which Gibbons links to its butyrate producers [00:00].
- Future work should use frailty metrics and microbial function (slide 21); Gibbons asked for studies to group people by frailty or intrinsic capacity (Otter: "in transit capacity") and combine that with multi-omic data [00:00].
- The chair held questions over to the panel at the end of the session, where Gibbons returned (see longevity-panel-microbiome-healthspan) [10:06].
- Funders named: NIH (NIDDK and NICHD) and The Global Grants for Gut Health (slide 22).

lessons.title: Supporting an improved healthspan in women with Biotics
lessons.summary:
Mónica Olivares, R&D director at Kerry, set out women's health as a market for probiotics and postbiotics. Their case is that research has long used men's bodies as the model, while women now look for solutions to their own needs; the deck cites Kerry's 2024 research that women spend on average nine years in poor health.

Kerry frames women's health by life stage, in three areas: the hormone lifecycle, healthy living and family living. Olivares mapped six of its branded biotics onto them, from a breast-milk probiotic for lactation to a yeast beta-glucan for immunity, and pitched its spore probiotic for protein absorption around menopause.

Two products got evidence. Plenibiotic, a heat-treated postbiotic, reduced water loss through the skin within four weeks. Most of the talk was a trial of HerPreg FERT2, a Lactobacillus salivarius probiotic, in 70 couples with unexplained infertility waiting for IVF: pregnancy success was 52% on the probiotic against 26% on placebo, which Olivares linked to the strain colonising the vagina and raising growth factors. Much of this is labelled preliminary.

Their conclusion: biotics are a huge opportunity in women's health. The one question, on Plenibiotic beyond four weeks, got the answer that the difference held to six weeks. The talk is from February 2025, so its figures may be dated.
takeaways: Kerry's case for the market (Kerry WOW Research 2024): a woman spends an average of nine years in poor health, and the women's health gap equates to 75 million years of life lost a year (slide 2).
Demand (same source): 80% of women are concerned about women's health issues such as menopause, menstruation and fertility, and 75% are adopting a long-term approach to health (slide 3).
Kerry's frame: women's health is "strongly lifestage linked", in three areas (hormone lifecycle, healthy living, family living), with six branded biotics mapped to them (slide 4) (slide 5).

FERT2 trial (Kerry's own, randomised, placebo-controlled, 70 couples, 3 billion a day for 4 to 9 months before IVF): successful pregnancy 52% on the probiotic (n=27) against 26% on placebo (n=30), which Kerry calls significant; the slide gives no p-value (read from the chart) (slide 12) (slide 15).

Preliminary results: L. salivarius was found in the vagina in 89.5% of the probiotic group against 7.7% of controls, and vaginal VEGF rose 2.6 times and TGF-beta 1.9 times; higher levels went with pregnancy (slide 18) (slide 19) (slide 20).
Plenibiotic (Kerry's own studies): in people with high starting water loss, transepidermal water loss was significantly lower after 4 weeks than on placebo (p<0.05) (slide 8).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: a probiotics and postbiotics talk with nothing on creatine, protein or nitrate. It touches us only through the markets: women's health and healthy ageing, where we also pitch CreaWin.
- My reading: Kerry's women's-health figures (nine years in poor health, 80% concerned) are a market frame we could cite, with Kerry named, when pitching creatine for women; they are Kerry's own research (slide 2) (slide 3).
- BC30, Kerry's spore-forming probiotic, is pitched as supporting "protein absorption" and is for food and drink only (slide 5); in the talk Olivares tied it to muscle loss in menopause [00:00]. My reading: Kerry is pitching a protein-plus-probiotic story to women at menopause, which is where IsoClr: Pea and CreaWin go; worth knowing as a co-ingredient and a competing message.
quotes: "Biotic solutions, such as probiotics and postbiotics, are particularly well-suited to support women’s comprehensive health needs." (slide 22)
"Oral administration of probiotic strain FERT2 results in efficient vaginal colonization by L.salivarius" (slide 18)
"Higher diversity and lack or less abundance of Lactobacillus has been related to infertility." (slide 11)
"We have a huge opportunity with biotics in the women's health space" [00:00]
lessons.detail:
- Other market figures (Kerry WOW Research 2024): more than 300 million women menstruating on any day, 80% with period pain at some point; about 40% of fertility disorders due to ovulatory disorders, 85% of those linked to PCOS; 80% of mothers stop breastfeeding before they want to; one billion women peri- or post-menopausal, 12% of the population (slide 2).
- The product map: BC30 and Plenibiotic for the hormone lifecycle; Wellmune, BC30 and Plenibiotic for healthy living; LC40, BfM26 and HerPreg FERT2 for family living (slide 5).
- LC40 (L. fermentum CECT5716) is from the breast milk of healthy mothers and is described as clinically shown to reduce harmful bacteria that can cause pain during lactation; BfM26 (B. breve CECT7263) is "the first Bifidobacterium isolated from human breastmilk"; Wellmune is described as the first ingredient clinically studied as an oral innate immune trainer (slide 5).
- Plenibiotic: rice-derived, heat-inactivated L. paracasei 327; 50 mg for digestive health, 100 mg for skin; kosher, halal, vegan, non-GMO; 92% of consumers believe an inside-out approach matters for beauty and a third start taking steps for healthy ageing and skin at 30 (FMCG Gurus, Kerry WOW Research) (slide 6).
- Plenibiotic skin results: change in water loss about -1.2 against -0.6 g/hm2 on placebo (read from the chart); less flaky facial skin and less skin cracking against placebo; studies Kumagai et al. 2017 and Saito et al. 2017; the slide lists "Potential Health benefit messaging" such as "supports skin moisture retention" (slide 8) (slide 9).
- FERT2 positioning: 90 mg serving; one in six people experience infertility; one in five infertile couples have unexplained infertility; references "Fernandez et al. In preparation" (slide 10).
- Trial design: Universidad Complutense de Madrid and Hospital Clínico San Carlos (logos); couples on an IVF waiting list of more than four months; probiotic or placebo from day 0 to IVF at months 4 to 6, continued to 12 weeks of pregnancy (slide 12) (slide 13).
- Flow: 285 assessed, 70 randomised, 35 per arm; 8 lost in the probiotic arm and 5 in the placebo arm, leaving 27 and 30 analysed (slide 14).
- Other outcomes: failed IVF 22% against 34%; IVF cancelled for poor embryo quality 18% against 23%, and for other reasons 8% against 17% (probiotic against control, read from the chart) (slide 15).
- Vaginal microbiota: no differences in alpha or beta diversity between groups; Lactobacillus above 95% in most samples; L. salivarius DNA 4.60 against 2.25 log10 copies/mL (slide 16) (slide 17) (slide 18).
- Growth factors at time 2: TGF-beta1 2.33 against 1.25 pg/mL (p=0.002) and VEGF 349 against 110 pg/mL (p=0.018), probiotic against placebo (read from the table) (slide 19).
- Spoken, not on the slide: the spore-forming probiotic (BC30 on slide 5) can "improve the absorption of protein", which Olivares called "especially interesting during menopause" because of muscle mass loss [00:00].
- Spoken: Wellmune in stressed women improved the immune response, reduced upper respiratory infections and "also improve mood"; stressed women have more digestive symptoms than stressed men, and digestive symptoms are common in menopause [00:00].
- Spoken fertility context: one in six people experience infertility (Olivares cited the World Health Organization), and Europe has more than 1.5 million fertility treatments a year [00:00].
- In the talk FERT2 is for couples: "we are addressing both in the COVID women and men" (Otter's words), with benefits also observed in men, not presented [00:00].
- Otter has the trial led by "COVID University of Manchester, the group of Dr Vanier Rodriguez" with a Madrid hospital; the slide logos are Universidad Complutense de Madrid and Hospital Clínico San Carlos, so the university is most likely Complutense (my reading) [00:00] (slide 12).
- Olivares said the lack of a difference in vaginal diversity between groups may be because "the sample size is too small" [00:00].
- Q&A: asked by the chair whether the Plenibiotic effect lasted beyond four weeks, Olivares said the study ran six weeks, the largest differences were at four weeks and the difference held [17:23].
- Markings: slide 12 carries "Kerry Group Confidential" and slide 20 "CONFIDENTIAL AND PROPRIETARY", though the deck was shown at a public conference; slides 17 to 21 are marked "PRELIMINARY RESULTS" (slide 12) (slide 20).

lessons.title: Gut microbiota & sports
lessons.summary:
Silvia Barbaresi of Minutia.AI spoke on the gut microbiome in sport. Barbaresi asked whether the gut microbiota is a "grand unified theory" linking the organs, and argued that it shapes training adaptation, performance and injury risk through a gut-muscle axis and a gut-joint axis.

The science section draws on published reviews. Gut microbes and their metabolites are linked to inflammation, energy use and muscle; one bacterium is shown clearing lactate, others are tied to motivation to exercise. Because each gut is different, Barbaresi says interventions must be personal: "one does not fit all".

Their argument then turns to their company's product. Barbaresi claims the microbiome is too complex for human experts alone, and presents Minutia Twin, described as the first digital twin of the human gut microbiome. A stool test feeds the model, which simulates diet and probiotic changes and produces a report with dietary advice for athletes.

The evidence is early. A pilot trial in 20 endurance athletes was ongoing, baseline data are said to match the literature, and the closing slides show the model projecting a higher VO2max. Every slide is marked confidential by the company. The talk is from February 2025, so its figures may be dated.
takeaways: Their thesis: the gut-muscle and gut-joint axes "play a key role" in sports performance and injury prevention, and gut-based interventions "are always customized" (slide 5).

Mechanisms cited from the literature: Veillonella atypica clears lactate and releases propionate; E. rectale and C. eutactus are linked to dopamine and motivation to exercise; Bacteroides uniformis to energy metabolism and insulin sensitivity (Jin et al., EMBO Molecular Medicine 2024) (slide 8).

The product: Minutia Twin, presented as the first digital twin of the human gut microbiome, with a sports version (Minutia Performance) to simulate the gut-muscle axis and predict each person's response to diet (slide 10).

The service: stool metagenomics plus a questionnaire, ideally blood, urine and VO2max, then a report with a gut performance index for endurance and strength and dietary advice (slide 11) (slide 12) (slide 13).

Evidence so far: a pilot in 20 runners and triathletes (VO2max above 45 ml/kg/min, 10 intervention, 10 control) with the University of Split and cmbio; only baseline results are shown (slide 14) (slide 15) (slide 16).

The model's own projection, not a measured result: one athlete's VO2max from 44.0 to 53.5 ml/kg/min, or 57.5 in a second scenario that changes F. prausnitzii and butyrate (read from the screen) (slide 18) (slide 22).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance medium: sports performance is our core market, and the talk ties gut health to muscle, recovery and endurance. It touches our ingredients only indirectly; none is named.
- My reading: the digital twin takes protein intake, arginine and citrulline malate intake as inputs beside VO2max (read from the screen). Personalised platforms like this could end up recommending ingredients; it would be worth asking whether nitrate (Oxystorm) or creatine could be modelled (slide 18).
- My reading: the evidence is a model and an unfinished pilot of 20; nothing here supports a claim for us, and a projected VO2max is not a result (slide 14) (slide 18).
quotes: "The GUT-Muscle Axis and the GUT-Joint Axis play a key role in sports performance and injury prevention." (slide 5)
"Gut Microbiota-based interventions are always customized" (slide 5)
"the dynamics of the gut microbiome and its complex interplay with nutrition and physical performance surpass the capacity of human experts to unravel its complexities." (slide 9)
lessons.detail:
- The scale of the microbiome: 46 million genes (oral plus gut), more than 2,000 species, more than 100 trillion cells and more than 90% difference between individuals (Tierney et al., Cell Host & Microbe 2019) (slide 3).
- Three offers to sports teams: injury prevention (an inflammatory-state and leaky-gut forecast of likely injuries), a "booster" for consistent performance, and a "talent scouter" with a Performance Quotient estimate from metrics such as VO2max, 1RM and Borg CR10 (slide 4).
- Injury risk: beyond poor diet and high training load, ageing, genetics and antibiotic use are said to raise injury risk; leaky gut with circulating LPS is linked to joint and muscle inflammation; their own article in Sports Injury Bulletin, March 2023 (slide 5).
- Gut-muscle axis: microbial metabolites are said to support muscle through control of inflammation and oxidative stress, glucose and fat oxidation and mitochondrial activity; irisin and IL-6 from contracting muscle stimulate gut release of ghrelin, leptin and GLP-1 (Liu et al. 2023). The figure lists SCFAs and urolithins A and B against muscle mass and function (read from the chart) (slide 6).
- The gut microbiota is described as an "independent organ" linked to heart, brain, muscle, lungs and liver, mainly with aerobic and endurance exercise (slide 7).
- The "elephant paradox": scientists looking at single biomarkers miss the whole picture (slide 9).
- The model captures bacterial abundances, metabolites, demographics and lifestyle, physical performance, diet and physiology; it is described as a probabilistic mechanistic framework with "highly explainable results" (slide 10).
- Example report: gut microbiome performance indices of 2.9 for endurance and 3.5 for strength out of 5, and a nutritional advice page that includes a vitamin B complex (read from the screen) (slide 13).
- Baseline athletes: Prevotella copri was the most abundant species at about 8% (read from the chart); carbohydrate oxidation was the leading enriched function, which Barbaresi calls higher metabolic flexibility (slide 15) (slide 16).
- Model inputs visible on screen include protein intake, fat intake, dietary fibre, arginine glutamate, arginine intake, citrulline malate intake, Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium, F. prausnitzii, lactate, IL-6 and VO2max (read from the screen) (slide 17) (slide 18).
- Their role: the report cover on slide 12 names Barbaresi as co-founder and chief scientific officer, MSc biotechnology and PhD sport nutrition (read from the image) (slide 12).
- Marking: every slide carries "CONFIDENTIAL" and "Minutia.AI Proprietary & Confidential information. All rights reserved." This is the company's own marking on a talk given at a public conference; the session is not confidential in our store (slide 1).

lessons.title: Postbiotics: The new frontier in microbial biotechnology

speakers.name: Javier Morán
speakers.organisation: IUIA-UCAM (University Institute of Food Innovation, Universidad Católica San Antonio de Murcia)
speakers.role: Full Professor of Food Innovation and Director of the University Institute of Food Innovation

lessons.summary:
Prof Javier Morán of the Food Innovation Institute at UCAM in Murcia spoke on how postbiotics can reach the EU market. Morán starts from a stability problem: a probiotic product holds dead and unculturable cells as well as the live counts declared on the label. That gap, Morán says, created the postbiotic concept. Regulation, not science, then decides new launches.

Morán sets out three routes. The first is food. Morán shows the EU's recent novel-food decisions on microbes, then their own case. A sourdough bread made with lactic acid bacteria went to the German authority for a status decision. The answer was that it is not a novel food. Their study found the bacteria in the sourdough but none alive in the baked bread, and the species matched those used before 1997.

The second route is medical devices. EU device rules exclude products containing living organisms, and some notified bodies also reject heat-killed ones. Morán argues that validated inactivation shows the cells are inviable and so fit the rules.

The third route is processing aids. There a strain replaced nitrite to give sausage its cured colour. Morán closes on microbiome skin care. The regulatory picture is as of February 2025.
takeaways: Postbiotics began with a stability problem: the chart shows dead and "viable unculturable" cells growing over shelf life beside the colony-forming units declared on the label (read from the chart) (slide 2).
Regulation is the key point for new launches, placed above science, market and marketing (slide 3).

Food route: a sourdough bread fermented with lactic acid bacteria was ruled not a novel food after a consultation through Germany's BVL, because traditional sourdough bread was eaten to a significant degree in the EU before 15 May 1997 (slide 6).

Their study: the sourdough held 5 x 10^7 CFU/g and the baked bread 0 CFU/g, so the bacteria are inactivated in baking while their metabolites remain; the species found matched pre-1997 literature and the EFSA QPS list (slide 8).

Medical devices: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 defines "inviable" as incapable of metabolism or multiplication; Morán argues validated inactivation and viability tests show heat-killed microbes meet the rules, though certain notified bodies read it otherwise (slide 13).
Processing aids: Lactobacillus fermentum at 10^8 CFU/g in place of nitrite "essentially replicated" the pigment and colour of nitrite-cured sausage (slide 16).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: postbiotics sit outside our range, and the talk names none of creatine, clear pea protein or Oxystorm. It touches us only indirectly.
- My reading: the food route turns on the same test our ingredients face, a significant history of use in the EU before 15 May 1997. It is a worked example of getting a status decision from one member state (slide 6).
- My reading: the nitric oxide slide is about meat curing, not dietary nitrate for performance. It gives nothing to Oxystorm's positioning (slide 16).
quotes: "The product is not a novel food." (slide 6)
"LAB inactivated during baking due to high temperatures; metabolites remain in the bread." (slide 9)
"Thermally inactivated microorganisms are inviable, but their metabolites remain functional" (slide 13)
lessons.detail:
- EU decisions on microbes, as the deck lists them in February 2025: Bacteroides xylanisolvens DSM 23964 approved as a novel food (2014); Mycobacterium setense manresensis approved with a use restriction (2015); Akkermansia muciniphila MucT approved with a shelf-life restriction (2021); P. freudenreichii biomass not a novel food, being consumed in fermented cheeses (2021); IBalance, 13 heat-treated microorganisms, a novel food with no history of consumption (2022); sourdough bread not a novel food, dated 2025; M. aurum Aogashima DSM33539 and Anaerobutyricum soehngenii CH106 pending (slide 5).
- The same slide says presence in the human microbiota does not guarantee safety, and that QPS listing is the gold standard; none of the six novel microbes it compares is on the QPS list (slide 5).
- The sourdough case rests on a technical dossier for the Menorca bakery S'Avia Rita, a BVL letter of 1 July 2024 and the Commission consultation result; the paper is Morán and Kilasoniya, Foods 2024, 13, 2042 (slide 6).
- Method: plate counts on MRS agar, then Oxford Nanopore sequencing, giving 13,080 reads for the sourdough, 14,575 for the dough and 14,774 for the bread (slide 8).
- Species used in sourdough before 1997 are listed country by country for Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and Sweden (slide 7).
- Their conclusions table says studies confirm lactic acid bacteria improve bread digestibility and nutritional value, and that there is no evidence sourdough is used as a medicine (slide 9).
- The device argument is set out in a preprint by Morán and Kilasoniya, posted 9 July 2024 and marked not peer-reviewed (slide 12).
- Processing aids under Regulation 1333/2008 are not consumed as food in themselves and may leave only harmless, technically unavoidable residues; they may still fall under GMO, novel-food or additive rules (slide 15).
- In the sausage case, of the four strains imaged only L. fermentum shows a fluorescence signal (read from the image) (slide 16).
- The cosmetics section shows a Le Santi "microbiome skincare" range carrying a "Biotic Complex" on pack, with no text from the speaker (slide 18).
- No slide is marked "Confidential". The closing slide remembers José Luis Mendoza Pérez, 1949-2023 (slide 19).

lessons.title: Aligning HTS Data and AI for Biotech R&D: Data, Model and Probiotic Media Optimisation

speakers.name: Xiangdong Zhao
speakers.organisation: Differential Bio (the slide also shows the TUM logo)

speakers.name: Martin Patz
speakers.organisation: Differential Bio (the slide also shows the TUM logo)

lessons.summary:
Xiangdong Zhao, who works on microbiology, and Martin Patz, who works on data and AI, of Differential Bio argued that data and AI can solve hard problems in probiotic development, if the data and the model are matched. Most laboratories today hold small datasets, under 10,000 points. That suits simple models, not complex goals such as predicting health benefits or scale-up.

Their answer is to grow data cheaply. They run fermentations in microtitre plates, using the many small wells as miniature reactors. They show what changes at that scale: oxygen transfer, shaking, air held in the plastic and the headspace, and the edge effect on outer wells. Sealing and careful set-up make each well a reliable vessel.

The case study is growth media for the probiotic strain Lactobacillus rhamnosus Gorbach-Goldin. A liquid-handling robot mixed 3,000 media formulations, and a neural network learned growth from them. It then chose 44 new recipes, tested in anaerobic tubes. The preferred plant-based recipe gave four times the cell count of standard MRS media at a lower media cost. They put the approach at about two weeks against eight to twelve by hand. These are the company's own results, presented in February 2025.
takeaways: Their three messages: data and AI have "huge potential" in probiotics development; align the dataset and the modelling approach with the goal; customise microtitre-plate screening to unlock it as a high-throughput fermentation platform (slide 28).
Datasets today are mostly under 10,000 points and suit simple uses; microbiome impact, health benefits, single-step scale-up and process control need far more data (slide 8).
Downscaling to microtitre plates has minimal effect at the single-cell level; the main impacts come from the high surface-to-volume ratio, which brings earlier and faster growth (slide 15).
Sealing the plate with an airtight seal gave less than 5% variation in OD600 and pH, so each well qualifies as an independent fermentation vessel (slide 18).

Case study method: 3,000 formulations of 10 MRS components by robot, a neural network trained on maximum OD, then 44 predicted recipes validated by CFU counts in 15 mL anaerobic tube fermentations (slide 22).
Their result for L. rhamnosus Gorbach-Goldin: 4x higher CFU and 16% lower media cost than baseline MRS, replacing animal-based components while reusing existing ones (slide 26).
lessons.for_us:
- Relevance low: this is a methods and AI talk for probiotic producers. It touches our range only indirectly.
- My reading: cheaper, plant-based growth media would cut probiotic producers' costs, which reaches us only through a probiotic partner's pricing.
- My reading: their plant-based media used soy peptone (slide 22). Whether pea-derived peptones could serve the same purpose is an open question the deck does not raise.
- My reading: the wider point travels. The same screen-then-model loop could be put to our own process questions, if the data existed to train on (slide 27).
quotes: "Data and AI have huge potential to solve complex problems in probiotics development." (slide 28)
"Status quo is small datasets (<10k), not suitable for complex use-cases" (slide 8)
"In-silico model is able to predict medium formula" (slide 25)
lessons.detail:
- Results by others on the opening slide: 62% cost reduction from optimising the medium for the meat starter culture Latilactobacillus sakei (Galante et al., 2023), and 5.3x higher yield of human interferon in Pichia pastoris with machine learning (Hashizume and Ying, 2024) (slide 4).
- Mismatch costs either way: a model too large for the data cannot be trained or the problem is too difficult; a model too small reaches its capacity and cannot benefit from more data (slide 9).
- Scale trade-off: industrial and pilot runs are highly relevant to production yet costly, while microtitre plates and microfluidics grow datasets cheaply; their plan is to build a cell response model there and translate it by 3D modelling (slide 11).
- A well holds 350 µL (read from the image). Intracellular pH stayed higher in plates than in a shaking flask, which they read as better cell vitality (slide 14).
- Surface-to-volume ratio is given as 24/8 = 3 for the larger block against 6/1 = 6 for the smaller (read from the diagram); the higher ratio raises early oxygen transfer and drives earlier, higher growth (slide 15).
- Shaking has little effect early but raises cell numbers late, which they put down to falling surface tension as cells accumulate (slide 16).
- Saturating the polystyrene plate with nitrogen, or replacing the headspace air, slows growth; anaerobicity can be reached by preventing air permeability or by using oxidisers (slide 17).
- Peripheral wells suffer evaporation, temperature drift and air diffusion, which can mislead cellular assays (slide 18).
- Media components varied: glucose, soy peptone, yeast extract, sodium acetate, dipotassium phosphate, ammonium citrate, magnesium sulfate, manganese sulfate, Tween 80 and meat extract. Plate conditions were 0.5 million CFU/mL cryo-inoculation, 37 °C static incubation, airtight seal, OD read every half hour for 24 hours (slide 22).
- Model fit: R² of 0.8941 on the plant-based and cost comparisons, 0.9011 for the preferred media and 0.6631 for the tube CFU validation (read from the charts) (slide 23) (slide 24) (slide 25).
- The preferred formula is -16.3% against the MRS price line (read from the chart), and quadruples the CFU count at the higher scale (slide 24) (slide 25).
- Speed claim: HTS and model-driven work at 1x in about two weeks and cheaply, against manual and iterative work at 4x the effort over 8 to 12 weeks and costly; the model is kept as a reusable digital asset (slide 27).
- The deck carries a "© Differential Bio" footer throughout but no slide is marked "Confidential". Slides 29 to 31 are a backup section: strain screening results transfer qualitatively from plate to 2 L benchtop fermenter (slide 30), and a table of typical MRS compositions from Hayek et al., 2019 (slide 31).
